<div><tool-result call-id="toolu_01YCKikPuuYEP2n1wV3riWe5"><script type="application/json">{"version":1,"status":"success","result":{"type":"text","value":"467:\u003cdiv>\u003ctool-call id=\"toolu_01SZRHaawVcG8vTaJJVmTX6m\">\u003cscript type=\"application/json\">{\"...[truncated, total 50041 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"467:\u003cdiv>\u003ctool-call id=\"toolu_01SZRHaawVcG8vTaJJVmTX6m\">\u003cscript type=\"application/json\">{\"version\":2,\"name\":\"write\",\"input\":{\"file_path\":\"person-grid-walkthrough.qmd\",\"content\":\"---\\ntitle: \\\"`person-grid.R`: a parametrized pictogram generator\\\"\\nsubtitle: \\\"Walkthrough: h...[truncated, total 13533 chars]\"},\"caption\":\"person-grid-walkthrough.qmd\",\"captionLink\":\"person-grid-walkthrough.qmd\",\"inputPreview\":{\"type\":\"code\",\"value\":\"---\\ntitle: \\\"`person-grid.R`: a parametrized pictogram generator\\\"\\nsubtitle: \\\"Walkthrough: how the script works, and how to use it in Quarto\\\"\\nformat:\\n  html:\\n    code-fold: false\\n    toc: true\\n---\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: setup\\n#| include: false\\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = \\\"center\\\")\\n```\\n\\n## Aims\\n\\n`person-grid.R` draws \\\"restroom-sign style\\\" person icons — plain polygons,\\nnot an icon font or image file — and arranges any number of them into a\\ngrid. It's the base building block behind several other figures in this\\nbook: a single icon reused by `testing-sequence.R` (a person at a computer)\\nand by `peer-review-workflow.R` (author/editor/reviewer roles), plus two\\nfigures used directly:\\n\\n- a **diversity sample** figure — a grid of icons varying in silhouette,\\n  age, disability, and skin tone, to make \\\"any group of people will vary\\\"\\n  concrete rather than abstract;\\n- an **effect grid** figure — the same grid mechanism, but with each icon's\\n  fill colour driven by a numeric value (e.g. an effect size or score) on a\\n  diverging blue–white–orange scale, to show \\\"people vary in how they\\n  respond\\\" to some intervention or condition.\\n\\nThis document explains how the script is built, then how to call it from a\\nQuarto chunk.\\n\\n## Prerequisites / assumptions\\n\\n- **Packages**: `ggplot2` only (loaded by the script itself). No icon\\n  fonts or external image assets — every icon is drawn from coordinates,\\n  so it renders identically wherever Quarto builds the document.\\n- **Sourcing**: standalone — nothing else needs to be sourced first. (It\\n  is, however, a dependency *of* `testing-sequence.R` and\\n  `peer-review-workflow.R` — see their own walkthroughs.)\\n- **Reader background**: basic familiarity with `ggplot2` (`geom_polygon()`,\\n  `aes()`, `theme_void()`) is assumed; no statistics background needed.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: source-script\\nsource(\\\"person-grid.R\\\")\\n```\\n\\n## How it works: the process\\n\\nEach icon is just a handful of flat shapes (head, torso, legs or\\nwheelchair, optional cane) assembled as polygons in a local coordinate\\nframe, then offset into a grid position. Colour and demographic\\ncomposition are decided by sampling from user-specified proportions. The\\npipeline for building the whole grid looks like this:\\n\\n```{mermaid}\\nflowchart LR\\n    A[\\\"person_parts()\\\\n(one icon's polygons)\\\"] --> E[\\\"assemble + offset\\\\ninto grid positions\\\"]\\n    B[\\\"sample_counts()\\\\n(silhouette / age / disability mix)\\\"] --> E\\n    C[\\\"diverging_colors() or\\\\nsampled skin tones\\\\n(fill colour)\\\"] --> E\\n    D[\\\"choose_ncol()\\\\n(grid shape)\\\"] --> E\\n    E --> F[\\\"ggplot() + geom_polygon()\\\\n+ scale_fill_identity()\\\"]\\n```\\n\\nIn short: **geometry** (what shape is each icon) is decided independently\\nfrom **composition** (how many of each kind) and **colour** (what fill\\neach gets), and all three are combined only at the very end when the\\npolygon data frame is built and handed to `ggplot()`.\\n\\n## Element-by-element walkthrough\\n\\n### Low-level geometry: `circle_pts()` and `person_parts()`\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-circle-pts\\n#| eval: false\\ncircle_pts \\u003c- function(cx, cy, r, n = 24) {\\n  t \\u003c- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n + 1)[-(n + 1)]\\n  data.frame(x = cx + r * cos(t), y = cy + r * sin(t))\\n}\\n```\\n\\n`circle_pts()` is a tiny helper that turns a centre + radius into `n`\\npoints around a circle (used for the head, and for the wheelchair wheel).\\nIt's deliberately generic — nothing about it is specific to drawing people.\\n\\n`person_parts(kind, age, disabled, scale, ox, oy)` is where one icon's\\nshape is actually defined. It builds a **named list** of polygons (head,\\ntorso, legs, etc.) in a fixed local coordinate frame (head centred at\\n`x = 0, y = 1.62`), then at the very end:\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-offset-logic\\n#| eval: false\\nout \\u003c- lapply(names(parts), function(nm) {\\n  p \\u003c- parts[[nm]]\\n  data.frame(part = nm, x = ox + scale * p$x, y = oy + scale * p$y)\\n})\\ndo.call(rbind, out)\\n```\\n\\nscales and offsets every part by `(ox, oy)` — this is *the* mechanism that\\nlets the same local shape be placed anywhere in a grid (or, in\\n`testing-sequence.R`, next to a monitor icon) just by changing `ox`/`oy`.\\n\\nThree design choices worth knowing about, because they explain shapes you\\nmight otherwise find surprising in the rendered figure:\\n\\n- `kind` controls the leg silhouette: `\\\"A\\\"` (trouser-coded, two separate leg\\n  bars), `\\\"B\\\"` (skirt-coded, one flared polygon), or `\\\"N\\\"` — literally half\\n  of each — an inclusive, non-binary-coded silhouette rather than a third\\n  stereotyped shape.\\n- `disabled = TRUE` swaps the torso/legs for a single wheelchair wheel plus\\n  a footrest peg, redesigned (per a code comment in the script) as one big\\n  unbroken shape rather than several small ones, because small shapes stop\\n  reading clearly once icons are shrunk down in a large grid.\\n- `age = \\\"elder\\\"` adds a cane polygon; `age = \\\"child\\\"` doesn't change the\\n  shape at all — it's handled later, as an overall `scale` multiplier in\\n  `person_grid()`, not inside `person_parts()`.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-person-parts\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"A single adult icon, drawn directly from person_parts()\\\"\\none_person \\u003c- person_parts(\\\"A\\\", \\\"adult\\\", disabled = FALSE)\\nggplot(one_person, aes(x, y, group = part)) +\\n  geom_polygon(fill = \\\"#3B6EA5\\\") +\\n  coord_equal() +\\n  theme_void()\\n```\\n\\n### Composition sampling: `sample_counts()`\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-sample-counts\\n#| eval: false\\nsample_counts \\u003c- function(n, props, seed) {\\n  stopifnot(\\n    \\\"`props` must have non-negative values, with at least one positive\\\" =\\n      all(props >= 0) && sum(props) > 0\\n  )\\n  props \\u003c- props / sum(props)\\n  set.seed(seed)\\n  raw \\u003c- props * n\\n  counts \\u003c- floor(raw)\\n  remainder \\u003c- n - sum(counts)\\n  if (remainder > 0) {\\n    order \\u003c- order(-(raw - counts))\\n    for (i in seq_len(remainder)) {\\n      idx \\u003c- order[((i - 1) %% length(order)) + 1]\\n      counts[idx] \\u003c- counts[idx] + 1\\n    }\\n  }\\n  sample(rep(names(props), counts))\\n}\\n```\\n\\nGiven target proportions (e.g. `c(adult = 0.70, child = 0.15, elder =\\n0.15)`) and a grid size `n`, this turns proportions into **exact integer\\ncounts** using the largest-remainder method (the same allocation method\\nused for apportioning seats to parties in some electoral systems): take the\\nfloor of each `proportion * n`, then hand out the few leftover icons to\\nwhichever categories had the largest fractional remainder. This hits the\\nrequested mix as closely as integers allow, rather than independently\\nsampling each icon (which could, by chance, give you 0 children out of 60\\neven at `child = 0.15`). The final `sample()` call shuffles the result so\\nicons of the same kind aren't clumped together in the grid.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-sample-counts\\nsample_counts(10, c(adult = 0.7, child = 0.15, elder = 0.15), seed = 1)\\n```\\n\\nNote the `stopifnot` requires *at least one* positive proportion, but zero\\nis allowed for the others — so `disabled_prop = 0` (the default in some\\ncontexts) is fine: it just means that category gets 0 of the `n` icons, not\\nan error.\\n\\n### Colour: `diverging_colors()`\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-diverging-colors\\n#| eval: false\\ndiverging_colors \\u003c- function(value, neg = \\\"#0072B2\\\", mid = \\\"#F2F1EC\\\", pos = \\\"#E69F00\\\") {\\n  span \\u003c- max(abs(value), 1e-9)\\n  tt \\u003c- value / span                     # -1 .. 1, 0 = null\\n  ramp_lo \\u003c- grDevices::colorRamp(c(neg, mid))\\n  ramp_hi \\u003c- grDevices::colorRamp(c(mid, pos))\\n  to_hex \\u003c- function(m) grDevices::rgb(m[, 1], m[, 2], m[, 3], maxColorValue = 255)\\n  vapply(tt, function(t) {\\n    if (t \\u003c= 0) to_hex(ramp_lo(t + 1))\\n    else        to_hex(ramp_hi(t))\\n  }, character(1))\\n}\\n```\\n\\nThis is the colour engine behind `person_grid()`'s `mode = \\\"value\\\"` —\\ne.g. colouring icons by an effect size or score. It's a **symmetric,\\ndiverging** scale: `0` is always treated as the reference/\\\"null\\\" point\\n(light, near-white), regardless of where your data happen to sit, and the\\ntwo endpoints (default blue/orange — the Okabe–Ito colour-blind-safe\\npalette, not a red/green or red/blue scale) are reached only at\\n`max(abs(value))`. That symmetry matters pedagogically: a `value` vector\\nof `c(-1, 3)` will *not* make `-1` look strongly negative, because `3` sets\\nthe scale — worth knowing if your values aren't already roughly symmetric\\naround zero.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-diverging-colors\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"The diverging scale at a few sample values\\\"\\nvals \\u003c- c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2)\\ndata.frame(value = vals, fill = diverging_colors(vals)) |>\\n  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = 1, fill = fill)) +\\n  geom_tile(width = 0.9, height = 0.9) +\\n  scale_fill_identity() +\\n  theme_void()\\n```\\n\\n### Automatic grid shape: `choose_ncol()`\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-choose-ncol\\n#| eval: false\\nchoose_ncol \\u003c- function(n, dx, dy, aspect) {\\n  ncols \\u003c- seq_len(n)\\n  nrows \\u003c- ceiling(n / ncols)\\n  grid_ratio \\u003c- (ncols * dx) / (nrows * dy)\\n  ncols[which.min(abs(log(grid_ratio / aspect)))]\\n}\\n```\\n\\nGiven `n` icons and a target width:height `aspect` ratio (default 16:9),\\nthis brute-forces every possible number of columns from 1 to `n` and picks\\nwhichever makes the resulting grid's bounding box closest to that aspect\\nratio — so the figure fills a slide with minimal leftover margin, without\\nyou having to hand-pick `ncol` for every `n`. It compares ratios on a *log*\\nscale, so \\\"twice too wide\\\" and \\\"twice too tall\\\" count as equally bad,\\nrather than the search being biased toward wide grids.\\n\\n### Putting it together: `person_grid()`\\n\\nThis is the function you actually call. It:\\n\\n1. Resolves `ncol` (via `choose_ncol()` if left as `\\\"auto\\\"`).\\n2. Samples silhouette/age/disability composition via `sample_counts()`.\\n3. Resolves fill colour — either sampled skin tones (`mode = \\\"diversity\\\"`)\\n   or `diverging_colors(value)` (`mode = \\\"value\\\"`).\\n4. Loops over `1:n`, computing each icon's grid row/column (and hence\\n   `ox`/`oy`), calling `person_parts()` for its shape (children are drawn\\n   at `scale = 0.65`), and stamping on that icon's fill colour.\\n5. Row-binds every icon's polygons into one data frame and builds a single\\n   `ggplot()` call — one `geom_polygon()` for the whole grid, not `n`\\n   separate layers, grouped by a per-icon `poly_id`.\\n6. Also returns `meta` (a tidy one-row-per-icon summary) and `alt_text` (a\\n   plain-language description of the composition, generated from the same\\n   sampling draws used to build the icons) — handy for `fig-alt`.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-person-grid-diversity\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"person_grid() in diversity mode\\\"\\n#| fig-width: 7\\n#| fig-height: 3\\ndiversity_demo \\u003c- person_grid(n = 24, seed = 11)\\ndiversity_demo$plot\\n```\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-person-grid-value\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"person_grid() in value mode, coloured by a simulated effect size\\\"\\n#| fig-width: 7\\n#| fig-height: 3\\nset.seed(2716)\\nvalue_demo \\u003c- person_grid(n = 24, mode = \\\"value\\\", value = rnorm(24, mean = 0, sd = 1.2))\\nvalue_demo$plot\\n```\\n\\n## Quarto usage / integration\\n\\nMinimal setup-chunk line:\\n\\n```r\\nsource(\\\"person-grid.R\\\")\\n```\\n\\nReal usage from `doing-being-science.qmd` (the diversity-sample slide):\\n\\n````{verbatim}\\n```{r}\\n#| label: fig-diversity-sample\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"The people in any group will vary in many ways: just look around you\\\"\\n#| fig-alt: !expr diversity_grid$alt_text\\n#| fig-width: 8\\n#| fig-height: 4.5\\n\\ndiversity_grid \\u003c- person_grid(n = 125, seed = 11)\\ndiversity_grid$plot\\n```\\n````\\n\\nAnd the value-mode / effect-size variant:\\n\\n````{verbatim}\\n```{r}\\n#| label: fig-effect-grid-demo\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"People vary and how conditions or interventions affect us will vary: from strongly negative (dark blue) to null (near-white) to strongly positive (dark red) impacts\\\"\\n#| fig-alt: !expr effect_grid$alt_text\\n#| fig-width: 8\\n#| fig-height: 4.5\\n\\nset.seed(2716)\\neffect_grid \\u003c- person_grid(n = 60, mode = \\\"value\\\", value = rnorm(60, mean = 0, sd = 1.2))\\neffect_grid$plot\\n```\\n````\\n\\nTwo things worth keeping in mind when reusing this pattern:\\n\\n- `fig-alt` is set via `!expr` to pull the *already-computed*\\n  `alt_text` field out of the object returned by `person_grid()` — so the\\n  alt text always matches what was actually sampled, rather than being\\n  hand-written and liable to drift out of sync.\\n- Because `coord_equal(expand = FALSE)` is used internally, the figure's\\n  panel is exactly the icons' bounding box with no extra margin — set\\n  `fig-width`/`fig-height` to roughly match the grid's aspect ratio so\\n  Reveal/HTML doesn't stretch it oddly.\\n\\n### Parameter quick reference\\n\\n| Parameter | Default | Meaning |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| `n` | `30` | Number of icons. |\\n| `ncol` | `\\\"auto\\\"` | Icons per row; `\\\"auto\\\"` picks the best fit to `aspect`. |\\n| `aspect` | `16/9` | Target width:height ratio used only when `ncol = \\\"auto\\\"`. |\\n| `comp_kind` | `c(A=.45, B=.45, N=.10)` | Silhouette mix (trouser / skirt / half-half). |\\n| `comp_age` | `c(adult=.70, child=.15, elder=.15)` | Age-presentation mix. |\\n| `disabled_prop` | `0.12` | Proportion drawn with the wheelchair silhouette. |\\n| `mode` | `\\\"diversity\\\"` | `\\\"diversity\\\"` (sampled skin tone) or `\\\"value\\\"` (diverging fill from `value`). |\\n| `skin_tones` | 6 hex colours | Palette sampled from when `mode = \\\"diversity\\\"`. |\\n| `value` | `NULL` | Numeric vector, length `n`; required when `mode = \\\"value\\\"`. |\\n| `seed` | `1` | Reproducibility seed for every sampling step. |\\n| `dx`, `dy` | `1.15, 2.15` | Icon spacing (horizontal, vertical). |\\n\\n## See also\\n\\n- [testing-sequence-walkthrough.qmd](testing-sequence-walkthrough.qmd) —\\n  reuses `person_parts()`, `sample_counts()`, and `diverging_colors()` to\\n  build a \\\"person at a computer\\\" icon.\\n- [peer-review-workflow-walkthrough.qmd](peer-review-workflow-walkthrough.qmd) —\\n  reuses the composite icon from `testing-sequence.R` (and so, transitively,\\n  this script) for the author/editor/reviewer roles.\\n\",\"language\":\"markdown\"}}\u003c/script>\u003c/tool-call>\u003c/div>\n473:\u003cdiv>\u003ctool-call id=\"toolu_01K47T3kQtsMAkm2NnJB33Uu\">\u003cscript type=\"application/json\">{\"version\":2,\"name\":\"write\",\"input\":{\"file_path\":\"testing-sequence-walkthrough.qmd\",\"content\":\"---\\ntitle: \\\"`testing-sequence.R`: one person, two people, a sample — at a computer\\\"\\nsubtit...[truncated, total 9920 chars]\"},\"caption\":\"testing-sequence-walkthrough.qmd\",\"captionLink\":\"testing-sequence-walkthrough.qmd\",\"inputPreview\":{\"type\":\"code\",\"value\":\"---\\ntitle: \\\"`testing-sequence.R`: one person, two people, a sample — at a computer\\\"\\nsubtitle: \\\"Walkthrough: how the script works, and how to use it in Quarto\\\"\\nformat:\\n  html:\\n    code-fold: false\\n    toc: true\\n---\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: setup\\n#| include: false\\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = \\\"center\\\")\\n```\\n\\n## Aims\\n\\n`testing-sequence.R` extends the pictogram generator in `person-grid.R`\\nwith a \\\"person sitting at a computer\\\" composite icon, and uses it to draw\\nthe narrative sequence: **one** person doing a data-collection task → **two**\\npeople doing it → a whole **sample** of people doing it (shown as a grid,\\nwith no individual scores). It also provides a faceted \\\"grid of grids\\\"\\nversion for showing several independent *studies*, each with its own\\nsample of people. Paired with `sampling-distributions.R`'s synthetic score\\nfigures, this is the icon half of a two-track illustration of sampling and\\nmeasurement error.\\n\\n## Prerequisites / assumptions\\n\\n- **Packages**: `ggplot2` only.\\n- **Sourcing**: `person-grid.R` **must** be sourced first — this script\\n  reuses `person_parts()`, `sample_counts()`, and `diverging_colors()`\\n  from it directly (not via a package namespace, so order matters).\\n- **Reader background**: read\\n  [person-grid-walkthrough.qmd](person-grid-walkthrough.qmd) first if the\\n  underlying icon mechanics (geometry, composition sampling, colour modes)\\n  aren't already familiar — this document assumes them.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: source-scripts\\nsource(\\\"person-grid.R\\\")\\nsource(\\\"testing-sequence.R\\\")\\n```\\n\\n## How it works: the process\\n\\n```{mermaid}\\nflowchart LR\\n    A[\\\"person_parts()\\\\n(from person-grid.R)\\\"] --> C[\\\"person_at_computer()\\\\n(person + monitor, one role column)\\\"]\\n    B[\\\"monitor_parts()\\\\n(screen geometry,\\\\npositioned relative to the head)\\\"] --> C\\n    C --> D[\\\"testing_icons()\\\\nloop over n icons,\\\\nplace in a grid,\\\\noptional score labels\\\"]\\n    D --> E[\\\"testing_icons_studies()\\\\nrepeat testing_icons() per study,\\\\nfacet_wrap(~study)\\\"]\\n```\\n\\nThe key idea is **composition over inheritance**: rather than writing a new\\nicon from scratch, `monitor_parts()` draws just the screen/stand, and\\n`person_at_computer()` glues one `person_parts()` output and one\\n`monitor_parts()` output into a single polygon set, tagged with a `role`\\ncolumn (`\\\"person\\\"` vs `\\\"monitor\\\"`) so the two pieces can be filled\\ndifferently. Everything above that (grids, score labels, faceted studies)\\nis built the same way `person_grid()` was.\\n\\n## Element-by-element walkthrough\\n\\n### Screen geometry: `monitor_parts()`\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-monitor-parts\\n#| eval: false\\nmonitor_parts \\u003c- function(scale = 1, ox = 0, oy = 0,\\n                           center_y = 1.62, x_offset = 0.80) {\\n  bezel_hw \\u003c- 0.40\\n  bezel_hh \\u003c- 0.34\\n  # ... bezel / screen / neck / base polygons, all offset from x_offset ...\\n}\\n```\\n\\nThis draws four stacked polygons (bezel, inset screen, neck, base — an\\ninverted-T stand) in the **same local coordinate frame** `person_parts()`\\nuses (head centred at `x = 0, y = 1.62`). Two defaults matter:\\n\\n- `center_y = 1.62` — the monitor is vertically centred *on the head*, not\\n  on the whole body, so the composite reads as \\\"looking at a screen\\\"\\n  rather than \\\"a person standing next to an unrelated box\\\".\\n- `x_offset = 0.80` — a fixed horizontal gap from the body's centre line.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-monitor-parts\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"monitor_parts() alone\\\"\\nggplot(monitor_parts(), aes(x, y, group = part)) +\\n  geom_polygon(fill = \\\"grey70\\\") +\\n  coord_equal() +\\n  theme_void()\\n```\\n\\n### The composite icon: `person_at_computer()`\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-person-at-computer\\n#| eval: false\\nperson_at_computer \\u003c- function(kind = \\\"A\\\", age = \\\"adult\\\", disabled = FALSE,\\n                                scale = 1, ox = 0, oy = 0,\\n                                person_color = \\\"#3B6EA5\\\",\\n                                screen_color = \\\"#CFE8FF\\\",\\n                                frame_color = \\\"#555555\\\") {\\n  p \\u003c- person_parts(kind, age, disabled, scale, ox, oy)\\n  p$role \\u003c- \\\"person\\\"\\n  p$fill \\u003c- person_color\\n\\n  m \\u003c- monitor_parts(scale = scale, ox = ox, oy = oy)\\n  m$role \\u003c- \\\"monitor\\\"\\n  m$fill \\u003c- ifelse(m$part == \\\"screen\\\", screen_color, frame_color)\\n\\n  rbind(p, m)\\n}\\n```\\n\\nThis simply calls `person_parts()` and `monitor_parts()` with the *same*\\n`scale`/`ox`/`oy`, stamps a `fill` colour on each (the monitor's bezel/neck/\\nbase all get `frame_color`, only the inset `screen` part gets\\n`screen_color`), and row-binds the two polygon sets. Because both pieces\\nshare the same offset, the composite moves as one unit when placed in a\\ngrid later.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-person-at-computer\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"One composite icon\\\"\\none_icon \\u003c- person_at_computer(kind = \\\"A\\\")\\nggplot(one_icon, aes(x, y, group = paste(part, role), fill = fill)) +\\n  geom_polygon() +\\n  scale_fill_identity() +\\n  coord_equal() +\\n  theme_void()\\n```\\n\\n### The main sequence function: `testing_icons()`\\n\\nThis mirrors `person_grid()`'s structure closely (composition sampling,\\ncolour modes, grid placement), with two differences specific to the\\nnarrative sequence it's built for:\\n\\n- an optional `scores` argument: when supplied (length must equal `n`),\\n  each icon gets an `\\\"x = \\u003cscore>\\\"` label underneath it — used for the\\n  one-person and two-person steps. Left `NULL` for the \\\"sample\\\" step,\\n  where the narrative says scores exist but deliberately doesn't show\\n  them.\\n- it inherits `person_grid()`'s two colour modes (`\\\"diversity\\\"` /\\n  `\\\"value\\\"`) unchanged, so the same colour-by-effect-size trick is\\n  available here too, not just on plain person icons.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-testing-icons-one\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"n = 1, with a score label\\\"\\ntesting_icons(n = 1, scores = 27)$plot\\n```\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-testing-icons-two\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"n = 2, with score labels\\\"\\ntesting_icons(n = 2, scores = c(31, 24))$plot\\n```\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-testing-icons-sample\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"n = 20, no scores shown -- 'a sample of people'\\\"\\n#| fig-width: 7\\n#| fig-height: 3.5\\ntesting_icons(n = 20, seed = 7)$plot\\n```\\n\\n### Many studies at once: `testing_icons_studies()`\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-testing-icons-studies\\n#| eval: false\\ntesting_icons_studies \\u003c- function(n_studies, n_per_study, ncol = NULL,\\n                                   seed = 1, ...) {\\n  panels \\u003c- vector(\\\"list\\\", n_studies)\\n  for (s in seq_len(n_studies)) {\\n    g \\u003c- testing_icons(n = n_per_study, seed = seed + s, ...)\\n    g$data$study \\u003c- paste(\\\"Study\\\", s)\\n    panels[[s]] \\u003c- g$data\\n  }\\n  df \\u003c- do.call(rbind, panels)\\n  df$poly_id \\u003c- paste(df$study, df$poly_id)\\n  # ... ggplot() + facet_wrap(~study) ...\\n}\\n```\\n\\nThis is the icon analogue of `sampling-distributions.R`'s\\n`plot_histogram_grid()`/`plot_dotpile_grid()`: it calls `testing_icons()`\\nonce per \\\"study\\\" with an offset seed (`seed + s`), so each panel is an\\n**independently drawn** sample (not the same 20 icons repeated), tags each\\npanel's polygons with a `study` column, and facets. Note `poly_id` is\\nre-prefixed with `study` — without this, icon 1 in Study 1 and icon 1 in\\nStudy 2 would share a `poly_id` and `ggplot` would try to connect/group\\nthem incorrectly across panels.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-testing-icons-studies\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"Six independent 20-person samples ('studies')\\\"\\n#| fig-width: 8\\n#| fig-height: 5\\ntesting_icons_studies(n_studies = 6, n_per_study = 20, ncol = 3, seed = 104)$plot\\n```\\n\\n## Quarto usage / integration\\n\\nSetup-chunk lines (order matters):\\n\\n```r\\nsource(\\\"person-grid.R\\\")\\nsource(\\\"testing-sequence.R\\\")\\n```\\n\\nReal usage from `doing-being-science.qmd` — one person, paired in a\\ntwo-column layout with a `sampling-distributions.R` dot plot of the same\\nsimulated score (`d_one$observed_score`), so the icon's label and the\\npoint on the number line visibly match:\\n\\n````{verbatim}\\n```{r}\\n#| label: fig-one-person-icon\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"You do the vocabulary test\\\"\\n#| fig-width: 4\\n#| fig-height: 3.75\\n#| echo: false\\n\\nd_one \\u003c- simulate_vocab_data(n = 1, seed = 101)\\ntesting_icons(n = 1, scores = d_one$observed_score)$plot\\n```\\n````\\n\\nThe \\\"many studies\\\" step:\\n\\n````{verbatim}\\n```{r}\\n#| label: fig-many-studies-icons\\n#| fig-width: 8\\n#| fig-height: 5\\n\\ntesting_icons_studies(n_studies = 6, n_per_study = 20, ncol = 3, seed = 104)$plot\\n```\\n````\\n\\nA couple of integration notes:\\n\\n- The icon grid's `seed` only controls *cosmetic* sampling (silhouette,\\n  age, disability, skin tone) — it has no bearing on simulated scores. If\\n  you want an icon's label to match a score drawn elsewhere (as in the\\n  one-person/two-person slides), pass that score in explicitly via\\n  `scores =`, rather than relying on the seeds to line up.\\n- `#| echo: false` is used on the slide chunks so only the figure shows on\\n  the slide, not the simulation code — drop it if you want to show the\\n  code for teaching purposes.\\n\\n### Parameter quick reference (`testing_icons()`)\\n\\n| Parameter | Default | Meaning |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| `n` | — | Number of icons. |\\n| `scores` | `NULL` | Optional length-`n` vector; adds `\\\"x = \\u003cscore>\\\"` labels. |\\n| `ncol` | `NULL` (auto) | Icons per row. |\\n| `comp_kind`, `comp_age`, `disabled_prop` | as `person_grid()` | Composition mix. |\\n| `mode` | `\\\"diversity\\\"` | `\\\"diversity\\\"` or `\\\"value\\\"` (see `person-grid.R`). |\\n| `skin_tones`, `value` | as `person_grid()` | Colour controls. |\\n| `seed` | `1` | Cosmetic-sampling reproducibility (not score data). |\\n| `dx`, `dy` | `1.9, 2.5` | Icon spacing. |\\n\\n`testing_icons_studies()` adds `n_studies`, `n_per_study`, and forwards\\neverything else to `testing_icons()` via `...` (except `scores`, which\\nisn't supported in the faceted version).\\n\\n## See also\\n\\n- [person-grid-walkthrough.qmd](person-grid-walkthrough.qmd) — the\\n  dependency this script builds on; read first.\\n- [sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd](sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd) —\\n  the synthetic-data figures this icon sequence is paired with in the\\n  slide deck (same narrative, data side instead of icon side).\\n- [peer-review-workflow-walkthrough.qmd](peer-review-workflow-walkthrough.qmd) —\\n  reuses `person_at_computer()` from this script.\\n\",\"language\":\"markdown\"}}\u003c/script>\u003c/tool-call>\u003c/div>\n479:\u003cdiv>\u003ctool-call id=\"toolu_01EQHzZAdEasoFP8G8MaXJoY\">\u003cscript type=\"application/json\">{\"version\":2,\"name\":\"write\",\"input\":{\"file_path\":\"peer-review-workflow-walkthrough.qmd\",\"content\":\"---\\ntitle: \\\"`peer-review-workflow.R`: the peer-review cycle as a flow diagram\\\"\\nsubtitle: \\\"...[truncated, total 10176 chars]\"},\"caption\":\"peer-review-workflow-walkthrough.qmd\",\"captionLink\":\"peer-review-workflow-walkthrough.qmd\",\"inputPreview\":{\"type\":\"code\",\"value\":\"---\\ntitle: \\\"`peer-review-workflow.R`: the peer-review cycle as a flow diagram\\\"\\nsubtitle: \\\"Walkthrough: how the script works, and how to use it in Quarto\\\"\\nformat:\\n  html:\\n    code-fold: false\\n    toc: true\\n---\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: setup\\n#| include: false\\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = \\\"center\\\")\\n```\\n\\n## Aims\\n\\n`peer-review-workflow.R` draws a single, fixed diagram of the peer-reviewed\\npublication cycle — author submits to editor, editor sends out to two\\nreviewers (fan-out), reviewers report back (fan-in), editor decides, with a\\ndashed loop-back arrow for \\\"reject with revise & resubmit → repeat\\\". It\\nreuses the \\\"person at a computer\\\" icon from `testing-sequence.R` across\\nfour roles (author, editor, reviewer ×2) rather than drawing a new icon\\nstyle, so the peer-review figure visually matches the testing-sequence\\nfigures elsewhere in the deck.\\n\\nUnlike the other four scripts in this set, this one is **not\\nparametrized** for general reuse — it's a single bespoke diagram, built\\nwith hand-placed coordinates for this specific six-icon layout. This\\ndocument explains that layout logic so it can be adapted (e.g. a\\ndifferent number of reviewers) rather than treated as a black box.\\n\\n## Prerequisites / assumptions\\n\\n- **Packages**: `ggplot2` only.\\n- **Sourcing**: `person-grid.R` **and** `testing-sequence.R` must both be\\n  sourced first, in that order — this script calls\\n  `person_at_computer()` directly, which itself depends on\\n  `person_parts()`/`monitor_parts()`.\\n- **Reader background**: read\\n  [person-grid-walkthrough.qmd](person-grid-walkthrough.qmd) and\\n  [testing-sequence-walkthrough.qmd](testing-sequence-walkthrough.qmd)\\n  first — this script is a thin, specific application of both.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: source-scripts\\nsource(\\\"person-grid.R\\\")\\nsource(\\\"testing-sequence.R\\\")\\nsource(\\\"peer-review-workflow.R\\\")\\n```\\n\\n## How it works: the process\\n\\n```{mermaid}\\nflowchart TB\\n    A[\\\"pos: named list of\\\\nhand-placed (x, y) coordinates\\\\nfor each of the 6 icons\\\"] --> B[\\\"icon_df() / icon helper\\\\nbuilds each icon via\\\\nperson_at_computer(), tags it,\\\\ncolours it by role\\\"]\\n    A --> C[\\\"right_of() / left_of()\\\\ncompute arrow endpoints\\\\njust outside each icon,\\\\nnot at icon centres\\\"]\\n    C --> D[\\\"straight_arrows, curve_arrows,\\\\nloop_arrow: data frames of\\\\narrow endpoints\\\"]\\n    B --> E[\\\"single ggplot():\\\\nicons + segments + curves\\\\n+ role/step text labels\\\"]\\n    D --> E\\n```\\n\\nThe diagram is built from three largely independent ingredients that only\\ncome together in the final `ggplot()` call: **where** each icon sits\\n(`pos`), **what** each icon looks like (role-specific colour via\\n`person_at_computer()`), and **how** the icons connect (arrows computed\\nfrom positions, not drawn freehand).\\n\\n## Element-by-element walkthrough\\n\\n### Layout: the `pos` list and role colours\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-pos\\n#| eval: false\\nresearcher_col \\u003c- list(person = \\\"#3B6EA5\\\", screen = \\\"#CFE8FF\\\")\\neditor_col     \\u003c- list(person = \\\"#B0562D\\\", screen = \\\"#FFDCC5\\\")\\nreviewer_col   \\u003c- list(person = \\\"#3B9E5F\\\", screen = \\\"#D3F5DF\\\")\\n\\npos \\u003c- list(\\n  researcher1 = c(0,    0),\\n  editor1     = c(5.0,  0),\\n  reviewerA   = c(10.5, 3.4),\\n  reviewerB   = c(10.5, -3.4),\\n  editor2     = c(16.0, 0),\\n  researcher2 = c(21.0, 0)\\n)\\n```\\n\\nEvery coordinate here is hand-chosen, not computed from a formula (unlike\\n`person-grid.R`'s automatic grid spacing). The author and editor appear\\n**twice** (`researcher1`/`researcher2`, `editor1`/`editor2`) at different\\nx-positions, because the same two people appear at both the start and end\\nof the cycle — this is a flow diagram of a *process*, not a single\\nsnapshot of who's present. The two reviewers are offset vertically\\n(`+3.4`/`-3.4`) at the same x-position, to draw the fan-out/fan-in\\nvisually as a split-and-rejoin. Each role gets its own `person`/`screen`\\ncolour pair, reused across every icon that plays that role.\\n\\n### Building each icon: the `icon_df()` helper\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-icon-df\\n#| eval: false\\nicon_df \\u003c- function(name, kind, cols) {\\n  p \\u003c- pos[[name]]\\n  d \\u003c- person_at_computer(kind = kind, ox = p[1], oy = p[2],\\n                           person_color = cols$person, screen_color = cols$screen)\\n  d$icon \\u003c- name\\n  d\\n}\\n\\nicons \\u003c- rbind(\\n  icon_df(\\\"researcher1\\\", \\\"A\\\", researcher_col),\\n  icon_df(\\\"editor1\\\",     \\\"B\\\", editor_col),\\n  icon_df(\\\"reviewerA\\\",   \\\"A\\\", reviewer_col),\\n  icon_df(\\\"reviewerB\\\",   \\\"B\\\", reviewer_col),\\n  icon_df(\\\"editor2\\\",     \\\"B\\\", editor_col),\\n  icon_df(\\\"researcher2\\\", \\\"A\\\", researcher_col)\\n)\\nicons$poly_id \\u003c- paste(icons$icon, icons$part, icons$role)\\n```\\n\\nThis is a direct application of `person_at_computer()` (from\\n`testing-sequence.R`) at each named position, looked up from `pos`. The\\n`kind` argument (`\\\"A\\\"`/`\\\"B\\\"`) here is just varying the leg silhouette for\\nvisual variety across the six icons — it carries no role meaning (unlike\\n`person_color`/`screen_color`, which *does* encode role). As with every\\nother script in this set, `poly_id` is rebuilt to be unique per icon\\n*and* per sub-part, so `ggplot`'s `group` aesthetic doesn't connect\\npolygons that happen to share a part name (e.g. every icon's `\\\"head\\\"`)\\nacross different icons.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-icon-df\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"The six positioned icons, before any arrows are added\\\"\\nresearcher_col \\u003c- list(person = \\\"#3B6EA5\\\", screen = \\\"#CFE8FF\\\")\\neditor_col     \\u003c- list(person = \\\"#B0562D\\\", screen = \\\"#FFDCC5\\\")\\nreviewer_col   \\u003c- list(person = \\\"#3B9E5F\\\", screen = \\\"#D3F5DF\\\")\\npos \\u003c- list(\\n  researcher1 = c(0, 0), editor1 = c(5.0, 0),\\n  reviewerA = c(10.5, 3.4), reviewerB = c(10.5, -3.4),\\n  editor2 = c(16.0, 0), researcher2 = c(21.0, 0)\\n)\\nicon_df \\u003c- function(name, kind, cols) {\\n  p \\u003c- pos[[name]]\\n  d \\u003c- person_at_computer(kind = kind, ox = p[1], oy = p[2],\\n                           person_color = cols$person, screen_color = cols$screen)\\n  d$icon \\u003c- name\\n  d\\n}\\ndemo_icons \\u003c- rbind(\\n  icon_df(\\\"researcher1\\\", \\\"A\\\", researcher_col),\\n  icon_df(\\\"editor1\\\", \\\"B\\\", editor_col),\\n  icon_df(\\\"reviewerA\\\", \\\"A\\\", reviewer_col),\\n  icon_df(\\\"reviewerB\\\", \\\"B\\\", reviewer_col),\\n  icon_df(\\\"editor2\\\", \\\"B\\\", editor_col),\\n  icon_df(\\\"researcher2\\\", \\\"A\\\", researcher_col)\\n)\\ndemo_icons$poly_id \\u003c- paste(demo_icons$icon, demo_icons$part, demo_icons$role)\\nggplot(demo_icons, aes(x, y, group = poly_id, fill = fill)) +\\n  geom_polygon() +\\n  scale_fill_identity() +\\n  coord_equal() +\\n  theme_void()\\n```\\n\\n### Arrows: `right_of()`/`left_of()` and three arrow data frames\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-arrow-helpers\\n#| eval: false\\nright_of \\u003c- function(name, dy = 0.9) c(pos[[name]][1] + 1.25, pos[[name]][2] + dy)\\nleft_of  \\u003c- function(name, dy = 0.9) c(pos[[name]][1] - 0.55, pos[[name]][2] + dy)\\n```\\n\\nArrows are anchored just outside each icon (`+1.25`/`-0.55` from the\\nicon's x-position, with a small `+0.9` vertical nudge) rather than at icon\\ncentres — centring the arrows would draw them straight through the icon\\npolygons. Three kinds of connections are built from these anchors:\\n\\n- `straight_arrows` — plain `geom_segment()` arrows: author → editor, and\\n  editor → author (submission and final decision).\\n- `curve_arrows` — `geom_curve()` arrows with an explicit `curvature`\\n  value per row (`+0.30` or `-0.30`) for the fan-out (editor → two\\n  reviewers) and fan-in (two reviewers → editor) — the sign of `curvature`\\n  controls which way each curve bows, matching the reviewer's vertical\\n  offset so the curves don't cross awkwardly.\\n- `loop_arrow` — a single dashed `geom_curve()` well below the main row\\n  (`y = -7.0`), representing \\\"reject, revise & resubmit\\\" looping back from\\n  the end to the start.\\n\\n### Text labels and final assembly\\n\\nTwo more data frames (`step_captions`, `role_labels`) place bold numbered\\nstep captions (e.g. \\\"1. Submit manuscript\\\") and small role labels\\n(\\\"Author\\\", \\\"Editor\\\", \\\"Reviewer 1\\\"/\\\"2\\\") at further hand-offset positions. A\\ncode comment in the script flags that *Reviewer 1*'s label needed a\\ndifferent vertical offset than the generic pattern to clear its icon\\nwithout crowding the step caption beneath it — a reminder that this\\ndiagram's positions were tuned by eye, so changing icon spacing or icon\\nsize will likely require re-tuning label offsets too, rather than\\ncascading automatically.\\n\\nEverything (polygons, segments, curves, loop arrow, annotation, two sets\\nof text labels) is layered onto **one** `ggplot()` object and returned as\\n`peer_review_workflow()$plot`.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-peer-review-workflow\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"The full peer-review workflow diagram\\\"\\n#| fig-width: 9\\n#| fig-height: 6\\npeer_review_workflow()$plot\\n```\\n\\n## Quarto usage / integration\\n\\nSetup-chunk lines (order matters: both dependencies before this script):\\n\\n```r\\nsource(\\\"person-grid.R\\\")\\nsource(\\\"testing-sequence.R\\\")\\nsource(\\\"peer-review-workflow.R\\\")\\n```\\n\\nReal usage from `doing-being-science.qmd`:\\n\\n````{verbatim}\\n```{r}\\n#| label: fig-peer-review-workflow\\n#| fig-cap: \\\"The peer-reviewed publication cycle: submission, review, and decision, repeating until accept or reject\\\"\\n#| fig-width: 9\\n#| fig-height: 6\\n\\npeer_review_workflow()$plot\\n```\\n````\\n\\n`peer_review_workflow()` takes **no arguments** — there's nothing to\\nconfigure via chunk options beyond `fig-width`/`fig-height` (the plot uses\\n`coord_equal(clip = \\\"off\\\", ylim = c(-8.8, 5.8))` internally, so it has a\\nfixed aspect ratio; picking a `fig-width`/`fig-height` far from roughly\\n9:6 will add letterboxing rather than reflowing the diagram).\\n\\n### If you need to adapt this diagram\\n\\nBecause nothing here is parametrized, adapting it (e.g. three reviewers\\ninstead of two, or a different number of decision rounds) means editing\\nthe script directly rather than passing new arguments:\\n\\n1. Add/remove entries in `pos` (and give any new role a colour list like\\n   `reviewer_col`).\\n2. Add/remove the corresponding `icon_df()` calls.\\n3. Add/remove rows in `curve_arrows` for the new fan-out/fan-in\\n   connections, with signed `curvature` chosen to avoid crossing.\\n4. Re-check `role_labels`/`step_captions` y-offsets by eye — as noted\\n   above, these were tuned per-icon, not computed generically.\\n\\n## See also\\n\\n- [testing-sequence-walkthrough.qmd](testing-sequence-walkthrough.qmd) —\\n  the source of the `person_at_computer()` icon reused four times here.\\n- [person-grid-walkthrough.qmd](person-grid-walkthrough.qmd) — the\\n  underlying geometry/colour primitives.\\n\",\"language\":\"markdown\"}}\u003c/script>\u003c/tool-call>\u003c/div>\n485:\u003cdiv>\u003ctool-call id=\"toolu_01GbhsgUYXZRE5ViBa3qoibg\">\u003cscript type=\"application/json\">{\"version\":2,\"name\":\"write\",\"input\":{\"file_path\":\"sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd\",\"content\":\"---\\ntitle: \\\"`sampling-distributions.R`: simulating and plotting test scores\\\"\\nsubtitle: \\\"Wa...[truncated, total 13873 chars]\"},\"caption\":\"sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd\",\"captionLink\":\"sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd\",\"inputPreview\":{\"type\":\"code\",\"value\":\"---\\ntitle: \\\"`sampling-distributions.R`: simulating and plotting test scores\\\"\\nsubtitle: \\\"Walkthrough: how the script works, and how to use it in Quarto\\\"\\nformat:\\n  html:\\n    code-fold: false\\n    toc: true\\n---\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: setup\\n#| include: false\\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = \\\"center\\\")\\n```\\n\\n## Aims\\n\\n`sampling-distributions.R` simulates scores on a hypothetical 0–40 item\\nvocabulary test, from the trial (item) level up, and draws the synthetic\\ndata half of the sampling/measurement-error narrative: one dot → two dots\\n→ a \\\"pile of dots\\\" showing a sample's distribution → a histogram → a grid\\nof histograms (repeated studies) → a scatterplot against a continuous\\ncovariate. It's the data-generating and plotting counterpart to\\n`testing-sequence.R`'s icon sequence (same narrative, numbers instead of\\npictograms).\\n\\nThe simulation is deliberately built **trial-level up** rather than\\ngenerating a continuous score and rounding/clipping it: every simulated\\nperson's score is the sum of 40 independent correct/incorrect item\\nresponses, so it is *structurally* impossible for a simulated score to\\nfall outside `[0, 40]` — there's no clipping step anywhere in the script,\\nbecause none is needed.\\n\\n## Prerequisites / assumptions\\n\\n- **Packages**: `ggplot2`, and `ggdist` for the dot-pile figures\\n  (`plot_dotpile()`, `plot_dotpile_grid()`).\\n- **Sourcing**: standalone — no other script in this set needs to be\\n  sourced first.\\n- **Reader background**: some familiarity with classical test theory\\n  terms (reliability, true score) is helpful but not required — the key\\n  ideas are explained below. Basic `ggplot2` familiarity assumed.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: source-script\\nlibrary(ggdist)\\nsource(\\\"sampling-distributions.R\\\")\\n```\\n\\n## How it works: the process\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: model-equation\\n#| echo: false\\n#| results: asis\\ncat(\\n  \\\"$$\\\",\\n  \\\"\\\\\\\\text{Ability (logit scale):} \\\\\\\\quad \\\\\\\\theta_i \\\\\\\\sim N(\\\\\\\\theta_\\\\\\\\mu, \\\\\\\\theta_\\\\\\\\sigma)\\\",\\n  \\\"$$\\\",\\n  \\\"$$\\\",\\n  \\\"\\\\\\\\text{Per-item probability:} \\\\\\\\quad p_i = \\\\\\\\text{plogis}(\\\\\\\\theta_i)\\\",\\n  \\\"$$\\\",\\n  \\\"$$\\\",\\n  \\\"\\\\\\\\text{Observed score:} \\\\\\\\quad Y_i \\\\\\\\sim \\\\\\\\text{Binomial}(40, p_i) \\\\\\\\quad \\\\\\\\in \\\\\\\\{0, \\\\\\\\dots, 40\\\\\\\\}\\\",\\n  \\\"$$\\\",\\n  sep = \\\"\\\\n\\\"\\n)\\n```\\n\\nA `Binomial(40, p_i)` draw is the vectorized equivalent of summing 40\\nindependent Bernoulli (correct/incorrect) trials, so the model above\\n*is* the trial-level process described in the aims, just computed\\nefficiently rather than looped item-by-item.\\n\\n```{mermaid}\\nflowchart LR\\n    A[\\\"calibrate_ability()\\\\nsolve theta_mu, theta_sigma\\\\nto hit target mu + reliability\\\\n(or mu + sd_true)\\\"] --> B[\\\"simulate_vocab_data()\\\\ndraw theta_i per person,\\\\np_i = plogis(theta_i),\\\\nscore_i ~ Binomial(40, p_i)\\\"]\\n    B --> C[\\\"plot_dots() / plot_dotpile() /\\\\nplot_histogram() / plot_scatter()\\\"]\\n    B --> D[\\\"simulate_studies()\\\\nrepeat simulate_vocab_data()\\\\nper independent 'study'\\\"]\\n    D --> E[\\\"plot_histogram_grid() /\\\\nplot_dotpile_grid()\\\\n(facet_wrap(~study))\\\"]\\n```\\n\\nThe central design idea: **you don't set the ability distribution's mean\\nand spread directly.** You set the things that matter pedagogically — the\\ntest's mean score (`mu`) and its reliability (`reliability`, or\\nalternatively a target spread `sd_true`) — and `calibrate_ability()`\\nnumerically solves for the underlying `theta_mu`/`theta_sigma` that\\nreproduce them, because for a fixed test length, mean/reliability/spread\\nare mathematically linked, not three independently free knobs.\\n\\n## Element-by-element walkthrough\\n\\n### Calibration machinery: `expect_theta()` and `implied_moments()`\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-expect-theta\\n#| eval: false\\nexpect_theta \\u003c- function(f, theta_mu, theta_sigma) {\\n  integrate(function(theta) f(theta) * dnorm(theta, theta_mu, theta_sigma),\\n            lower = theta_mu - 10 * theta_sigma,\\n            upper = theta_mu + 10 * theta_sigma)$value\\n}\\n```\\n\\n`expect_theta()` computes $E[f(\\\\theta)]$ for $\\\\theta \\\\sim N(\\\\theta_\\\\mu,\\n\\\\theta_\\\\sigma)$ by plain numerical integration (base R `integrate()`, no\\nextra dependency) — used to get exact expectations like $E[p_i]$ or\\n$E[p_i^2]$ without resorting to Monte Carlo.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-implied-moments\\n#| eval: false\\nimplied_moments \\u003c- function(theta_mu, theta_sigma, n_items) {\\n  p_bar  \\u003c- expect_theta(plogis, theta_mu, theta_sigma)\\n  p2_bar \\u003c- expect_theta(function(th) plogis(th)^2, theta_mu, theta_sigma)\\n  pq_bar \\u003c- expect_theta(function(th) plogis(th) * (1 - plogis(th)), theta_mu, theta_sigma)\\n\\n  mean_score  \\u003c- n_items * p_bar\\n  var_true    \\u003c- n_items^2 * (p2_bar - p_bar^2)\\n  var_error   \\u003c- n_items * pq_bar\\n  reliability \\u003c- var_true / (var_true + var_error)\\n  # ...\\n}\\n```\\n\\nGiven a candidate `(theta_mu, theta_sigma)`, this works out what mean\\nscore, \\\"true\\\"-score variance (between-person spread), measurement-error\\nvariance (within-person, item-sampling noise), and reliability\\n(`var_true / (var_true + var_error)`) that choice *implies* — i.e. it runs\\nthe model forward analytically. `calibrate_ability()` then runs this\\nbackward: searching for the `(theta_mu, theta_sigma)` whose\\n`implied_moments()` output matches your targets.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-implied-moments\\nimplied_moments(theta_mu = 0, theta_sigma = 1.3, n_items = 40)\\n```\\n\\n### Solving for ability parameters: `calibrate_ability()`\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-calibrate-ability-signature\\n#| eval: false\\ncalibrate_ability \\u003c- function(mu, reliability = 0.80, sd_true = NULL, n_items = 40) {\\n  # ...\\n}\\n```\\n\\nTwo calibration targets are supported, and they're **mutually\\nexclusive** — for a fixed `mu` and `n_items`, fixing one determines the\\nother:\\n\\n- `reliability` (the default path) — \\\"how repeatable is this test\\\"; use\\n  this when the figure is about test-retest/parallel-forms reliability.\\n- `sd_true` — \\\"how spread out is this population\\\"; use this when a figure\\n  needs independent control of between-person spread (e.g. two panels\\n  with the same mean but visibly different spread), supplied instead of\\n  `reliability`.\\n\\nInternally, both paths use the same robust pattern: a nested `uniroot()`\\nsearch (an outer search over `theta_sigma`, and for each candidate, an\\ninner search over `theta_mu` so the mean score matches `mu` exactly), with\\nthe search bracket doubled automatically if the initial range doesn't\\ncontain a root, and an informative error (rather than a cryptic numerical\\nfailure) if the target isn't achievable — e.g. `reliability` above about\\n0.99 would require an implausibly large, numerically unstable ability\\nspread for a 40-item test. `sd_true` additionally has a closed-form\\nfeasibility check: the theoretical ceiling is `sqrt(mu * (n_items - mu))`,\\napproached only as the ability spread goes to infinity.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-calibrate-ability\\ncal \\u003c- calibrate_ability(mu = 30, reliability = 0.80)\\ncal$moments\\n```\\n\\n### Simulating one sample: `simulate_vocab_data()`\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-simulate-vocab-data-core\\n#| eval: false\\ncal \\u003c- calibrate_ability(mu, reliability = reliability, sd_true = sd_true, n_items = n_items)\\n# ... correlation setup (see below) ...\\ntheta \\u003c- cal$theta_mu + cal$theta_sigma * theta_z\\np_correct \\u003c- plogis(theta)\\nobserved_score \\u003c- rbinom(n, size = n_items, prob = p_correct)\\n```\\n\\nAfter calibration, simulating is simple: draw standardized ability\\n`theta_z` per person (optionally correlated with a covariate — see next\\nsection), scale/shift it to `theta`, convert to `p_correct` via\\n`plogis()`, and draw `observed_score` as a single vectorized\\n`rbinom(n, 40, p_correct)` call — bounded to `[0, 40]` by construction.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-simulate-vocab-data\\nd \\u003c- simulate_vocab_data(n = 10, mu = 30, reliability = 0.80, seed = 1)\\nd\\nrange(simulate_vocab_data(n = 10000, seed = 2)$observed_score)\\n```\\n\\n### Inducing a covariate correlation: `r_with_x`\\n\\nThis is the part of the script most worth reading carefully if you're\\nadapting it, because of **attenuation**: any correlation involving a\\nnoisy *observed* variable is weaker than the correlation involving the\\nunderlying *true* ability, because measurement error adds noise that\\ndilutes the relationship. Classical test theory gives\\n$\\\\text{corr}(\\\\text{observed}, \\\\theta) = \\\\sqrt{\\\\text{reliability}}$, so to\\nhit a target **observed**-score correlation `r_with_x`, the script works\\nbackward through that relationship:\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: show-attenuation-logic\\n#| eval: false\\nmax_r \\u003c- sqrt(reliability)\\nif (abs(r_with_x) > max_r) {\\n  warning(...)  # cap r_with_x at the achievable ceiling\\n  r_with_x \\u003c- sign(r_with_x) * max_r\\n}\\nr_theta_x \\u003c- if (r_with_x == 0) 0 else r_with_x / max_r\\n# theta_z is then a mix of standardized x and independent noise,\\n# correlated with x at r_theta_x so that, after measurement error,\\n# the *observed* score ends up correlated with x at (approximately) r_with_x\\n```\\n\\nTwo consequences worth knowing: (1) `r_with_x` is specified on the\\n*observed*-score scale — i.e. it's (approximately) the correlation you'll\\nactually see in `plot_scatter()`, not some larger hidden value; (2) at\\nlow `reliability`, only a limited range of `r_with_x` is achievable at\\nall (capped at `sqrt(reliability)`), and the function warns rather than\\nsilently failing if you ask for more than that.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-r-with-x\\nd_cor \\u003c- simulate_vocab_data(n = 2000, r_with_x = 0.5, seed = 3)\\ncor(d_cor$x, d_cor$observed_score)\\n```\\n\\nOne more detail handled explicitly: `scale(x)` is undefined (`NaN`) when\\n`n \\u003c 2` or `x` has zero variance, and `0 * NaN` is `NaN` in R — so the\\nstandardization path is skipped entirely whenever `r_theta_x == 0`,\\npreventing an `NA` score from leaking in even at the default\\n`r_with_x = 0` with `n = 1`.\\n\\n### Repeated studies: `simulate_studies()` and `simulate_parallel_forms()`\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-simulate-studies\\nstudies \\u003c- simulate_studies(n_studies = 3, n_per_study = 15, seed = 4)\\ntapply(studies$observed_score, studies$study, mean)\\n```\\n\\n`simulate_studies()` just calls `simulate_vocab_data()` once per study\\n(without resetting the seed between calls, so each study's sample differs\\nbut the whole sequence stays reproducible from one top-level `seed`),\\nrow-binding the results with a `study` label — this is what feeds the\\n`_grid()` plotting functions below.\\n\\n`simulate_parallel_forms()` is a different use case: it draws **one**\\n`theta_i` per person but **two** independent test administrations\\n(`form1`, `form2`) from that same `theta_i` — i.e. the same person tested\\ntwice (or on two equivalent forms). This is how the script's own\\nreliability calibration can be checked empirically:\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-parallel-forms\\npf \\u003c- simulate_parallel_forms(n = 20000, mu = 30, reliability = 0.80, seed = 5)\\ncor(pf$form1, pf$form2)\\n```\\n\\n### Figures: `plot_dots()`, `plot_dotpile()`, `plot_histogram()`, `plot_scatter()`, and their `_grid()` variants\\n\\nThese are comparatively simple `ggplot2` wrappers; the interesting parts\\nare the choices, not the mechanics:\\n\\n- `plot_dots()` — one or two scores as points on a number line, with `y`\\n  nudged just above 0 so points sit on the axis line rather than being\\n  bisected by it.\\n- `plot_dotpile()` — a sample's distribution as discrete points via\\n  `ggdist::stat_dots()`, by design **not** a smoothed density curve or a\\n  binned histogram, so the figure reads as \\\"these are the actual\\n  individual scores\\\", not an idealized shape.\\n- `plot_dotpile_grid()` — the faceted version; `binwidth` is fixed\\n  explicitly rather than left to `ggdist`'s per-panel default, because\\n  that default sizes each panel's dot diameter to that panel's own\\n  tallest stack — which would make dots visibly different sizes across\\n  panels, undermining a \\\"same scale, different samples\\\" comparison.\\n- `plot_histogram()` / `plot_histogram_grid()` — standard binned\\n  histograms, for the \\\"distribution looks approximately normal\\\" step.\\n- `plot_scatter()` — score against a covariate, with an optional\\n  `geom_smooth(method = \\\"lm\\\")` fitted line.\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-figures\\n#| fig-width: 7\\n#| fig-height: 2.2\\nplot_dots(d$observed_score[1])\\n```\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-dotpile\\n#| fig-width: 7\\n#| fig-height: 2.5\\nplot_dotpile(simulate_vocab_data(n = 30, seed = 6)$observed_score)\\n```\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-histogram-grid\\n#| fig-width: 8\\n#| fig-height: 4\\nplot_histogram_grid(simulate_studies(6, 40, seed = 7))\\n```\\n\\n```{r}\\n#| label: demo-scatter\\n#| fig-width: 6\\n#| fig-height: 4\\nplot_scatter(simulate_v...[truncated, total 50041 chars]","language":"text"},"elapsedMs":33}</script></tool-result></div>

## 1. Overall purpose and context

The file documents a multi-session chat about developing figure-generating R scripts for a Quarto teaching book (`teaching-critical-thinking`, revealjs deck `doing-being-science.qmd`), then writing **tutorial-style "walkthrough" `.qmd` documents** for each script. Five scripts were documented: `person-grid.R`, `testing-sequence.R`, `peer-review-workflow.R`, `sampling-distributions.R`, `concept-map.R` — each producing `<script>-walkthrough.qmd`. The explicit style model cited (line 402) was **"Andrew Heiss / Solomon Kurz-style walkthroughs"** — i.e., data-science/stats blog-post tutorials that combine aims, prerequisites, conceptual overview, element-by-element annotated code, and runnable examples, rather than dense reference docs or a plain reproduction of source files (line 404, plan at line 419).

## 2. Structure/format conventions for "walk-through" style docs

A consistent outline was used across all five `.qmd` files (established in the plan at line 419, piloted on `person-grid-walkthrough.qmd`, lines 467ff):

1. **YAML header**: `title: "`script.R`: one-line purpose"`, `subtitle: "Walkthrough: how the script works, and how to use it in Quarto"`, `format: html: {code-fold: false, toc: true}`.
2. **Setup chunk** (`#| include: false`) setting `knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center")`.
3. **`## Aims`** — a short paragraph on what figures the script produces and why they exist pedagogically, ending with 3 **"Learning objectives" bullets** in the form "After working through this, you should be able to: ..." (added later as a deliberate pattern, line 979).
4. **`## Prerequisites / assumptions`** — bullet list: Packages required, Sourcing order/dependencies (which other `.R` scripts must be sourced first and why), Reader background assumed. Followed by an actual `source()` chunk.
5. **`## How it works: the process`** — short prose plus a small **Mermaid `flowchart`** diagram summarizing the internal pipeline (e.g., geometry → composition/colour → grid assembly → `ggplot()`), so readers get a map before code detail.
6. **`## Element-by-element walkthrough`** — one `###` subsection per function/helper group, each containing:
   - A code chunk with `#| eval: false` showing the actual (sometimes trimmed) function source;
   - Explanatory prose describing what it does and *why* it's built that way (non-obvious design decisions);
   - Key "worth knowing" design-decision asides formatted as **Quarto callout divs** (`::: {.callout-note title="..."} ... :::`), not plain prose — this was an explicit stylistic upgrade (AskUser decision at line 721-740: "Use callouts" chosen over "keep as prose");
   - A runnable demo chunk (executed, not `eval: false`) producing a minimal output/plot, so the doc doubles as a working vignette.
   - The single **most distinctive design-decision code snippet** per script was required to be shown explicitly in full rather than only described in prose (this was an explicit later refinement — e.g., the `kind` A/B/N leg-silhouette branch in person-grid, the full `monitor_parts()` body in testing-sequence, the `curve_arrows` data frame in peer-review-workflow, the `scale()`/NaN guard in sampling-distributions, the `dx`-vs-`rx` overlap check in concept-map).
7. **`## Quarto usage / integration`** — setup-chunk source lines; 1–2 **real usage snippets lifted verbatim from `doing-being-science.qmd`** (wrapped in `` ````{verbatim} ```` `` fences so the nested chunk markers display literally), with integration notes (e.g., `fig-alt` via `!expr`, aspect-ratio/sizing caveats); then a **`### Parameter quick reference`** markdown table (columns: Parameter | Default | Meaning).
8. **`### Common errors`** table — added as a deliberate late addition, placed right after the parameter table, with columns **Message | Likely cause**, mapping the script's actual `stopifnot`/`warning()` text (or, for parameter-free scripts, visual symptoms) to causes.
9. **`## Exercises`** — a numbered list of practice tasks (present in all docs, referenced at lines 769, 901, 920).
10. **`## See also`** — cross-links to the other walkthrough docs that are dependencies or thematic pairings (e.g., `testing-sequence-walkthrough.qmd` links back to `person-grid-walkthrough.qmd`).

Tone: second-person, conversational but precise; prose explains *rationale* for design choices, not just mechanics. Code and explanation are tightly interleaved — never a whole-file dump; each subsection isolates one function.

## 3. Explicit stylistic rules / dos and don'ts agreed upon

- **Don't** just reproduce the whole `.R` file at once — break it into logical chunks with explanatory prose and runnable examples (line 404).
- **Do** show the single most distinctive/pedagogically important design-decision snippet as real code rather than only describing it in prose (explicit refinement applied to all 5 docs, lines 687, 740, 830-850).
- **Do** convert "worth knowing" design-decision asides into Quarto `.callout-note`/`.callout-tip` divs rather than leaving them as plain paragraphs (explicit AskUser confirmation, line 721-729, "Use callouts" recommended and chosen).
- **Do** add an explicit "Common errors" / symptoms table (message → likely cause) next to the parameter quick-reference table in every doc, sourced from the script's actual `stopifnot`/`warning` text (lines 769, 901, 920, 981).
- **Do** add 3 "learning objectives" bullets at the end of Aims, phrased as "After working through this, you should be able to..." (line 979).
- **Do** keep each `.qmd` standalone and renderable on its own (own YAML header, own `source()` calls), even though none were wired into `_quarto.yml`'s book `chapters:` list (explicitly deferred/out of scope, lines 419, plan notes).
- **Do** verify every doc renders cleanly via `quarto render` after each change, deleting generated `.html`/`_files` artifacts afterward (process followed consistently, e.g. lines 775, 973-975).
- **Do** pull "real usage" chunk examples directly/adapted from the actual slide deck (`doing-being-science.qmd`) rather than inventing synthetic examples, to keep docs grounded (lines 432, 441, 459-463).
- Naming convention: flat files alongside the `.R` scripts, named `<script>-walkthrough.qmd` (confirmed default, line 419 plan, no `docs/` subfolder).
- Build/documentation order followed each script's dependency chain: `person-grid.R` (no deps) → `testing-sequence.R` → `peer-review-workflow.R` → `sampling-distributions.R` (standalone) → `concept-map.R` (standalone).

## 4. Scripts, datasets, examples used to illustrate the style

- **`person-grid.R`** — "restroom-sign style" pictogram generator (plain ggplot2 polygons: head/torso/legs/wheelchair/cane), two colour modes (`"diversity"` sampled skin tones vs `"value"` diverging blue/orange scale). Used to illustrate: geometry helpers (`circle_pts()`, `person_parts()`), composition sampling via largest-remainder method (`sample_counts()`), colour engine (`diverging_colors()`), automatic grid shape (`choose_ncol()`), top-level `person_grid()`.
- **`testing-sequence.R`** — extends person-grid with a "person at a computer" composite icon (`monitor_parts()`, `person_at_computer()`), builds the one-person/two-people/sample-grid narrative sequence (`testing_icons()`) plus a faceted multi-study grid (`testing_icons_studies()`).
- **`peer-review-workflow.R`** — a bespoke, non-parametrized flow diagram of the peer-review cycle (author→editor→2 reviewers fan-out/fan-in→editor→author, plus a dashed reject/resubmit loop), reusing `person_at_computer()` across 4 roles with hand-placed coordinates (`pos` list, `icon_df()`, `right_of()`/`left_of()`, `curve_arrows`).
- **`sampling-distributions.R`** — the data-generation/plotting half of the same narrative: simulates a 0–40 item vocabulary test (modeled explicitly on the **Shipley vocabulary test**, per the original design brief at line 29), trial-level up (`theta_i ~ N`, `p_i = plogis(theta_i)`, `score_i ~ Binomial(40, p_i)`), calibrated via `calibrate_ability()` to hit a target mean and either `reliability` (~0.80 parallel-forms target) or `sd_true`; produces `plot_dots()`, `plot_dotpile()` (via `ggdist::stat_dots`, deliberately not a density/histogram), `plot_histogram()`, `plot_histogram_grid()`, `plot_dotpile_grid()`, `plot_scatter()` against a covariate with settable `r_with_x`.
- **`concept-map.R`** — a general N-column, many-to-many curved-link diagram in the style of **McElreath's *Statistical Rethinking* Figure 1.2** (theories → process models → statistical models), used in the deck under the slide "The theory is not the hypothesis is not the statistical test result" (`doing-being-science.qmd` line ~482).
- These were integrated into `doing-being-science.qmd` as a 5-slide two-column sequence under the heading **"Given the logic, the challenges: People are kind of random"**: one person/one score → two people → 20-person sample → six independent studies (icon grids) → six corresponding score distributions (dotpile grids), each icon figure paired with a matching `simulate_vocab_data()`/`plot_dots()` output sharing the same seed/score.

## 5. Psychological testing, sampling, NHST, power, Neyman-Pearson mentions

- The original design brief (line 29, repeated at line ~295) explicitly frames the whole figure sequence as illustrating **"sampling and measurement error, leading to thoughts about sampling distributions and frequentist null hypothesis significance testing (NHST)."**
- The task is modeled on a **Shipley-style vocabulary test** (0–40 items), with **classical test theory** concepts: measurement error (`y = a + bx_i + e_i`, `e_i ~ N(0, σ)`), **reliability** (~80% parallel-forms/test-retest correlation target), and **sampling variability across repeated studies** (used to motivate sampling distributions).
- In the deck, a `callout-tip` on measurement explicitly cites **validity** (@borsboom2004: "the thing exists and variations in it causally produce variations in measurement values") and **reliability** (@revelle2019 definition) (lines 461).
- No occurrences were found of **power, alpha/Type I/Type II error, p-values, significance testing procedures, or Neyman-Pearson error-rate framing** — the conversation references NHST only at the conceptual/narrative-framing level (as the destination the sampling-distribution sequence is building toward) and never develops power analysis or Neyman-Pearson decision-theoretic content in the scripts or documentation.

Marek et al. documented a\nstatistical-error taxonomy -- false negatives, false positives,\n**magnitude/inflation error (Type M)**, and **sign error (Type S)** -- each\nas a function of sample size, and showed that smaller samples' significant\neffects are disproportionately the most inflated and sign-flipped ones (the\n\"underpowered paradox\": stricter significance thresholds select for, rather\nthan screen out, the most inflated estimates). That richer structure is the\nsubject of Aim 5, covered in a separate future document.\n:::\n\n## Design: Aim 1 (effect size x sample size) and Aim 2 (discovery/replication split)\n\nBoth aims share one data-generating run: RE specification fixed at\n\"correct\" (random intercepts only, for `ResponseId`/`participant_id` and\n`text.id`/`text_id`); variance components fixed at their empirical values;\nthe full joint sample-size grid (30 `(n_p, n_t)` cells); 50 replicates/cell.\nA grid cell's `(n_p, n_t)` is the **total** sample -- Aim 2 splits each cell\ninto two roughly-equal-sized discovery/replication halves.\n\n**Aim 1** runs three **one-at-a-time** effect-size sweeps -- each holding\nthe other two effects fixed at their empirical values while varying the\nswept effect:\n\n| Sweep | Effect | Grid (centered on empirical estimate) |\n|---|---|---|\n| (i) | `zHLVA` (main effect, participant-level) | 0, 0.18, 0.363 (observed), 0.7, 1.0 |\n| (ii) | `zPCREFp` (main effect, text-level) | 0, 0.05, ~0.095 (observed), 0.2, 0.35 |\n| (iii) | `zHLVA:zPCREFp` (interaction) | 0, 0.025, 0.054 (observed), 0.10, 0.20 |\n\nDiagnostics extend the project's existing four (bias, sign reliability,\ncoverage, RMSE) with a Marek-style decomposition, directly computable here\nbecause the true value is known exactly: **Type S (sign) error rate** (among\nCI-excludes-0 draws, proportion with the wrong sign), **Type M\n(magnitude/inflation) ratio** (`|estimate|/|true value|` among\nCI-excludes-0 draws), and **power** on its own scale.\n\n**Question Aim 1 answers:** is the sign-instability pattern found in Phase 1\n(near-coin-flip sign consistency for the interaction at *n* = 2 texts) (a) a\nproperty of the *specific* small effect size observed, (b) specific to the\ninteraction term, or (c) a general property of being estimated from the\n*text* margin (in which case `zPCREFp`, also text-level, should show a\nsimilar pattern)? Both variants can be compared once built; the run below uses\n`\"participants_only\"`.\n\nThe significance-threshold/multiple-comparisons sweep (Marek's\nP\u003c0.05-to-Bonferroni comparison) is explicitly **deferred** here -- see\n\"Flagged future work\" below.\n\n## Shared data-generating function\n\nGeneralizes `simulate_interaction_data()` (from\n`power-simulation-vocabulary-cohesion.qmd`) and `generate_data_s3()` (from\n`simulation_study_complete.qmd`): crossed participant x text design with\n`k`-texts-per-participant subsetting (clamped to `n_texts`), independently\nsettable effect sizes for all three effects, independently settable\nintercept variances for both margins, and optional by-margin slope\nvariance/correlation (zero by default here, so Aims 1-2 reduce to the\nintercept-only DGP; non-zero values are used only by Aim 5, covered\nelsewhere).\n\n```{r}\n#| label: generate-data-p2\n\ngenerate_data_p2 \u003c- function(\n    n_participants = 200,\n    n_texts        = 20,\n    k              = min(10, n_texts),\n    questions_per_text = 4,\n    b_intercept    = 2.093,\n    b_hlva         = 0.363,\n    b_pcref        = 0.095,\n    b_interaction  = 0.054,\n    sd_participant = 0.69,\n    sd_text        = 0.41,\n    sd_pcref_slope = 0,\n    sd_hlva_slope  = 0,\n    cor_part       = 0,\n    cor_text       = 0,\n    cohesion_design = c(\"natural\", \"widened\"),\n    reliability_hlva = 1,\n    reliability_pcref = 1,\n    seed           = NULL\n) {\n  cohesion_design \u003c- match.arg(cohesion_design)\n  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)\n  k \u003c- min(k, n_texts)\n\n  # zHLVA measurement reliability -- Aim 6 strategy E; reliability_hlva = 1\n  # (default) reproduces the exact prior behavior used in Aims 1-5.\n  zHLVA_true \u003c- rnorm(n_participants, 0, 1)\n  zHLVA_obs  \u003c- sqrt(reliability_hlva) * zHLVA_true +\n    sqrt(1 - reliability_hlva) * rnorm(n_participants, 0, 1)\n\n  participants \u003c- tibble(\n    participant_id = 1:n_participants,\n    zHLVA          = zHLVA_true,\n    zHLVA_obs      = zHLVA_obs,\n    u_participant  = re_part[, 1],\n    s_pcref        = re_part[, 2]\n  )\n\n  # Text-level random effects: intercept + zHLVA slope (correlated) -- Aim 5\n  Sigma_text \u003c- matrix(\n    c(sd_text^2, cor_text * sd_text * sd_hlva_slope,\n      cor_text * sd_text * sd_hlva_slope, sd_hlva_slope^2),\n    nrow = 2\n  )\n  re_text \u003c- if (sd_hlva_slope > 0) {\n    MASS::mvrnorm(n_texts, mu = c(0, 0), Sigma = Sigma_text)\n  } else {\n    cbind(rnorm(n_texts, 0, sd_text), 0)\n  }\n\n  # zPCREFp sampling design -- Aim 6 strategy D (widened cohesion range) --\n  # and measurement reliability -- Aim 6 strategy E.\n  zPCREFp_true \u003c- if (cohesion_design == \"widened\") {\n    rep(c(-1.5, 1.5), length.out = n_texts) + rnorm(n_texts, 0, 0.3)\n  } else {\n    rnorm(n_texts, 0, 1)\n  }\n  zPCREFp_obs \u003c- sqrt(reliability_pcref) * zPCREFp_true +\n    sqrt(1 - reliability_pcref) * rnorm(n_texts, 0, 1)\n\n  texts \u003c- tibble(\n    text_id  = 1:n_texts,\n    zPCREFp  = zPCREFp_true,\n    zPCREFp_obs = zPCREFp_obs,\n    u_text   = re_text[, 1],\n    s_hlva   = re_text[, 2]\n  )\n\n  assignments \u003c- tibble(participant_id = 1:n_participants) |>\n    dplyr::mutate(assigned = purrr::map(participant_id,\n                          ~ sample(1:n_texts, size = k, replace = FALSE))) |>\n    tidyr::unnest(assigned) |>\n    dplyr::rename(text_id = assigned)\n\n  assignments |>\n    dplyr::left_join(participants, by = \"participant_id\") |>\n    dplyr::left_join(texts,        by = \"text_id\") |>\n    dplyr::slice(rep(1:dplyr::n(), each = questions_per_text)) |>\n    dplyr::mutate(\n      question_id = rep(1:questions_per_text, times = dplyr::n() / questions_per_text),\n      eta = b_intercept +\n        (b_hlva  + s_hlva)  * zHLVA +\n        (b_pcref + s_pcref) * zPCREFp +\n        b_interaction * zHLVA * zPCREFp +\n        u_participant + u_text,\n      prob     = plogis(eta),\n      response = rbinom(dplyr::n(), 1, prob)\n    ) |>\n    dplyr::mutate(zHLVA_fit = zHLVA_obs, zPCREFp_fit = zPCREFp_obs) |>\n    dplyr::select(participant_id, text_id, question_id,\n                  zHLVA = zHLVA_fit, zPCREFp = zPCREFp_fit, response)\n}\n```\n\nNote: `library(MASS)` is deliberately **not** attached (only `MASS::mvrnorm`\nis called via `::`), because `MASS::select()` masks `dplyr::select()` and\nbreaks the pipeline above if attached. The fitted model always sees\n`zHLVA`/`zPCREFp` as **observed** (possibly measurement-error-attenuated)\nvalues, while the response is generated from the **true** latent values --\nwith the default `reliability_hlva = reliability_pcref = 1` used throughout\nAims 1-2, observed and true are identical.\n\n## Shared fitting and outcome-classification helpers\n\nReused from `sampling-variability-corridor-of-stability.qmd`'s\n`fit_reduced_model()` / `extract_terms_of_interest()` /\n`fit_reduced_model_guarded()` pattern, extended with a third RE\nspecification (`\"full_slopes\"`, used only by Aim 5) alongside the\n`\"correct\"`/`\"misspecified\"` pair used here and by Aim 3.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fit-model-p2\n\nextract_terms_of_interest_p2 \u003c- function(fit) {\n  terms \u003c- c(\"zHLVA\", \"zPCREFp\", \"zHLVA:zPCREFp\")\n  co \u003c- tryCatch(summary(fit)$coefficients, error = function(e) NULL)\n  if (is.null(co)) return(NULL)\n  avail \u003c- intersect(terms, rownames(co))\n  tibble(term = avail, estimate = co[avail, \"Estimate\"], std.error = co[avail, \"Std. Error\"])\n}\n\nfit_model_p2 \u003c- function(data, re_spec = c(\"correct\", \"misspecified\", \"full_slopes\")) {\n  re_spec \u003c- match.arg(re_spec)\n  form \u003c- switch(re_spec,\n    correct      = response ~ zHLVA * zPCREFp + (1 | participant_id) + (1 | text_id),\n    misspecified = response ~ zHLVA * zPCREFp + (1 | participant_id),\n    full_slopes  = response ~ zHLVA * zPCREFp + (1 + zPCREFp | participant_id) + (1 + zHLVA | text_id)\n  )\n  warn_msgs \u003c- character(0)\n  fit \u003c- tryCatch(\n    withCallingHandlers(\n      glmer(form, data = data, family = binomial, control = glmerControl(optimizer = \"bobyqa\")),\n      warning = function(w) { warn_msgs \u003c\u003c- c(warn_msgs, conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart(\"muffleWarning\") }\n    ),\n    error = function(e) e\n  )\n  if (inherits(fit, \"error\")) return(list(status = \"error\", coefs = NULL))\n  status \u003c- if (length(warn_msgs) > 0 &&\n                any(grepl(\"failed to converge|Model failed|large eigenvalue|unable to evaluate\",\n                          warn_msgs, ignore.case = TRUE))) {\n    \"optimizer_warning\"\n  } else if (isSingular(fit)) {\n    \"converged_singular\"\n  } else {\n    \"converged_clean\"\n  }\n  list(status = status, coefs = extract_terms_of_interest_p2(fit))\n}\n\nfit_model_p2_guarded \u003c- function(data, re_spec, timeout_secs = 15) {\n  setTimeLimit(elapsed = timeout_secs, transient = TRUE)\n  res \u003c- tryCatch(\n    fit_model_p2(data, re_spec),\n    error = function(e) list(status = \"error\", coefs = NULL)\n  )\n  setTimeLimit(elapsed = Inf, transient = FALSE)\n  res\n}\n```\n\n## Sample-size grid and Aim 1 sweep grids\n\n```{r}\n#| label: sample-size-grid\n\nn_p_grid \u003c- c(25, 100, 375, 725, 1300, 1497)\nn_t_grid \u003c- c(2, 10, 35, 85, 136)\njoint_grid \u003c- tidyr::expand_grid(n_p = n_p_grid, n_t = n_t_grid)\nnrow(joint_grid)\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: aim1-sweep-grids\n\nb_hlva_grid        \u003c- c(0, 0.18, 0.363, 0.7, 1.0)\nb_pcref_grid       \u003c- c(0, 0.05, 0.095, 0.2, 0.35)\nb_interaction_grid \u003c- c(0, 0.025, 0.054, 0.10, 0.20)\n```\n\n## Discovery/replication data-generating pair (Aim 2)\n\nFor `split_margin = \"participants_only\"`, both halves share the same\n`n_t_total` texts (avoiding degenerate 1-text halves at the smallest grid\npoint, `n_t = 2`); only the participant pool is split. For `split_margin =\n\"both\"`, both margins split independently.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: generate-data-p2-pair\n\ngenerate_data_p2_pair \u003c- function(\n    n_p_total, n_t_total, k = min(10, n_t_total), questions_per_text = 4,\n    b_intercept = 2.093, b_hlva = 0.363, b_pcref = 0.095, b_interaction = 0.054,\n    sd_participant = 0.69, sd_text = 0.41,\n    sd_pcref_slope = 0, sd_hlva_slope = 0, cor_part = 0, cor_text = 0,\n    split_margin = c(\"participants_only\", \"both\"),\n    seed\n) {\n  split_margin \u003c- match.arg(split_margin)\n  set.seed(seed)\n\n  n_p_half \u003c- max(1, floor(n_p_total / 2))\n  n_t_half \u003c- if (split_margin == \"both\") max(1, floor(n_t_total / 2)) else n_t_total\n\n  make_texts \u003c- function(n_t) {\n    Sigma_text \u003c- matrix(c(sd_text^2, cor_text * sd_text * sd_hlva_slope,\n                            cor_text * sd_text * sd_hlva_slope, sd_hlva_slope^2), nrow = 2)\n    re_text \u003c- if (sd_hlva_slope > 0) MASS::mvrnorm(n_t, c(0, 0), Sigma_text) else cbind(rnorm(n_t, 0, sd_text), 0)\n    tibble(text_id = 1:n_t, zPCREFp = rnorm(n_t, 0, 1), u_text = re_text[, 1], s_hlva = re_text[, 2])\n  }\n  make_participants \u003c- function(n_p) {\n    Sigma_part \u003c- matrix(c(sd_participant^2, cor_part * sd_participant * sd_pcref_slope,\n                            cor_part * sd_participant * sd_pcref_slope, sd_pcref_slope^2), nrow = 2)\n    re_part \u003c- if (sd_pcref_slope > 0) MASS::mvrnorm(n_p, c(0, 0), Sigma_part) else cbind(rnorm(n_p, 0, sd_participant), 0)\n    tibble(participant_id = 1:n_p, zHLVA = rnorm(n_p, 0, 1), u_participant = re_part[, 1], s_pcref = re_part[, 2])\n  }\n  build_dataset \u003c- function(participants, texts) {\n    kk \u003c- min(k, nrow(texts))\n    assignments \u003c- tibble(participant_id = participants$participant_id) |>\n      dplyr::mutate(assigned = purrr::map(participant_id, ~ sample(texts$text_id, size = kk, replace = FALSE))) |>\n      tidyr::unnest(assigned) |> dplyr::rename(text_id = assigned)\n    assignments |>\n      dplyr::left_join(participants, by = \"participant_id\") |>\n      dplyr::left_join(texts, by = \"text_id\") |>\n      dplyr::slice(rep(1:dplyr::n(), each = questions_per_text)) |>\n      dplyr::mutate(\n        question_id = rep(1:questions_per_text, times = dplyr::n() / questions_per_text),\n        eta = b_intercept + (b_hlva + s_hlva) * zHLVA + (b_pcref + s_pcref) * zPCREFp +\n          b_interaction * zHLVA * zPCREFp + u_participant + u_text,\n        prob = plogis(eta), response = rbinom(dplyr::n(), 1, prob)\n      ) |>\n      dplyr::select(participant_id, text_id, question_id, zHLVA, zPCREFp, response)\n  }\n\n  texts_shared      \u003c- make_texts(n_t_half)\n  participants_disc \u003c- make_participants(n_p_half)\n  participants_repl \u003c- make_participants(n_p_half)\n  texts_repl        \u003c- if (split_margin == \"both\") make_texts(n_t_half) else texts_shared\n\n  list(\n    discovery   = build_dataset(participants_disc, texts_shared),\n    replication = build_dataset(participants_repl, texts_repl)\n  )\n}\n```\n\n## Diagnostics and combined per-cell runner\n\nCoverage/CI-width/Type S/Type M diagnostics use **Wald confidence intervals**\n(`estimate +/- 1.96 * std.error`) rather than profile-likelihood CIs, for\nspeed -- consistent with the project's `glmer`-as-fast-workhorse convention.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: aim1-aim2-diagnostics-and-runner\n\ndiagnose_coefs_p2 \u003c- function(coefs, true_vals) {\n  coefs |>\n    dplyr::mutate(\n      true_value      = true_vals[term],\n      ci_lower        = estimate - 1.96 * std.error,\n      ci_upper        = estimate + 1.96 * std.error,\n      ci_width        = ci_upper - ci_lower,\n      excludes_zero   = ci_lower > 0 | ci_upper \u003c 0,\n      correct_sign    = sign(estimate) == sign(true_value),\n      sign_error      = excludes_zero & !correct_sign,\n      inflation_ratio = ifelse(true_value != 0, abs(estimate) / abs(true_value), NA_real_),\n      bias            = estimate - true_value,\n      covers_truth    = ci_lower \u003c= true_value & true_value \u003c= ci_upper\n    )\n}"},"elapsedMs":13}</script></tool-result></div>
