0.177 | 0.603 |\n| 35 | 0.997 | 0.860 | 0.930 | 0.917 | 0.300 | 0.577 |\n| 85 | 0.993 | 0.930 | 0.897 | 0.920 | 0.420 | 0.570 |\n| 136 | 0.993 | 0.937 | 0.913 | 0.910 | 0.510 | 0.620 |\n\n**This resolves the question the design set out to answer, and the answer is\nnot what the \"reverse cohesion effect\" framing might suggest.** At `n_t =\n2`, `zPCREFp`'s sign reliability (0.553) is *worse* than the interaction's\n(0.717) -- barely better than a coin flip -- while `zHLVA` (the\nparticipant-level effect) is comparatively well-behaved (0.940). This is a\n**text-margin property, not an interaction-specific property**: the\ntext-level main effect is at least as unstable as the interaction at the\nsmallest realistic text sample size, and by this particular diagnostic, more\nso.\n\n`zPCREFp`'s power also shows the \"underpowered paradox\" signature directly:\npower is *higher* at `n_t = 2` (0.627) than at `n_t = 10` (0.177) -- not\nbecause small samples are better powered, but because the noisiest, most\ndegenerate cell produces wildly inflated estimates that cross the\nsignificance threshold more often *while being wrong about the sign* half\nthe time. A researcher who only sees \"significant, p \u003c .05\" from a 2-text\nstudy cannot distinguish this from a well-powered result.\n\n### Aim 1 -- fuller metrics table\n\nThe table above reports sign reliability and power only. For completeness\nagainst Marek et al.'s (2022) full diagnostic set, this expands to Type S\nerror rate, Type M ratio, median bias, coverage, and RMSE, all at each\nterm's own empirically-observed effect size, pooled across the six\nparticipant sample sizes.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: aim1-full-metrics-table\n\naim1_metrics_by_nt \u003c- aim1_all |>\n  dplyr::group_by(term, n_t) |>\n  dplyr::summarise(\n    power            = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE),\n    sign_reliability = mean(correct_sign, na.rm = TRUE),\n    type_s_rate      = mean(sign_error[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),\n    type_m_ratio     = median(inflation_ratio[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),\n    median_bias      = median(bias, na.rm = TRUE),\n    coverage         = mean(covers_truth, na.rm = TRUE),\n    rmse_raw         = sqrt(mean(bias^2, na.rm = TRUE)),\n    rmse_trimmed     = sqrt(mean(pmin(bias^2, quantile(bias^2, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)), na.rm = TRUE)),\n    n_fits           = dplyr::n(),\n    .groups = \"drop\"\n  )\n\naim1_metrics_by_nt |>\n  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric) & !c(n_t, n_fits), ~round(., 3))) |>\n  dplyr::arrange(term, n_t)\n```\n\n`rmse_raw` is included for completeness but is itself dominated by rare\npathological fits at small `n_t` (e.g. an outlying -20.3 estimate at\n`n_t = 2`); `rmse_trimmed` (winsorizing squared bias at its 95th percentile\nbefore averaging) is the more trustworthy summary of typical-case error\nmagnitude and should be preferred when comparing across cells.\n\n### Aim 1 -- visualizations\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-aim1-metrics-vs-nt\n#| fig-cap: \"Aim 1: power, sign reliability, Type S error rate, and Type M exaggeration ratio vs. text sample size (n_t), at each term's own empirically-observed effect size, pooled across all six participant sample sizes and 50 replicates/cell.\"\n\nplot_metrics_vs_x(\n  aim1_metrics_by_nt, x_var = \"n_t\",\n  metrics = c(\"power\", \"sign_reliability\", \"type_s_rate\", \"type_m_ratio\"),\n  metric_labels = aim1_metric_labels,\n  x_lab = \"Text sample size (n_t, log scale)\"\n)\n```\n\nThis is the visual counterpart of the table above and of Aim 1's prose\nfinding: `zPCREFp` has the *worst* sign reliability and the *highest* Type\nS/Type M values at `n_t = 2`, worse even than the interaction -- while also\nhaving power *higher* at `n_t = 2` than at `n_t = 10`, the \"underpowered\nparadox\" signature (a significant result here is more likely to be wrong,\nnot more trustworthy).\n\n### What the \"underpowered paradox\" looks like at the level of individual estimates\n\nThe summary diagnostics above (power, sign reliability, Type S/M rates) are\nall *aggregates* over 50 replicate fits per cell. It can be easier to see\nwhy the paradox happens by looking at the individual replicate estimates\nthemselves, rather than only their summary statistics. The two panels below\nshow every individual estimate from Aim 1's fits at `n_p = 1497` -- the\n**largest** participant sample size in the grid, held constant across every\nrow and column so that the funnel shown reflects the text margin (`n_t`)\nspecifically, not participant-margin noise -- for `zPCREFp` (top) and the\n`zHLVA:zPCREFp` interaction (bottom): one dot per replicate fit, one column\nper simulated true effect size, one row per text sample size.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-aim1-distribution-explainer\n#| fig-width: 12\n#| fig-height: 8.5\n#| fig-cap: \"Aim 1: individual estimates (one dot per replicate fit, n_p held constant at its largest grid value, 1497) for zPCREFp (top) and the zHLVA:zPCREFp interaction (bottom), by text sample size (rows, narrower at top) and true effect size (columns, labeled \\\"true = ...\\\"). Dashed vertical line = the true value being simulated in that column. Red = a 95% CI that excludes zero (\\\"significant\\\"); grey = not significant. A handful of pathological estimates beyond the plotted range (all at n_t = 2) are clipped to the axis edge for readability.\"\n\nillustrative_n_p \u003c- max(n_p_grid)\n\nmake_aim1_distribution_panel \u003c- function(data, term_name, x_clip, illustrative_n_p,\n                                          show_x_axis = TRUE) {\n  df \u003c- data |>\n    dplyr::filter(term == term_name, n_p == illustrative_n_p) |>\n    dplyr::mutate(\n      n_t_f = factor(n_t, levels = n_t_grid),\n      significant = ifelse(excludes_zero, \"Significant (95% CI excludes 0)\", \"Not significant\"),\n      estimate_clipped = pmax(pmin(estimate, x_clip), -x_clip)\n    )\n\n  ggplot(df, aes(x = estimate_clipped, y = n_t_f, color = significant, fill = significant)) +\n    ggdist::stat_dots(\n      side = \"both\", scale = 0.85, alpha = 0.55,\n      binwidth = ggplot2::unit(c(1.3, 2.2), \"mm\"),\n      overflow = \"compress\"\n    ) +\n    geom_vline(aes(xintercept = effect_value), linetype = \"dashed\", color = \"black\", linewidth = 0.5) +\n    facet_wrap(~effect_value, nrow = 1,\n               labeller = as_labeller(function(x) paste0(\"true = \", x))) +\n    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-x_clip, 0, x_clip)) +\n    scale_color_manual(values = c(\"Significant (95% CI excludes 0)\" = \"#b2182b\",\n                                   \"Not significant\" = \"grey45\")) +\n    scale_fill_manual(values = c(\"Significant (95% CI excludes 0)\" = \"#b2182b\",\n                                  \"Not significant\" = \"grey45\")) +\n    labs(\n      x = if (show_x_axis) paste0(term_name, \" estimate (clipped to [-\", x_clip, \", \", x_clip, \"])\") else NULL,\n      y = \"n_t\", color = NULL, fill = NULL\n    ) +\n    theme_bw(base_size = 10) +\n    theme(\n      panel.border = element_rect(color = \"grey35\", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.7),\n      panel.spacing = unit(1.1, \"lines\"),\n      strip.background = element_rect(fill = \"grey85\", color = \"grey35\"),\n      strip.text = element_text(face = \"bold\", size = 8.5),\n      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),\n      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),\n      legend.position = \"bottom\"\n    )\n}\n\npanel_dist_pcref \u003c- make_aim1_distribution_panel(\n  aim1_pcref, \"zPCREFp\", x_clip = 2, illustrative_n_p = illustrative_n_p, show_x_axis = FALSE\n) + labs(title = \"zPCREFp (text-level main effect)\")\n\npanel_dist_interaction \u003c- make_aim1_distribution_panel(\n  aim1_interaction, \"zHLVA:zPCREFp\", x_clip = 1.5, illustrative_n_p = illustrative_n_p, show_x_axis = TRUE\n) + labs(title = \"zHLVA:zPCREFp (interaction)\")\n\n(panel_dist_pcref / panel_dist_interaction) +\n  patchwork::plot_layout(guides = \"collect\") &\n  theme(legend.position = \"bottom\")\n```\n\nThree things are visible here that the summary tables/plots only imply.\nFirst, the funnel shape itself, present in **both** rows: each cloud of\ndots is wide at the bottom (`n_t = 2`) and collapses to a tight cluster\naround the dashed true-value line by the top (`n_t = 136`) -- the textbook\n\"wide at small *N*, narrow at large *N*\" funnel, for every true effect size\nsimulated. Second, and this is the paradox in its most direct form: in\n`zPCREFp`'s leftmost column (`true = 0`, i.e. **no true effect at all**), a\nsubstantial share of the `n_t = 2` dots are still colored red --\nindividually indistinguishable, in a real analysis, from a genuine\ndiscovery. Those red dots at `n_t = 2` are false positives purely from\nnoise, and they are just as red (just as \"significant\", p \u003c .05) as the\ntrue positives further right. A significance threshold cannot tell these\napart; only a larger text sample -- more rows lower down turning into\nfewer, tighter, more-often-correctly-colored rows higher up -- can.\n\nThird, comparing the two rows directly answers whether the interaction's\nfunnel looks like `zPCREFp`'s: **not really**. At `n_t = 2`, the\ninteraction's dots are mostly grey, not red, across every column including\nits own empirically-observed effect size (`true = 0.054`) -- consistent\nwith its much lower power at that cell (0.127, vs. `zPCREFp`'s 0.627 from\nthe table above). Where `zPCREFp`'s problem at `n_t = 2` is \"too many\nconfidently-wrong answers,\" the interaction's is closer to \"usually no\nanswer at all, and on the rare occasions there is one, it is not obviously\nmore trustworthy than `zPCREFp`'s\" -- the same underlying text-margin\nscarcity, but manifesting as a power problem more than a false-discovery\nproblem for this particular term.\n\n### Why can an estimate be \"significant\" when the true effect is exactly zero?\n\nThis is the question the `true = 0` column above raises most sharply, and\nit is worth answering mechanistically rather than leaving it as a\nstatistical curiosity. Two different things are going on, and it is\nimportant to distinguish them.\n\n**It is not simply the ordinary 5% false-positive rate.** A correctly\ncalibrated 95% CI is *expected* to exclude a true value of zero 5% of the\ntime, by construction -- that is what \"95%\" means. But the observed rate at\n`n_t = 2` is far above that: the table below shows that 66.3% of the\n`zPCREFp` fits at `n_t = 2` under a true null are \"significant,\" roughly\n13x the nominal rate. Something is actively miscalibrated here, not merely\nunlucky.\n\n**The mechanism is a random-effects identifiability breakdown, not sampling\nbad luck on the covariate itself.** With only `n_t = 2` texts, there is\nexactly one degree of freedom available to describe how the two sampled\ntexts differ from each other -- two points determine a line perfectly, with\nnothing left over to check whether that line is trustworthy. The \"correct\"\nmodel asks `glmer` to split any such between-text difference into two\npieces: a text-level random intercept (`(1 | text_id)`, capturing\nidiosyncratic, unexplained differences between texts) and the fixed\n`zPCREFp` slope (capturing the cohesion effect specifically). Estimating a\nrandom-intercept *variance* from only 2 groups is close to impossible --\nthere is essentially no information to distinguish \"these two texts differ\na lot by chance\" from \"these two texts differ a lot systematically.\" In\npractice, `lme4` resolves this by pinning the text-level variance at (or\nextremely near) its zero boundary -- a **singular fit**:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-aim1-singular-fit-diagnostic\n\nnull_nt2_diagnostic \u003c- aim1_pcref |>\n  dplyr::filter(term == \"zPCREFp\", n_t == 2, effect_value == 0)\n\ncat(\"Fit status, all 300 replicates (n_t = 2, true zPCREFp effect = 0):\\n\")\ntable(null_nt2_diagnostic$status)\n\nnull_nt2_diagnostic |>\n  dplyr::group_by(excludes_zero) |>\n  dplyr::summarise(\n    n = dplyr::n(),\n    `median |estimate|` = round(median(abs(estimate), na.rm = TRUE), 3),\n    `median std. error` = round(median(std.error, na.rm = TRUE), 3),\n    .groups = \"drop\"\n  )\n```\n\nEvery single one of these 300 replicates converges to a singular fit --\nthe text-level random-intercept variance collapses to zero every time\n`n_t = 2`, regardless of how many participants are simulated. Once that\nvariance is pinned at zero, the model has nowhere else to put the two\nsampled texts' chance difference except into the only fixed-effect\npredictor that differs between them -- `zPCREFp`. This inflates the fixed-\neffect point estimate (median |estimate| = 0.734 among the \"significant\"\nfits, versus a true value of exactly 0) and simultaneously produces an\noverconfident, too-narrow Wald standard error (median SE = 0.106 among the\n\"significant\" fits, versus 0.294 among the fits that correctly stayed\nnon-significant) -- because the SE formula implicitly assumes the\nrandom-effects variance structure has been reliably estimated, an\nassumption that fails precisely at this boundary. Inflated estimate +\ndeflated SE together push a large share of purely-noise-driven fits across\nthe 95%-CI-excludes-zero line.\n\nIn short: at `n_t = 2`, the model is not really testing \"does cohesion\npredict comprehension\" -- it is testing \"do these two specific,\nrandomly-sampled texts differ,\" and then attributing 100% of whatever\ndifference it finds to cohesion, because there is no other place left for\nthat difference to go. This is a more extreme version of the same\nfamily of problem documented elsewhere in this project as random-effects\nmisspecification (Aim 3's omitted-`text.id` bias, and Phase 1's finding\nthat pseudoreplication introduces genuine bias, not just imprecision) --\n[Next offset: 897; 418 more lines, ~20.8KB]"},"elapsedMs":0}</script></tool-result></div>

Figure 3 (the power surface below) and Figure 4 (the\npower curves) both plot the same quantity, P(95% CI excludes zero), but\nFigure 4 sweeps the true effect size down to and through zero. At that\npoint, P(significant) is no longer \"power\" in the strict sense: it is the\n**false-positive rate**, since there is nothing there to detect. Rather\nthan color that `effect size = 0` line as if it were simply the lightest\npoint on the same power-curve palette -- which would imply it answers the\nsame question as its non-zero neighbors -- Figure 4 draws it in a distinct,\ncolorblind-friendly bright orange, held constant across all three rows. It\nanswers a different question (\"how often does noise alone\ncross the significance threshold?\") from the colored curves next to it\n(\"how often is a real effect of this size detected?\"), and this is exactly\nthe distinction the \"underpowered paradox\" discussion above turns on.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-aim1-power-surface\n#| fig-width: 8\n#| fig-height: 4\n#| fig-cap: \"Aim 1: power surface across the full joint (n_p, n_t) grid, at each term's own empirically-observed effect size. This is the direct 2-D analog of a Marek et al. (2022)-style Figure 3 sample-size surface: both axes are the two sample-size margins, and tile fill is the probability a 95% Wald CI excludes zero.\"\n\naim1_surface \u003c- aim1_all |>\n  dplyr::group_by(term, n_p, n_t) |>\n  dplyr::summarise(power = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = \"drop\")\n\nplot_power_heatmap(aim1_surface, fill_var = \"power\", fill_label = \"Power\")\n```\n\nThe surface makes visible what the by-`n_t` table (pooled over `n_p`)\ncannot: `zHLVA`'s power saturates near 100% once `n_p` reaches ~100,\n*independent* of `n_t` -- it is a purely participant-margin-limited effect.\n`zPCREFp` and the interaction, by contrast, need growth on **both** margins\nsimultaneously to reach comparable power; increasing `n_p` alone at `n_t =\n2` caps out around 78-92% and 14-24% respectively, well short of what larger\n`n_t` unlocks at the same `n_p`.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-aim1-power-curves\n#| fig-width: 10\n#| fig-height: 9.5\n#| fig-cap: \"Aim 1: classic power curves -- P(significant) vs. participant sample size (n_p, log scale), one row per term, faceted by text sample size (n_t) across columns. Each row uses its own sequential color palette (darker = larger effect size); the thicker line/larger points mark each term's empirically-observed effect size.\"\n\naim1_power_by_effect \u003c- aim1_sweep_combined |>\n  dplyr::group_by(term, effect_value, n_p, n_t) |>\n  dplyr::summarise(power = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = \"drop\")\n\n# Each term sweeps a different set of effect-size values (see the sweep\n# grids above), so a single shared color scale across all three rows would\n# either compress each term's own 5-point range into indistinguishable\n# shades or mix three unrelated numeric scales under one legend. at `n_t = 2`, the bright orange\nfalse-positive-rate curve (true effect = 0) stays **non-monotonic and never\nnear zero across the entire `n_p` range** (~20-60%) -- i.e., a sizeable\nshare of fits at This is the clearest single illustration in this\ndocument of the underpowered paradox's mechanism: at the modal literature\ntext sample size, growing the participant sample does not rescue the\nfalse-positive problem -- it is a text-margin problem, not a\nparticipant-margin one. The highlighted \"(observed)\" curve in each row --\nthe effect size actually estimated from this project's real data -- sits in\nthe middle of its own sweep by construction, letting readers see directly\nhow much power/error-rate behavior would differ if the true effect were\nsmaller or larger than what was actually observed.\n\n## Aim 2: discovery/replication rates\n\n| `n_t` | zHLVA replication | zPCREFp replication | interaction replication |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 2 | 0.478 | 0.473 | **0.013** |\n| 10 | 0.803 | 0.157 | 0.250 |\n| 35 | 0.797 | 0.163 | 0.267 |\n| 85 | 0.820 | 0.237 | 0.273 |\n| 136 | 0.797 | 0.340 | 0.297 |\n\nA different, complementary picture emerges here: under the stricter\n\"significant in both independent halves, same sign\" criterion, the\n**interaction is the most fragile of the three** at `n_t = 2` (1.3%\nreplication vs. ~47-48% for both main effects) -- because it is so rarely\neven significant in the first place with half the already-small sample. answer?\") -- and\nboth indicate `n_t = 2` is inadequate, just via different mechanisms.\n\n### Aim 2 -- fuller metrics table and visualizations\n\nIn addition to the raw replication rate above, this adds discovery rate\n(P[significant in the first, discovery half]) and conditional replication\n(P[replicates | discovery-significant] -- \"given I got a significant result\nin one half, would it hold up in an independent second half?\"), the more\ndirectly decision-relevant quantity for a researcher who has already seen a\nsignificant discovery-sample result.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: aim2-full-metrics-table\n\naim2_metrics_by_nt \u003c- aim2_all |>\n  dplyr::group_by(term, n_t) |>\n  dplyr::summarise(\n    discovery_rate           = mean(discovery_significant, na.rm = TRUE),\n    replication_rate         = mean(replicated, na.rm = TRUE),\n    conditional_replication  = mean(replicated[discovery_significant], na.rm = TRUE),\n    n_fits                   = dplyr::n(),\n fig-aim2-metrics-vs-nt\n#| fig-width: 9\n#| fig-cap: \"Aim 2: discovery rate, (unconditional) replication rate, and conditional replication rate vs. text sample size, at each term's own empirically-observed effect size.\"\n\nplot_metrics_vs_x(\n  aim2_metrics_by_nt, x_var = \"n_t\",\n  metrics = c(\"discovery_rate\", \"replication_rate\", \"conditional_replication\"),\n conditional on having found a significant\ninteraction in the discovery half, the interaction's replication rate (~22%\nat `n_t = 2`, rising to ~70-92% at larger `n_t`) is *lower* than `zHLVA`'s at\nevery `n_t` but is **not as catastrophically low** as its unconditional\nreplication rate (1.3% at `n_t = 2`) might suggest in isolation -- most of\nthat unconditional fragility comes from rarely being significant in the\ndiscovery half at all (a power problem), rather than from significant\ndiscoveries failing to hold up (a pure replication problem). Both framings\nmatter for different audiences: a reviewer asking \"is this literature's\nreplication rate adequate\" should look at the unconditional rate; a\nresearcher who has already observed one significant result and is deciding\nwhether to trust it should look at the conditional rate.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-aim2-replication-surface\n#| fig-width: 8\n#| fig-height: 4\n#| fig-cap: \"Aim 2: unconditional replication-rate surface across the full joint (n_p, n_t) grid, at each term's own empirically-observed effect size -- the discovery/replication analog of the Aim 1 power surface above.\"\n\naim2_surface \u003c- aim2_all |>\n  dplyr::group_by(term, n_p, n_t) |>\n  dplyr::summarise(replication_rate = mean(replicated, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = \"drop\")\n\nplot_power_heatmap(aim2_surface, fill_var = \"replication_rate\", fill_label = \"Replication\\nrate\")\n```\n\nSame qualitative pattern as Aim 1's power surface, but stricter: `zHLVA`\nagain saturates on the participant margin alone (100% replication once\n`n_p >= 375`, at any `n_t`), while `zPCREFp` and the interaction remain\nbelow 70% replication everywhere on this grid except the single\nlargest-both-margins cell -- reinforcing that halving the sample (as Aim 2's\ndiscovery/replication design necessarily does) makes the two\ntext-margin-dependent effects substantially harder to recover than Aim 1's\nfull-sample power numbers alone would suggest.\n\n## Aim 1 & Aim 2: discussion\n\nComparing the two aims' diagnostics side by side clarifies what each is, and\nisn't, telling us:\n\n- **Aim 1** (conditional on significance) says `zPCREFp` is the *least*\n  trustworthy term at `n_t = 2` -- its significant results are the most\n  likely to have the wrong sign.\n- **Aim 2** (unconditional, halved samples) says the **interaction** is the\n  most fragile overall -- not because its significant results are\n  especially untrustworthy, but because it is rarely significant at all\n  once the sample is halved.\n- Both agree that `n_t = 2` -- the modal text sample size in this project's\n  literature review (Phase 1's overlay finding: ~95% of reviewed studies\n  fall outside the trustworthy region) -- is inadequate for any of the\n  three effects, via different mechanisms depending on which question is\n  asked.\n- `zHLVA`, the sole participant-level effect among the three, is\n  comparatively well-behaved on both diagnostics and saturates on the\n  participant margin alone, independent of text sample size -- consistent\n  with Phase 1's finding that participant-margin effects are far less\n  sensitive to this project's chronic text-sample scarcity than text-margin\n  effects are.\n\nA full cross-aim synthesis, tying these findings together with Aims 3-6\n(random-effects misspecification, variance-component sensitivity, slope/\ncovariance recovery, and design remedies), will appear once those aims have\ntheir own reporting-ready documents.\n\n## Flagged future work\n\n- **The significance-threshold/multiple-comparisons sweep** (Marek et al.'s\n  P\u003c0.05-to-Bonferroni comparison) was explicitly deferred at the design\n  stage, given the real core model's 26-term fixed-effects formula. Nothing in this section\nis required to understand the results above; it documents how they were\nproduced.\n\n### Relationship to existing project simulation infrastructure\n\nThis work explicitly reused conventions already established in\n`simulation_study_complete.qmd` (Simulations 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6) and\n`power-simulation-vocabulary-cohesion.qmd`, rather than inventing new ones:\n\n- **One-at-a-time sweeps, not a full factorial.** Existing simulations vary\n  one dimension (effect size, a single variance component, or a single\n  intercept-slope correlation) at a time while holding others fixed at a\n  realistic value, to avoid combinatorial explosion. Phase 2 follows the\n  same pattern (six aims, altogether) rather than crossing effect size x\n  variance x covariance x misspecification x design strategy x\n  two-dimensional sample size all at once.\n- **Fitting**: `glmer` (fast) as the sweep workhorse, with `brms`\n  spot-checks at a handful of cells using the project's precompile-once,\n  `update()`-per-replicate pattern to avoid Stan recompilation cost across\n  replicates (not run for Aims 1-2 specifically; see flagged future work).\n- **Parallelization**: `furrr::future_pmap_dfr()` with `multisession`,\n  `furrr_options(seed = TRUE)`, hierarchical seeds, 4 workers with a\n  `setTimeLimit()` guard, following Phase 1's memory-safety lessons.\n- **Outcome-quality classification**: converged-clean / converged-singular\n  / optimizer-warning / error, reused verbatim from Phase 1's helper\n  functions.\n\n### Confirmed decisions (made before building Aims 1-2)\n\n1. **Scope**: all six aims cover **three effects** -- `zHLVA` (main),\n   `zPCREFp` (main), and `zHLVA:zPCREFp` (interaction) -- rather than the\n   interaction alone.\n2. **Aim 2 split axis**: left configurable (`split_margin =\n   \"participants_only\"` vs. `\"both\"`) rather than fixed; both variants can\n   be run and compared. The results above use `\"participants_only\"`.\n3. **Significance-threshold sweep**: deferred (see \"Flagged future work\").\n4. **Pacing**: build and review Aim 1 (together with Aim 2) first, as the\n   more traditional power-analysis-style starting point extended with the\n   replication-split question.\n5. **Replicate count**: 50 resamples/cell, matching Phase 1 Step 3's\n   memory-safe, coarsened configuration.\n\n### Timing benchmark\n\nA small number of representative cells (small/moderate/large) were timed\nonce each for the `\"correct\"` and `\"misspecified\"` RE specifications (the\ntwo used by Aims 1-3), before committing to the full grid:\n\n| Cell | n_p | n_t | `correct` | `misspecified` |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| small | 25 | 2 | 0.34s (singular) | 0.03s (clean) |\n| moderate | 375 | 35 | 0.71s (clean) | 0.30s (clean) |\n| large | 1497 | 136 | 3.53s (clean) | 1.43s (clean) |\n\nMean per-fit time across these three cells (a rough, order-of-magnitude\nestimate, not a proper average over the full grid's cell-size\ndistribution): `correct` ~1.53s, `misspecified` ~0.59s. (The original\nbenchmark also timed a `\"full_slopes\"` arm for Aim 5's covariance sweep,\nusing reference slope-variance/correlation values extracted from the fitted\ncore model; that arm is out of scope for this Aims-1/2-only document and is\nreported instead in the Aim 5 document.)\n\nExtrapolated cost: Aim 1 (22,500 fits, `correct` spec) ~9.6h serial / ~2.4h\non 4 workers; Aim 2 (~22,500 fits, `correct` spec) ~9.6h serial / ~2.4h\nparallel. Marek et al. documented a\nstatistical-error taxonomy -- false negatives, false positives,\n**magnitude/inflation error (Type M)**, and **sign error (Type S)** -- each\nas a function of sample size, and showed that smaller samples' significant\neffects are disproportionately the most inflated and sign-flipped ones (the\n\"underpowered paradox\": stricter significance thresholds select for, rather\nthan screen out, the most inflated estimates). That richer structure is the\nsubject of Aim 5, covered in a separate future document.\n:::\n\n## Design: Aim 1 (effect size x sample size) and Aim 2 (discovery/replication split)\n\nBoth aims share one data-generating run: RE specification fixed at\n\"correct\" (random intercepts only, for `ResponseId`/`participant_id` and\n`text.id`/`text_id`); variance components fixed at their empirical values;\nthe full joint sample-size grid (30 `(n_p, n_t)` cells); 50 replicates/cell.\nA grid cell's `(n_p, n_t)` is the **total** sample -- Aim 2 splits each cell\ninto two roughly-equal-sized discovery/replication halves.\n\n**Aim 1** runs three **one-at-a-time** effect-size sweeps -- each holding\nthe other two effects fixed at their empirical values while varying the\nswept effect:\n\n| Sweep | Effect | Grid (centered on empirical estimate) |\n|---|---|---|\n| (i) | `zHLVA` (main effect, participant-level) | 0, 0.18, 0.363 (observed), 0.7, 1.0 |\n| (ii) | `zPCREFp` (main effect, text-level) | 0, 0.05, ~0.095 (observed), 0.2, 0.35 |\n| (iii) | `zHLVA:zPCREFp` (interaction) | 0, 0.025, 0.054 (observed), 0.10, 0.20 |\n\nDiagnostics extend the project's existing four (bias, sign reliability,\ncoverage, RMSE) with a Marek-style decomposition, directly computable here\nbecause the true value is known exactly: **Type S (sign) error rate** (among\nCI-excludes-0 draws, proportion with the wrong sign), **Type M\n(magnitude/inflation) ratio** (`|estimate|/|true value|` among\nCI-excludes-0 draws), and **power** on its own scale.\n\n**Question Aim 1 answers:** is the sign-instability pattern found in Phase 1\n(near-coin-flip sign consistency for the interaction at *n* = 2 texts) (a) a\nproperty of the *specific* small effect size observed, (b) specific to the\ninteraction term, or (c) a general property of being estimated from the\n*text* margin (in which case `zPCREFp`, also text-level, should show a\nsimilar pattern)? Two different things are going on, and it is\nimportant to distinguish them.\n\n**It is not simply the ordinary 5% false-positive rate.** A correctly\ncalibrated 95% CI is *expected* to exclude a true value of zero 5% of the\ntime, by construction -- that is what \"95%\" means. But the observed rate at\n`n_t = 2` is far above that: the table below shows that 66.3% of the\n`zPCREFp` fits at `n_t = 2` under a true null are \"significant,\" roughly\n13x the nominal rate. Something is actively miscalibrated here, not merely\nunlucky.\n\n**The mechanism is a random-effects identifiability breakdown, not sampling\nbad luck on the covariate itself.** With only `n_t = 2` texts, there is\nexactly one degree of freedom available to describe how the two sampled\ntexts differ from each other -- two points determine a line perfectly, with\nnothing left over to check whether that line is trustworthy. The \"correct\"\nmodel asks `glmer` to split any such between-text difference into two\npieces: a text-level random intercept (`(1 | text_id)`, capturing\nidiosyncratic, unexplained differences between texts) and the fixed\n`zPCREFp` slope (capturing the cohesion effect specifically). Estimating a\nrandom-intercept *variance* from only 2 groups is close to impossible --\nthere is essentially no information to distinguish \"these two texts differ\na lot by chance\" from \"these two texts differ a lot systematically.\" In\npractice, `lme4` resolves this by pinning the text-level variance at (or\nextremely near) its zero boundary -- a **singular fit**:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-aim1-singular-fit-diagnostic\n\nnull_nt2_diagnostic \u003c- aim1_pcref |>\n  dplyr::filter(term == \"zPCREFp\", n_t == 2, effect_value == 0)\n\ncat(\"Fit status, all 300 replicates (n_t = 2, true zPCREFp effect = 0):\\n\")\ntable(null_nt2_diagnostic$status)\n\nnull_nt2_diagnostic |>\n  dplyr::group_by(excludes_zero) |>\n  dplyr::summarise(\n    n = dplyr::n(),\n    `median |estimate|` = round(median(abs(estimate), na.rm = TRUE), 3),\n    `median std. error` = round(median(std.error, na.rm = TRUE), 3),\n    .groups = \"drop\"\n  )\n```\n\nEvery single one of these 300 replicates converges to a singular fit --\nthe text-level random-intercept variance collapses to zero every time\n`n_t = 2`, regardless of how many participants are simulated. Once that\nvariance is pinned at zero, the model has nowhere else to put the two\nsampled texts' chance difference except into the only fixed-effect\npredictor that differs between them -- `zPCREFp`. This inflates the fixed-\neffect point estimate (median |estimate| = 0.734 among the \"significant\"\nfits, versus a true value of exactly 0) and simultaneously produces an\noverconfident, too-narrow Wald standard error (median SE = 0.106 among the\n\"significant\" fits, versus 0.294 among the fits that correctly stayed\nnon-significant) -- because the SE formula implicitly assumes the\nrandom-effects variance structure has been reliably estimated, an\nassumption that fails precisely at this boundary. ## Summary of findings

**Files:** `/Users/robertdavies/Dropbox/teaching-critical-thinking/synthetic-data-analyses-power-error-replication-aims-1-2-draft.qmd` (1313 lines) and the companion `...-reportable.qmd` (997 lines).

### 1. Purpose and audience

Both documents report **Phase 2** of a larger research project (not generic teaching material): a parametric-simulation ("Aims 1–2") follow-up to an empirical resampling study (**"Phase 1,"** `sampling-variability-corridor-of-stability.qmd`). The goal is to port **Marek et al. (2022)**'s brain-wide-association-study reproducibility framework (false positives/negatives, Type S sign error, Type M magnitude/inflation error, discovery/replication splits) onto a psycholinguistic reading-comprehension dataset, testing whether a previously observed "reverse cohesion effect" sign-instability is a generic text-sample-size phenomenon rather than specific to one effect (draft lines 1–76, 92–139).

- **Draft** (`-draft.qmd`): the "reference/working copy" — contains all prose **and** the live, runnable DGP/model-fitting R code (`generate_data_p2()`, `fit_model_p2()`, etc.), plus an appendix "Development history" with full process narrative (decisions, timing benchmarks, smoke tests, launch records) and a closing "Follow-up note" saying the code is kept live for possible future modification (lines 155–274, 1175–1313).
- **Reportable** (`-reportable.qmd`): explicitly the "reportable version" (line 38) — identical prose, tables, and figures, but all DGP/fitting code chunks are **stripped out and replaced with `callout-tip` blocks** pointing back to the draft (lines 172–179, 189–194, 220–223, 231–235). Only code that loads pre-computed `.rds` results and makes plots is retained. Audience is a reader who wants to see results and reasoning without wading through simulation machinery — essentially a "clean report" distilled from the "working" draft.

Both are aimed at the same internal research audience (anyone reviewing this specific project's statistical findings), not students in general; however, their contrast (draft-with-code vs. reportable-without-code) is itself a template pattern that could be reused pedagogically.

### 2. Data-generating process (DGP)

Single shared generator `generate_data_p2()` (draft lines 170–274), generalizing two earlier project functions (`simulate_interaction_data()` from `power-simulation-vocabulary-cohesion.qmd` and `generate_data_s3()` from `simulation_study_complete.qmd`). It simulates a **crossed participant × text design** for a binary comprehension-accuracy outcome:

- Participants (`n_participants`) each have a latent trait `zHLVA` ~ N(0,1) (vocabulary-ish measure), a random intercept `u_participant` ~ N(0, sd_participant²), and optionally a correlated random slope for `zPCREFp` (zero by default).
- Texts (`n_texts`) each have `zPCREFp` ~ N(0,1) (text cohesion measure; alternative "widened" design samples bimodally at ±1.5 + noise), a random intercept `u_text` ~ N(0, sd_text²), and optionally a correlated random slope for `zHLVA`.
- Each participant is assigned `k` texts (`k = min(10, n_texts)`), each text-pair answered via `questions_per_text = 4` binary items.
- Linear predictor: `eta = b_intercept + (b_hlva + s_hlva)*zHLVA + (b_pcref + s_pcref)*zPCREFp + b_interaction*zHLVA*zPCREFp + u_participant + u_text`; `prob = plogis(eta)`; `response ~ Bernoulli(prob)` (logistic/binomial GLMM DGP).
- Empirically-grounded parameter values (from the real "Phase 1" fitted model): `b_intercept = 2.093`, `b_hlva = 0.363`, `b_pcref = 0.095`, `b_interaction = 0.054`, `sd_participant = 0.69` (sd(ResponseId) ≈0.61–0.62 empirically), `sd_text = 0.41` (sd(text.id) ≈0.70–0.72 empirically) — lines 78–87, 170–182.
- Optional **measurement-reliability attenuation** (`reliability_hlva`, `reliability_pcref`, defaults =1, i.e., no attenuation for Aims 1–2; used only in a later "Aim 6" not covered here) — observed predictor = √reliability·true + √(1-reliability)·noise (lines 206–240).
- A paired-sample variant `generate_data_p2_pair()` (lines 371–424) builds **discovery/replication halves** for Aim 2, with `split_margin` either `"participants_only"` (shared text pool, independent participants) or `"both"` (independent participants and texts).

**Sample-size grids** reused from Phase 1 Step 3 (lines 80–81, 347–348): participants n_p ∈ {25, 100, 375, 725, 1300, 1497}; texts n_t ∈ {2, 10, 35, 85, 136}; full joint grid = 30 cells.

**Effect-size sweep grids (Aim 1)**, one-at-a-time, holding other two effects at empirical values (lines 120–124, 356–358):
- zHLVA: 0, 0.18, 0.363 (observed), 0.7, 1.0
- zPCREFp: 0, 0.05, 0.095 (observed), 0.2, 0.35
- zHLVA:zPCREFp interaction: 0, 0.025, 0.054 (observed), 0.10, 0.20

50 replicates per cell (consistent with Phase 1's "memory-safe" configuration, line 1220).

### 3. R code structure/approach

- **Packages**: `tidyverse` (dplyr/tidyr/purrr/ggplot2), `lme4` (glmer fitting), `patchwork` (multi-panel figures), `RColorBrewer`, `ggdist` (dot plots), plus `MASS::mvrnorm` called via `::` only (deliberately not attached, to avoid masking `dplyr::select()`, draft lines 276–282), and `furrr` for parallelization in the actual production run (not shown in the live code, only described, lines 1201–1203, 1293–1301).
- **Style**: tidyverse pipe (`|>`) throughout, heavy use of fully qualified `dplyr::`/`tidyr::`/`purrr::` namespacing (avoiding `library()` attach collisions), functional/vectorized generation (`purrr::map`, `tidyr::unnest`) rather than loops.
- **Model fitting** (`fit_model_p2()`, lines 303–329): `glmer(response ~ zHLVA*zPCREFp + REs, family=binomial, control=glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"))`, three possible RE specs via `match.arg`: `"correct"` (random intercepts for both participant_id and text_id), `"misspecified"` (participant intercept only), `"full_slopes"` (used only in a later "Aim 5," not in this document). Convergence/singularity captured via `withCallingHandlers`/`tryCatch`, classified into `converged_clean` / `converged_singular` / `optimizer_warning` / `error`. A guarded wrapper `fit_model_p2_guarded()` adds a `setTimeLimit()` (default 15s) safety net (lines 331–339).
- **Diagnostics function** `diagnose_coefs_p2()` (lines 436–450): computes Wald 95% CIs (`estimate ± 1.96*SE`), `excludes_zero` (significance), `correct_sign`, `sign_error` (Type S), `inflation_ratio` (Type M, `|est|/|true|`), `bias`, `covers_truth` (CI coverage) — all against the exactly-known true simulated value.
- **Replication combiner** `combine_replication_p2()` (lines 452–465): joins discovery and replication-half diagnostics, flags `replicated` = both significant AND same sign.
- **Per-cell orchestration**: `run_aim1_aim2_cell(sweep, effect_value, n_p, n_t, rep, split_margin)` (lines 467–505) generates one full-sample dataset (Aim 1) and one discovery/replication pair (Aim 2) per grid cell with deterministic hierarchical seeds (`seed_base <- rep*1e7 + n_p*1e3 + n_t + sweep_idx*1e5 + round(effect_value*1000)`), fits models, and returns `list(aim1=..., aim2=...)`.
- **Scale of the full run**: 3 sweeps × 5 effect values × 30 (n_p,n_t) cells × 50 reps × 3 glmer fits/combo = **67,500 total `glmer` fits**, run once as a detached background job (`run_aim1_aim2_full.R`) using `furrr::plan(multisession, workers=4)`, ~99–101 min per sweep, ~5h total (draft lines 508–512, 1223–1301). Results saved as `.rds` files in `results_phase2/` (`aim1_hlva.rds`, `aim1_pcref.rds`, `aim1_interaction.rds`, `aim2_hlva.rds`, `aim2_pcref.rds`, `aim2_interaction.rds`) and simply loaded (`readRDS`) by both documents, not regenerated — both documents are "load-and-report," not "simulate-and-report" (lines 514–539).
- **Summarization**: `summarize_p2_metrics()` / inline `group_by`+`summarise` chains compute, per (term, n_t) or (term, n_p, n_t): `power` (mean excludes_zero), `sign_reliability` (mean correct_sign), `type_s_rate` (mean sign_error among significant), `type_m_ratio` (median inflation ratio among significant), `median_bias`, `coverage`, `rmse_raw`, `rmse_trimmed` (95th-percentile-winsorized), and for Aim 2: `discovery_rate`, `replication_rate`, `conditional_replication`.
- **Visualization helpers** (reused across Aims 1 & 2, draft/reportable lines ~600–632): `plot_metrics_vs_x()` (facetted line plots of multiple metrics vs. n_t, log-x, Dark2 palette) and `plot_power_heatmap()` (n_p × n_t tile heatmap with percent labels, viridis fill) — generic, designed to be reused for future Aims 3–6. Additional bespoke figures: a `ggdist::stat_dots()` "distribution explainer" panel (individual-estimate dot plots faceted by true effect size × n_t, draft lines 736–795) and custom per-term power-curve panels with sequential ColorBrewer palettes and a fixed Okabe-Ito orange for the "true effect = 0" (false-positive) curve (draft lines 941–1009).

### 4. Key concepts demonstrated, tied to specific chunks

- **Sampling distributions / sampling error vs. measurement error**: the DGP conflates two error sources — sampling variability from random participant/text draws and random-intercept noise (`u_participant`, `u_text`), plus optional measurement unreliability (`reliability_hlva`/`reliability_pcref`, lines 206–240) representing classical true-score/attenuation structure (true score + independent error), though reliability=1 throughout Aims 1–2 so this mechanism is dormant here (reserved for a later "Aim 6").
- **NHST / significance**: operationalized purely via Wald 95% CI excluding zero (`excludes_zero` in `diagnose_coefs_p2()`, lines 436–450) — no explicit p-values computed; CI-based testing framing throughout.
- **Power**: `power = mean(excludes_zero)` restricted to non-zero true effect sizes; demonstrated via the Aim 1 fuller-metrics table (lines 673–694), the power-surface heatmap (`fig-aim1-power-surface`, lines 920–931) and the classic power-curve figure (`fig-aim1-power-curves`, lines 941–1009) sweeping n_p/n_t/effect size.
- **Type I error (false positives)**: shown at the `effect_value = 0` column/curve — explicitly distinguished from "power" conceptually in prose (lines 901–919) and visually (orange curve held constant across panels). A dedicated diagnostic chunk (`fig-aim1-singular-fit-diagnostic`, lines 854–871) shows 300/300 replicates at n_t=2 under the true null converging to **singular fits**, with 66.3% "significant" (~13× nominal rate) — a mechanistic explanation of inflated Type I error via **random-effects identifiability breakdown** (only 2 texts → intercept variance collapses to the zero boundary → all residual text-level variation forced into the fixed slope) — lines 824–899.
- **Type II error / underpowered paradox**: Marek-style narrative that small samples' significant results are the *most* inflated/sign-flipped ("stricter thresholds select for, not screen out, the worst estimates") — demonstrated by zPCREFp's power being *higher* at n_t=2 than n_t=10 (lines 657–663, 1012–1029).
- **Type S (sign) error and Type M (magnitude/inflation) error**: computed directly because true values are known exactly (`sign_error`, `inflation_ratio` in `diagnose_coefs_p2()`), summarized in `aim1_metrics_by_nt` and plotted in `fig-aim1-metrics-vs-nt` (lines 673–721).
- **Neyman-Pearson / error-rate framing**: whole Aim 1 design is framed around comparing error-rate taxonomies (power, sign reliability/Type S, Type M, coverage, RMSE) across three effects and sample-size margins rather than single point-estimate behavior — a deliberately Neyman-Pearson-flavored "long-run error rate" perspective versus Fisherian single-test p-values.
- **Replication / discovery-replication split (Marek Fig. 3e analog)**: Aim 2 entirely (`generate_data_p2_pair`, `combine_replication_p2`, `run_aim1_aim2_cell`'s aim2 branch) — unconditional replication rate vs. conditional replication rate (`P(replicates | discovery-significant)`), each decomposed to show power vs. true replication failure (lines 1031–1128).
- **Coverage / CI calibration**: `covers_truth` in diagnostics, reported in the "fuller metrics table" (lines 673–694).
- **Model misspecification** (briefly, cross-referenced rather than run here): "correct" vs. "misspecified" random-effects structure is defined in `fit_model_p2()` but Aims 1–2 use only "correct"; misspecification sweep is "Aim 3," referenced but not executed in this document (lines 303–309, 1168–1173).

### 5. Narrative/pedagogical structure and build-up

Both documents follow an identical sequence (the reportable version just removes code, not structure or findings):

1. **Framing/motivation**: Phase 1 (real-data resampling) vs. Phase 2 (parametric simulation) distinction; literature grounding in Marek et al. (2022); a parameter-value table grounding every simulated input in the real fitted model (lines 51–105).
2. **Design statement**: explicit statement of Aim 1 (effect-size × sample-size sweep with full error taxonomy) and Aim 2 (discovery/replication split) and the specific research question each answers (lines 107–158).
3. **Shared infrastructure build-up**: DGP function → fitting/classification helpers → sample-size/sweep grids → discovery/replication pair generator → diagnostics/runner → plotting helpers (lines 155–632) — each introduced with a short rationale referencing prior project documents it's "generalizing."
4. **Results, Aim 1**: starts with a compact summary table (sign reliability & power), then escalates depth: fuller metrics table → facetted line plot → individual-estimate "distribution explainer" (pedagogically unpacking *why* the aggregate numbers look that way) → a focused mechanistic digression ("Why can an estimate be significant when true effect = 0?") diagnosing the singular-fit mechanism → explicit conceptual clarification of power vs. false-positive rate → 2D power-surface heatmap → full power-curve grid (lines 634–1029). This is a clear concept-scaffolding progression: summary stat → full diagnostic set → visual intuition → individual-level mechanism → formal distinction (power vs Type I) → multi-dimensional sweep.
5. **Results, Aim 2**: same escalation pattern (summary table → fuller metrics/visual → surface heatmap) and explicit side-by-side discussion contrasting what Aim 1 vs. Aim 2 diagnostics each reveal (lines 1031–1152).
6. **Discussion**: bullet synthesis comparing Aim 1 and Aim 2's different (non-contradictory) conclusions about which effect is "least trustworthy" (lines 1130–1157).
7. **Flagged future work**: explicitly deferred items (multiple-comparisons/Bonferroni sweep) and pointers to Aims 3–6 (lines 1159–1173).
8. **Collapsed "Development history" appendix**: process narrative — relation to prior simulation infrastructure/conventions, confirmed design decisions, timing benchmarks, a live small-scale "smoke test" (kept runnable even in the draft, cached, ~6s, lines 1251–1291), and the cost/launch record of the actual multi-hour background job (lines 1175–1302). In the reportable version this section is retained as prose/tables but its own code (the smoke test) is also stripped (reportable lines 962–969).
9. **Closing "Follow-up note"**: clarifies that DGP/fitting code is preserved unmodified in the draft for potential future revision, and that no new simulations were run in this pass (draft 1304–1313; reportable 987–997) — i.e. both documents are explicit snapshots of a one-time, already-executed simulation study, with the draft retaining "live" code as a reusable/extensible asset and the reportable version serving as the clean deliverable.

This draft/reportable pairing — same prose and figures, differing only in whether simulation/fitting code chunks are shown inline vs. replaced by "see companion document" callouts — is itself a reusable documentation pattern worth carrying into any new scripts built from this work.

<div><tool-result call-id="toolu_01NaeRirCF4rJB7fvrbD7P2S"><script type="application/json">{"version":1,"status":"success","result":{"type":"text","value":"[File: 35.3KB, 764 lines, showing lines 1-501 (output byte budget reached)]\n1\t---\n2\ttitle:...[truncated, total 24530 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"[File: 35.3KB, 764 lines, showing lines 1-501 (output byte budget reached)]\n---\ntitle: \"Tutorial: the Aims 1-2 synthetic-data simulation pipeline\"\nsubtitle: \"How the data behind the power / error-rate / replication figures is generated, walked through piece by piece\"\ndate: today\nformat:\n  html:\n    toc: true\n    toc-depth: 3\n    number-sections: true\n    theme: cosmo\n    embed-resources: true\n    code-fold: false\nexecute:\n  warning: false\n  message: false\n---\n\n::: {.callout-note}\n## What this document is (and isn't)\n\nThis is a **teaching walk-through** of the simulation/analysis pipeline\nbehind `synthetic-data-analyses-power-error-replication-aims-1-2-draft.qmd`\n(Aims 1-2 of the Phase 2 parametric simulation program). It extracts every\npiece of code and commentary needed to understand **how the input data for\nthat document's tables and figures is produced** -- the data-generating\nfunction, the model-fitting logic, the sample-size/effect-size grids, and\nthe per-cell orchestration that ties them together -- stopping exactly where\nthat data becomes ready to plot.\n\nIt deliberately does **not** cover: the actual visualization code (`ggplot`\ncalls, plotting helpers), the substantive findings/discussion, or the\nsmall-scale smoke test used to validate the pipeline before the full run\n(that smoke test *is* a nice minimal worked example if you want to run this\ncode yourself interactively -- see the closing note).\n\nCode below is reproduced verbatim from the source document (function names,\ndefaults, and comments unchanged) so it can be cross-checked directly\nagainst it.\n:::\n\n## The big picture\n\nAims 1-2 answer: *if we knew the true effect sizes and variance components\nexactly, how would our ability to detect and correctly characterize three\nspecific effects (`zHLVA`, `zPCREFp`, their interaction) change with\nparticipant sample size, text sample size, and the size of the effect\nitself?* Answering this requires, for many different combinations of\n\"true\" parameter values and sample sizes:\n\n1. **Simulate** a synthetic dataset with those exact, known-true properties.\n2. **Fit** the same statistical model a real analysis would use.\n3. **Classify** the fit's outcome against the known truth (right sign? CI\n   excludes zero? how far off is the estimate?).\n4. **Repeat** many times (replicates) per combination, and repeat across\n   every combination in the design.\n\nThe rest of this document walks through the code that does exactly that, in\nthe order a reader would need to understand it.\n\n## Step 1: packages\n\n```{r}\n#| label: setup\n\nlibrary(tidyverse)\nlibrary(lme4)\n```\n\nOnly two packages are needed for the *generation* side of the pipeline:\n`tidyverse` (for `dplyr`/`tidyr` data wrangling and `purrr::map`/`pmap` for\niterating over grids) and `lme4` (`glmer`, for fitting the mixed-effects\nlogistic regression models). Everything downstream of this point works with\nplain R and these two packages -- no modeling-specific niceties are needed\nuntil the visualization stage, which is out of scope here.\n\n## Step 2: the data-generating function\n\nThe core building block is a function that, given a set of \"true\" parameter\nvalues and sample sizes, simulates one complete synthetic dataset that\nlooks like the real study's data structure: participants, each answering\nmultiple-choice questions about several texts, with a known true effect of\nparticipant vocabulary (`zHLVA`) and text cohesion (`zPCREFp`), plus their\ninteraction, on accuracy.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: generate-data-p2\n\ngenerate_data_p2 \u003c- function(\n    n_participants = 200,\n    n_texts        = 20,\n    k              = min(10, n_texts),\n    questions_per_text = 4,\n    b_intercept    = 2.093,\n    b_hlva         = 0.363,\n    b_pcref        = 0.095,\n    b_interaction  = 0.054,\n    sd_participant = 0.69,\n    sd_text        = 0.41,\n    sd_pcref_slope = 0,\n    sd_hlva_slope  = 0,\n    cor_part       = 0,\n    cor_text       = 0,\n    cohesion_design = c(\"natural\", \"widened\"),\n    reliability_hlva = 1,\n    reliability_pcref = 1,\n    seed           = NULL\n) {\n  cohesion_design \u003c- match.arg(cohesion_design)\n  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)\n  k \u003c- min(k, n_texts)\n\n  # Participant-level random effects: intercept + zPCREFp slope (correlated) -- Aim 5\n  Sigma_part \u003c- matrix(\n    c(sd_participant^2, cor_part * sd_participant * sd_pcref_slope,\n      cor_part * sd_participant * sd_pcref_slope, sd_pcref_slope^2),\n    nrow = 2\n  )\n  re_part \u003c- if (sd_pcref_slope > 0) {\n    MASS::mvrnorm(n_participants, mu = c(0, 0), Sigma = Sigma_part)\n  } else {\n    cbind(rnorm(n_participants, 0, sd_participant), 0)\n  }\n\n  # zHLVA measurement reliability -- Aim 6 strategy E; reliability_hlva = 1\n  # (default) reproduces the exact prior behavior used in Aims 1-5.\n  zHLVA_true \u003c- rnorm(n_participants, 0, 1)\n  zHLVA_obs  \u003c- sqrt(reliability_hlva) * zHLVA_true +\n    sqrt(1 - reliability_hlva) * rnorm(n_participants, 0, 1)\n\n  participants \u003c- tibble(\n    participant_id = 1:n_participants,\n    zHLVA          = zHLVA_true,\n    zHLVA_obs      = zHLVA_obs,\n    u_participant  = re_part[, 1],\n    s_pcref        = re_part[, 2]\n  )\n\n  # Text-level random effects: intercept + zHLVA slope (correlated) -- Aim 5\n  Sigma_text \u003c- matrix(\n    c(sd_text^2, cor_text * sd_text * sd_hlva_slope,\n      cor_text * sd_text * sd_hlva_slope, sd_hlva_slope^2),\n    nrow = 2\n  )\n  re_text \u003c- if (sd_hlva_slope > 0) {\n    MASS::mvrnorm(n_texts, mu = c(0, 0), Sigma = Sigma_text)\n  } else {\n    cbind(rnorm(n_texts, 0, sd_text), 0)\n  }\n\n  # zPCREFp sampling design -- Aim 6 strategy D (widened cohesion range) --\n  # and measurement reliability -- Aim 6 strategy E.\n  zPCREFp_true \u003c- if (cohesion_design == \"widened\") {\n    rep(c(-1.5, 1.5), length.out = n_texts) + rnorm(n_texts, 0, 0.3)\n  } else {\n    rnorm(n_texts, 0, 1)\n  }\n  zPCREFp_obs \u003c- sqrt(reliability_pcref) * zPCREFp_true +\n    sqrt(1 - reliability_pcref) * rnorm(n_texts, 0, 1)\n\n  texts \u003c- tibble(\n    text_id  = 1:n_texts,\n    zPCREFp  = zPCREFp_true,\n    zPCREFp_obs = zPCREFp_obs,\n    u_text   = re_text[, 1],\n    s_hlva   = re_text[, 2]\n  )\n\n  assignments \u003c- tibble(participant_id = 1:n_participants) |>\n    dplyr::mutate(assigned = purrr::map(participant_id,\n                          ~ sample(1:n_texts, size = k, replace = FALSE))) |>\n    tidyr::unnest(assigned) |>\n    dplyr::rename(text_id = assigned)\n\n  assignments |>\n    dplyr::left_join(participants, by = \"participant_id\") |>\n    dplyr::left_join(texts,        by = \"text_id\") |>\n    dplyr::slice(rep(1:dplyr::n(), each = questions_per_text)) |>\n    dplyr::mutate(\n      question_id = rep(1:questions_per_text, times = dplyr::n() / questions_per_text),\n      eta = b_intercept +\n        (b_hlva  + s_hlva)  * zHLVA +\n        (b_pcref + s_pcref) * zPCREFp +\n        b_interaction * zHLVA * zPCREFp +\n        u_participant + u_text,\n      prob     = plogis(eta),\n      response = rbinom(dplyr::n(), 1, prob)\n    ) |>\n    dplyr::mutate(zHLVA_fit = zHLVA_obs, zPCREFp_fit = zPCREFp_obs) |>\n    dplyr::select(participant_id, text_id, question_id,\n                  zHLVA = zHLVA_fit, zPCREFp = zPCREFp_fit, response)\n}\n```\n\nWalking through this piece by piece:\n\n**a. Arguments and their defaults (lines defining the signature).** Every\n\"true\" quantity the simulation needs is a function argument with a default\nequal to this project's real, empirically-estimated value (e.g.\n`b_hlva = 0.363` is the real fitted `zHLVA` coefficient). This is\ndeliberate: calling `generate_data_p2()` with no arguments reproduces the\n\"realistic\" scenario, and any Aim-specific sweep just overrides the one or\ntwo arguments it cares about (e.g. Aim 1 overrides `b_hlva`/`b_pcref`/\n`b_interaction`; Aim 6 overrides `cohesion_design`/`reliability_hlva`).\n`sd_pcref_slope`, `sd_hlva_slope`, `cor_part`, `cor_text` default to zero --\nthey only matter for Aim 5's richer random-slopes design, so Aims 1-2 never\ntouch them and effectively get a simpler random-**intercepts**-only model.\n\n**b. Participant-level random effects.** `Sigma_part` is a 2x2\nvariance-covariance matrix for a participant's random intercept and (Aim\n5-only) random `zPCREFp` slope. When `sd_pcref_slope = 0` (Aims 1-2's case),\nbuilding this correlated bivariate draw would be wasted work and\nnumerically fragile (a rank-deficient covariance matrix), so the code\nbranches: if there's no slope variance, it just draws ordinary independent\nnormal random intercepts (`rnorm`) and hard-codes the slope column to zero.\n`MASS::mvrnorm()` (correlated bivariate normal draws) is only reached when\nAim 5 actually asks for slope variation.\n\n**c. `zHLVA` and measurement reliability.** Every participant gets a \"true\"\n`zHLVA` value drawn from a standard normal. `zHLVA_obs` is a\nreliability-attenuated version: `reliability_hlva = 1` (the Aims 1-2\ndefault) makes `zHLVA_obs` identical to `zHLVA_true`; a value below 1 (used\nonly in Aim 6's measurement-reliability strategy) blends in independent\nnoise, simulating an imperfect vocabulary test.\n\n**d. Assembling the `participants` tibble.** One row per participant,\ncarrying both the true and observed `zHLVA`, plus the random-intercept/slope\ndraws from (b).\n\n**e-g. Mirror image for texts.** Steps (e) text-level random effects, (f)\n`zPCREFp`'s true value (with an optional \"widened\" sampling design used only\nby Aim 6, which spaces cohesion values at two extremes rather than sampling\nthem continuously) and its own reliability attenuation, and (g) assembling\nthe `texts` tibble, all repeat the same logic as (b)-(d) with participant\nand text swapped.\n\n**h. Crossing participants with texts.** Real participants don't read every\ntext -- each is assigned a random subset of `k` texts (default: up to 10,\nclamped to however many texts actually exist in this run, since a run with\n`n_texts = 2` can't give every participant 10 distinct texts). `purrr::map`\ndraws one random sample of text IDs per participant, and `tidyr::unnest()`\nturns that list-column into one row per (participant, assigned text) pair.\n\n**i. Expanding to the question level.** The real outcome (`response`) is\nrecorded per-question, not per-text (each text has multiple comprehension\nquestions). `dplyr::slice(rep(..., each = questions_per_text))` duplicates\nevery participant-text row `questions_per_text` (default 4) times, and a\nrepeating `1:questions_per_text` sequence labels which question each\nduplicate represents.\n\n**j. The actual data-generating step.** `eta` is the model's linear\npredictor on the logit scale: an intercept, the `zHLVA` and `zPCREFp` main\neffects (each augmented by that participant's or text's own random slope,\nwhich is zero for Aims 1-2), the fixed interaction term, and the\nparticipant's and text's random intercepts. `plogis(eta)` converts that to\na probability, and `rbinom(..., 1, prob)` draws the actual 0/1 `response`\n-- this is the only genuinely random step tied to the *outcome* itself\n(everything upstream generates covariates and random effects; this line is\nwhere \"did this participant get this question right\" is actually decided).\n\n**k. Final selection: true vs. observed covariates.** The very last\n`mutate()`/`select()` swaps in the (possibly reliability-attenuated)\n*observed* `zHLVA`/`zPCREFp` values as what the fitted model will see, while\n`eta` was computed from the *true* values. When `reliability_* = 1` (Aims\n1-2), these are identical and this distinction is invisible; the separation\nexists so Aim 6's measurement-reliability strategy can reuse this same\nfunction unmodified.\n\n::: {.callout-tip}\n**A small but important implementation note:** `library(MASS)` is\ndeliberately never attached in the source document (only `MASS::mvrnorm()`\nis called, via `::`). This is because `MASS` also defines a `select()`\nfunction that would silently shadow `dplyr::select()` if attached, breaking\nthe pipeline above the moment it's loaded after `tidyverse`. This is a\ncommon `MASS`/`dplyr` gotcha worth knowing if you reuse this pattern\nelsewhere.\n:::\n\n## Step 3: fitting the model and classifying the result\n\nOnce a dataset exists, it needs to be fit with the same kind of model a\nreal analysis would use, and the fit's outcome needs to be captured in a\nstructured way (including failure modes) so later steps can build\ndiagnostics from it.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fit-model-p2\n\nextract_terms_of_interest_p2 \u003c- function(fit) {\n  terms \u003c- c(\"zHLVA\", \"zPCREFp\", \"zHLVA:zPCREFp\")\n  co \u003c- tryCatch(summary(fit)$coefficients, error = function(e) NULL)\n  if (is.null(co)) return(NULL)\n  avail \u003c- intersect(terms, rownames(co))\n  tibble(term = avail, estimate = co[avail, \"Estimate\"], std.error = co[avail, \"Std. Error\"])\n}\n\nfit_model_p2 \u003c- function(data, re_spec = c(\"correct\", \"misspecified\", \"full_slopes\")) {\n  re_spec \u003c- match.arg(re_spec)\n  form \u003c- switch(re_spec,\n    correct      = response ~ zHLVA * zPCREFp + (1 | participant_id) + (1 | text_id),\n    misspecified = response ~ zHLVA * zPCREFp + (1 | participant_id),\n    full_slopes  = response ~ zHLVA * zPCREFp + (1 + zPCREFp | participant_id) + (1 + zHLVA | text_id)\n  )\n  warn_msgs \u003c- character(0)\n  fit \u003c- tryCatch(\n    withCallingHandlers(\n      glmer(form, data = data, family = binomial, control = glmerControl(optimizer = \"bobyqa\")),\n      warning = function(w) { warn_msgs \u003c\u003c- c(warn_msgs, conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart(\"muffleWarning\") }\n    ),\n    error = function(e) e\n  )\n  if (inherits(fit, \"error\")) return(list(status = \"error\", coefs = NULL))\n  status \u003c- if (length(warn_msgs) > 0 &&\n                any(grepl(\"failed to converge|Model failed|large eigenvalue|unable to evaluate\",\n                          warn_msgs, ignore.case = TRUE))) {\n    \"optimizer_warning\"\n  } else if (isSingular(fit)) {\n    \"converged_singular\"\n  } else {\n    \"converged_clean\"\n  }\n  list(status = status, coefs = extract_terms_of_interest_p2(fit))\n}\n\nfit_model_p2_guarded \u003c- function(data, re_spec, timeout_secs = 15) {\n  setTimeLimit(elapsed = timeout_secs, transient = TRUE)\n  res \u003c- tryCatch(\n    fit_model_p2(data, re_spec),\n    error = function(e) list(status = \"error\", coefs = NULL)\n  )\n  setTimeLimit(elapsed = Inf, transient = FALSE)\n  res\n}\n```\n\nThree functions, each doing one job:\n\n**`extract_terms_of_interest_p2()`** pulls just the three coefficients this\nwhole program cares about (`zHLVA`, `zPCREFp`, their interaction) out of a\nfitted model's coefficient table, as a tidy `term`/`estimate`/`std.error`\ntibble. `intersect(terms, rownames(co))` guards against a term being\nmissing entirely (which can happen on a badly degenerate fit) rather than\nerroring.\n\n**`fit_model_p2()`** does the actual fitting. Three things worth noting:\n- The formula is chosen via `re_spec`, a three-way switch between `\"correct\"`\n  (random intercepts for both participant and text -- the specification\n  Aims 1-2 always use), `\"misspecified\"` (participant intercept only, used\n  by Aim 3 to quantify the cost of omitting a grouping factor), and\n  `\"full_slopes\"` (adds correlated random slopes, used only by Aim 5).\n- `withCallingHandlers()` around the `glmer()` call **captures warnings\n  without stopping execution** -- `invokeRestart(\"muffleWarning\")` lets the\n  fit continue and the warning's text is stashed in `warn_msgs` for\n  inspection afterward, rather than letting it print to the console\n  thousands of times over a large simulation.\n- The `status` classification turns those captured warnings (plus `lme4`'s\n  own `isSingular()` check) into one of three buckets: `optimizer_warning`\n  (the optimizer itself flagged non-convergence), `converged_singular` (a\n  random-effect variance pinned at its zero boundary -- expected and common\n  at small `n_t`, as later diagnostics show), or `converged_clean`. This\n  three-way classification is what later analysis uses to report *how\n  often* fits broke down, not just what they estimated when they didn't.\n\n**`fit_model_p2_guarded()`** wraps `fit_model_p2()` in a per-fit wall-clock\ntimeout (`setTimeLimit()`, default 15 seconds) so that one pathological fit\nin a 60,000+-fit simulation run can't hang the entire background job\nindefinitely; a fit that blows through the timeout is treated the same as\nany other error.\n\n## Step 4: the sample-size and effect-size grids\n\n```{r}\n#| label: sample-size-grid\n\nn_p_grid \u003c- c(25, 100, 375, 725, 1300, 1497)\nn_t_grid \u003c- c(2, 10, 35, 85, 136)\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: aim1-sweep-grids\n\nb_hlva_grid        \u003c- c(0, 0.18, 0.363, 0.7, 1.0)\nb_pcref_grid       \u003c- c(0, 0.05, 0.095, 0.2, 0.35)\nb_interaction_grid \u003c- c(0, 0.025, 0.054, 0.10, 0.20)\n```\n\n`n_p_grid` (participant counts) and `n_t_grid` (text counts) together\ndefine 6 x 5 = 30 `(n_p, n_t)` \"cells\" -- every combination of participant\nand text sample size the simulation will visit. These particular values\nwere carried over unchanged from an earlier, real-data resampling analysis\n(Phase 1), so that this parametric-simulation program's results can be laid\ndirectly alongside that earlier analysis's real-data findings.\n\nThe three effect-size grids implement Aim 1's **one-at-a-time sweep**\ndesign: each grid has 5 values centered on that term's real,\nempirically-estimated effect size (the middle value in every grid),\nflanked by two smaller and two larger hypothetical true effects. Sweeping\none term while holding the other two fixed at their real values -- rather\nthan crossing all three simultaneously -- keeps the design a manageable\n\"3 sweeps\" rather than a combinatorial explosion, at the cost of not being\nable to see three-way interactions between the swept effects (not a\nconcern here, since the real fitted model has no such three-way term among\nthese predictors).\n\n## Step 5: generating a discovery/replication pair (for Aim 2)\n\nAim 2 asks a different question from Aim 1: not \"how well does one fit\nrecover the truth,\" but \"if I split my sample into two independent halves,\ndoes a significant finding in one replicate in the other?\" That needs a\nfunction that generates *two* related datasets at once, sharing (or not)\npart of the design.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: generate-data-p2-pair\n\ngenerate_data_p2_pair \u003c- function(\n    n_p_total, n_t_total, k = min(10, n_t_total), questions_per_text = 4,\n    b_intercept = 2.093, b_hlva = 0.363, b_pcref = 0.095, b_interaction = 0.054,\n    sd_participant = 0.69, sd_text = 0.41,\n    sd_pcref_slope = 0, sd_hlva_slope = 0, cor_part = 0, cor_text = 0,\n    split_margin = c(\"participants_only\", \"both\"),\n    seed\n) {\n  split_margin \u003c- match.arg(split_margin)\n  set.seed(seed)\n\n  n_p_half \u003c- max(1, floor(n_p_total / 2))\n  n_t_half \u003c- if (split_margin == \"both\") max(1, floor(n_t_total / 2)) else n_t_total\n\n  make_texts \u003c- function(n_t) {\n    Sigma_text \u003c- matrix(c(sd_text^2, cor_text * sd_text * sd_hlva_slope,\n                            cor_text * sd_text * sd_hlva_slope, sd_hlva_slope^2), nrow = 2)\n    re_text \u003c- if (sd_hlva_slope > 0) MASS::mvrnorm(n_t, c(0, 0), Sigma_text) else cbind(rnorm(n_t, 0, sd_text), 0)\n    tibble(text_id = 1:n_t, zPCREFp = rnorm(n_t, 0, 1), u_text = re_text[, 1], s_hlva = re_text[, 2])\n  }\n  make_participants \u003c- function(n_p) {\n    Sigma_part \u003c- matrix(c(sd_participant^2, cor_part * sd_participant * sd_pcref_slope,\n                            cor_part * sd_participant * sd_pcref_slope, sd_pcref_slope^2), nrow = 2)\n    re_part \u003c- if (sd_pcref_slope > 0) MASS::mvrnorm(n_p, c(0, 0), Sigma_part) else cbind(rnorm(n_p, 0, sd_participant), 0)\n    tibble(participant_id = 1:n_p, zHLVA = rnorm(n_p, 0, 1), u_participant = re_part[, 1], s_pcref = re_part[, 2])\n  }\n  build_dataset \u003c- function(participants, texts) {\n    kk \u003c- min(k, nrow(texts))\n    assignments \u003c- tibble(participant_id = participants$participant_id) |>\n      dplyr::mutate(assigned = purrr::map(participant_id, ~ sample(texts$text_id, size = kk, replace = FALSE))) |>\n      tidyr::unnest(assigned) |> dplyr::rename(text_id = assigned)\n    assignments |>\n      dplyr::left_join(participants, by = \"participant_id\") |>\n      dplyr::left_join(texts, by = \"text_id\") |>\n      dplyr::slice(rep(1:dplyr::n(), each = questions_per_text)) |>\n      dplyr::mutate(\n        question_id = rep(1:questions_per_text, times = dplyr::n() / questions_per_text),\n        eta = b_intercept + (b_hlva + s_hlva) * zHLVA + (b_pcref + s_pcref) * zPCREFp +\n          b_interaction * zHLVA * zPCREFp + u_participant + u_text,\n        prob = plogis(eta), response = rbinom(dplyr::n(), 1, prob)\n      ) |>\n      dplyr::select(participant_id, text_id, question_id, zHLVA, zPCREFp, response)\n  }\n\n  texts_shared      \u003c- make_texts(n_t_half)\n  participants_disc \u003c- make_participants(n_p_half)\n  participants_repl \u003c- make_participants(n_p_half)\n  texts_repl        \u003c- if (split_margin == \"both\") make_texts(n_t_half) else texts_shared\n\n  list(\n    discovery   = build_dataset(participants_disc, texts_shared),\n    replication = build_dataset(participants_repl, texts_repl)\n  )\n}\n```\n\nThis is deliberately a self-contained re-implementation of\n`generate_data_p2()`'s logic (three internal helpers `make_texts()`,\n`make_participants()`, `build_dataset()`, each doing the same job as the\ncorresponding piece of Step 2) rather than a call to it, because it needs\nto build *two* datasets that share some pieces and not others, controlled\nby `split_margin`:\n\n- **`n_p_half`/`n_t_half`**: given a cell's *total* sample size, halve the\n  participant count always; halve the text count only if `split_margin =\n  \"both\"`. With `split_margin = \"participants_only\"` (what Aims 1-2 use),\n  `n_t_half` is just the full `n_t_total` -- both halves see the *same*\n  texts.\n- **Why avoid splitting texts at small `n_t`**: the comment in the source\n  document notes this choice specifically avoids degenerate 1-text halves\n  at the smallest grid point (`n_t = 2`) -- splitting 2 texts into two\n  halves of 1 would make the text-level random intercept trivially\n  unidentifiable in a different, less interesting way than the phenomenon\n  Aim 1/2 are trying to study.\n- **Building the pair**: `texts_shared` is generated once; `discovery` and\n  `replication` each get their *own*, independently-sampled participants\n  (`participants_disc`/`participants_repl`), but share `texts_shared`\n  unless `split_margin = \"both\"` asks for independent `texts_repl` too.\n  Each half is then expanded to the full participant x text x question\n  dataset via the shared `build_dataset()` helper -- functionally identical\n  to steps (h)-(j) of `generate_data_p2()`.\n\n## Step 6: diagnostics and the per-grid-cell orchestrator\n\nEverything above produces raw data and raw model fits. dplyr::mutate(term = factor(term, levels = term_levels))\n\n# Full effect-size sweep, all points (not just the own-effect-size slice) --\n# used for the Aim 1 power-curves figure dplyr::filter(term == \"zHLVA:zPCREFp\")\n) |> dplyr::mutate(term = factor(term, levels = term_levels))\n```\n\nPiece by piece:\n\n- **The `file.exists()` guard.** Before touching anything else, the code\n  checks that all six expected `.rds` files exist and fails loudly with a\n  specific, actionable error message if any are missing, rather than\n  letting a later step fail confusingly (or silently proceed with stale\n  data). This is a good habit any time a document depends on\n  externally-produced files it doesn't (and shouldn't) regenerate itself.\n- **Loading the six files.** Each sweep's Aim 1 and Aim 2 results were\n  saved separately by the background job, so there are six objects to\n  read in: `aim1_hlva`, `aim1_pcref`, `aim1_interaction` and their Aim 2\n  counterparts. Each is a long tibble with one row per (term, effect\n  value, `n_p`, `n_t`, replicate) combination.\n- **`own_effect` and `term_levels`.** `own_effect` records each term's\n  real, empirically-observed value -- the same numbers used as defaults\n  back in Step 2/6 -- so that later filtering can pick out \"the row where\n  the swept effect equals its real value\" without hard-coding that number\n  three separate times. `term_levels` fixes a consistent factor ordering\n  (`zHLVA`, `zPCREFp`, interaction) used throughout so tables and plots\n  always present the three terms in the same order.\n- **`aim1_all` / `aim2_all`: the \"own effect size\" slice.** Each sweep's\n  saved results contain data for *all five* swept effect-size values (0,\n  small, real, large, larger), but most tables/figures only want *each\n  term's own real value* -- e.g. `zHLVA`'s row from the `hlva` sweep at\n  `effect_value == 0.363`, not from the `pcref` or `interaction` sweeps\n  (where `zHLVA` was just held fixed as a covariate, not the focus). The\n  three `filter()` + `bind_rows()` calls pick exactly one term from each of\n  the three sweeps' output and stack them into one tidy tibble.\n- **`aim1_sweep_combined`: the full sweep, kept separate.** One figure (the\n  power-curves figure, showing how power changes as the *true effect size\n  itself* varies) genuinely needs every effect-size value, not just the\n  real one -- so this object keeps all five values per term rather than\n  filtering down to one.\n\nAt this point, `aim1_all`, `aim2_all`, and `aim1_sweep_combined` are exactly\nthe data structures every downstream table and figure consumes. Nothing\npast this point generates new data -- everything from here on is\nsummarizing (`group_by()`/`summarise()`) and plotting what these three\ntibbles already contain.\n\n::: {.callout-tip}\n## If you want to actually run this yourself\n\nThe full 67,500-fit design is a multi-hour job and shouldn't be your first\nattempt at reproducing this. The source document\n(`synthetic-data-analyses-power-error-replication-aims-1-2-draft.qmd`)\ncontains a small, self-contained **smoke test** in its collapsed\n\"Development history\" section that calls exactly the functions walked\nthrough above (`run_aim1_aim2_cell()`, and transitively everything else) on\na tiny 24-combination grid, completing in about 6 seconds -- a good\nstarting point for experimenting with this code interactively before\nattempting anything at full scale.\n:::"},"elapsedMs":1}</script></tool-result></div>

It is a restructured development version of\n`synthetic-data-analyses-power-error-replication-aims-1-2-draft.qmd` (which\nis left unchanged as the reference/working copy), reframed around this\nproject's actual, broader purpose: **mapping how power, the full Type\nI/II/S/M error taxonomy, and discovery/replication rates vary with effect\nsize and sample size, for all three effects this project cares about**\n(the `zHLVA` participant-level main effect, the `zPCREFp` text-level main\neffect, and their interaction) -- not only the specific sign-instability\nquestion that originally motivated the design (see below). Aims 3-6 and the\nnormative-F1-ANOVA-malpractice extension will get their own documents\nlater, built the same way.\n\nAll tables and figures below are computed from pre-existing, already-run\nresults saved in `results_phase2/aim1_*.rds` and `results_phase2/aim2_*.rds`\n(no full-grid recomputation happens when this document is rendered).
