The DGP/fitting code below is kept live (not just for reference) because\nit may be revisited for informative modifications in a follow-up pass; see\nthe closing note.\n:::\n\n::: {.callout-important}\n## Terminology check: Type I vs. Type II\n\nThroughout this document, **Type I error** = a false positive (rejecting a\ntrue null -- concluding an effect exists when it does not), and **Type II\nerror** = a false negative (failing to reject a false null -- missing a\nreal effect). This is the standard convention, and matches how the rest of\nthis document already uses \"false-positive rate\" (e.g. the `n_t = 2`\n`zPCREFp` discussion below). If a different convention was intended when\nthis restructuring was requested, flag it and the language below can be\nadjusted.\n:::\n\n```{r}\n#| label: setup\n\nlibrary(tidyverse)\nlibrary(lme4)\nlibrary(patchwork)\nlibrary(RColorBrewer)\nlibrary(ggdist)\n```\n\n## Relationship to Phase 1 and motivating framework\n\nPhase 1 (`sampling-variability-corridor-of-stability.qmd`) was an\n**empirical resampling** study of this project's one real dataset,\nanswering \"how unstable is our *actual* estimate at smaller *N*?\" Phase 2 is\na **parametric simulation** study, answering the complementary question:\n\"how unstable would an estimate be across a *range* of plausible true\neffects, variances, and model specifications -- are Phase 1's findings a\ngeneric property of this kind of crossed design, or specific to this\nproject's particular dataset?\"\n\nAims 1-2 port Marek et al.'s (2022) brain-wide-association-study\nreproducibility framework onto this setting. Marek et al. documented a\nstatistical-error taxonomy -- false negatives, false positives,\n**magnitude/inflation error (Type M)**, and **sign error (Type S)** -- each\nas a function of sample size, and showed that smaller samples' significant\neffects are disproportionately the most inflated and sign-flipped ones (the\n\"underpowered paradox\": stricter significance thresholds select for, rather\nthan screen out, the most inflated estimates). They also used an explicit\n**discovery/replication split** design to quantify out-of-sample replication\nprobability directly. Aims 1-2 were originally motivated by testing whether\nthis project's own documented sign-instability (the \"reverse cohesion\neffect\" finding -- see project memory) is a domain-specific instance of the\nsame generic phenomenon; the design covers **three effects** rather than\nthe interaction alone (the `zHLVA` main effect, the `zPCREFp` main effect,\nand their `zHLVA:zPCREFp` interaction) precisely so that question could be\nanswered by comparison.\n\nThat motivating question, however, is narrower than what this document is\nactually useful for. Once all three effects are run through the same\neffect-size x sample-size grid with the same diagnostic taxonomy, the\nresults answer a more general question that different readers will care\nabout differently:\n\n- A reader planning a **new study** mainly wants **power** and **discovery\n  rate**: how large a sample, on which margin, is needed to reliably detect\n  a given effect?\n- A reader trying to **interpret an existing significant finding** (their\n  own or someone else's) mainly wants **Type S (sign) error rate** and\n  **Type M (magnitude) ratio**: conditional on a result being \"significant,\"\n  how likely is it to have the wrong sign, or to be substantially inflated?\n- A reader thinking about **meta-scientific reproducibility** mainly wants\n  the **discovery/replication rates** from Aim 2: if this study were run\n  twice independently, how often would both runs agree?\n\nAll three questions are answered for all three effects below; the original\nsign-instability question is one specific instance of the first two,\nrevisited explicitly in \"Aim 1: is small-text-*N* instability a\ntext-margin property or an interaction-specific property?\" below.\n\nThe table below defines each diagnostic used throughout this document and\nstates exactly how it is computed here. All are derived from\n`diagnose_coefs_p2()`'s per-replicate-fit columns (`estimate`, `std.error`,\n`true_value`, and the **Wald** 95% CI `estimate +/- 1.96 * std.error`), then\naggregated by `summarize_p2_metrics()` / the `aim1-full-metrics-table`\nchunk over whichever grouping is in play (typically `term` x `n_t`, pooled\nover `n_p` and the 50 replicates/cell).\n\n| Diagnostic | Standard definition | Computed here as |\n|---|---|---|\n| `power` | P(reject H0 \\| true effect is non-zero) -- probability of correctly detecting a real effect. | `mean(excludes_zero)`, restricted to rows at the term's non-zero (typically empirically-observed) effect size. `excludes_zero` = the 95% Wald CI does not contain 0. |\n| `type_1_rate` | P(reject H0 \\| true effect is exactly zero) -- the false-positive rate; nominally ~0.05 for a correctly calibrated 95% CI. | `mean(excludes_zero)`, restricted to rows at `effect_value == 0` on the same sweep. |\n| `sign_reliability` | P(estimated sign matches true sign), unconditional on significance. | `mean(correct_sign)` over **all** fits (significant or not), where `correct_sign = sign(estimate) == sign(true_value)`. |\n| `type_s_rate` | Type S (sign) error rate: P(estimated sign is wrong \\| the result is significant) -- Gelman & Carlin's (2014)/Marek et al.'s (2022) usage. | `mean(sign_error[excludes_zero])`, i.e. computed only among rows where the CI excludes zero; `sign_error = excludes_zero & !correct_sign`. |\n| `type_m_ratio` | Type M (magnitude/inflation) ratio: how much larger a *significant* estimate typically is than the true effect. | `median(inflation_ratio[excludes_zero])`, where `inflation_ratio = abs(estimate) / abs(true_value)` (undefined/`NA` when `true_value == 0`, since inflation relative to zero is not meaningful); the median (not mean) is used to resist the heavy right skew of this ratio at small `n_t`. |\n| `median_bias` | Bias: the typical signed deviation of the estimate from the true value. | `median(bias)` over all fits, where `bias = estimate - true_value`. Median rather than mean, again for robustness to the occasional extreme estimate at small `n_t`. |\n| `coverage` | Nominal 95% CI coverage: the proportion of CIs that actually contain the true value (should be ~0.95 if well-calibrated). | `mean(covers_truth)`, where `covers_truth = ci_lower \u003c= true_value & true_value \u003c= ci_upper`. |\n| `rmse_raw` | Root-mean-squared error of the estimate around the true value. | `sqrt(mean(bias^2))` over all fits. Included for completeness but dominated by rare pathological fits at `n_t = 2` (see prose below the fuller metrics table). |\n| `rmse_trimmed` | RMSE, robustified against extreme outliers. | `sqrt(mean(pmin(bias^2, quantile(bias^2, 0.95))))` -- squared bias is winsorized at its own 95th percentile (within each group) before averaging, so a handful of extreme singular-fit estimates cannot dominate the summary. Preferred over `rmse_raw` for cross-cell comparison. |\n\nTwo things to note about this taxonomy as implemented: first, `type_s_rate`\nand `type_m_ratio` are both computed *conditional on significance*\n(`excludes_zero`), matching Marek et al.'s (2022) framing of \"what does a\nsignificant result look like at this sample size\" -- they are not defined,\nand are `NA`, for the (usually large) share of non-significant fits.\nSecond, all coverage/CI-based diagnostics here use **Wald** intervals\n(`estimate +/- 1.96 * std.error`) rather than profile-likelihood or\nbootstrap CIs, for computational speed across tens of thousands of `glmer`\nfits -- this is a possible source of miscalibration in its own right,\ndistinct from the random-effects-identifiability mechanism discussed later\nin this document, and is not separately investigated here.\n\n| Input | Value(s) | Source |\n|---|---|---|\n| Sample-size grid (participants) | 25, 100, 375, 725, 1300, 1497 | Phase 1 Step 3's joint grid |\n| Sample-size grid (texts) | 2, 10, 35, 85, 136 | Phase 1 Step 3's joint grid |\n| Effect size, `zHLVA` | 0.363 | Phase 1 Step 0 full-data fit |\n| Effect size, `zPCREFp` | 0.094-0.098 | Phase 1 Step 0 / Step 5 |\n| Effect size, `zHLVA:zPCREFp` | 0.054 | Phase 1 Step 0 / Step 5 (glmer and brms agree) |\n| Variance component, `sd(ResponseId)` | 0.69 | Full core model (`dev.all.studies.noratings.ptqs.normal.0.1.normal.0.1.lkj.2.study.ri.rds`), extracted in `phase2-effect-variance-misspecification.qmd`'s `extract-aim5-reference` chunk -- differs from Phase 1's simpler reduced-model estimate (~0.61-0.62) because the full model's 26 fixed effects absorb some of that between-participant variance |\n| Variance component, `sd(text.id)` | 0.41 | Same source as above -- differs from Phase 1's reduced-model estimate (~0.70-0.72), same reason |\n| RE-misspecification contrast | \"correct\" `(1\\|ResponseId)+(1\\|text.id)` vs. \"misspecified\" `(1\\|ResponseId)` only | Phase 1, all steps |\n\nReusing the same sample-size grid means these results can be laid\nside-by-side against Phase 1's real-data panels directly.\n\n::: {.callout-important}\n## Note: the real core model's random-effects structure is richer than this DGP\n\nThe real fitted core model's random-effects terms let participants vary in\ntheir *slopes* for all five text-level predictors (including `zPCREFp`), and\nlet texts vary in their *slopes* for the participant-level predictors\n(including `zHLVA`), each correlated with its own grouping factor's\nintercept. Aims 1-2 (like Aim 3-4 and 6) use a simpler, random-**intercept**-\nonly \"correct\"/\"misspecified\" data-generating process, following Phase 1's\nreduced model -- they answer a coarser question (omitting a grouping\nfactor's clustering altogether) and should not be read as testing the real\nmodel's richer slope/covariance structure. That richer structure is the\nsubject of Aim 5, covered in a separate future document.\n:::\n\n## Design: Aim 1 (effect size x sample size) and Aim 2 (discovery/replication split)\n\nBoth aims share one data-generating run: RE specification fixed at\n\"correct\" (random intercepts only, for `ResponseId`/`participant_id` and\n`text.id`/`text_id`); variance components fixed at their empirical values;\nthe full joint sample-size grid (30 `(n_p, n_t)` cells); 50 replicates/cell.\nA grid cell's `(n_p, n_t)` is the **total** sample -- Aim 2 splits each cell\ninto two roughly-equal-sized discovery/replication halves.\n\n**Aim 1** runs three **one-at-a-time** effect-size sweeps -- each holding\nthe other two effects fixed at their empirical values while varying the\nswept effect:\n\n| Sweep | Effect | Grid (centered on empirical estimate) |\n|---|---|---|\n| (i) | `zHLVA` (main effect, participant-level) | 0, 0.18, 0.363 (observed), 0.7, 1.0 |\n| (ii) | `zPCREFp` (main effect, text-level) | 0, 0.05, ~0.095 (observed), 0.2, 0.35 |\n| (iii) | `zHLVA:zPCREFp` (interaction) | 0, 0.025, 0.054 (observed), 0.10, 0.20 |\n\nDiagnostics extend the project's existing four (bias, sign reliability,\ncoverage, RMSE) with a Marek-style decomposition, directly computable here\nbecause the true value is known exactly: **Type S (sign) error rate** (among\nCI-excludes-0 draws, proportion with the wrong sign), **Type M\n(magnitude/inflation) ratio** (`|estimate|/|true value|` among\nCI-excludes-0 draws), and **power** on its own scale.\n\n**The original motivating question Aim 1 answers** (one specific instance\nof its general purpose): is the sign-instability pattern found in Phase 1\n(near-coin-flip sign consistency for the interaction at *n* = 2 texts) (a) a\nproperty of the *specific* small effect size observed, (b) specific to the\ninteraction term, or (c) a general property of being estimated from the\n*text* margin (in which case `zPCREFp`, also text-level, should show a\nsimilar pattern)? Comparing all three effects on the same diagnostics\ndistinguishes these explanations directly. But the same grid and diagnostics\nalso answer the broader questions above (power/discovery for study\nplanning, Type S/M for interpreting an existing result) for **any** of the\nthree effects, independent of that original motivating question -- readers\nwho don't care about the reverse-cohesion-effect history can use the tables\nand figures below directly for whichever effect and diagnostic interests\nthem.\n\n**Aim 2** ports Marek et al.'s replication design (their Fig. 3e): for each\ngrid cell (all three effects), split the simulated sample into two\nindependent, equal-sized discovery/replication halves, fit both, and compute\nthe proportion of replicates in which a discovery-significant effect also\nreplicates (same sign, both significant) out-of-sample. The split axis is\nconfigurable (`split_margin`): `\"participants_only\"` (same text pool in both\nhalves, new participants only) vs. `\"both\"` (independent participants *and*\ntexts). Both variants can be compared once built; the run below uses\n`\"participants_only\"`.\n\nThe significance-threshold/multiple-comparisons sweep (Marek's\nP\u003c0.05-to-Bonferroni comparison) is explicitly **deferred** here -- see\n\"Flagged future work\" below.\n\n## Shared data-generating function\n\nGeneralizes `simulate_interaction_data()` (from\n`power-simulation-vocabulary-cohesion.qmd`) and `generate_data_s3()` (from\n`simulation_study_complete.qmd`): crossed participant x text design with\n`k`-texts-per-participant subsetting (clamped to `n_texts`), independently\nsettable effect sizes for all three effects, independently settable\nintercept variances for both margins, and optional by-margin slope\nvariance/correlation (zero by default here, so Aims 1-2 reduce to the\nintercept-only DGP; non-zero values are used only by Aim 5, covered\nelsewhere).\n\n```{r}\n#| label: generate-data-p2\n\ngenerate_data_p2 \u003c- function(\n    n_participants = 200,\n    n_texts        = 20,\n    k              = min(10, n_texts),\n    questions_per_text = 4,\n    b_intercept    = 2.093,\n    b_hlva         = 0.363,\n    b_pcref        = 0.095,\n    b_interaction  = 0.054,\n    sd_participant = 0.69,\n    sd_text        = 0.41,\n    sd_pcref_slope = 0,\n    sd_hlva_slope  = 0,\n    cor_part       = 0,\n    cor_text       = 0,\n    cohesion_design = c(\"natural\", \"widened\"),\n    reliability_hlva = 1,\n    reliability_pcref = 1,\n    seed           = NULL\n) {\n  cohesion_design \u003c- match.arg(cohesion_design)\n  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)\n  k \u003c- min(k, n_texts)\n\n  # Participant-level random effects: intercept + zPCREFp slope (correlated) -- Aim 5\n  Sigma_part \u003c- matrix(\n    c(sd_participant^2, cor_part * sd_participant * sd_pcref_slope,\n      cor_part * sd_participant * sd_pcref_slope, sd_pcref_slope^2),\n    nrow = 2\n  )\n  re_part \u003c- if (sd_pcref_slope > 0) {\n    MASS::mvrnorm(n_participants, mu = c(0, 0), Sigma = Sigma_part)\n  } else {\n    cbind(rnorm(n_participants, 0, sd_participant), 0)\n  }\n\n  # zHLVA measurement reliability -- Aim 6 strategy E; reliability_hlva = 1\n  # (default) reproduces the exact prior behavior used in Aims 1-5.\n  zHLVA_true \u003c- rnorm(n_participants, 0, 1)\n  zHLVA_obs  \u003c- sqrt(reliability_hlva) * zHLVA_true +\n    sqrt(1 - reliability_hlva) * rnorm(n_participants, 0, 1)\n\n  participants \u003c- tibble(\n    participant_id = 1:n_participants,\n    zHLVA          = zHLVA_true,\n    zHLVA_obs      = zHLVA_obs,\n    u_participant  = re_part[, 1],\n    s_pcref        = re_part[, 2]\n  )\n\n  # Text-level random effects: intercept + zHLVA slope (correlated) -- Aim 5\n  Sigma_text \u003c- matrix(\n    c(sd_text^2, cor_text * sd_text * sd_hlva_slope,\n      cor_text * sd_text * sd_hlva_slope, sd_hlva_slope^2),\n    nrow = 2\n  )\n  re_text \u003c- if (sd_hlva_slope > 0) {\n    MASS::mvrnorm(n_texts, mu = c(0, 0), Sigma = Sigma_text)\n  } else {\n    cbind(rnorm(n_texts, 0, sd_text), 0)\n  }\n\n  # zPCREFp sampling design -- Aim 6 strategy D (widened cohesion range) --\n  # and measurement reliability -- Aim 6 strategy E.\n  zPCREFp_true \u003c- if (cohesion_design == \"widened\") {\n    rep(c(-1.5, 1.5), length.out = n_texts) + rnorm(n_texts, 0, 0.3)\n  } else {\n    rnorm(n_texts, 0, 1)\n  }\n  zPCREFp_obs \u003c- sqrt(reliability_pcref) * zPCREFp_true +\n    sqrt(1 - reliability_pcref) * rnorm(n_texts, 0, 1)\n\n  texts \u003c- tibble(\n    text_id  = 1:n_texts,\n    zPCREFp  = zPCREFp_true,\n    zPCREFp_obs = zPCREFp_obs,\n    u_text   = re_text[, 1],\n    s_hlva   = re_text[, 2]\n  )\n\n  assignments \u003c- tibble(participant_id = 1:n_participants) |>\n    dplyr::mutate(assigned = purrr::map(participant_id,\n                          ~ sample(1:n_texts, size = k, replace = FALSE))) |>\n    tidyr::unnest(assigned) |>\n    dplyr::rename(text_id = assigned)\n\n  assignments |>\n    dplyr::left_join(participants, by = \"participant_id\") |>\n    dplyr::left_join(texts,        by = \"text_id\") |>\n    dplyr::slice(rep(1:dplyr::n(), each = questions_per_text)) |>\n    dplyr::mutate(\n      question_id = rep(1:questions_per_text, times = dplyr::n() / questions_per_text),\n      eta = b_intercept +\n        (b_hlva  + s_hlva)  * zHLVA +\n        (b_pcref + s_pcref) * zPCREFp +\n        b_interaction * zHLVA * zPCREFp +\n        u_participant + u_text,\n      prob     = plogis(eta),\n      response = rbinom(dplyr::n(), 1, prob)\n    ) |>\n    dplyr::mutate(zHLVA_fit = zHLVA_obs, zPCREFp_fit = zPCREFp_obs) |>\n    dplyr::select(participant_id, text_id, question_id,\n                  zHLVA = zHLVA_fit, zPCREFp = zPCREFp_fit, response)\n}\n```\n\nNote: `library(MASS)` is deliberately **not** attached (only `MASS::mvrnorm`\nis called via `::`), because `MASS::select()` masks `dplyr::select()` and\nbreaks the pipeline above if attached. The fitted model always sees\n`zHLVA`/`zPCREFp` as **observed** (possibly measurement-error-attenuated)\nvalues, while the response is generated from the **true** latent values --\nwith the default `reliability_hlva = reliability_pcref = 1` used throughout\nAims 1-2, observed and true are identical.\n\n## Shared fitting and outcome-classification helpers\n\nReused from `sampling-variability-corridor-of-stability.qmd`'s\n`fit_reduced_model()` / `extract_terms_of_interest()` /\n`fit_reduced_model_guarded()` pattern, extended with a third RE\nspecification (`\"full_slopes\"`, used only by Aim 5) alongside the\n`\"correct\"`/`\"misspecified\"` pair used here and by Aim 3.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fit-model-p2\n\nextract_terms_of_interest_p2 \u003c- function(fit) {\n  terms \u003c- c(\"zHLVA\", \"zPCREFp\", \"zHLVA:zPCREFp\")\n  co \u003c- tryCatch(summary(fit)$coefficients, error = function(e) NULL)\n  if (is.null(co)) return(NULL)\n  avail \u003c- intersect(terms, rownames(co))\n  tibble(term = avail, estimate = co[avail, \"Estimate\"], std.error = co[avail, \"Std. Error\"])\n}\n\nfit_model_p2 \u003c- function(data, re_spec = c(\"correct\", \"misspecified\", \"full_slopes\")) {\n  re_spec \u003c- match.arg(re_spec)\n  form \u003c- switch(re_spec,\n    correct      = response ~ zHLVA * zPCREFp + (1 | participant_id) + (1 | text_id),\n    misspecified = response ~ zHLVA * zPCREFp + (1 | participant_id),\n    full_slopes  = response ~ zHLVA * zPCREFp + (1 + zPCREFp | participant_id) + (1 + zHLVA | text_id)\n  )\n  warn_msgs \u003c- character(0)\n  fit \u003c- tryCatch(\n    withCallingHandlers(\n      glmer(form, data = data, family = binomial, control = glmerControl(optimizer = \"bobyqa\")),\n      warning = function(w) { warn_msgs \u003c\u003c- c(warn_msgs, conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart(\"muffleWarning\") }\n    ),\n    error = function(e) e\n  )\n  if (inherits(fit, \"error\")) return(list(status = \"error\", coefs = NULL))\n  status \u003c- if (length(warn_msgs) > 0 &&\n                any(grepl(\"failed to converge|Model failed|large eigenvalue|unable to evaluate\",\n                          warn_msgs, ignore.case = TRUE))) {\n    \"optimizer_warning\"\n  } else if (isSingular(fit)) {\n    \"converged_singular\"\n  } else {\n    \"converged_clean\"\n  }\n  list(status = status, coefs = extract_terms_of_interest_p2(fit))\n}\n\nfit_model_p2_guarded \u003c- function(data, re_spec, timeout_secs = 15) {\n  setTimeLimit(elapsed = timeout_secs, transient = TRUE)\n  res \u003c- tryCatch(\n    fit_model_p2(data, re_spec),\n    error = function(e) list(status = \"error\", coefs = NULL)\n  )\n  setTimeLimit(elapsed = Inf, transient = FALSE)\n  res\n}\n```\n\n## Sample-size grid and Aim 1 sweep grids\n\n```{r}\n#| label: sample-size-grid\n\nn_p_grid \u003c- c(25, 100, 375, 725, 1300, 1497)\nn_t_grid \u003c- c(2, 10, 35, 85, 136)\njoint_grid \u003c- tidyr::expand_grid(n_p = n_p_grid, n_t = n_t_grid)\nnrow(joint_grid)\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: aim1-sweep-grids\n\nb_hlva_grid        \u003c- c(0, 0.18, 0.363, 0.7, 1.0)\nb_pcref_grid       \u003c- c(0, 0.05, 0.095, 0.2, 0.35)\nb_interaction_grid \u003c- c(0, 0.025, 0.054, 0.10, 0.20)\n```\n\n## Discovery/replication data-generating pair (Aim 2)\n\nFor `split_margin = \"participants_only\"`, both halves share the same\n`n_t_total` texts (avoiding degenerate 1-text halves at the smallest grid\npoint, `n_t = 2`); only the participant pool is split. For `split_margin =\n\"both\"`, both margins split independently.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: generate-data-p2-pair\n\ngenerate_data_p2_pair \u003c- function(\n    n_p_total, n_t_total, k = min(10, n_t_total), questions_per_text = 4,\n[Next offset: 455; 1753 more lines, ~95.4KB]"},"elapsedMs":12}</script></tool-result></div>

This is now visible on every diagnostic in this document\n  (the fuller metrics table's explicit Type I column, the reordered power\n  surface/curves, and the three-panel funnel plot), not just the original\n  sign-reliability/power comparison -- the general pattern (text-margin\n  terms behave qualitatively differently from the participant-margin term,\n  regardless of which specific error-taxonomy diagnostic is examined) holds\n  up consistently, which is itself the more general finding this\n  restructured document is built to surface.\n\nA full cross-aim synthesis, tying these findings together with Aims 3-6\n(random-effects misspecification, variance-component sensitivity, slope/\ncovariance recovery, and design remedies), will appear once those aims have\ntheir own reporting-ready documents.\n\n## Flagged future work\n\n- **The significance-threshold/multiple-comparisons sweep** (Marek et al.'s\n  P\u003c0.05-to-Bonferroni comparison) was explicitly deferred at the design\n  stage, given the real core model's 26-term fixed-effects formula. Whether to commit to a full Scenario 6 run remains a\n     separate, still-open decision; this benchmark only removes the cost\n     uncertainty, not the decision itself.\n\n::: {.callout-note}\n## Scenario 6 benchmark (completed)\n\n6 candidate cells at the proposed extremes (`n_p` up to 5000, `n_t` up to\n300), 2 replicates each, `\"correct\"` RE spec, timed with the same\n`generate_data_p2()`/`fit_model_p2()` helpers used throughout this\ndocument (full detail and the underlying findings are in\n`cost-estimate-expanded-grid-replicates-aims1-2-PLAN.qmd`'s \"Scenario 6\nbenchmark\" section):\n\n| Cell | `n_p` | `n_t` | Rows | Mean fit time | Status |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Text-margin only | 1497 | 200 | 59,880 | 2.93s | clean, both reps |\n| Text-margin only | 1497 | 300 | 59,880 | 3.50s | clean, both reps |\n| Participant-margin only | 3000 | 136 | 120,000 | 7.18s | clean, both reps |\n| Participant-margin only | 5000 | 136 | 200,000 | 12.18s | clean, both reps |\n| Both margins | 3000 | 300 | 120,000 | 7.65s | clean, both reps |\n| Both margins (max) | 5000 | 300 | 200,000 | 11.68s | clean, both reps |\n\nAll 12 fits converged cleanly (no singular fits, optimizer warnings, or\ntimeouts). A second,\npractically useful finding: because `generate_data_p2()` caps each\nparticipant at `k = min(10, n_texts)` assigned texts, extending `n_t`\n*alone* past 10 adds no rows and costs essentially nothing extra (the\n`n_t = 200`/`300` cells cost the same as the existing `n_t = 136`\nbaseline at matched `n_p`) -- only extending `n_p`, or adding more\ntexts-per-participant, increases cost.\n\nAs one concrete illustration: a dedicated sweep restricted to just these 6\ncells, at the existing Aims 1-2 structure (3 sweeps x 5 effect values x 50\nreplicates/cell), would cost ~9.4h serial / ~2.4h on 4 workers (Aim 1\nonly, 4,500 fits) or ~28.2h serial / ~7.0h on 4 workers (full Aim 1 + Aim\n2 structure, 13,500 fits, upper-bound estimate). A full densified-and-\nextended Scenario 6 grid (the original \"~130-150 cells\" estimate) can now\nbe costed with the same confidence as Scenarios 1-4 via `rows x 0.06 /\n1000` seconds per fit, once a specific grid is chosen.\n:::\n  3. **A dedicated `b_intercept` sweep** was judged worth scoping as its\n     own small follow-up study to check whether logistic regression's\n     non-collapsibility makes the text-margin instability findings above\n     sensitive to this project's unusually high (~89%) baseline accuracy.\n     It has since been designed and costed in full (see\n     `cost-estimate-b-intercept-sweep-PLAN.qmd`), summarized here:\n\n     ::: {.callout-note}\n     ## `b_intercept` sweep design and cost (run)\n\n     A 5-point one-at-a-time sweep over target baseline accuracies (0.50,\n     0.65, 0.80, **0.89 -- observed**, 0.95, i.e. `b_intercept` = 0, 0.619,\n     1.386, 2.093, 2.944), holding the three focal effect sizes at their\n     empirically-observed values, at **4 representative cells** rather\n     than the full 30-cell grid: the existing small (25, 2), moderate\n     (375, 35), and large (1497, 136) benchmark cells, plus a new\n     `n_t = 2` pathology cell at large `n_p` (1497, 2) -- benchmarked\n     specifically for this plan at 0.78s/fit (mean of 2 reps, both\n     `converged_singular`) -- chosen to isolate whether the text-margin\n     identifiability breakdown itself is intercept-sensitive. Aim 1\n     diagnostics only (no discovery/replication split), 50 replicates/\n     cell: **1,000 total fits, ~22 minutes serial, ~5.6 minutes\n     wall-clock on 4 workers** -- cheap enough to run interactively, no\n     background job needed. A design check run as part of this planning\n     pass found the simulated data's actual mean response rate runs\n     1-2 percentage points below the naive `plogis(b_intercept)` target\n     at every grid point (expected, from the same non-collapsibility/\n     Jensen's-inequality logic this sweep investigates) -- the achieved,\n     not nominal, baseline should be reported in any write-up.\n     :::\n\n     The sweep was subsequently run in full; see \"`b_intercept` sweep:\n     results\" below (its own top-level section, placed after this list,\n     since its code chunk did not nest cleanly inside this indented\n     callout/list structure).\n- **The shareable self-contained workflow** (a standalone `.R` process\n  script + bash runner, updated generation/visualization tutorials sourcing\n  from it, and a final trimmed reporting document) is planned as a\n  follow-on piece of work once the extension decisions above are settled,\n  so that any new grid only needs to be run once against the final\n  pipeline.\n\nAims 3-6's own flagged-future-work items (Aim 3's `brms` spot-checks, Aim\n4's flat interaction-CI-width finding, Aim 5's deferred joint\ncorrelation x variance sweep, Aim 6's remedy-specific follow-ups, and the\n`furrr` load-imbalance engineering note) are unchanged and documented in\n`phase2-effect-variance-misspecification.qmd`; they will surface again in\ntheir own future documents rather than being duplicated here.\n\n## `b_intercept` sweep: results\n\nThe sweep designed and costed above (design summary: \"`b_intercept`\nsweep design and cost\" callout in \"Flagged future work\") was run (script:\n`run_b_intercept_sweep.R`) -- **sequentially rather than with `furrr`'s 4\nworkers**, given the real memory pressure this machine was found to be\nunder when this sweep was designed (swap ~87% full at the time); actual\nruntime was **20.7 minutes** (vs. the ~5.6-minute parallel estimate),\nstill cheap enough to run interactively. Results are saved to\n`results_phase2/aim1_intercept_sweep.rds` (1,000 fits x 3 terms = 3,000\nrows) and loaded directly below, not recomputed.\n\nSee `cost-estimate-b-intercept-sweep-PLAN.qmd` for the fuller design,\nexecution, and results write-up (including the same findings below in\nmore detail, a projected-vs-achieved cost comparison, and the follow-on\n\"Scenario 5 + intercept variation\" work this sweep's findings motivated).\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-b-intercept-sweep-results\n#| fig-width: 9\n#| fig-height: 6\n#| fig-cap: \"b_intercept sweep: power vs. target baseline accuracy, by representative cell and term. Vertical dotted line marks this project's real, observed baseline (~89%).\"\n\nintercept_sweep_results \u003c- readRDS(\"results_phase2/aim1_intercept_sweep.rds\")\n\nintercept_sweep_summary \u003c- intercept_sweep_results |>\n  dplyr::group_by(label, n_p, n_t, target_accuracy, term) |>\n  dplyr::summarise(\n    power            = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE),\n    sign_reliability = mean(correct_sign, na.rm = TRUE),\n    type_s_rate      = mean(sign_error[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),\n    type_m_ratio     = median(inflation_ratio[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),\n    coverage         = mean(covers_truth, na.rm = TRUE),\n    .groups = \"drop\"\n  ) |>\n  dplyr::mutate(cell_label = paste0(label, \" (n_p=\", n_p, \", n_t=\", n_t, \")\"))\n\nggplot(intercept_sweep_summary, aes(x = target_accuracy, y = power, color = term)) +\n  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.890, linetype = \"dotted\", color = \"grey40\") +\n  geom_line() +\n  geom_point() +\n  facet_wrap(~cell_label, scales = \"free_y\") +\n  scale_color_brewer(palette = \"Dark2\") +\n  labs(x = \"Target baseline accuracy (plogis(b_intercept))\", y = \"Power\", color = \"Term\") +\n  theme_minimal()\n```\n\n**Headline finding: power for all three effects generally declines as\nbaseline accuracy rises toward this project's real ~89% value**, most\nclearly for the interaction and `zPCREFp` -- confirming the concern that\nmotivated this sweep. At the \"moderate\" cell (n_p=375, n_t=35), the\ninteraction's power declines close to monotonically from 84% (50%\naccuracy) to 28% (95% accuracy); at the \"small\" cell (n_p=25, n_t=2),\n`zHLVA`'s power declines from 32% to 6% over the same range. The `n_t =\n2` pathology cell's Type S rate for `zPCREFp` also *worsens* toward\nhigher accuracy (36% -> 55% wrong-sign-given-significant), as does its\nType M ratio (4.2x -> 7.5x) -- so the text-margin identifiability\nbreakdown documented throughout the main part of this document is not\nmerely co-occurring with this project's high baseline accuracy, it is\nmeasurably *exacerbated* by it.\n\n**A specific mechanistic finding, investigated directly**: at the\n\"large\" cell (n_p=1497, n_t=136), the interaction's power looks like it\ndrops suddenly -- a flat 100% from 50-89% accuracy, then a step down to\n78% only at the most extreme point (95%) -- which could look like a\ndiscontinuity or an artifact. Inspecting the underlying per-replicate\n`estimate/std.error` ratios shows this is not a sudden change in the\ndata-generating mechanism: the median ratio declines smoothly and\ncontinuously across the *entire* sweep (5.70 -> 5.58 -> 4.92 -> 3.73 ->\n2.86), and so does the minimum (3.26 -> 3.25 -> 2.53 -> 2.05 -> 1.17).\nWhat changes abruptly is only whether that smooth decline crosses the\nfixed 95%-significance threshold (a ratio of 1.96): because the starting\nmargin at 50% accuracy is generous (median ratio ~5.7, nearly 3x the\nthreshold), it takes until the most extreme grid point for enough\nreplicates' ratios to dip below 1.96 (11 of 50 do, at 95% accuracy; zero\ndo at every lower level, including 89%, where the *minimum* ratio was\nalready down to 2.05 -- a near miss). This is a textbook case of a\nsmoothly-varying quantity producing an apparently sudden change in a\n*thresholded* summary (power) -- compounded by a genuine, accelerating\nincrease in standard error as the baseline approaches the ceiling: mean\nSE rises from 0.0095 to 0.0174 across the sweep, and the *rate* of\nincrease itself accelerates (successive ratios 1.02x, 1.14x, 1.22x,\n1.30x), loosely tracking the Fisher-information-style prediction that\nvariance in a Bernoulli outcome scales with `1/(p(1-p))` (a naive\n`1/sqrt(p(1-p))` calculation predicts a 2.29x relative SE increase from\n50% to 95% accuracy; the observed increase, 1.83x, is smaller, plausibly\nbuffered by the participant/text random-effects variance components, but\npoints the same direction). This prediction -- that a denser grid near\nthe top of the accuracy range would reveal a smooth decline rather than\na true discontinuity at exactly 95% -- was tested directly (see\n\"Follow-up: ceiling-densification check\" immediately below) and\nconfirmed.\n\n### Follow-up: ceiling-densification check (confirmed)\n\nTwo more intercept values, 92% and 97% target accuracy, were added at\nthe same 4 cells and 50 replicates/cell (script:\n`run_b_intercept_sweep_ceiling_extension.R`; 400 additional fits, 8.7\nminutes serial), specifically to test the smooth-decline prediction\nabove. Results are saved separately\n(`results_phase2/aim1_intercept_sweep_ceiling_extension.rds`) and\ncombined with the original sweep below.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-b-intercept-ceiling-extension\n#| fig-width: 9\n#| fig-height: 6\n#| fig-cap: \"b_intercept sweep with ceiling densification: power vs. target baseline accuracy, by representative cell and term, now at 7 accuracy points (adding 92% and 97% to the original 5). Vertical dotted line marks this project's real, observed baseline (~89%).\"\n\nintercept_sweep_ceiling_ext \u003c- readRDS(\"results_phase2/aim1_intercept_sweep_ceiling_extension.rds\")\n\nintercept_sweep_combined \u003c- dplyr::bind_rows(intercept_sweep_results, intercept_sweep_ceiling_ext)\n\nintercept_sweep_combined_summary \u003c- intercept_sweep_combined |>\n  dplyr::group_by(label, n_p, n_t, target_accuracy, term) |>\n  dplyr::summarise(power = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = \"drop\") |>\n  dplyr::mutate(cell_label = paste0(label, \" (n_p=\", n_p, \", n_t=\", n_t, \")\"))\n\nggplot(intercept_sweep_combined_summary, aes(x = target_accuracy, y = power, color = term)) +\n  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.890, linetype = \"dotted\", color = \"grey40\") +\n  geom_line() +\n  geom_point() +\n  facet_wrap(~cell_label, scales = \"free_y\") +\n  scale_color_brewer(palette = \"Dark2\") +\n  labs(x = \"Target baseline accuracy (plogis(b_intercept))\", y = \"Power\", color = \"Term\") +\n  theme_minimal()\n```\n\n**Confirmed**: at the \"large\" cell, the interaction's power across all 7\npoints is 100%, 100%, 100%, 100%, **92%, 78%, 68%** (50%/65%/80%/89%/\n**92%/95%/97%** accuracy) -- a smooth, monotonic decline once the two\nnew points fill in the gap, not a discontinuity at exactly 95%. The\nunderlying `estimate/std.error` ratios decline just as smoothly across\nall 7 points (median: 5.70, 5.58, 4.92, 3.73, **3.31, 2.86, 2.32**;\nminimum: 3.26, 3.25, 2.53, 2.05, **1.31, 1.17, 0.297**), and mean SE\nkeeps rising with the same accelerating pattern (0.0095, 0.0097, 0.0110,\n0.0134, **0.0146, 0.0174, 0.0221**). The same pattern generalizes beyond\nthe one cell originally flagged: the \"moderate\" cell's interaction power\nalso continues declining smoothly past the original grid's endpoint,\nfrom 48% (89%) down to 36%, 28%, and 22% at 92%/95%/97% accuracy. The\napparent \"cliff\" in the original 5-point grid was, as predicted, a grid-\nsparsity artifact rather than a true discontinuity -- confirming that\nthis project's underpowered-paradox-adjacent findings do not depend on a\nsudden qualitative change happening to fall near the observed baseline;\nthe underlying erosion is continuous and only *looks* abrupt because of\nwhere the significance threshold happens to sit relative to a sparse\ngrid.\n\n**Interpretation**: this project's own real baseline accuracy (~89%)\nsits close enough to the region where these effects begin measurably\neroding that the main Aims 1-2 document's findings should be read as\nsomewhat conservative, not baseline-independent -- a comprehension test\nwith a more moderate pass rate would likely show *better* power and\n*less* severe Type S/M error for the same underlying effect sizes, not\nworse.\n\n::: {.callout-note collapse=\"true\"}\n## Development history (collapsed -- process detail, not reportable findings)\n\nThis section preserves the process/decision narrative that accompanied the\noriginal build of Aims 1-2, condensed from `phase2-effect-variance-misspecification-PLAN.qmd`\nand `phase2-effect-variance-misspecification.qmd`. Nothing in this section\nis required to understand the results above; it documents how they were\nproduced.\n\n### Relationship to existing project simulation infrastructure\n\nThis work explicitly reused conventions already established in\n`simulation_study_complete.qmd` (Simulations 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6) and\n`power-simulation-vocabulary-cohesion.qmd`, rather than inventing new ones:\n\n- **One-at-a-time sweeps, not a full factorial.** Existing simulations vary\n  one dimension (effect size, a single variance component, or a single\n  intercept-slope correlation) at a time while holding others fixed at a\n  realistic value, to avoid combinatorial explosion. Phase 2 follows the\n  same pattern (six aims, altogether) rather than crossing effect size x\n  variance x covariance x misspecification x design strategy x\n  two-dimensional sample size all at once.\n- **Fitting**: `glmer` (fast) as the sweep workhorse, with `brms`\n  spot-checks at a handful of cells using the project's precompile-once,\n  `update()`-per-replicate pattern to avoid Stan recompilation cost across\n  replicates (not run for Aims 1-2 specifically; see flagged future work).\n- **Parallelization**: `furrr::future_pmap_dfr()` with `multisession`,\n  `furrr_options(seed = TRUE)`, hierarchical seeds, 4 workers with a\n  `setTimeLimit()` guard, following Phase 1's memory-safety lessons.\n- **Outcome-quality classification**: converged-clean / converged-singular\n  / optimizer-warning / error, reused verbatim from Phase 1's helper\n  functions.\n\n### Confirmed decisions (made before building Aims 1-2)\n\n1. **Scope**: all six aims cover **three effects** -- `zHLVA` (main),\n   `zPCREFp` (main), and `zHLVA:zPCREFp` (interaction) -- rather than the\n   interaction alone.\n2. **Aim 2 split axis**: left configurable (`split_margin =\n   \"participants_only\"` vs. `\"both\"`) rather than fixed; both variants can\n   be run and compared. More\nbroadly, `zPCREFp`'s `n_t=2` replication rate meets or exceeds every larger\n`n_t` at the same `n_p` in 9 of 11 `n_p` cells -- the same underpowered-\nparadox signature carrying over from Aim 1's power surface into Aim 2's\nstricter replication criterion, not a genuine advantage of the smallest\ntext sample.\n\n### A broader synthesis\n\nPutting the two reader questions from the top of this section back together\nwith everything above:\n\n- **For planning**: `zHLVA` (the participant-level effect) needs only a\n  moderate participant sample (saturates by `n_p~100`-`375`) and is\n  comparatively insensitive to text sample size once `n_t>=6`. `zPCREFp`\n  and the interaction need growth on **both** margins, and specifically\n  need `n_t` to clear roughly 20-30 texts before the small-`n_t` pathology\n  fully resolves -- a design implication independent of whether a\n  particular study happens to land in the \"paradoxically inflated\" `n_t=2`\n  regime or not. Baseline accuracy should also be budgeted for: a\n  comprehension test calibrated closer to 50-75% accuracy (rather than this\n  project's ~89%) would show *better* power for the same underlying effect\n  sizes.\n- **For evaluation**: a \"significant\" `zPCREFp` or interaction result from\n  a study with very few texts (especially `n_t=2`, the modal value in this\n  project's own literature review) should be read with real suspicion --\n  not because small samples are underpowered in the usual sense, but\n  because the specific `n_t=2` identifiability breakdown documented below\n  inflates both the raw significance rate and the replication rate at\n  exactly that sample size, for reasons unrelated to whether a real effect\n  is present.\n- The \"underpowered paradox\" is the sharpest single illustration of the\n  evaluation-side risk, and is retained here as such -- but as this section\n  has shown, it does not characterize every diagnostic (sign reliability,\n  Type S, Type M all behave conventionally), and it is only one of several\n  observations relevant to planning and evaluation questions, not the\n  single organizing finding of this analysis.\n\nFull mechanistic detail on *why* `n_t=2` produces this pattern (the\nrandom-effects-identifiability argument, the singular-fit diagnostic, and\nthe Wald-SE-deflation mechanism) is given in \"Why can an estimate be\n'significant' when the true effect is exactly zero?\" above.\n\n## Development note\n\nThis document was produced entirely from already-computed `.rds` files\n(`run_scenario5_full.R`, `run_scenario5_intercept_sweep.R`); no new\nsimulation was run to produce it. I have thorough coverage of all three documents now. Let me compile the final answer.

## Summary of findings

All three files live in `/Users/robertdavies/Dropbox/teaching-critical-thinking/` and are part of a single "Phase 2 parametric simulation program" (Aims 1–2) studying a reading-comprehension study (`zHLVA` = participant vocabulary, `zPCREFp` = text cohesion, their interaction, outcome = binary comprehension accuracy). **This is not classic "test-score/true-score-theory" content** (no CTT reliability formulas, no simple group-comparison t-tests) — instead "measurement error" appears only as an optional reliability-attenuation feature (`reliability_hlva`, `reliability_pcref`, lines 104-105, 124-128, 151-158 of the tutorial), and "power/error/replication" concepts are explored via mixed-effects logistic regression (`glmer`) simulations, not a simple t-test/ANOVA teaching example.

### 1. Purpose, audience, and workflow across the three files

- **`synthetic-data-…-draft-development.qmd`** (2206 lines) is the primary **working/reporting document**: a restructured, broadened version of an earlier "Aims 1-2" report, self-described (lines 24-45) as covering Aim 1 (effect-size × sample-size sweep with a full error taxonomy) and Aim 2 (discovery/replication split), for the accuracy outcome only. It mixes narrative, live code, tables, figures, a "Flagged future work" section, and a collapsed "Development history" (process notes, timing benchmarks, smoke test) — i.e., development notebook + near-final report combined.
- **`synthetic-data-…-draft-review.qmd`** (1543 lines) is explicitly a **downstream review document** (title: "Review: densified grid (Scenario 5) …", lines 1-44): it analyzes new results (an 11×9 densified sample-size grid, 100 reps/cell, plus a full-grid `b_intercept` sweep) computed via background jobs, explicitly states it "does not modify or supersede" the development document, and cross-references it throughout, flagging/explaining discrepancies (e.g., the "grid-density caveat," lines 1410-1451) rather than treating them as contradictions.
- **`simulation-pipeline-tutorial-aims-1-2.qmd`** (763 lines) is a **separate pedagogical walkthrough**, explicitly framed (lines 18-39) as *not* a report but a "teaching walk-through" that extracts and explains, piece-by-piece, only the data-generation/model-fitting/orchestration code behind the Aims 1-2 report — deliberately excluding plotting code, findings/discussion, and the smoke test (though it points to it).

**Workflow**: development.qmd (original build + findings) → review.qmd (re-analysis at a denser grid, reviewing/validating/extending) → simulation-pipeline-tutorial (a teaching artifact extracted from the development doc's code, written after the fact to explain the pipeline mechanics to a reader/learner, independent of the substantive findings).

### 2. Data-generating process

Common DGP across all three (`generate_data_p2()`, tutorial lines 88-191, development lines 252-356): a crossed participant × text design.
- Participants (default n=200) each get a true `zHLVA ~ N(0,1)` and a participant random intercept `~N(0, sd_participant=0.69)` (optionally correlated random slope for `zPCREFp`, Aim-5-only, default 0).
- Texts (default n=20) get true `zPCREFp ~ N(0,1)` (or a "widened" two-cluster design `rep(c(-1.5,1.5)) + N(0,0.3)` for Aim 6) and a text random intercept `~N(0, sd_text=0.41)`.
- Each participant is randomly assigned `k = min(10, n_texts)` texts, each expanded to `questions_per_text=4` (default) item-level rows.
- Outcome: logistic model, `eta = b_intercept(2.093) + (b_hlva(0.363)+slope)*zHLVA + (b_pcref(0.095)+slope)*zPCREFp + b_interaction(0.054)*zHLVA*zPCREFp + u_participant + u_text`; `prob=plogis(eta)`; `response ~ Bernoulli(prob)`.
- Optional measurement-reliability attenuation (`reliability_hlva`, `reliability_pcref`, default 1 = no error) blends true scores with independent noise — the only "measurement error" concept present, used only by Aim 6 (not actually run in these documents).
- Sample-size grids: `n_p_grid = c(25,100,375,725,1300,1497)`, `n_t_grid = c(2,10,35,85,136)` (30 cells; development/tutorial), densified in review.qmd's "Scenario 5" to 11×9=99 log-spaced cells with 100 reps/cell (vs. 50).
- Effect-size sweep grids (one-at-a-time, 5 points each centered on empirical estimate): `b_hlva_grid = c(0,0.18,0.363,0.7,1.0)`, `b_pcref_grid = c(0,0.05,0.095,0.2,0.35)`, `b_interaction_grid = c(0,0.025,0.054,0.10,0.20)`.
- `b_intercept` sweep (development lines 1863-2066; review's Scenario-5 full-grid version): target baseline accuracies 50/65/80/89(observed)/95%, later densified at the ceiling to add 92%/97%.
- Aim 2 discovery/replication pairs generated by `generate_data_p2_pair()` (tutorial lines 415-468), splitting total N into two halves — `split_margin="participants_only"` (shared texts) vs `"both"` (independent texts too).

### 3. R code structure/approach

- Tidyverse-centric (`dplyr`, `tidyr`, `purrr`), `lme4::glmer` for fitting, `MASS::mvrnorm` called only via `::` (never attached, to avoid masking `dplyr::select`) — explicitly flagged as a reusable gotcha (tutorial lines 268-276).
- Review doc additionally loads `patchwork`, `RColorBrewer`, `ggdist`, `scico` for visualization.
- Core functions: `generate_data_p2()` / `generate_data_p2_pair()` (DGP), `fit_model_p2()`/`fit_model_p2_guarded()` (fit with `re_spec` in `"correct"`/`"misspecified"`/`"full_slopes"`, warning-capturing via `withCallingHandlers`, timeout via `setTimeLimit`), `extract_terms_of_interest_p2()`, `diagnose_coefs_p2()` (computes CI, significance, sign/magnitude errors, bias, coverage), `combine_replication_p2()`, and the orchestrator `run_aim1_aim2_cell()` (tutorial lines 508-578; development lines 516-595) which deterministically seeds and runs both Aim 1 and Aim 2 fits per cell.
- Full design: 3 sweeps × 5 effect values × 30 cells × 50 reps = 22,500 combinations × 3 fits (Aim1 full + Aim2 discovery/replication) = 67,500 total `glmer` fits, run as a detached background script `run_aim1_aim2_full.R` with `furrr::plan(multisession, workers=4)` (~5h). Scenario 5 (review doc) used 11×9 grid ×100 reps ×8 workers (~14.2h actual vs ~35.9h estimated at 4 workers). Results cached to `.rds` files under `results_phase2/` and loaded, never recomputed inline — explicitly justified (tutorial lines 648-653) as good practice ("a simulation of this size should not be run inside the document that reports on it").
- Summarization: `group_by()`/`summarise()` over `term × n_p × n_t` (or pooled margins) computing power, type_1_rate, sign_reliability, type_s_rate, type_m_ratio, median_bias, coverage, rmse_raw/trimmed (development doc's diagnostic table lines 129-139). Visualization: heatmap "surfaces" (viridis/cividis/scico diverging "vik" palette), power/error curves faceted by term×n_t, dot "funnel" plots of individual estimates.

### 4. Key concepts and code mapping

- **Sampling distributions / replication variability**: 50–100 replicates per grid cell, varying only the random seed (`rep` index) — visualized in the "funnel plot" (`fig-aim1-distribution-explainer` / `-s5`, development line 1099, review line 717).
- **Measurement error vs sampling error**: measurement error modeled only via `reliability_hlva/pcref` attenuation (Aim 6, not actually exercised in these docs' results); sampling error is the Wald SE from `glmer`, propagating into CIs.
- **NHST / power / Type I & II error**: explicit terminology callout (development lines 48-59) defining Type I = false positive, Type II = false negative; `power = mean(excludes_zero)` at non-zero effect; `type_1_rate = mean(excludes_zero)` at effect=0 (`diagnose_coefs_p2`, `summarize_p2_metrics`).
- **Type S / Type M errors (Marek et al. 2022 framing)**: `sign_error`/`type_s_rate` and `inflation_ratio`/`type_m_ratio`, computed conditional on significance — directly coded in `diagnose_coefs_p2()` (tutorial lines 508-522) and summarized in the diagnostics table (development lines 129-139).
- **Discovery/replication (Aim 2)**: `generate_data_p2_pair()` + `combine_replication_p2()`, mirroring Marek et al.'s Fig. 3e design; reported as unconditional and conditional replication rate.
- **"Underpowered paradox"**: central narrative finding — small `n_t` (esp. `n_t=2`) singular/degenerate random-effects fits paradoxically inflate apparent significance/power/replication for `zPCREFp`, explained mechanistically via a "Why can an estimate be significant when the true effect is exactly zero?" subsection (development ~line 1201, review ~line 829) tied to random-effects identifiability and Wald-SE deflation.
- **Neyman-Pearson/process-control framing**: not explicitly named as such in these three files (no direct use of that phrase found), but the Type I/II/S/M taxonomy and fixed-threshold (95% CI / p<.05) framing throughout is the implicit NP decision-procedure lens; multiple-comparisons/threshold-sweep extension is explicitly deferred (development lines 233-235, 1776-1781).

### 5. Pedagogical structure of the tutorial

`simulation-pipeline-tutorial-aims-1-2.qmd` is organized as 8 numbered "Steps" (packages → DGP function → model-fitting/classification → sample-size/effect grids → discovery/replication pair function → diagnostics/orchestrator → note on the external background run → loading saved results into report-ready tibbles), each followed by a detailed prose walkthrough that goes argument-by-argument / line-block-by-line-block through the code (e.g., "a. Arguments and defaults," "b. Participant-level random effects," …), explaining both *what* each code chunk does and *why* (e.g., why `MASS` isn't attached, why Wald CIs are used for speed, why seeds are deterministically hashed). Tone is explanatory/expository, assuming R/tidyverse familiarity but walking a reader unfamiliar with this specific pipeline through it; it explicitly scopes out plotting and substantive results, and ends with a callout pointing to the 24-cell, ~6-second smoke test in the development doc as a hands-on starting point.

### 6. TODOs / open issues / unresolved items (mainly in development.qmd)

- **"Flagged future work"** section (development lines 1774-1911):
  - Significance-threshold / multiple-comparisons (Bonferroni) sweep explicitly deferred/untested.
  - Three "extension decisions": (1) densify grid + double replicates → became review.qmd's Scenario 5 (now done); (2) extend sample-size range beyond real N (Scenario 6) — cost benchmark completed (lines 1823-1862) but the decision to actually run it remains open; (3) `b_intercept` sweep — designed, costed, and run (results included), with a follow-up ceiling-densification confirmed.
  - "Shareable self-contained workflow" (standalone `.R` script + bash runner, updated tutorials, trimmed reporting doc) is noted as planned future work, not yet done.
  - Aims 3–6's own flagged items (Aim 3 `brms` spot-checks, Aim 4's flat interaction-CI-width finding, Aim 5's deferred joint correlation×variance sweep, Aim 6 remedies, `furrr` load-imbalance) are acknowledged but deferred to future documents.
  - Wald CIs (vs. profile-likelihood/bootstrap) flagged as a possible separate source of miscalibration, not investigated (lines 146-151).
- **review.qmd**: frames itself as provisional/first-pass ("analyzed here for the first time," line 27); explicitly calls out and resolves an apparent discrepancy (grid-density pooling artifact, lines 1410-1451) as something a reader might mistake for a real finding; "Development note" (closing section) points to `AGENTS.md` and a cost-estimate planning doc for further rationale, implying ongoing/external tracking of next steps rather than closure within the document itself.
- Both working documents repeatedly caution that the simplified random-intercept-only DGP is "coarser" than the real fitted model's richer random-slope structure (Aim 5's subject, not yet documented) — an acknowledged simplification/limitation rather than a resolved issue.

Author submits manuscript to editor.\n#'   2. Editor sends manuscript out to two reviewers (fan-out).\n#'   3. Reviewers submit reviews back to editor (fan-in).\n#'   4. Editor makes a decision and informs the author.\n#' A dashed loop-back arrow underneath represents \"reject with\n#' revise & resubmit -> repeat\" until accept/reject.\n#'\n#' Requires person-grid.R and testing-sequence.R sourced first\n#' (same folder).\n#'\n#' Quarto usage:\n#'   ```{r}\n#'   source(\"person-grid.R\")\n#'   source(\"testing-sequence.R\")\n#'   source(\"peer-review-workflow.R\")\n#'   peer_review_workflow()$plot\n#'   ```\n#' ============================================================\n\nlibrary(ggplot2)\n\n#' Build the peer-review workflow diagram.\n#' @return list(plot = ggplot object)\npeer_review_workflow \u003c- function() {\n\n  researcher_col \u003c- list(person = \"#3B6EA5\", screen = \"#CFE8FF\")\n  editor_col     \u003c- list(person = \"#B0562D\", screen = \"#FFDCC5\")\n  reviewer_col   \u003c- list(person = \"#3B9E5F\", screen = \"#D3F5DF\")\n\n  pos \u003c- list(\n    researcher1 = c(0,    0),\n    editor1     = c(5.0,  0),\n    reviewerA   = c(10.5, 3.4),\n    reviewerB   = c(10.5, -3.4),\n    editor2     = c(16.0, 0),\n    researcher2 = c(21.0, 0)\n  )\n\n  icon_df \u003c- function(name, kind, cols) {\n    p \u003c- pos[[name]]\n    d \u003c- person_at_computer(kind = kind, ox = p[1], oy = p[2],\n                             person_color = cols$person, screen_color = cols$screen)\n    d$icon \u003c- name\n    d\n  }\n\n  icons \u003c- rbind(\n    icon_df(\"researcher1\", \"A\", researcher_col),\n    icon_df(\"editor1\",     \"B\", editor_col),\n    icon_df(\"reviewerA\",   \"A\", reviewer_col),\n    icon_df(\"reviewerB\",   \"B\", reviewer_col),\n    icon_df(\"editor2\",     \"B\", editor_col),\n    icon_df(\"researcher2\", \"A\", researcher_col)\n  )\n  icons$poly_id \u003c- paste(icons$icon, icons$part, icons$role)\n\n  right_of \u003c- function(name, dy = 0.9) c(pos[[name]][1] + 1.25, pos[[name]][2] + dy)\n  left_of  \u003c- function(name, dy = 0.9) c(pos[[name]][1] - 0.55, pos[[name]][2] + dy)\n\n  straight_arrows \u003c- rbind(\n    data.frame(rbind(c(right_of(\"researcher1\"), left_of(\"editor1\")))),\n    data.frame(rbind(c(right_of(\"editor2\"),     left_of(\"researcher2\"))))\n  )\n  names(straight_arrows) \u003c- c(\"x\", \"y\", \"xend\", \"yend\")\n\n  curve_arrows \u003c- data.frame(rbind(\n    c(right_of(\"editor1\")[1],   right_of(\"editor1\")[2],   left_of(\"reviewerA\")[1], left_of(\"reviewerA\")[2],  0.30),\n    c(right_of(\"editor1\")[1],   right_of(\"editor1\")[2],   left_of(\"reviewerB\")[1], left_of(\"reviewerB\")[2], -0.30),\n    c(right_of(\"reviewerA\")[1], right_of(\"reviewerA\")[2], left_of(\"editor2\")[1],   left_of(\"editor2\")[2],   -0.30),\n    c(right_of(\"reviewerB\")[1], right_of(\"reviewerB\")[2], left_of(\"editor2\")[1],   left_of(\"editor2\")[2],    0.30)\n  ))\n  names(curve_arrows) \u003c- c(\"x\", \"y\", \"xend\", \"yend\", \"curvature\")\n\n  loop_arrow \u003c- data.frame(\n    x = pos$researcher2[1] + 0.35, y = -7.0,\n    xend = pos$researcher1[1] + 0.35, yend = -7.0\n  )\n\n  step_captions \u003c- data.frame(\n    x = c(pos$researcher1[1] + 0.35, pos$editor1[1] + 0.35,\n          (pos$reviewerA[1] + pos$reviewerB[1]) / 2, pos$editor2[1] + 0.35),\n    y = -6.0,\n    label = c(\"1. Submit\\nmanuscript\",\n              \"2. Editor sends\\nto review\",\n              \"3. Reviewers\\nsubmit reviews\",\n              \"4. Decision: accept /\\nR&R / reject\")\n  )\n\n  role_labels \u003c- data.frame(\n    x = c(pos$researcher1[1] + 0.35, pos$editor1[1] + 0.35,\n          pos$reviewerA[1] + 0.35, pos$reviewerB[1] + 0.35,\n          pos$editor2[1] + 0.35, pos$researcher2[1] + 0.35),\n    # Reviewer A's label needs the same +2.4 clearance from icon centre\n    # used for the on-centerline roles; the previous +1.4 offset landed\n    # on the icon itself. Reviewer B keeps its original offset since its\n    # label already clears the icon without crowding the step captions\n    # below it.\n    y = c(2.4, 2.4, pos$reviewerA[2] + 2.4, -4.8, 2.4, 2.4),\n    label = c(\"Author\", \"Editor\", \"Reviewer 1\", \"Reviewer 2\", \"Editor\", \"Author\")\n  )\n\n  plot \u003c- ggplot() +\n    geom_polygon(data = icons, aes(x, y, group = poly_id, fill = fill)) +\n    geom_segment(data = straight_arrows,\n                 aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),\n                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, \"cm\"), type = \"closed\"),\n                 linewidth = 0.6, color = \"grey30\")\n\n  for (i in seq_len(nrow(curve_arrows))) {\n    plot \u003c- plot + geom_curve(data = curve_arrows[i, ],\n                               aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),\n                               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, \"cm\"), type = \"closed\"),\n                               linewidth = 0.6, color = \"grey30\",\n                               curvature = curve_arrows$curvature[i])\n  }\n\n  plot \u003c- plot +\n    geom_curve(data = loop_arrow,\n               aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),\n               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, \"cm\"), type = \"closed\"),\n               linewidth = 0.5, color = \"grey55\", linetype = \"dashed\",\n               curvature = -0.15) +\n    annotate(\"text\", x = (pos$researcher1[1] + pos$researcher2[1]) / 2 + 0.35,\n             y = -7.9, label = \"reject with revise & resubmit \\u2192 repeat the cycle\",\n             size = 3.3, color = \"grey40\", fontface = \"italic\") +\n    geom_text(data = role_labels, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.1, color = \"grey20\") +\n    geom_text(data = step_captions, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.4,\n              lineheight = 0.95, fontface = \"bold\") +\n    scale_fill_identity() +\n    coord_equal(clip = \"off\", ylim = c(-8.8, 5.8)) +\n    theme_void() +\n    theme(plot.margin = margin(20, 25, 20, 25))\n\n  list(plot = plot)\n}\n"},"elapsedMs":0}</script></tool-result></div>

<div><tool-result call-id="toolu_01B9XMLXgzbPUbsGdmFwgU53"><script type="application/json">{"version":1,"status":"success","result":{"type":"text","value":"[File: 9.1KB, 221 lines, showing lines 1-221]\n1\t#' =======================================...[truncated, total 10134 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"[File: 9.1KB, 221 lines, showing lines 1-221]\n#' ============================================================\n#' concept-map.R\n#'\n#' A general \"N columns of ellipses, many-to-many curved links between\n#' adjacent columns\" diagram, in the style of McElreath's Statistical\n#' Rethinking Figure 1.2 (theories -> process models -> statistical\n#' models). Built from plain polygons + ggplot2::geom_curve, so it\n#' needs nothing beyond ggplot2.\n#'\n#' Quarto usage (the exact figure you described):\n#'\n#'   ```{r}\n#'   #| label: fig-theory-process-stats\n#'   #| fig-cap: \"Many theories and processes can imply the same statistical result\"\n#'   source(\"concept-map.R\")\n#'\n#'   columns \u003c- list(\n#'     c(\"Words we experience more are easier to access\",\n#'       \"Experience does not matter to access\",\n#'       \"Words we experience early in life are easier to access\"),\n#'     c(\"Neural network connections change\",\n#'       \"Neural word representations change\",\n#'       \"Word recognition decisions change\"),\n#'     c(\"Experience correlates with word recognition speed\",\n#'       \"Experience does not correlate with word recognition speed\")\n#'   )\n#'   titles \u003c- c(\"Theories\", \"Process models\", \"Statistical models\")\n#'\n#'   # edges[[k]]: which item in column k links to which item in column k+1\n#'   # (1-based indices, one row per link -- repeat a `from` or `to` for\n#'   # many-to-many links)\n#'   edges \u003c- list(\n#'     data.frame(from = c(1,1,2,3,3), to = c(1,2,3,1,2)),   # theories -> processes\n#'     data.frame(from = c(1,2,3,3),   to = c(1,1,2,1))       # processes -> stats\n#'   )\n#'\n#'   concept_map(columns, edges, titles)$plot\n#'   ```\n#' ============================================================\n\nlibrary(ggplot2)\n\n# ---- geometry ------------------------------------------------------------\n\nellipse_pts \u003c- function(cx, cy, rx, ry, n = 72) {\n  t \u003c- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n)\n  data.frame(x = cx + rx * cos(t), y = cy + ry * sin(t))\n}\n\nwrap_label \u003c- function(label, width = 16) {\n  paste(strwrap(label, width = width), collapse = \"\\n\")\n}\n\n# ---- main function ---------------------------------------------------\n\n#' @param columns    a list of character vectors, one per column, each\n#'                   holding that column's node labels top-to-bottom.\n#' @param edges      a list of length length(columns)-1; edges[[k]] is a\n#'                   data frame with columns `from` and `to`: 1-based\n#'                   indices into columns[[k]] and columns[[k+1]]\n#'                   respectively. Repeat an index for many-to-many links.\n#' @param titles     optional character vector of column headings.\n#' @param rx, ry     ellipse half-width / half-height. Either a single\n#'                   value (applied to every column) or a vector of\n#'                   length length(columns) giving a separate size per\n#'                   column -- useful when one column's labels are much\n#'                   longer than another's (e.g. long theory sentences\n#'                   vs. short process names).\n#' @param dx, dy     horizontal spacing between columns / vertical\n#'                   spacing between ellipses within a column. Note `dx`\n#'                   is a single fixed gap regardless of per-column `rx`;\n#'                   a warning is issued if it's too small to clear two\n#'                   adjacent columns' ellipses.\n#' @param wrap_width characters per line before wrapping label text.\n#'                   Single value or one per column, as for `rx`/`ry`.\n#' @param fill_colors  one fill colour per column; recycled/extended\n#'                   with a default pastel palette if too few given.\n#' @param curvature  passed to geom_curve (0 = straight lines).\n#' @param arrows     if TRUE (default), draw a small arrowhead at each\n#'                   curve's target end. Set FALSE for plain connecting\n#'                   lines, closer to McElreath's original figure (which\n#'                   shows correspondence between columns, not\n#'                   directional causality).\n#'\n#' @return list(plot = ggplot object, nodes = node data frame,\n#'   edges = edge data frame used for the curves)\nconcept_map \u003c- function(columns, edges, titles = NULL,\n                         rx = 1.15, ry = 0.62, dx = 3.3, dy = 1.55,\n                         wrap_width = 16,\n                         fill_colors = c(\"#F6DCC7\", \"#CFE3F5\", \"#D9E8CE\", \"#E9D8F0\", \"#F5E3B0\"),\n                         edge_color = \"#888888\", edge_alpha = 0.7, curvature = 0.2,\n                         arrows = TRUE) {\n  k \u003c- length(columns)\n  stopifnot(length(edges) == k - 1)\n  if (length(fill_colors) \u003c k) {\n    fill_colors \u003c- grDevices::colorRampPalette(fill_colors)(k)\n  }\n\n  # rx/ry/wrap_width can be a single value (applied to every column) or\n  # a vector with one entry per column.\n  recycle_per_column \u003c- function(val, name) {\n    if (length(val) == 1) return(rep(val, k))\n    if (length(val) == k) return(val)\n    stop(sprintf(\"`%s` must have length 1 or length(columns) = %d, not %d.\",\n                 name, k, length(val)))\n  }\n  rx \u003c- recycle_per_column(rx, \"rx\")\n  ry \u003c- recycle_per_column(ry, \"ry\")\n  wrap_width \u003c- recycle_per_column(wrap_width, \"wrap_width\")\n\n  # dx is a single fixed column spacing; if per-column rx makes two\n  # neighbouring ellipses wider than that gap, warn rather than silently\n  # rendering overlapping ellipses.\n  for (ci in seq_len(k - 1)) {\n    min_dx \u003c- rx[ci] + rx[ci + 1]\n    if (dx \u003c= min_dx) {\n      warning(sprintf(\n        paste(\"dx = %.2f may be too small for columns %d and %d\",\n              \"(rx = %.2f and %.2f): their ellipses may overlap.\",\n              \"Consider increasing dx.\"),\n        dx, ci, ci + 1, rx[ci], rx[ci + 1]\n      ))\n    }\n  }\n\n  # Validate edge indices up front, so a typo (e.g. an off-by-one, or a\n  # `from`/`to` swapped) fails with a message naming the column and the\n  # offending index -- rather than silently dropping the edge (as NA\n  # coordinates) later and only surfacing a generic ggplot warning.\n  for (ci in seq_len(k - 1)) {\n    e \u003c- edges[[ci]]\n    n_from \u003c- length(columns[[ci]])\n    n_to \u003c- length(columns[[ci + 1]])\n    bad_from \u003c- e$from[!(e$from %in% seq_len(n_from))]\n    bad_to \u003c- e$to[!(e$to %in% seq_len(n_to))]\n    if (length(bad_from) > 0) {\n      stop(sprintf(\n        \"edges[[%d]]$from has out-of-range value(s) %s: column %d ('%s') only has %d item(s), so valid indices are 1..%d.\",\n        ci, paste(unique(bad_from), collapse = \", \"), ci,\n        if (!is.null(titles)) titles[ci] else paste(\"column\", ci), n_from, n_from\n      ))\n    }\n    if (length(bad_to) > 0) {\n      stop(sprintf(\n        \"edges[[%d]]$to has out-of-range value(s) %s: column %d ('%s') only has %d item(s), so valid indices are 1..%d.\",\n        ci, paste(unique(bad_to), collapse = \", \"), ci + 1,\n        if (!is.null(titles)) titles[ci + 1] else paste(\"column\", ci + 1), n_to, n_to\n      ))\n    }\n  }\n\n  # node layout: column i at x = (i-1)*dx, items centred vertically,\n  # using that column's own rx/ry/wrap_width.\n  nodes \u003c- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(k), function(ci) {\n    labels \u003c- columns[[ci]]\n    m \u003c- length(labels)\n    data.frame(\n      col = ci, idx = seq_len(m),\n      x = (ci - 1) * dx,\n      y = (m - 1) / 2 * dy - (seq_len(m) - 1) * dy,\n      label = vapply(labels, wrap_label, character(1), width = wrap_width[ci]),\n      fill = fill_colors[ci],\n      rx = rx[ci], ry = ry[ci],\n      stringsAsFactors = FALSE\n    )\n  }))\n  nodes$node_id \u003c- paste(nodes$col, nodes$idx)\n\n  node_xy \u003c- function(ci, i) {\n    row \u003c- nodes[nodes$col == ci & nodes$idx == i, ]\n    c(x = row$x, y = row$y, rx = row$rx)\n  }\n\n  # edge endpoints: right edge of source ellipse -> left edge of target,\n  # each using its own node's rx (so differently-sized ellipses still\n  # meet at their actual boundaries).\n  edge_df \u003c- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(k - 1), function(ci) {\n    e \u003c- edges[[ci]]\n    do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(e)), function(j) {\n      p1 \u003c- node_xy(ci, e$from[j])\n      p2 \u003c- node_xy(ci + 1, e$to[j])\n      data.frame(x = p1[\"x\"] + p1[\"rx\"], y = p1[\"y\"],\n                 xend = p2[\"x\"] - p2[\"rx\"], yend = p2[\"y\"])\n    }))\n  }))\n\n  # ellipse polygons, each at its own node's rx/ry\n  ellipse_df \u003c- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(nodes)), function(i) {\n    n \u003c- nodes[i, ]\n    e \u003c- ellipse_pts(n$x, n$y, n$rx, n$ry)\n    e$node_id \u003c- n$node_id\n    e$fill \u003c- n$fill\n    e\n  }))\n\n  title_df \u003c- NULL\n  if (!is.null(titles)) {\n    top_y \u003c- max(nodes$y + nodes$ry) + 0.6\n    title_df \u003c- data.frame(x = unique(nodes$x), y = top_y, label = titles)\n  }\n\n  plot \u003c- ggplot() +\n    geom_curve(data = edge_df, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),\n               curvature = curvature, color = edge_color, alpha = edge_alpha,\n               linewidth = 0.6,\n               arrow = if (arrows) arrow(length = unit(0.12, \"cm\"), type = \"closed\") else NULL) +\n    geom_polygon(data = ellipse_df, aes(x, y, group = node_id, fill = fill),\n                 color = \"#555555\", linewidth = 0.4) +\n    scale_fill_identity() +\n    geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.2, lineheight = 0.9) +\n    coord_equal() +\n    theme_void()\n\n  if (!is.null(title_df)) {\n    plot \u003c- plot + geom_text(data = title_df, aes(x, y, label = label),\n                              fontface = \"bold\", size = 4.5)\n  }\n\n  list(plot = plot, nodes = nodes, edges = edge_df)\n}\n"},"elapsedMs":0}</script></tool-result></div>
