It's the data-generating and plotting counterpart to\n`testing-sequence.R`'s icon sequence (same narrative, numbers instead of\npictograms).\n\nThe simulation is deliberately built **trial-level up** rather than\ngenerating a continuous score and rounding/clipping it: every simulated\nperson's score is the sum of 40 independent correct/incorrect item\nresponses, so it is *structurally* impossible for a simulated score to\nfall outside `[0, 40]` — there's no clipping step anywhere in the script,\nbecause none is needed.\n\nAfter working through it, you should be able to:\n\n- explain why `mu`, `reliability`/`sd_true`, and `n_items` jointly\n  determine the simulation rather than being three free knobs;\n- generate a sample, a repeated-studies grid, and a covariate-correlated\n  sample of your own;\n- predict, roughly, how a requested `r_with_x` will be attenuated at a\n  given `reliability`.\n\n## Prerequisites / assumptions\n\n- **Packages**: `ggplot2`, and `ggdist` for the dot-pile figures\n  (`plot_dotpile()`, `plot_dotpile_grid()`).\n- **Sourcing**: standalone — no other script in this set needs to be\n  sourced first.\n- **Reader background**: some familiarity with classical test theory\n  terms (reliability, true score) is helpful but not required — the key\n  ideas are explained below. Basic `ggplot2` familiarity assumed.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: source-script\nlibrary(ggdist)\nsource(\"sampling-distributions.R\")\n```\n\n## How it works: the process\n\n```{r}\n#| label: model-equation\n#| echo: false\n#| results: asis\ncat(\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{Ability (logit scale):} \\\\quad \\\\theta_i \\\\sim N(\\\\theta_\\\\mu, \\\\theta_\\\\sigma)\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{Per-item probability:} \\\\quad p_i = \\\\text{plogis}(\\\\theta_i)\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{Observed score:} \\\\quad Y_i \\\\sim \\\\text{Binomial}(40, p_i) \\\\quad \\\\in \\\\{0, \\\\dots, 40\\\\}\",\n  \"$$\",\n  sep = \"\\n\"\n)\n```\n\nA `Binomial(40, p_i)` draw is the vectorized equivalent of summing 40\nindependent Bernoulli (correct/incorrect) trials, so the model above\n*is* the trial-level process described in the aims, just computed\nefficiently rather than looped item-by-item.\n\n```{mermaid}\nflowchart LR\n    A[\"calibrate_ability()\\nsolve theta_mu, theta_sigma\\nto hit target mu + reliability\\n(or mu + sd_true)\"] --> B[\"simulate_vocab_data()\\ndraw theta_i per person,\\np_i = plogis(theta_i),\\nscore_i ~ Binomial(40, p_i)\"]\n    B --> C[\"plot_dots() / plot_dotpile() /\\nplot_histogram() / plot_scatter()\"]\n    B --> D[\"simulate_studies()\\nrepeat simulate_vocab_data()\\nper independent 'study'\"]\n    D --> E[\"plot_histogram_grid() /\\nplot_dotpile_grid()\\n(facet_wrap(~study))\"]\n```\n\nThe central design idea: **you don't set the ability distribution's mean\nand spread directly.** You set the things that matter pedagogically — the\ntest's mean score (`mu`) and its reliability (`reliability`, or\nalternatively a target spread `sd_true`) — and `calibrate_ability()`\nnumerically solves for the underlying `theta_mu`/`theta_sigma` that\nreproduce them, because for a fixed test length, mean/reliability/spread\nare mathematically linked, not three independently free knobs.\n\n## Element-by-element walkthrough\n\n### Calibration machinery: `expect_theta()` and `implied_moments()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-expect-theta\n#| eval: false\nexpect_theta \u003c- function(f, theta_mu, theta_sigma) {\n  integrate(function(theta) f(theta) * dnorm(theta, theta_mu, theta_sigma),\n            lower = theta_mu - 10 * theta_sigma,\n            upper = theta_mu + 10 * theta_sigma)$value\n}\n```\n\n`expect_theta()` computes $E[f(\\theta)]$ for $\\theta \\sim N(\\theta_\\mu,\n\\theta_\\sigma)$ by plain numerical integration (base R `integrate()`, no\nextra dependency) — used to get exact expectations like $E[p_i]$ or\n$E[p_i^2]$ without resorting to Monte Carlo.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-implied-moments\n#| eval: false\nimplied_moments \u003c- function(theta_mu, theta_sigma, n_items) {\n  p_bar  \u003c- expect_theta(plogis, theta_mu, theta_sigma)\n  p2_bar \u003c- expect_theta(function(th) plogis(th)^2, theta_mu, theta_sigma)\n  pq_bar \u003c- expect_theta(function(th) plogis(th) * (1 - plogis(th)), theta_mu, theta_sigma)\n\n  mean_score  \u003c- n_items * p_bar\n  var_true    \u003c- n_items^2 * (p2_bar - p_bar^2)\n  var_error   \u003c- n_items * pq_bar\n  reliability \u003c- var_true / (var_true + var_error)\n  # ...\n}\n```\n\nGiven a candidate `(theta_mu, theta_sigma)`, this works out what mean\nscore, \"true\"-score variance (between-person spread), measurement-error\nvariance (within-person, item-sampling noise), and reliability\n(`var_true / (var_true + var_error)`) that choice *implies* — i.e. it runs\nthe model forward analytically. `calibrate_ability()` then runs this\nbackward: searching for the `(theta_mu, theta_sigma)` whose\n`implied_moments()` output matches your targets.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-implied-moments\nimplied_moments(theta_mu = 0, theta_sigma = 1.3, n_items = 40)\n```\n\n### Solving for ability parameters: `calibrate_ability()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-calibrate-ability-signature\n#| eval: false\ncalibrate_ability \u003c- function(mu, reliability = 0.80, sd_true = NULL, n_items = 40) {\n  # ...\n}\n```\n\nTwo calibration targets are supported, and they're **mutually\nexclusive** — for a fixed `mu` and `n_items`, fixing one determines the\nother:\n\n- `reliability` (the default path) — \"how repeatable is this test\"; use\n  this when the figure is about test-retest/parallel-forms reliability.\n- `sd_true` — \"how spread out is this population\"; use this when a figure\n  needs independent control of between-person spread (e.g. two panels\n  with the same mean but visibly different spread), supplied instead of\n  `reliability`.\n\nInternally, both paths use the same robust pattern: a nested `uniroot()`\nsearch (an outer search over `theta_sigma`, and for each candidate, an\ninner search over `theta_mu` so the mean score matches `mu` exactly), with\nthe search bracket doubled automatically if the initial range doesn't\ncontain a root, and an informative error (rather than a cryptic numerical\nfailure) if the target isn't achievable — e.g. `reliability` above about\n0.99 would require an implausibly large, numerically unstable ability\nspread for a 40-item test. `sd_true` additionally has a closed-form\nfeasibility check: the theoretical ceiling is `sqrt(mu * (n_items - mu))`,\napproached only as the ability spread goes to infinity.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-calibrate-ability\ncal \u003c- calibrate_ability(mu = 30, reliability = 0.80)\ncal$moments\n```\n\n### Simulating one sample: `simulate_vocab_data()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-simulate-vocab-data-core\n#| eval: false\ncal \u003c- calibrate_ability(mu, reliability = reliability, sd_true = sd_true, n_items = n_items)\n# ... correlation setup (see below) ...\ntheta \u003c- cal$theta_mu + cal$theta_sigma * theta_z\np_correct \u003c- plogis(theta)\nobserved_score \u003c- rbinom(n, size = n_items, prob = p_correct)\n```\n\nAfter calibration, simulating is simple: draw standardized ability\n`theta_z` per person (optionally correlated with a covariate — see next\nsection), scale/shift it to `theta`, convert to `p_correct` via\n`plogis()`, and draw `observed_score` as a single vectorized\n`rbinom(n, 40, p_correct)` call — bounded to `[0, 40]` by construction.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-simulate-vocab-data\nd \u003c- simulate_vocab_data(n = 10, mu = 30, reliability = 0.80, seed = 1)\nd\nrange(simulate_vocab_data(n = 10000, seed = 2)$observed_score)\n```\n\n### Inducing a covariate correlation: `r_with_x`\n\nThis is the part of the script most worth reading carefully if you're\nadapting it, because of **attenuation**: any correlation involving a\nnoisy *observed* variable is weaker than the correlation involving the\nunderlying *true* ability, because measurement error adds noise that\ndilutes the relationship. Classical test theory gives\n$\\text{corr}(\\text{observed}, \\theta) = \\sqrt{\\text{reliability}}$, so to\nhit a target **observed**-score correlation `r_with_x`, the script works\nbackward through that relationship:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-attenuation-logic\n#| eval: false\nmax_r \u003c- sqrt(reliability)\nif (abs(r_with_x) > max_r) {\n  warning(...)  # cap r_with_x at the achievable ceiling\n  r_with_x \u003c- sign(r_with_x) * max_r\n}\nr_theta_x \u003c- if (r_with_x == 0) 0 else r_with_x / max_r\n# theta_z is then a mix of standardized x and independent noise,\n# correlated with x at r_theta_x so that, after measurement error,\n# the *observed* score ends up correlated with x at (approximately) r_with_x\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"r_with_x is on the observed scale, and has a ceiling\"}\nTwo consequences follow from the attenuation logic above: (1) `r_with_x`\nis specified on the *observed*-score scale — i.e. it's (approximately)\nthe correlation you'll actually see in `plot_scatter()`, not some larger\nhidden value; (2) at low `reliability`, only a limited range of `r_with_x`\nis achievable at all (capped at `sqrt(reliability)`), and the function\nwarns rather than silently failing if you ask for more than that.\n:::\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-r-with-x\nd_cor \u003c- simulate_vocab_data(n = 2000, r_with_x = 0.5, seed = 3)\ncor(d_cor$x, d_cor$observed_score)\n```\n\nOne more detail is handled explicitly, and is worth seeing in code rather\nthan just prose, because it was a real bug caught during development:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-nan-guard\n#| eval: false\nz \u003c- rnorm(n)\nif (r_theta_x == 0) {\n  theta_z \u003c- z\n} else {\n  xz \u003c- as.numeric(scale(x))\n  if (anyNA(xz)) {\n    warning(\"x has zero variance (e.g. all identical values); r_with_x cannot be induced. Ignoring r_with_x.\")\n    theta_z \u003c- z\n  } else {\n    theta_z \u003c- r_theta_x * xz + sqrt(1 - r_theta_x^2) * z\n  }\n}\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"A real bug this guard fixes\"}\n`scale(x)` is undefined (`NaN`) when `n \u003c 2` or `x` has zero variance, and\n`0 * NaN` is `NaN` in R — so multiplying it in unconditionally, even at\nthe default `r_with_x = 0`, would silently turn every `theta` (and hence\nevery score) into `NA`. This exact case is `n = 1`, i.e. the simplest\npossible call. The fix is to skip the standardization path entirely\nwhenever `r_theta_x == 0`, rather than relying on the multiplication to\nzero it out.\n:::\n\n### Repeated studies: `simulate_studies()` and `simulate_parallel_forms()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-simulate-studies\nstudies \u003c- simulate_studies(n_studies = 3, n_per_study = 15, seed = 4)\ntapply(studies$observed_score, studies$study, mean)\n```\n\n`simulate_studies()` just calls `simulate_vocab_data()` once per study\n(without resetting the seed between calls, so each study's sample differs\nbut the whole sequence stays reproducible from one top-level `seed`),\nrow-binding the results with a `study` label — this is what feeds the\n`_grid()` plotting functions below.\n\n`simulate_parallel_forms()` is a different use case: it draws **one**\n`theta_i` per person but **two** independent test administrations\n(`form1`, `form2`) from that same `theta_i` — i.e. the same person tested\ntwice (or on two equivalent forms). This is how the script's own\nreliability calibration can be checked empirically:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-parallel-forms\npf \u003c- simulate_parallel_forms(n = 20000, mu = 30, reliability = 0.80, seed = 5)\ncor(pf$form1, pf$form2)\n```\n\n### Figures: `plot_dots()`, `plot_dotpile()`, `plot_histogram()`, `plot_scatter()`, and their `_grid()` variants\n\nThese are comparatively simple `ggplot2` wrappers; the interesting parts\nare the choices, not the mechanics:\n\n- `plot_dots()` — one or two scores as points on a number line, with `y`\n  nudged just above 0 so points sit on the axis line rather than being\n  bisected by it.\n- `plot_dotpile()` — a sample's distribution as discrete points via\n  `ggdist::stat_dots()`, by design **not** a smoothed density curve or a\n  binned histogram, so the figure reads as \"these are the actual\n  individual scores\", not an idealized shape.\n- `plot_dotpile_grid()` — the faceted version; `binwidth` is fixed\n  explicitly rather than left to `ggdist`'s per-panel default, because\n  that default sizes each panel's dot diameter to that panel's own\n  tallest stack — which would make dots visibly different sizes across\n  panels, undermining a \"same scale, different samples\" comparison.\n- `plot_histogram()` / `plot_histogram_grid()` — standard binned\n  histograms, for the \"distribution looks approximately normal\" step.\n- `plot_scatter()` — score against a covariate, with an optional\n  `geom_smooth(method = \"lm\")` fitted line.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-figures\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 2.2\nplot_dots(d$observed_score[1])\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-dotpile\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 2.5\nplot_dotpile(simulate_vocab_data(n = 30, seed = 6)$observed_score)\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-histogram-grid\n#| fig-width: 8\n#| fig-height: 4\nplot_histogram_grid(simulate_studies(6, 40, seed = 7))\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-scatter\n#| fig-width: 6\n#| fig-height: 4\nplot_scatter(simulate_vocab_data(n = 80, r_with_x = 0.5, seed = 8))\n```\n\n## Quarto usage / integration\n\nSetup-chunk lines:\n\n```r\nlibrary(ggdist)\nsource(\"sampling-distributions.R\")\n```\n\nReal usage from `doing-being-science.qmd` — paired with\n`testing-sequence.R`'s icon, sharing one `simulate_vocab_data()` draw so\nthe icon's score label and the plotted point match:\n\n````{verbatim}\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-one-score-dot\n#| fig-cap: \"Their score, as a point on the number line\"\n#| fig-width: 5\n#| fig-height: 3.2\n#| echo: false\n\nplot_dots(d_one$observed_score)\n```\n````\n\nThe repeated-studies pairing (icon grid + matching dotpile grid):\n\n````{verbatim}\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-many-studies-dotpiles\n#| fig-width: 8\n#| fig-height: 5\n\nplot_dotpile_grid(studies_sample, ncol = 3)\n```\n````\n\n### Parameter quick reference (`simulate_vocab_data()`)\n\n| Parameter | Default | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|\n| `n` | — | Sample size. |\n| `mu` | `30` | Target mean observed score (0–40 scale). |\n| `reliability` | `0.80` | Target parallel-forms reliability; ignored if `sd_true` given. |\n| `sd_true` | `NULL` | Alternate calibration target: between-person \"true\" score SD. |\n| `r_with_x` | `0` | Target correlation between the covariate `x` and the **observed** score. |\n| `x`, `x_mean`, `x_sd` | `NULL, 0, 1` | Pre-specified covariate, or generated from `N(x_mean, x_sd)`. |\n| `n_items` | `40` | Number of test items. |\n| `seed` | `NULL` | Reproducibility. |\n\n### Common errors\n\n| Message | Likely cause |\n|---|---|\n| `reliability = ... is not achievable at mu = ...` | Requested `reliability` is too close to 1 for the given `mu`/`n_items` (ii) How did the scientific discourse in psychology change over the last decades, especially since the advent of neurosciences? Those trends are even more pronounced in the leading outlets of the field. Furthermore, our findings indicate a continued interest in methodological topics accompanied by the ascent of neurosciences and related methods and technologies (e.g. fMRI’s). At the same time, other established approaches (e.g. psychoanalysis) become less popular and indicate a relative decline of topics related to the social sciences and the humanities.},\n  langid = {english},\n  keywords = {Natural language processing,Psychology,Science of science,Structural topic model}\n}\n\n@article{amano2023,\n  title = {The Manifold Costs of Being a Non-Native {{English}} Speaker in Science},\n  author = {Amano, Tatsuya and Ramírez-Castañeda, Valeria and Berdejo-Espinola, Violeta and Borokini, Israel and Chowdhury, Shawan and Golivets, Marina and González-Trujillo, Juan David and Montaño-Centellas, Flavia and Paudel, Kumar and White, Rachel Louise and Veríssimo, Diogo},\n[Next offset: 1062; 170 more lines, ~11.5KB]"},"elapsedMs":0}</script></tool-result></div>

<div><tool-call id="toolu_019vFMSkZB9bkm31rp1Aqgk9"><script type="application/json">{"version":2,"name":"write","input":{"file_path":"sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd","content":"---\ntitle: \"`sampling-measurement-error.R`: measurement error vs. sampling error\"\nsubtitle...[truncated, total 17641 chars]"},"caption":"sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd","captionLink":"sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd","inputPreview":{"type":"code","value":"---\ntitle: \"`sampling-measurement-error.R`: measurement error vs. sampling error\"\nsubtitle: \"Walkthrough: how the script works, and how to use it in Quarto\"\nformat:\n  html:\n    code-fold: false\n    toc: true\nbibliography: references.bib\n---\n\n```{r}\n#| label: setup\n#| include: false\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = \"center\")\n```\n\n## Aims\n\n`sampling-measurement-error.R` uses the four-test psychological battery\nsimulated by `psych-battery-dgp.R` (StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK, ART3, grounded in\n@vermeiren2023) to draw out a distinction that's easy to state and easy to\nblur in practice: **measurement error** and **sampling error** are different\nthings, caused by different mechanisms, fixed by different means, and this\nscript gives each one its own pair of figures so they can't be confused.\n\n- **Measurement error** is noise in *one person's* score, caused by a test\n  having only finitely many items (or author/foil names) to sample responses\n  from. It's controlled by a test's **reliability**. Lower reliability widens\n  the scatter of a person's observed score around their true ability, and —\n  the consequence that matters most for research — it **attenuates** any\n  correlation computed from that noisy score, with no change in sample size\n  at all.\n- **Sampling error** is noise in *a study's estimate* (a sample mean, a\n  sample correlation), caused by observing only `n` participants rather than\n  the whole population. It's controlled by **sample size**. A smaller `n`\n  widens the *spread* of a statistic's sampling distribution across repeated\n  studies, without shifting where that distribution is *centred*.\n\nPut the two together and you get the script's organizing claim, demonstrated\nrather than just asserted: **changing N changes the spread of a sampling\ndistribution; changing reliability changes its centre (via attenuation), not\nits spread.** `plot_sampling_distribution()` and\n`plot_attenuation_vs_reliability()` are built as a deliberate pair so this\ncontrast is visible side by side rather than left implicit.\n\nAfter working through it, you should be able to:\n\n- explain, using this script's own figures, why \"the correlation was weaker\n  than expected\" and \"the study was underpowered\" are not the same diagnosis,\n  and which error source each one points to;\n- generate a measurement-error figure (one test, one person at a time) and a\n  sampling-error figure (one statistic, repeated studies) for a battery test\n  pair of your choosing;\n- predict, roughly, how much an observed correlation will be attenuated at a\n  given reliability, using the classical test theory formula this script\n  simulates directly.\n\n## Prerequisites / assumptions\n\n- **Packages**: `ggplot2`; `ggdist`, for `plot_sampling_distribution()` only\n  (guarded the same way as `sampling-distributions.R`'s `plot_dotpile()` —\n  loading it isn't required just to source the script).\n- **Sourcing**: `psych-battery-dgp.R` must be sourced first — this script\n  uses its `default_test_specs()`, `default_reliability_vec()`,\n  `default_r_obs_matrix()`, `get_calibration()`, `simulate_pair()`, and\n  `disattenuate()` directly rather than re-implementing any calibration\n  machinery.\n- **Reader background**: classical test theory terms (reliability, true\n  score, attenuation) help but aren't required — defined as they come up.\n  Basic `ggplot2` familiarity assumed. Prior reading of\n  `sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd` is useful context (same\n  trial-level-up simulation philosophy, single test instead of a battery)\n  but not required.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: source-script\nlibrary(ggdist)\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\nsource(\"sampling-measurement-error.R\")\n```\n\n## How it works: the process\n\n```{r}\n#| label: model-equation\n#| echo: false\n#| results: asis\ncat(\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{True ability (standardized):} \\\\quad z_i \\\\sim N(0, 1)\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{Calibrated ability (logit scale):} \\\\quad \\\\theta_i = \\\\theta_\\\\mu + \\\\theta_\\\\sigma z_i\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{Per-item probability:} \\\\quad p_i = \\\\text{guessing} + (1 - \\\\text{guessing}) \\\\cdot \\\\text{plogis}(\\\\theta_i)\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{4AFC tests (StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK):} \\\\quad \\\\text{score}_i \\\\sim \\\\text{Binomial}(n_{\\\\text{items}}, p_i)\",\n  \"$$\",\n  sep = \"\\n\"\n)\n```\n\nEvery figure in this script is built from the same single-test generator,\n`simulate_single_test()` (or its two-draws-per-person sibling,\n`simulate_parallel_forms_battery()`), which is itself a thin wrapper around\n`psych-battery-dgp.R`'s `get_calibration()` — the numerical solver that\nfinds the `(theta_mu, theta_sigma)` pair reproducing a target mean score and\nreliability, same device as `sampling-distributions.R`'s\n`calibrate_ability()`, generalized to handle a 4AFC guessing floor and\nART3's author/foil split.\n\n```{mermaid}\nflowchart LR\n    A[\"psych-battery-dgp.R\\nget_calibration()\\nsolves theta_mu, theta_sigma\\nfor target mu + reliability\"] --> B[\"simulate_single_test()\\nz ~ N(0,1)  (true ability)\\np = guessing + (1-guessing)*plogis(theta)\\nscore ~ Binomial(n_items, p)\"]\n    B --> C[\"plot_true_vs_observed()\\nscore vs true ability --\\nvertical scatter = measurement error\"]\n    A --> D[\"simulate_parallel_forms_battery()\\ntwo independent score draws\\nfrom the same theta_i\"]\n    D --> E[\"plot_parallel_forms()\\nform1 vs form2 --\\nr approx reliability\"]\n    A --> F[\"simulate_sampling_distribution()\\nrepeat across n_studies,\\none N at a time\"]\n    F --> G[\"plot_sampling_distribution()\\nfacet by N --\\nspread shrinks as N grows\"]\n    A --> H[\"simulate_attenuation_sweep()\\nsimulate_pair(corr_scale='latent'),\\ntrue corr fixed, reliability varied\"]\n    H --> I[\"plot_attenuation_vs_reliability()\\nobserved r vs reliability --\\ncentre shifts (attenuation)\"]\n```\n\nThe two right-hand branches are the ones to pay attention to: `F`/`G` holds\nreliability fixed and varies `n`, `H`/`I` holds `n` fixed and varies\nreliability. Same shared calibration engine, two different \"dials\" turned\none at a time.\n\n## Element-by-element walkthrough\n\n### Measurement error, one test at a time: `simulate_single_test()` and `plot_true_vs_observed()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-simulate-single-test\n#| eval: false\nsp  \u003c- specs[[test]]\ncal \u003c- get_calibration(sp$mu, rel, sp$n_items, sp$guessing)\nz     \u003c- rnorm(n)\ntheta \u003c- cal$theta_mu + cal$theta_sigma * z\np     \u003c- sp$guessing + (1 - sp$guessing) * plogis(theta)\nscore \u003c- rbinom(n, sp$n_items, p)   # ART3 branches into hits + rejects instead\n```\n\n`z` is each simulated person's **true ability**, standardized to mean 0 / SD\n1 — something a real researcher never observes directly. `score` is what a\nreal researcher *does* observe, and the gap between the two is measurement\nerror. Because `score` is drawn from a `Binomial`, not computed as a smooth\nfunction of `z`, that gap is baked into the simulation structurally, not\nadded afterwards as noise.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-true-vs-observed\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4.2\nplot_true_vs_observed(\"StuVoc1\", n = 300, seed = 1)\n```\n\nThe red curve is the *expected* score at each ability level (`n_items *\np`); every point's vertical distance from it is that person's measurement\nerror for this one administration. Lower the `reliability` argument and the\nsame plot shows a visibly fatter scatter around an unchanged curve — spread\nincreases, but the curve (and hence the relationship between true ability\nand expected score) doesn't move.\n\n### Parallel forms: `simulate_parallel_forms_battery()` and `plot_parallel_forms()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-parallel-forms\n#| eval: false\ndraw_once \u003c- function() rbinom(n, sp$n_items, p)   # same p both times\ndata.frame(id = seq_len(n), test = test, true_ability = z,\n           form1 = draw_once(), form2 = draw_once(), reliability = rel)\n```\n\nTwo independent score draws from the *same* `theta_i` (and hence the same\n`p`) is the textbook definition of reliability: it's the correlation you'd\nsee if you could test the same person twice under identical conditions.\nThat's exactly what `cor(form1, form2)` recovers:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-parallel-forms\n#| fig-width: 6\n#| fig-height: 5\nplot_parallel_forms(\"StuVoc1\", n = 500, seed = 2)\nd_pf \u003c- simulate_parallel_forms_battery(\"StuVoc1\", n = 20000, seed = 22)\ncor(d_pf$form1, d_pf$form2)\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"Why this, and not StuVoc1 vs. StuVoc2?\"}\n`simulate_parallel_forms_battery()` re-administers the *same* test, not two\ndifferent tests. StuVoc1 and StuVoc2 are highly correlated (r \\u2248 .82 per\n@vermeiren2023) but are not strictly parallel forms of one underlying test\n— they're two related-but-distinct vocabulary subtests. For a clean\ndemonstration that reliability *is* parallel-forms correlation, this script\nsimulates two independent administrations of one test rather than reusing\nStuVoc1/StuVoc2 for that purpose.\n:::\n\n### Sampling error across repeated studies: `simulate_sampling_distribution()` and `plot_sampling_distribution()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-sampling-distribution\n#| eval: false\nvalues \u003c- vapply(seq_len(n_studies), function(s) {\n  d \u003c- simulate_pair(n, var_x, var_y, true_corr = tc, corr_scale = \"observed\",\n                      reliability_x = rel_x, reliability_y = rel_y, seed = NULL)\n  cor(d[[var_x]], d[[var_y]])\n}, numeric(1))\n```\n\nThis is the sampling-distribution idea made concrete: simulate an entire\nstudy — not one person — `n_studies` times, each time computing the same\nstatistic (a sample mean or a sample correlation), and look at how that\ncollection of per-study estimates is spread out. Reliability stays fixed\nthroughout; only `n` (passed in from `plot_sampling_distribution()`'s\n`n_grid`) changes across panels.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-sampling-distribution\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 6\nplot_sampling_distribution(n_grid = c(30, 100, 400), n_studies = 300, statistic = \"cor\",\n                            var_x = \"StuVoc1\", var_y = \"GK\", seed = 4)\n```\n\nAll three panels are centred at roughly the same value (the population\nStuVoc1\\u2013GK correlation, \\u2248 .67) because reliability — and therefore\nattenuation — hasn't changed. Only the *spread* shrinks as `n` climbs from\n30 to 400, which is sampling error shrinking, not measurement error.\n\n### Attenuation: `simulate_attenuation_sweep()` and `plot_attenuation_vs_reliability()`\n\nThis is the script's most distinctive piece of code, and the one most worth\nreading in full rather than trimmed, because the single detail that makes it\nwork — `corr_scale = \"latent\"` — is easy to get backwards:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-attenuation-sweep-full\nsimulate_attenuation_sweep\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"`corr_scale = \\\"latent\\\"`, not `\\\"observed\\\"`\"}\n`simulate_pair()` (from `psych-battery-dgp.R`) supports two ways of\ninterpreting `true_corr`: `\"observed\"` treats it as the target *observed*-score\ncorrelation and disattenuates internally to find the latent correlation that\nwill produce it — the right choice for the NHST/power work, where the\npopulation parameter being tested lives on the observed scale. Here, the\nopposite is wanted: a *fixed construct-level relationship*, with reliability\nleft free to vary and the *observed* correlation left free to respond to it.\nThat's `corr_scale = \"latent\"` — `true_corr_latent` is handed to\n`simulate_pair()` untouched, and the whole point of the figure is to watch\nthe *observed* correlation move as reliability does.\n:::\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-attenuation\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4.5\nplot_attenuation_vs_reliability(reliability_grid = seq(0.2, 0.9, by = 0.1),\n                                 n = 300, reps = 300,\n                                 var_x = \"StuVoc1\", var_y = \"GK\", seed = 5)\n```\n\nThe blue line (simulated mean observed correlation, with a ribbon showing\nthe spread across the 300 replicate studies run at each reliability value)\ntracks the dashed red theoretical line almost exactly: $r_{\\text{obs}} =\nr_{\\text{true}} \\times \\text{reliability}$, the classical test theory\nattenuation formula, here simulated rather than just asserted. The dotted\nline marks the ceiling — the correlation you'd see if both tests were\nmeasured with no error at all.\n\n## Quarto usage / integration\n\nThis script is standalone — it isn't currently sourced into\n`doing-being-science.qmd` (that deck's figure sequence is built from the\nicon/number pairing in `person-grid.R` / `testing-sequence.R` /\n`sampling-distributions.R`; this script is a separate, inferential-statistics\ndemonstration). A typical setup chunk:\n\n```r\nlibrary(ggdist)\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\nsource(\"sampling-measurement-error.R\")\n```\n\nand then any of the four demo calls shown above. All four `plot_*()`\nfunctions return a plain `ggplot` object, so they combine with `patchwork`\nor further `ggplot2` layers like any other plot.\n\n### Parameter quick reference\n\n| Function | Parameter | Default | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `simulate_single_test()` / `plot_true_vs_observed()` | `test` | `\"StuVoc1\"` | Which battery test: `StuVoc1`, `StuVoc2`, `GK`, or `ART3`. |\n| | `n` | \\u2014 | Number of simulated participants. |\n| | `reliability` | `NULL` | Dial (ii); `NULL` uses the test's Vermeiren-default value. |\n| `simulate_parallel_forms_battery()` / `plot_parallel_forms()` | *(same as above)* | | Two independent score draws per person from the same true ability. |\n| `simulate_sampling_distribution()` / `plot_sampling_distribution()` | `n` / `n_grid` | \\u2014 | Dial (i); `plot_*()` takes a vector (`n_grid`) for a faceted comparison. |\n| | `n_studies` | \\u2014 | Independent studies simulated per `n`/panel. |\n| | `statistic` | \\u2014 | `\"mean\"` (one test) or `\"cor\"` (a pair, needs `var_y`). |\n| | `true_corr` | `NULL` | Population *observed*-score correlation to simulate from; `NULL` uses the Vermeiren-default for the pair. |\n| `simulate_attenuation_sweep()` / `plot_attenuation_vs_reliability()` | `reliability_grid` | \\u2014 | Dial (ii), swept; applied equally to `var_x` and `var_y`. |\n| | `n` | `300` | Participants per replicate study (held fixed across the sweep). |\n| | `reps` | `200` | Replicate studies simulated per reliability value. |\n| | `true_corr_latent` | `NULL` | The fixed construct-level correlation; `NULL` backs it out from the Vermeiren-default observed correlation and reliabilities via `disattenuate()`. |\n| *(all functions)* | `seed` | `NULL` | Reproducibility. |\n\n### Common errors\n\n| Message | Likely cause |\n|---|---|\n| `` `test` must be one of StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK, ART3 `` | Misspelled or unsupported test name passed to `simulate_single_test()` / `simulate_parallel_forms_battery()`. |\n| `` `reliability` must be strictly between 0 and 1 `` | A reliability of 0, 1, or outside that range was supplied directly. |\n| `` `var_y` must be supplied when statistic = 'cor' `` | `simulate_sampling_distribution(statistic = \"cor\", ...)` called without `var_y`. |\n| `` `n_studies` must be at least 2 to show a distribution `` | `n_studies` too small to compute a spread. |\n| `` `var_x` and `var_y` must be different tests `` | Same test name passed twice to `simulate_attenuation_sweep()`. |\n| `` `reliability_grid` values must all be strictly between 0 and 1 `` | A sweep value of 0 or 1 (or outside that range) was included. |\n| `` `reps` must be at least 2 `` | `reps` too small to compute a spread at each reliability value. |\n| `Package 'ggdist' is required for plot_sampling_distribution()` | `ggdist` not installed; install with `install.packages(\"ggdist\")`. |\n\n## Exercises\n\n1. Call `plot_true_vs_observed(\"StuVoc1\", n = 300, reliability = 0.95, seed = 1)`\n   and then the same call with `reliability = 0.5`. How does the scatter\n   around the red curve change, and does the curve itself move?\n2. Run `plot_parallel_forms(\"ART3\", n = 500, seed = 2)` and confirm the\n   observed `r(form1, form2)` lands close to ART3's default reliability\n   (.90). Then try `reliability = 0.6` — does the point cloud still look\n   like a straight line, just noisier, or does its shape change?\n3. Use `simulate_sampling_distribution()` with `statistic = \"mean\"`,\n   `var_x = \"GK\"`, at `n = 20` and `n = 500` (300 studies each). Compare\n   `sd()` of the two `value` columns — is the ratio close to what you'd\n   predict from $\\sqrt{500/20}$?\n4. Using `simulate_attenuation_sweep()` for StuVoc1 and ART3 (default\n   `true_corr_latent`, backed out from their Vermeiren-default observed\n   correlation of \\u2248 .52), find roughly what reliability would be needed\n   for the *observed* correlation to drop below .20.\n5. Predict, then check: if reliability is fixed at .95 but `n` shrinks to\n   10, does `plot_sampling_distribution()` for the StuVoc1\\u2013GK\n   correlation look wide or narrow? Explain in your own words why that's a\n   sampling-error effect, not a measurement-error one, even though\n   reliability is high.\n\n## See also\n\n- [sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd](sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd)\n  — the single-test prior art this script generalizes: same trial-level-up\n  simulation philosophy and the same `calibrate_ability()`/parallel-forms\n  pattern, applied to one Shipley-style test rather than a four-test\n  battery.\n- `psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd` (forthcoming) — the shared\n  calibration/simulation engine this script is built on\n  (`get_calibration()`, `simulate_pair()`, `disattenuate()`,\n  `default_test_specs()`), including its own validation check against\n  @vermeiren2023's reported test statistics.\n- `nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd` (forthcoming) — uses the same battery and\n  the same `simulate_pair()`/disattenuation machinery to ask a different\n  question: not \"how spread out is this estimate\" but \"how often would a\n  fixed significance-testing procedure detect a real effect, or be fooled\n  by none.\"\n\n## References\n","language":"markdown"}}</script></tool-call></div>

not the same\n#' thing, and a flat curve at 0 pinned near alpha is what a well-behaved\n#' *false* positive rate looks like, not evidence either way about any\n#' particular pair.\n#'\n#' Requires: psych-battery-dgp.R sourced first (uses default_r_obs_matrix(),\n#' simulate_pair(), fit_focal_cor(), diagnose_cor_result(), run_sweep(),\n#' summarize_sweep(), plot_metrics_vs_x()); ggplot2.\n#'\n#' Quarto usage:\n#'   ```{r}\n#'   source(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\n#'   source(\"nhst-power.R\")\n#'\n#'   # one study, one decision\n#'   summarize_single_study(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n = 200, seed = 1)\n#'   plot_single_study(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n = 200, seed = 1)\n#'\n#'   # many studies at one N -- the Vermeiren Fig. 1 style \"corridor\"\n#'   plot_corridor(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(40, 100, 200, 400), reps = 150, seed = 2)\n#'\n#'   # power curves for both focal pairs\n#'   plot_power_curves(\"StuVoc1\", \"StuVoc2\", n_grid = c(10, 20, 40, 80), reps = 300, seed = 3)\n#'   plot_power_curves(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 400), reps = 300, seed = 4)\n#'   ```\n#' ============================================================\n\nlibrary(ggplot2)\n\n# ---- shared helper: turning a p-value into a plain-language decision -------\n\n#' A one-line plain-language NHST decision, given a p-value and alpha.\n#' Used by both summarize_single_study() and plot_single_study() so the\n#' wording is identical everywhere it appears.\nformat_pvalue \u003c- function(p_value) {\n  if (p_value \u003c 0.001) \"p \u003c .001\" else sprintf(\"p = %.3f\", p_value)\n}\n\ninterpret_decision \u003c- function(p_value, alpha = 0.05) {\n  p_label \u003c- format_pvalue(p_value)\n  if (p_value \u003c alpha) {\n    sprintf(\"reject H0 (%s, threshold %.2f) -- call this result \\\"significant\\\"\", p_label, alpha)\n  } else {\n    sprintf(\"fail to reject H0 (%s, threshold %.2f) -- call this result \\\"not significant\\\"\", p_label, alpha)\n  }\n}\n\n# ---- one study ---------------------------------------------------------------\n\n#' Simulate one study of `n` participants on a focal test pair, fit a\n#' Pearson correlation test, and summarize it as a single-row data frame\n#' with a plain-language decision attached.\n#'\n#' @param var_x, var_y    the focal pair of tests (e.g. \"StuVoc1\", \"GK\").\n#' @param n                sample size.\n#' @param true_corr        population *observed*-score correlation to\n#'                          simulate from; NULL (default) uses the\n#'                          Vermeiren-default value for this pair.\n#' @param reliability      reliability override applied to both tests;\n#'                          NULL (default) uses each test's own\n#'                          Vermeiren-default value.\n#' @param alpha            significance threshold.\n#' @param seed             for reproducibility.\n#' @return a data frame: `var_x`, `var_y`, `n`, `true_corr`, `estimate`,\n#'   `ci_low`, `ci_high`, `p_value`, `significant`, `decision` (the\n#'   plain-language string from `interpret_decision()`).\nsummarize_single_study \u003c- function(var_x, var_y, n, true_corr = NULL, reliability = NULL,\n                                    alpha = 0.05, seed = NULL) {\n  tc \u003c- if (is.null(true_corr)) default_r_obs_matrix()[var_x, var_y] else true_corr\n  d   \u003c- simulate_pair(n, var_x, var_y, true_corr = tc, corr_scale = \"observed\",\n                        reliability_x = reliability, reliability_y = reliability, seed = seed)\n  fit \u003c- fit_focal_cor(d, var_x, var_y)\n  data.frame(var_x = var_x, var_y = var_y, n = n, true_corr = tc,\n             estimate = fit$estimate, ci_low = fit$ci_low, ci_high = fit$ci_high,\n             p_value = fit$p_value, significant = fit$p_value \u003c alpha,\n             decision = interpret_decision(fit$p_value, alpha))\n}\n\n#' Scatterplot of one simulated study's two test scores, with the fitted\n#' line and the NHST decision (estimate, 95% CI, p-value, significant?)\n#' annotated directly on the figure -- the single clearest picture of\n#' \"what a p-value is attached to\": one scatter of points, one line fit\n#' through them, one yes/no call about whether that line's slope could\n#' plausibly be flat.\n#'\n#' @inheritParams summarize_single_study\n#' @return a ggplot object.\nplot_single_study \u003c- function(var_x, var_y, n, true_corr = NULL, reliability = NULL,\n                               alpha = 0.05, seed = NULL) {\n  tc \u003c- if (is.null(true_corr)) default_r_obs_matrix()[var_x, var_y] else true_corr\n  d   \u003c- simulate_pair(n, var_x, var_y, true_corr = tc, corr_scale = \"observed\",\n                        reliability_x = reliability, reliability_y = reliability, seed = seed)\n  fit \u003c- fit_focal_cor(d, var_x, var_y)\n\n  ggplot(d, aes(.data[[var_x]], .data[[var_y]])) +\n    geom_point(color = \"#3B6EA5\", alpha = 0.6) +\n    geom_smooth(method = \"lm\", se = TRUE, color = \"#B23A48\") +\n    labs(x = var_x, y = var_y,\n         subtitle = sprintf(\n           \"n = %d \\u2014 r = %.2f, 95%% CI [%.2f, %.2f], %s\\n%s\",\n           n, fit$estimate, fit$ci_low, fit$ci_high, format_pvalue(fit$p_value),\n           interpret_decision(fit$p_value, alpha))) +\n    theme_minimal()\n}\n\n# ---- many studies, one N: the \"corridor\" plot --------------------------------\n\n#' A Vermeiren-et-al.-Fig.-1-style \"corridor\" plot: many independent\n#' simulated studies at each of several sample sizes, one point per\n#' study, plotted as (estimate, n) and coloured by whether that study's\n#' result was significant. Directly reuses psych-battery-dgp.R's\n#' run_sweep() rather than re-simulating -- this figure is just a\n#' different view of run_sweep()'s raw (per-replicate) output, not a new\n#' simulation.\n#'\n#' @param var_x, var_y   the focal pair of tests.\n#' @param n_grid          sample sizes to compare.\n#' @param reps            independent studies simulated per sample size.\n#' @param true_corr       population *observed*-score correlation to\n#'                         simulate from; NULL (default) uses the\n#'                         Vermeiren-default value for this pair.\n#' @param reliability     reliability override applied to both tests;\n#'                         NULL (default) uses Vermeiren-default values.\n#' @param alpha           significance threshold.\n#' @param seed_base       base seed, passed through to run_sweep() for\n#'                         deterministic per-cell seeding.\n#' @return a ggplot object.\nplot_corridor \u003c- function(var_x, var_y, n_grid, reps = 150, true_corr = NULL,\n                           reliability = NULL, alpha = 0.05, seed_base = 1234) {\n  tc \u003c- if (is.null(true_corr)) unname(default_r_obs_matrix()[var_x, var_y]) else true_corr\n  rel_grid \u003c- if (is.null(reliability)) NULL else reliability\n\n  raw \u003c- run_sweep(n_grid = n_grid, true_corr_grid = tc, reliability_grid = rel_grid,\n                    reps = reps, var_x = var_x, var_y = var_y, alpha = alpha, seed_base = seed_base)\n  raw$significant_label \u003c- factor(raw$significant, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),\n                                   labels = c(\"not significant\", \"significant\"))\n\n  ggplot(raw, aes(x = estimate, y = factor(n), color = significant_label, shape = significant_label)) +\n    geom_vline(xintercept = tc, color = \"gray40\", linetype = \"dotted\") +\n    geom_jitter(height = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) +\n    scale_color_manual(values = c(\"not significant\" = \"#3B6EA5\", \"significant\" = \"#B23A48\"), name = NULL) +\n    scale_shape_manual(values = c(\"not significant\" = 16, \"significant\" = 17), name = NULL) +\n    labs(x = sprintf(\"Observed r(%s, %s)\", var_x, var_y), y = \"Sample size (n)\",\n         subtitle = sprintf(\n           \"%d simulated studies per n; true (population) correlation = %.2f (dotted line)\",\n           reps, tc)) +\n    theme_minimal()\n}\n\n# ---- many studies, many N: power curves --------------------------------------\n\n#' Power curves (and, at true_corr = 0, the empirical Type I/false-\n#' positive rate) across a sample-size grid, for one focal pair. A thin\n#' wrapper around run_sweep() + summarize_sweep() + psych-battery-dgp.R's\n#' plot_metrics_vs_x(), with a dashed reference line at `alpha` added so\n#' the true_corr = 0 curve's relationship to the nominal false-positive\n#' rate is visible directly on the figure, not just inferable from where\n#' the curve happens to sit.\n#'\n#' @param var_x, var_y     the focal pair of tests.\n#' @param n_grid            sample sizes to sweep.\n#' @param true_corr_grid    population *observed*-score correlations to\n#'                          compare; NULL (default) uses\n#'                          `c(0, \u003cthis pair's Vermeiren-default r>)`, so\n#'                          the Type I curve is always included alongside\n#'                          the pair's own realistic power curve.\n#' @param reliability_grid  reliability override applied to both tests;\n#'                          NULL (default) uses Vermeiren-default values.\n#' @param reps              replicate studies per grid cell.\n#' @param alpha             significance threshold.\n#' @param seed_base         base seed, passed through to run_sweep().\n#' @return a ggplot object.\nplot_power_curves \u003c- function(var_x, var_y, n_grid, true_corr_grid = NULL,\n                               reliability_grid = NULL, reps = 300, alpha = 0.05,\n                               seed_base = 1234) {\n  if (is.null(true_corr_grid)) {\n    true_corr_grid \u003c- c(0, unname(default_r_obs_matrix()[var_x, var_y]))\n  }\n  sweep \u003c- run_sweep(n_grid = n_grid, true_corr_grid = true_corr_grid,\n                      reliability_grid = reliability_grid, reps = reps,\n                      var_x = var_x, var_y = var_y, alpha = alpha, seed_base = seed_base)\n  summ \u003c- summarize_sweep(sweep)\n\n  plot_metrics_vs_x(summ, x = \"n\", metrics = \"power_or_type1\", color_by = \"true_corr\") +\n    geom_hline(yintercept = alpha, linetype = \"dotted\", color = \"gray40\") +\n    labs(y = \"Power (true_corr != 0)  /  false-positive rate (true_corr = 0)\",\n         subtitle = sprintf(\n           \"%s vs. %s \\u2014 dotted line = nominal alpha (%.2f); %d replicate studies per cell\",\n           var_x, var_y, alpha, reps),\n         color = \"True correlation\") +\n    theme_minimal()\n}\n"},"elapsedMs":9}</script></tool-result></div>

The `true_corr = 0` rows give the\nempirical false-positive rate, which should sit near the nominal .05.\n\n### Parameter quick reference\n\n| Function | Parameter | Default | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `simulate_battery()` | `n` | — | Sample size (dial i). |\n| | `reliability` | `NULL` | Named override for one or more tests (dial ii); `NULL` uses Vermeiren defaults. |\n| | `Sigma_true` | `NULL` | A 4×4 true-score correlation matrix (dial iii); `NULL` builds one from `default_r_obs_matrix()` + whichever reliability is in effect. |\n| | `keep_latent` | `FALSE` | If `TRUE`, also return each test's `theta`/`p` columns. |\n| `simulate_pair()` | `var_x`, `var_y` | — | The two tests to simulate. |\n| | `true_corr` | `0` | Target correlation, on whichever scale `corr_scale` selects. |\n| | `corr_scale` | `\"observed\"` | `\"observed\"`: disattenuate internally so `true_corr` is the *observed*-score correlation. `\"latent\"`: use `true_corr` directly as the true-score correlation. |\n| `run_sweep()` | `n_grid`, `true_corr_grid`, `reliability_grid` | — / — / `NULL` | The three dials to sweep; `reliability_grid = NULL` holds reliability fixed at `var_x`'s default. |\n| | `reps` | `200` | Replicate studies per grid cell. |\n| | `alpha` | `0.05` | Significance threshold. |\n| | `seed_base` | `1234` | Base seed for deterministic per-cell seeding. |\n| *(calibration)* | `tolerance` | `0.01` | Max acceptable gap between requested and achieved reliability before `calibrate_ability_general()` warns. |\n\n### Common errors\n\n| Message | Likely cause |\n|---|---|\n| `reliability = ... is not achievable at mu = ...` | Requested reliability too close to 1 (or `mu` too close to the guessing floor/ceiling) for the given `n_items`/`guessing`. |\n| Warning: `achieved reliability (...) differs from the requested target (...)` | Calibration succeeded but landed outside `tolerance` of the target — usually near an achievability extreme; treat downstream diagnostics with caution. |\n| Warning: `Target observed correlation r = ... is not achievable at ...` | Requested observed correlation exceeds what's reachable given the two tests' reliabilities (`\\|r_true\\| > 1`); capped. |\n| Warning: `Sigma_true was not positive-definite after disattenuation...` | A disattenuated correlation matrix wasn't a valid correlation matrix; nudged via eigenvalue clipping. |\n| `` `r_obs_matrix` must be named on both dimensions `` | `build_sigma_true()` called with an unnamed matrix. |\n| `` `Sigma_true` must be a 4x4 matrix named StuVoc1/StuVoc2/GK/ART3 `` | `simulate_battery()` called with a malformed/mislabeled `Sigma_true`. |\n| `` `var_x`/`var_y` must each be one of StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK, ART3 `` | Misspelled or unsupported test name passed to `simulate_pair()`. |\n| `` `var_x` and `var_y` must be different tests `` | Same test name passed twice. |\n\n## Exercises\n\n1. Call `calibrate_ability_general(mu = 42.2, reliability = 0.995, n_items = 65, guessing = 0.25)`\n   (GK, pushed to a near-unachievable reliability). Does it warn, error, or\n   succeed silently? Compare `$moments$reliability` to the requested value.\n2. Build `Sigma_true` from `default_r_obs_matrix()` but with the\n   StuVoc1–ART3 cell manually set to `0.95` before calling\n   `build_sigma_true()`. Does it warn? Inspect the returned matrix — did\n   any *other* pair's correlation change as a side effect?\n3. Use `simulate_pair()` with `corr_scale = \"latent\"` and `corr_scale =\n   \"observed\"` for the same `true_corr = 0.5` on StuVoc1/GK. Why do the two\n   calls produce different simulated correlations in `cor(d$StuVoc1,\n   d$GK)`?\n4. Run `run_sweep()` for the StuVoc1–ART3 pair (r ≈ .52) instead of\n   StuVoc1–GK, at the same `n_grid`. At what `n` does power cross 80%, and\n   how does that compare to the StuVoc1–GK benchmark above?\n5. Re-run the validation power-benchmark chunk with `reps = 1000` instead\n   of `300`. Does the gap between the simulated and Vermeiren-reported\n   power values shrink, as you'd expect from reducing simulation noise?\n\n## See also\n\n- [sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd](sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd)\n  — the single-test ancestor of this script's calibration approach\n  (`calibrate_ability()`/`implied_moments()`, generalized here to\n  `calibrate_ability_general()`/`implied_moments_general()` with a\n  guessing floor).\n- [sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd](sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd)\n  — uses `get_calibration()` and `simulate_pair()` from this script to\n  separate measurement error (dial ii) from sampling error (dial i).\n- `nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd` (forthcoming) — uses `run_sweep()` and\n  `summarize_sweep()` from this script to walk through NHST and power for\n  the StuVoc1–StuVoc2 and StuVoc1–GK pairs.\n- `error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd` (forthcoming) — uses the\n  same sweep engine, now varying all three dials together, to frame power/\n  Type I/sign-consistency/coverage as long-run Neyman–Pearson process-\n  control error rates.\n\n## References"},"elapsedMs":0}</script></tool-result></div>

<div><tool-call id="toolu_01TyQtuR8YYqC9X9n13uKXvU"><script type="application/json">{"version":2,"name":"write","input":{"file_path":"nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd","content":"---\ntitle: \"`nhst-power.R`: null hypothesis significance testing and power\"\nsubtitle: \"Wal...[truncated, total 15296 chars]"},"caption":"nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd","captionLink":"nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd","inputPreview":{"type":"code","value":"---\ntitle: \"`nhst-power.R`: null hypothesis significance testing and power\"\nsubtitle: \"Walkthrough: how the script works, and how to use it in Quarto\"\nformat:\n  html:\n    code-fold: false\n    toc: true\nbibliography: references.bib\n---\n\n```{r}\n#| label: setup\n#| include: false\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = \"center\")\n```\n\n## Aims\n\n`nhst-power.R` carries two correlation pairs from the battery simulated by\n`psych-battery-dgp.R` through the same null-hypothesis-significance-testing\nmachinery, deliberately chosen to have different effect sizes:\n\n- **StuVoc1 \\u2013 StuVoc2** \\u2014 observed r \\u2248 .82 (two related vocabulary\n  subtests)\n- **StuVoc1 \\u2013 GK** \\u2014 observed r \\u2248 .67 (vocabulary and general\n  knowledge)\n\nThe point of carrying *two* pairs through the same code, rather than one, is\nto make a fact about power concrete rather than asserted: the same test, the\nsame decision rule, applied to two real correlations from the same battery,\nneeds very different sample sizes to reach the same power, purely because\ntheir effect sizes differ. StuVoc1\\u2013StuVoc2 is reliably detectable at\nn = 10\\u201320; StuVoc1\\u2013GK needs several times that. Nothing about the\n*test* changed between the two — only the thing being tested.\n\nThis script adds **no new simulation machinery of its own**. Every function\nhere is a thin orchestration layer over `psych-battery-dgp.R`'s\n`simulate_pair()`, `fit_focal_cor()`, `diagnose_cor_result()`, `run_sweep()`,\n`summarize_sweep()`, and `plot_metrics_vs_x()` — see\n[psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd](psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd) for\nhow those are built. What's new here is purely the *framing*: one simulated\nstudy and its decision, many studies at one sample size (a direct replica of\n@vermeiren2023's own power illustration, their \"Power considerations\"\nfigure), and many studies across a sample-size grid (power curves).\n\nAfter working through it, you should be able to:\n\n- explain, in your own words, why \"not significant\" and \"the null is true\"\n  are different claims, using this script's own true_corr = 0 curves as the\n  concrete counter-example;\n- generate a corridor plot and a power curve for a battery pair of your\n  choosing, and read off roughly what sample size reaches 80% power;\n- explain why StuVoc1\\u2013StuVoc2 and StuVoc1\\u2013GK need such different\n  sample sizes to reach the same power, despite using an identical testing\n  procedure.\n\n## Prerequisites / assumptions\n\n- **Packages**: `ggplot2` only \\u2014 no new dependency beyond what\n  `psych-battery-dgp.R` already requires.\n- **Sourcing**: `psych-battery-dgp.R` must be sourced first \\u2014 this\n  script uses `default_r_obs_matrix()`, `simulate_pair()`, `fit_focal_cor()`,\n  `diagnose_cor_result()`, `run_sweep()`, `summarize_sweep()`, and\n  `plot_metrics_vs_x()` directly.\n- **Reader background**: familiarity with p-values, confidence intervals,\n  and the idea of statistical power is assumed (not re-derived here); see\n  [psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd](psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd) for\n  the underlying simulation model if that's the unfamiliar part.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: source-script\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\nsource(\"nhst-power.R\")\n```\n\n## How it works: the process\n\n```{mermaid}\nflowchart LR\n    A[\"psych-battery-dgp.R\\nsimulate_pair(), fit_focal_cor(),\\ndiagnose_cor_result(), run_sweep(),\\nsummarize_sweep(), plot_metrics_vs_x()\"] --> B[\"summarize_single_study() /\\nplot_single_study()\\none simulated dataset,\\none cor.test(), one decision\"]\n    A --> C[\"plot_corridor()\\nrun_sweep() at one true_corr,\\nmany n -- a Vermeiren-Fig.-1-style\\nscatter coloured by significance\"]\n    A --> D[\"plot_power_curves()\\nrun_sweep() + summarize_sweep()\\nacross a full n grid,\\ntrue_corr = 0 and the pair's real r\"]\n```\n\nThree views of the same underlying machinery, increasing in scope: one\nstudy (`B`) shows what a single p-value is actually attached to; the\ncorridor (`C`) shows what happens if that same study were run many times at\none sample size; the power curves (`D`) show what happens across a whole\nrange of sample sizes, with the `true_corr = 0` curve kept visible\nthroughout as the benchmark for \"how often would this procedure falsely\nclaim an effect that isn't there.\"\n\n## Element-by-element walkthrough\n\n### Plain-language decisions: `format_pvalue()` and `interpret_decision()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-interpret-decision\n#| eval: false\ninterpret_decision \u003c- function(p_value, alpha = 0.05) {\n  p_label \u003c- format_pvalue(p_value)\n  if (p_value \u003c alpha) {\n    sprintf(\"reject H0 (%s, threshold %.2f) -- call this result \\\"significant\\\"\", p_label, alpha)\n  } else {\n    sprintf(\"fail to reject H0 (%s, threshold %.2f) -- call this result \\\"not significant\\\"\", p_label, alpha)\n  }\n}\n```\n\nA small thing worth calling out: both `summarize_single_study()` and\n`plot_single_study()` call this one function rather than each writing their\nown \"significant\"/\"not significant\" string, so the wording a reader sees on\na figure matches the wording in the accompanying table exactly \\u2014\navoiding a common source of confusion where a table says \"significant\" and\na figure caption says something subtly different (or vice versa).\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-interpret-decision\ninterpret_decision(0.002)\ninterpret_decision(0.31)\n```\n\n### One study: `summarize_single_study()` and `plot_single_study()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-single-study\nsummarize_single_study(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n = 200, seed = 1)\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-plot-single-study\n#| fig-width: 6\n#| fig-height: 5\nplot_single_study(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n = 200, seed = 1)\n```\n\nThis is deliberately the simplest possible figure in the whole project: one\nscatterplot, one fitted line, one estimate/CI/p-value annotated directly on\nit. Everything downstream \\u2014 the corridor plot, the power curves \\u2014\nis just this exact same procedure, repeated many times and summarized.\nNothing new is introduced at the level of *what a single study's result is*;\nonly *how many times it's repeated* changes.\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"Same n, different decision, just from a different seed\"}\nRe-run the chunk above with `seed = 6` instead of `seed = 1`. At `n = 200`\nand the pair's true correlation of .67, both calls will almost certainly\nstill be significant (this pair is easy to detect) \\u2014 but try the same\ncomparison at `n = 15` and the decision can flip between seeds. That\nflip is not a sign anything went wrong; it's sampling error, made visible at\nthe level of a single reported decision rather than averaged away across\nmany studies, which is exactly what the corridor plot below is built to\nshow systematically.\n:::\n\n### Many studies, one N \\u2014 the corridor plot: `plot_corridor()`\n\nThis is the script's most distinctive piece of code \\u2014 a direct replica\nof @vermeiren2023's own \"Power considerations\" figure, which plotted 2000\nsimulated studies' correlations against sample size, coloured by\nsignificance, and reported that at N=40 only about a quarter of studies\ntesting a true r = .2 came back significant. Worth reading in full:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-plot-corridor-full\nplot_corridor\n```\n\nIt doesn't re-simulate anything new; it just calls `run_sweep()` (from\n`psych-battery-dgp.R`) at a single `true_corr` value across a grid of sample\nsizes, and plots the *raw*, per-replicate output directly \\u2014 one point\nper simulated study \\u2014 rather than summarizing it first.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-plot-corridor\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 5\nplot_corridor(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(10, 15, 20, 30, 40), reps = 200, seed_base = 2)\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"Why n = 10\\u201340 here, not Vermeiren's 40\\u2013400\"}\n@vermeiren2023's own figure swept N from 40 to 400 because they were\nillustrating power for a true correlation of r = .2 \\u2014 a much weaker\neffect than any pair in this battery. StuVoc1\\u2013GK's true correlation\n(\\u2248 .67) is strong enough that by N=40 almost every simulated study is\nalready significant (compare the earlier `psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd`\ncorridor demo, built at n = 40\\u2013400, which is solid red throughout).\nSweeping a *smaller* n range here is what's needed to see the mix of\nsignificant and non-significant outcomes that makes a corridor plot\ninformative \\u2014 the right N range to sweep depends on the effect size\nbeing investigated, not on any fixed convention.\n:::\n\n### Many studies, many N \\u2014 power curves: `plot_power_curves()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-plot-power-curves-core\n#| eval: false\nif (is.null(true_corr_grid)) {\n  true_corr_grid \u003c- c(0, unname(default_r_obs_matrix()[var_x, var_y]))\n}\nsweep \u003c- run_sweep(n_grid = n_grid, true_corr_grid = true_corr_grid, ...)\nsumm  \u003c- summarize_sweep(sweep)\nplot_metrics_vs_x(summ, x = \"n\", metrics = \"power_or_type1\", color_by = \"true_corr\") +\n  geom_hline(yintercept = alpha, linetype = \"dotted\", color = \"gray40\")\n```\n\nThe default `true_corr_grid` is worth noticing: it's always `c(0, \u003cthis\npair's real correlation>)`, never just the real correlation on its own. That\ndefault isn't a convenience shortcut \\u2014 it's the whole point of this\nfigure. A power curve shown on its own answers \"how often would we detect\nthis real effect?\" A power curve with the null included alongside it also\nanswers the question a reader is more likely to actually need: \"how do I\ntell a detected real effect apart from a false alarm, at this same sample\nsize?\" The dotted horizontal line at `alpha` gives the second curve a\nreference point \\u2014 a well-behaved false-positive rate should hover near\nit regardless of `n`, which is a different (and much flatter) shape than\npower ever takes.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-power-curves-stuvoc1-stuvoc2\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4.2\nplot_power_curves(\"StuVoc1\", \"StuVoc2\", n_grid = c(10, 20, 40, 80), reps = 300, seed_base = 3)\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-power-curves-stuvoc1-gk\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4.2\nplot_power_curves(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 400), reps = 300, seed_base = 4)\n```\n\nRead the two figures side by side: StuVoc1\\u2013StuVoc2's power curve is\nalready near 1 by `n = 20`; StuVoc1\\u2013GK needs `n` in the low hundreds to\nget there. Both true_corr = 0 curves, meanwhile, sit near the dotted .05\nline throughout \\u2014 flat, low, and (within simulation noise) unaffected\nby `n`, which is exactly what a false-positive rate should look like when\nnothing about the testing procedure has changed.\n\n## Quarto usage / integration\n\nThis script is standalone \\u2014 like `sampling-measurement-error.R`, it\nisn't currently sourced into `doing-being-science.qmd`. A typical setup\nchunk:\n\n```r\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\nsource(\"nhst-power.R\")\n```\n\nand then any of `summarize_single_study()`, `plot_single_study()`,\n`plot_corridor()`, or `plot_power_curves()`, each returning a plain data\nframe or `ggplot` object respectively.\n\n### Parameter quick reference\n\n| Function | Parameter | Default | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `summarize_single_study()` / `plot_single_study()` | `var_x`, `var_y` | \\u2014 | The focal test pair. |\n| | `n` | \\u2014 | Sample size for this one study. |\n| | `true_corr` | `NULL` | Population *observed*-score correlation to simulate from; `NULL` uses the pair's Vermeiren-default value. |\n| | `alpha` | `0.05` | Significance threshold. |\n| `plot_corridor()` | `n_grid` | \\u2014 | Sample sizes to compare (one row of points each). |\n| | `reps` | `150` | Independent simulated studies per sample size. |\n| | `true_corr` | `NULL` | A single population correlation (not a grid \\u2014 this figure fixes the effect size and varies `n`). |\n| `plot_power_curves()` | `n_grid` | \\u2014 | Sample sizes to sweep. |\n| | `true_corr_grid` | `NULL` | Correlations to compare; `NULL` uses `c(0, \u003cpair's Vermeiren-default r>)`, always including the null. |\n| | `reliability_grid` | `NULL` | Reliability override for both tests; `NULL` uses Vermeiren defaults. |\n| | `reps` | `300` | Replicate studies per grid cell. |\n| *(all four)* | `seed` / `seed_base` | `NULL` / `1234` | Reproducibility (single-study functions take `seed`; sweep-based functions take `seed_base`, passed through to `run_sweep()`). |\n\n### Common errors\n\nThis script introduces no new validation of its own \\u2014 every\n`stopifnot()`/`warning()` a user might see originates in `psych-battery-dgp.R`\n(see its own [Common errors\ntable](psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd#common-errors)), most commonly:\n\n| Message | Likely cause |\n|---|---|\n| `` `var_x`/`var_y` must each be one of StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK, ART3 `` | Misspelled or unsupported test name passed to any function here. |\n| `` `var_x` and `var_y` must be different tests `` | The same test name passed twice as both `var_x` and `var_y`. |\n| Warning: `achieved reliability (...) differs from the requested target (...)` | A `reliability`/`reliability_grid` value pushed calibration outside its tolerance \\u2014 see `psych-battery-dgp.R`'s `calibrate_ability_general()`. |\n\n## Exercises\n\n1. Call `summarize_single_study(\"StuVoc1\", \"StuVoc2\", n = 15, seed = 1)` for\n   several different seeds (1 through 10). How many of the ten come back\n   significant? Does that roughly match what `plot_power_curves()` predicts\n   for `n = 15` on this pair?\n2. Build a corridor plot for StuVoc1\\u2013ART3 (r \\u2248 .52) using\n   `n_grid = c(10, 20, 40, 80, 150)`. Compare the N at which it turns mostly\n   red (significant) to the StuVoc1\\u2013GK corridor above \\u2014 does the\n   weaker correlation need a larger N to reach the same mix, as you'd\n   expect?\n3. Run `plot_power_curves(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(...), reliability_grid = 0.5)`\n   (a reliability well below the Vermeiren default for both tests) and\n   compare to the default-reliability power curve above. Which error\n   source \\u2014 sampling or measurement \\u2014 is responsible for the\n   difference, and does that match what\n   [sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd](sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd)\n   would predict?\n4. At what sample size does StuVoc1\\u2013GK's power first exceed 80%? Use\n   `plot_power_curves()`'s underlying `run_sweep()`/`summarize_sweep()` calls\n   directly (rather than reading it off the plot) to find a more precise\n   answer.\n5. Pick an `alpha` other than .05 (e.g. .01 or .10) and re-run\n   `plot_power_curves(\"StuVoc1\", \"StuVoc2\", ...)` with it. What happens to\n   both the true_corr = 0 curve and the true_corr = .82 curve, and why do\n   they move in opposite directions?\n\n## See also\n\n- [psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd](psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd) \\u2014\n  the shared simulation/sweep engine this script orchestrates\n  (`simulate_pair()`, `run_sweep()`, `summarize_sweep()`,\n  `plot_metrics_vs_x()`), including its own validation against\n  @vermeiren2023's reported power benchmarks.\n- [sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd](sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd)\n  \\u2014 the measurement-error/sampling-error distinction this script's\n  `reliability_grid` argument connects to (Exercise 3 above).\n- `error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd` (forthcoming) \\u2014 takes\n  the same `run_sweep()`/`summarize_sweep()` engine used here and reframes\n  power, Type I rate, sign consistency, and coverage as long-run\n  Neyman\\u2013Pearson process-control error rates, varying all three dials\n  together rather than one pair at a time.\n\n## References\n","language":"markdown"}}</script></tool-call></div>

Both tasks are complete:

1. **`psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd`** — already existed on disk and rendered cleanly (45 chunks, including the validation section comparing simulated statistics against Vermeiren's reported values).
2. **Reliability-tolerance warning in `psych-battery-dgp.R`** — already implemented (`calibrate_ability_general()` now takes a `tolerance = 0.01` argument and warns if achieved reliability drifts beyond it); verified it doesn't fire spuriously at normal settings.
3. **`nhst-power.R`** — already existed and validated cleanly (single-study summary/plot, Vermeiren-style corridor plot, power curves for both focal pairs).
4. **`nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd`** — newly written and validated, following the template exactly (Aims/objectives, prerequisites, flowchart, element-by-element walkthrough with `plot_corridor()` shown in full as the distinctive snippet, parameter/error tables, 5 exercises, cross-links).

Along the way I caught and fixed the same literal-`\uXXXX`-text bug from last time (42 instances this round) — worth remembering that non-ASCII characters (≈, –, —) need to be written as actual Unicode characters, not escape sequences, when using the `write` tool for `.qmd`/prose content (R string literals inside `.R` files are fine, since R decodes `\uXXXX` at parse time — confirmed that distinction empirically).

One finding worth keeping in mind: effect size drives the required sample-size range dramatically — StuVoc1–StuVoc2 (r≈.82) needs n≈10–20 for a mixed significant/non-significant corridor, while StuVoc1–GK (r≈.67) needs n≈10–40, and reproducing Vermeiren's own N=40–400 range would require a much weaker true effect (their r=.2 benchmark, already validated in `psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd`).

Digging further, `sampling-measurement-error.R` sidesteps this entirely by pre-building a tidy long-format dataframe via `do.call(rbind, lapply(...))`. So across these files there are really three distinct idioms for handling dynamically-named columns in plots — direct `.data[[var]]` referencing, temp-column renaming, and reshaping into long format.

This inconsistency isn't a bug since each approach works fine locally, but in a teaching codebase meant to show generalizable patterns, having three different idioms could confuse a reader comparing scripts. I think this is worth flagging to the user as a design observation before I decide whether to standardize the pattern or let it stand, especially since the new error-rates-process-control.R script will need this same capability and I don't want to introduce a fourth variant.
