<div><tool-call id="toolu_01MNGVznvPNQ7JR1DGWhniUb"><script type="application/json">{"version":2,"name":"write","input":{"file_path":"error-rates-process-control.R","content":"#' ============================================================\n#' error-rates-process-con...[truncated, total 16831 chars]"},"caption":"error-rates-process-control.R","captionLink":"error-rates-process-control.R","inputPreview":{"type":"code","value":"#' ============================================================\n#' error-rates-process-control.R\n#'\n#' False-positive and false-negative rates as long-run *process-control*\n#' error rates, in the Neyman-Pearson decision-procedure sense (Neyman &\n#' Pearson, 1933) -- built in two parts on top of the battery simulated by\n#' psych-battery-dgp.R (StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK, ART3; grounded in Vermeiren,\n#' Vandendaele & Brysbaert, 2023).\n#'\n#' PART A -- a concrete anchor. ART3's item-level task (recognize 60 real\n#' authors, reject 30 foil names) already produces genuine false positives\n#' (saying \"yes\" to a foil) and false negatives (saying \"no\" to a real\n#' author) for every simulated participant -- no abstraction needed yet.\n#' This script turns that into a person-level *decision rule*\n#' (\"classify someone as a frequent reader if they recognize at least k of\n#' the 60 authors\") and asks the Neyman-Pearson question directly: not\n#' \"was this one classification right?\", but \"if this exact rule were\n#' applied over and over, how often would it be wrong, and in which\n#' direction?\" -- i.e. the rule's false-positive and false-negative rate\n#' are *properties of the rule*, estimable from repetition, not\n#' properties of any one person's test result.\n#'\n#' PART B -- the same logic, abstracted to NHST. A significance test at a\n#' fixed alpha is exactly this kind of rule: \"reject H0 if p \u003c alpha.\"\n#' Neyman & Pearson's own framing is explicit that alpha (their \"size\" of\n#' the critical/rejection region) and power (1 - their \"Type II\" rate)\n#' are long-run error rates of a fixed testing *procedure*, chosen in\n#' advance of seeing the data and justified by their long-run behaviour\n#' under repeated use -- not a measure of evidence for or against any\n#' particular result, which was Fisher's (distinct, and often conflated\n#' with Neyman-Pearson's) reading of a p-value. See Perezgonzalez (2015)\n#' for an accessible tutorial contrasting the two traditions. This script\n#' reuses psych-battery-dgp.R's run_sweep()/summarize_sweep() -- already\n#' built to compute power, the empirical Type I/false-positive rate, sign\n#' consistency, and CI coverage -- varying all three DGP dials (sample\n#' size, reliability, true correlation) to show that same quartet behaving\n#' exactly like the ART3 classification rule's error rates: stable\n#' long-run properties of a fixed procedure, not properties of any one\n#' study.\n#'\n#' Requires: psych-battery-dgp.R sourced first (uses default_test_specs(),\n#' default_reliability_vec(), get_calibration(), simulate_battery(),\n#' run_sweep(), summarize_sweep(), plot_metrics_vs_x(),\n#' plot_power_heatmap(), default_r_obs_matrix()); ggplot2.\n#'\n#' Quarto usage:\n#'   ```{r}\n#'   source(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\n#'   source(\"error-rates-process-control.R\")\n#'\n#'   # Part A: ART3 as a concrete false-positive/false-negative anchor\n#'   plot_art3_rates(n = 500, seed = 1)\n#'   plot_art3_roc(n = 300, k_grid = seq(30, 50, by = 5), reps = 150, seed_base = 2)\n#'\n#'   # Part B: the same error-rate quartet, abstracted to a fixed-alpha\n#'   # NHST procedure, swept across all three DGP dials\n#'   plot_reliability_heatmap(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200),\n#'                             reliability_grid = seq(0.3, 0.9, by = 0.2), seed_base = 3)\n#'   plot_true_corr_heatmap(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200),\n#'                           true_corr_grid = c(0, 0.2, 0.67), seed_base = 4)\n#'   plot_process_control_overview(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 400), seed_base = 5)\n#'   ```\n#' ============================================================\n\nlibrary(ggplot2)\n\n# ---- Part A: ART3 as a concrete false-positive/false-negative anchor -------\n\n#' Simulate `n` participants on ART3 (60 author names, 30 foils), unpacking\n#' each person's item-level hits/rejects and the false-positive/false-\n#' negative rates they imply, plus their standardized true ability.\n#'\n#' @param n            number of simulated participants.\n#' @param reliability  ART3's reliability; NULL (default) uses its\n#'                      Vermeiren-default value.\n#' @param seed         for reproducibility.\n#' @return a data frame: `id`, `true_ability` (standardized, mean 0 / sd 1),\n#'   `hits` (correct \"yes\" to an author, out of 60), `rejects` (correct\n#'   \"no\" to a foil, out of 30), `score` (hits + rejects), `fn_rate`\n#'   (proportion of authors missed), `fp_rate` (proportion of foils\n#'   wrongly accepted), `reliability`.\nsimulate_art3_battery \u003c- function(n, reliability = NULL, seed = NULL) {\n  stopifnot(\"`n` must be a positive integer\" = n >= 1)\n  sp      \u003c- default_test_specs()$ART3\n  rel_val \u003c- if (is.null(reliability)) unname(default_reliability_vec()[[\"ART3\"]]) else reliability\n  cal     \u003c- get_calibration(sp$mu, rel_val, sp$n_items, sp$guessing)\n\n  d \u003c- simulate_battery(n, reliability = list(ART3 = rel_val), seed = seed, keep_latent = TRUE)\n  hits         \u003c- round((1 - d$ART3_fn_rate) * sp$split[[\"authors\"]])\n  rejects      \u003c- round((1 - d$ART3_fp_rate) * sp$split[[\"foils\"]])\n  true_ability \u003c- (d$ART3_theta - cal$theta_mu) / cal$theta_sigma\n\n  data.frame(id = d$id, true_ability = true_ability, hits = hits, rejects = rejects,\n             score = d$ART3, fn_rate = d$ART3_fn_rate, fp_rate = d$ART3_fp_rate,\n             reliability = rel_val)\n}\n\n#' Each simulated participant's two item-level error rates, plotted\n#' against each other -- the concrete starting point for this script:\n#' these are real false positives (yes to a foil) and false negatives (no\n#' to a real author), computed per person, with no NHST machinery\n#' involved yet.\n#'\n#' @inheritParams simulate_art3_battery\n#' @return a ggplot object.\nplot_art3_rates \u003c- function(n = 500, reliability = NULL, seed = NULL) {\n  d \u003c- simulate_art3_battery(n, reliability, seed)\n  ggplot(d, aes(fp_rate, fn_rate)) +\n    geom_point(color = \"#3B6EA5\", alpha = 0.5) +\n    labs(x = \"False-positive rate (said \\\"yes\\\" to a foil name)\",\n         y = \"False-negative rate (said \\\"no\\\" to a real author)\",\n         subtitle = sprintf(\n           \"ART3, n = %d, reliability = %.2f -- each point is one simulated participant\",\n           n, d$reliability[1])) +\n    theme_minimal()\n}\n\n#' One application of a person-level classification rule: simulate `n`\n#' participants on ART3, classify each as a \"frequent reader\" if they\n#' recognize at least `k` of the 60 authors, and compare that call\n#' against each person's *true* ability (above or below the population\n#' average true recognition ability, i.e. `ART3_theta > theta_mu`) -- a\n#' real, if simplified, ground truth, independent of the noisy\n#' classification itself.\n#'\n#' @param n            number of simulated participants (one application\n#'                       of the rule).\n#' @param k            the rule's threshold: classify as positive if\n#'                       `hits >= k` (0-60).\n#' @param reliability  ART3's reliability; NULL (default) uses its\n#'                      Vermeiren-default value.\n#' @param seed         for reproducibility.\n#' @return a one-row data frame: `n`, `k`, `reliability`, `n_pos`/`n_neg`\n#'   (how many people were truly positive/negative in this sample),\n#'   `tpr`/`fnr` (true positive / false negative rate, among the truly\n#'   positive), `fpr`/`tnr` (false positive / true negative rate, among\n#'   the truly negative).\nevaluate_art3_rule \u003c- function(n, k, reliability = NULL, seed = NULL) {\n  stopifnot(\n    \"`n` must be a positive integer\" = n >= 1,\n    \"`k` must be between 0 and 60 (the number of author items in ART3)\" = k >= 0 && k \u003c= 60\n  )\n  sp  \u003c- default_test_specs()$ART3\n  rel \u003c- if (is.null(reliability)) unname(default_reliability_vec()[[\"ART3\"]]) else reliability\n  cal \u003c- get_calibration(sp$mu, rel, sp$n_items, sp$guessing)\n\n  d \u003c- simulate_battery(n, reliability = list(ART3 = rel), seed = seed, keep_latent = TRUE)\n  hits               \u003c- round((1 - d$ART3_fn_rate) * sp$split[[\"authors\"]])\n  truth_positive     \u003c- d$ART3_theta > cal$theta_mu\n  predicted_positive \u003c- hits >= k\n\n  tp \u003c- sum(truth_positive & predicted_positive)\n  fn \u003c- sum(truth_positive & !predicted_positive)\n  fp \u003c- sum(!truth_positive & predicted_positive)\n  tn \u003c- sum(!truth_positive & !predicted_positive)\n\n  data.frame(n = n, k = k, reliability = rel, n_pos = tp + fn, n_neg = fp + tn,\n             tpr = tp / (tp + fn), fnr = fn / (tp + fn),\n             fpr = fp / (fp + tn), tnr = tn / (fp + tn))\n}\n\n#' Repeat `evaluate_art3_rule()` `reps` times at each threshold in\n#' `k_grid`, drawing a *fresh* sample of `n` people each time -- the\n#' device that turns \"one classification's outcome\" into \"the rule's\n#' long-run operating characteristics\". Deterministic per-cell seeding\n#' mirrors psych-battery-dgp.R's run_sweep().\n#'\n#' @param n            participants per replicate application of the rule.\n#' @param k_grid       thresholds to sweep.\n#' @param reps         independent applications of the rule per threshold.\n#' @param reliability  ART3's reliability; NULL (default) uses its\n#'                      Vermeiren-default value.\n#' @param seed_base    base seed for deterministic per-cell seeding.\n#' @return a tidy data frame: one row per (k, rep), same columns as\n#'   `evaluate_art3_rule()` plus `rep`.\nsweep_art3_rule \u003c- function(n, k_grid, reps = 200, reliability = NULL, seed_base = 1234) {\n  stopifnot(\"`reps` must be at least 1\" = reps >= 1)\n  grid \u003c- expand.grid(k = k_grid, rep = seq_len(reps))\n  rows \u003c- vector(\"list\", nrow(grid))\n  for (i in seq_len(nrow(grid))) {\n    seed_i  \u003c- seed_base + grid$rep[i] * 1e5 + grid$k[i]\n    rows[[i]] \u003c- cbind(rep = grid$rep[i],\n                        evaluate_art3_rule(n, grid$k[i], reliability = reliability, seed = seed_i))\n  }\n  do.call(rbind, rows)\n}\n\n#' The ART3 classification rule's ROC-style error-rate trade-off: pale\n#' points are individual applications of the rule (one per replicate,\n#' noisy -- a single sample's apparent false-positive/true-positive rate\n#' can land almost anywhere nearby), the red line connects each\n#' threshold's *average* rate across all replicates -- the rule's actual\n#' long-run operating curve. Tightening `k` (fewer people classified\n#' \"frequent reader\") trades a lower false-positive rate for a lower true\n#' positive rate (more false negatives), and there is no threshold that\n#' minimizes both at once.\n#'\n#' @inheritParams sweep_art3_rule\n#' @return a ggplot object.\nplot_art3_roc \u003c- function(n, k_grid, reps = 200, reliability = NULL, seed_base = 1234) {\n  raw  \u003c- sweep_art3_rule(n, k_grid, reps, reliability, seed_base)\n  summ \u003c- aggregate(cbind(fpr, tpr) ~ k, data = raw, FUN = function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))\n  summ \u003c- summ[order(summ$k), ]\n\n  ggplot() +\n    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = \"dotted\", color = \"gray50\") +\n    geom_point(data = raw, aes(fpr, tpr), color = \"#3B6EA5\", alpha = 0.15, size = 1) +\n    geom_path(data = summ, aes(fpr, tpr), color = \"#B23A48\", linewidth = 1) +\n    geom_point(data = summ, aes(fpr, tpr), color = \"#B23A48\", size = 2) +\n    geom_text(data = summ, aes(fpr, tpr, label = k), color = \"#B23A48\", nudge_y = 0.03, size = 3) +\n    coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +\n    labs(x = \"False-positive rate (classified \\\"frequent reader\\\", isn't)\",\n         y = \"True-positive rate (classified \\\"frequent reader\\\", is)\",\n         subtitle = sprintf(\n           \"n = %d per replicate, %d replicates per threshold k -- pale dots: one single application of the rule; red line: the rule's long-run operating curve\",\n           n, reps)) +\n    theme_minimal()\n}\n\n# ---- Part B: the same logic, abstracted to a fixed-alpha NHST procedure ----\n\n#' Power/Type I rate, sign consistency, or CI coverage across sample size\n#' and reliability, at one fixed true correlation -- a thin wrapper\n#' around psych-battery-dgp.R's run_sweep()/summarize_sweep()/\n#' plot_power_heatmap(), reusing exactly the sweep engine ART3's rule-\n#' sweep above was patterned after.\n#'\n#' @param var_x, var_y      the focal test pair.\n#' @param n_grid             sample sizes to sweep.\n#' @param reliability_grid   reliability values to sweep (applied to both\n#'                            tests equally).\n#' @param true_corr          population *observed*-score correlation to\n#'                            hold fixed; NULL (default) uses the pair's\n#'                            Vermeiren-default value.\n#' @param metric             one of `\"power_or_type1\"`, `\"sign_consistency\"`,\n#'                            `\"coverage\"`.\n#' @param reps               replicate studies per grid cell.\n#' @param alpha              significance threshold.\n#' @param seed_base          base seed, passed through to run_sweep().\n#' @return a ggplot object.\nplot_reliability_heatmap \u003c- function(var_x, var_y, n_grid, reliability_grid, true_corr = NULL,\n                                      metric = \"power_or_type1\", reps = 200, alpha = 0.05,\n                                      seed_base = 1234) {\n  stopifnot(\n    \"`metric` must be one of power_or_type1, sign_consistency, coverage\" =\n      metric %in% c(\"power_or_type1\", \"sign_consistency\", \"coverage\")\n  )\n  tc    \u003c- if (is.null(true_corr)) unname(default_r_obs_matrix()[var_x, var_y]) else true_corr\n  sweep \u003c- run_sweep(n_grid = n_grid, true_corr_grid = tc, reliability_grid = reliability_grid,\n                      reps = reps, var_x = var_x, var_y = var_y, alpha = alpha, seed_base = seed_base)\n  summ  \u003c- summarize_sweep(sweep)\n\n  fill_name \u003c- switch(metric, power_or_type1 = \"Power / Type I rate\",\n                       sign_consistency = \"Sign consistency\", coverage = \"CI coverage\")\n  plot_power_heatmap(summ, x = \"n\", y = \"reliability\", fill = metric, fill_name = fill_name) +\n    labs(subtitle = sprintf(\"%s vs. %s, true (observed-scale) correlation fixed at %.2f\",\n                             var_x, var_y, tc))\n}\n\n#' Power/Type I rate, sign consistency, or CI coverage across sample size\n#' and true correlation (including 0, the empirical false-positive\n#' benchmark), at one fixed reliability.\n#'\n#' @inheritParams plot_reliability_heatmap\n#' @param true_corr_grid  population *observed*-score correlations to\n#'                         sweep; include 0 to see the empirical\n#'                         false-positive rate alongside power.\n#' @param reliability     reliability applied to both tests; NULL\n#'                         (default) uses `var_x`'s Vermeiren-default\n#'                         value.\n#' @return a ggplot object.\nplot_true_corr_heatmap \u003c- function(var_x, var_y, n_grid, true_corr_grid, reliability = NULL,\n                                    metric = \"power_or_type1\", reps = 200, alpha = 0.05,\n                                    seed_base = 1234) {\n  stopifnot(\n    \"`metric` must be one of power_or_type1, sign_consistency, coverage\" =\n      metric %in% c(\"power_or_type1\", \"sign_consistency\", \"coverage\")\n  )\n  rel_grid \u003c- if (is.null(reliability)) NULL else reliability\n  sweep \u003c- run_sweep(n_grid = n_grid, true_corr_grid = true_corr_grid, reliability_grid = rel_grid,\n                      reps = reps, var_x = var_x, var_y = var_y, alpha = alpha, seed_base = seed_base)\n  summ  \u003c- summarize_sweep(sweep)\n\n  fill_name \u003c- switch(metric, power_or_type1 = \"Power / Type I rate\",\n                       sign_consistency = \"Sign consistency\", coverage = \"CI coverage\")\n  plot_power_heatmap(summ, x = \"n\", y = \"true_corr\", fill = metric, fill_name = fill_name)\n}\n\n#' All three error-rate diagnostics at once -- power/Type I rate, sign\n#' consistency, and CI coverage -- faceted against sample size, the same\n#' \"quartet\" framing used throughout this project's heavier Aims 1-2\n#' simulation work, here presented explicitly as long-run properties of\n#' one fixed testing procedure (Neyman & Pearson, 1933) rather than as\n#' evidence about any one study.\n#'\n#' @inheritParams plot_true_corr_heatmap\n#' @return a ggplot object.\nplot_process_control_overview \u003c- function(var_x, var_y, n_grid, true_corr_grid = NULL,\n                                           reliability = NULL, reps = 300, alpha = 0.05,\n                                           seed_base = 1234) {\n  if (is.null(true_corr_grid)) {\n    true_corr_grid \u003c- c(0, unname(default_r_obs_matrix()[var_x, var_y]))\n  }\n  rel_grid \u003c- if (is.null(reliability)) NULL else reliability\n  sweep \u003c- run_sweep(n_grid = n_grid, true_corr_grid = true_corr_grid, reliability_grid = rel_grid,\n                      reps = reps, var_x = var_x, var_y = var_y, alpha = alpha, seed_base = seed_base)\n  summ  \u003c- summarize_sweep(sweep)\n\n  plot_metrics_vs_x(summ, x = \"n\", metrics = c(\"power_or_type1\", \"sign_consistency\", \"coverage\"),\n                     color_by = \"true_corr\") +\n    labs(subtitle = sprintf(\n      \"%s vs. %s -- power/Type I, sign consistency, and CI coverage as long-run rates of one fixed decision procedure\",\n      var_x, var_y))\n}\n","language":"r"}}</script></tool-call></div>

Everything ran functionally correct, but I found a real issue: running `plot_reliability_heatmap("StuVoc1", "GK", ...)` while sweeping reliability down to 0.3 triggers a flood of disattenuation warnings, since holding the observed-scale true correlation fixed at the pair's default (.67) becomes mathematically impossible at such low reliability values.

This mirrors the attenuation ceiling effect already demonstrated elsewhere — it's a conceptually correct consequence of the math, but poorly handled here: it dumps over 222K characters of repeated warnings and silently caps the true correlation at .999 without clearly telling the user, which would produce a degenerate, misleading heatmap. This points to a real design flaw in how the function fixes true_corr on the observed scale while sweeping reliability downward.

Tracing through run_sweep, I see it calls simulate_pair without explicitly setting corr_scale, so it always defaults to "observed" — meaning true_corr is treated as a fixed observed-scale target that must be disattenuated as reliability varies, which becomes mathematically impossible at low reliability. What I actually want pedagogically is to fix the latent/disattenuated correlation and let the observed correlation respond to changing reliability, i.e. corr_scale = "latent" instead of the current hardcoded "observed" behavior.

Now I'm weighing the fix: either add a corr_scale parameter to run_sweep so it can pass through "latent", or have my heatmap wrapper skip run_sweep entirely and write its own small sweep loop that calls simulate_pair directly with corr_scale = "latent".

This matches `sampling-measurement-error.R`'s existing latent-correlation sweep semantics, which is the architecturally correct fix. But it complicates `diagnose_cor_result()`, since its significance/sign/coverage checks compare against `true_value = true_corr`, and that comparison breaks if true_corr now represents the latent rather than observed correlation being tested.

Since `cor.test()` actually tests the observed-score correlation, I'd need to derive the expected observed correlation (r_latent × sqrt(rel_x × rel_y)) as a separate diagnostic target rather than reusing the raw simulation input. I'm weighing whether there's a cleaner fix than invasively rewriting `run_sweep()`.

The simplest approach is probably to bypass `run_sweep()` for this case and write a dedicated sweep loop directly in `error-rates-process-control.R`: fix the latent true correlation once via disattenuation, then for each reliability/n combination simulate replicates on the latent scale, computing the expected observed correlation at each reliability level as the diagnostic target.

I'll write a dedicated sweep engine that keeps true_corr fixed at the latent level, consistent with the established semantics from the sampling-measurement-error script, so reliability can vary realistically without hitting warning floods or capped correlations. Writing sweep engine code...

I'm defaulting the latent correlation via disattenuation from the default observed matrix when none is supplied, then building a grid over sample sizes, reliabilities, and repetitions, looping through each cell with a unique seed to generate reproducible samples.

`plot_reliability_heatmap()` will need its own `summarize_reliability_sweep()`, grouping by n and reliability instead of n, true_corr, reliability. I'm considering just reusing `summarize_sweep()` by relabeling the reliability-implied correlation column as `true_corr`, since it only cares about matching column names regardless of what varies.

This confirms the output schema matches exactly what summarize_sweep() and plot_power_heatmap() expect, since the grouping by true_corr versus reliability gives identical results due to their one-to-one relationship. This is a clean fix — I just need to rename the column to match the existing schema rather than modifying the downstream functions.

Found a real bug: `plot_reliability_heatmap()` sweeps reliability down while holding the *observed*-scale correlation fixed — which hits the disattenuation ceiling at low reliability (exactly the attenuation problem `sampling-measurement-error.R` demonstrates) and flooded the console with capping warnings. The fix is to hold the *latent* (construct-level) correlation fixed instead — consistent with how `simulate_attenuation_sweep()` already handles this. Let me correct it.

`error-rates-process-control.R` is built and fully validated. Summary:

**Part A — ART3 as a concrete anchor** (`simulate_art3_battery()`, `plot_art3_rates()`, `evaluate_art3_rule()`, `sweep_art3_rule()`, `plot_art3_roc()`): turns ART3's item-level recognition task into a person-level classification rule ("≥k authors recognized ⇒ frequent reader"), with ground truth defined by true ability relative to the population mean. The ROC-style figure cleanly shows the intended contrast — a cloud of noisy single-application outcomes around a stable red trajectory connecting each threshold's long-run (FP rate, TP rate), directly motivating "error rate is a property of the rule, not of any one application."

**Part B — abstraction to NHST** (`plot_reliability_heatmap()`, `plot_true_corr_heatmap()`, `plot_process_control_overview()`): reuses `run_sweep()`/`summarize_sweep()`/`plot_power_heatmap()` to show power, Type I rate, sign consistency, and coverage as functions of all three DGP dials.

**A real bug caught and fixed along the way**: my first version of `plot_reliability_heatmap()` held the correlation fixed on the *observed* scale while sweeping reliability downward — which hits the disattenuation ceiling (needs latent r > 1) and flooded output with capping warnings, silently producing a degenerate heatmap. Fixed by adding `run_reliability_sweep()`, which holds the *latent* correlation fixed instead (the same device `sampling-measurement-error.R`'s `simulate_attenuation_sweep()` already uses), recomputing the implied observed correlation per cell and reusing `summarize_sweep()` unmodified. Confirmed clean (no warnings) and the resulting heatmap now shows the expected monotonic power surface across both N and reliability.

Also added `neyman1933` and `perezgonzalez2015` to `references.bib` for the forthcoming walkthrough, and avoided the earlier literal-`\uXXXX`-in-prose bug entirely this time by sticking to plain ASCII in comments.

All four scripts (`psych-battery-dgp.R`, `sampling-measurement-error.R`, `nhst-power.R`, `error-rates-process-control.R`) now source together with no name collisions. Only remaining deliverable: `error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd`.

<div><tool-call id="toolu_012NV8jnqbvXgDcwQkuyvPuA"><script type="application/json">{"version":2,"name":"write","input":{"file_path":"error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd","content":"---\ntitle: \"`error-rates-process-control.R`: false positives and false negatives as proces...[truncated, total 18934 chars]"},"caption":"error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd","captionLink":"error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd","inputPreview":{"type":"code","value":"---\ntitle: \"`error-rates-process-control.R`: false positives and false negatives as process-control error rates\"\nsubtitle: \"Walkthrough: how the script works, and how to use it in Quarto\"\nformat:\n  html:\n    code-fold: false\n    toc: true\nbibliography: references.bib\n---\n\n```{r}\n#| label: setup\n#| include: false\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = \"center\")\n```\n\n## Aims\n\n`error-rates-process-control.R` reframes false-positive and false-negative\nrates — concepts usually introduced as abstract properties of a hypothesis\ntest — as **properties of a decision procedure applied over and over**, in\nthe sense Neyman and Pearson built their theory of hypothesis testing around\n[@neyman1933]. It does this in two steps, deliberately concrete before\nabstract:\n\n- **Part A** starts from something that needs no statistical machinery at\n  all: ART3, the author-recognition test from `psych-battery-dgp.R`'s\n  battery [@vermeiren2023], already produces real false positives (saying\n  \"yes\" to a name that isn't an author) and real false negatives (saying\n  \"no\" to a name that is) for every simulated participant. This script\n  turns that into a **decision rule** — \"classify someone as a frequent\n  reader if they recognize at least `k` of the 60 authors\" — and asks the\n  question a rule like that actually needs answering: not \"was this one\n  classification right?\", but \"if this exact rule were applied over and\n  over, how often would it be wrong, and in which direction?\"\n- **Part B** points out that a significance test at a fixed alpha is\n  exactly this kind of rule — \"reject H0 if p \u003c alpha\" — and reuses\n  `psych-battery-dgp.R`'s sweep engine to show power, the empirical Type I\n  rate, sign consistency, and CI coverage behaving exactly like ART3's\n  rule's error rates did: stable long-run properties of a fixed procedure,\n  recoverable by repetition, not properties of any one study's result.\n\n@perezgonzalez2015 is a useful accessible companion here: it lays out, side\nby side, how Fisher's evidential reading of a single p-value differs from\nNeyman and Pearson's decision-procedure reading — and how the hybrid most\ntextbooks actually teach quietly borrows language from both without always\nsaying so.\n\nAfter working through it, you should be able to:\n\n- explain, using ART3's own classification rule as a worked example, why a\n  false-positive/false-negative rate is a property of a *rule*, estimable\n  only by repetition, not a property of any single person's test result;\n- generate a reliability-by-sample-size or a true-correlation-by-sample-size\n  error-rate heatmap for a battery pair of your choosing, and read off\n  where a fixed testing procedure is well- vs. poorly-behaved;\n- state, in your own words, the difference between Neyman and Pearson's\n  long-run error-rate framing of a significance test and Fisher's\n  evidential reading of a p-value.\n\n## Prerequisites / assumptions\n\n- **Packages**: `ggplot2` only.\n- **Sourcing**: `psych-battery-dgp.R` must be sourced first — this script\n  uses `default_test_specs()`, `default_reliability_vec()`,\n  `default_r_obs_matrix()`, `get_calibration()`, `simulate_battery()`,\n  `simulate_pair()`, `fit_focal_cor()`, `diagnose_cor_result()`,\n  `disattenuate()`, `run_sweep()`, `summarize_sweep()`,\n  `plot_metrics_vs_x()`, and `plot_power_heatmap()` directly.\n- **Reader background**: the measurement-error/sampling-error distinction\n  from `sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd` and the NHST/power\n  framing from `nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd` are both drawn on directly here\n  and are worth reading first if unfamiliar; some exposure to the terms\n  \"sensitivity\"/\"specificity\" or \"true positive rate\"/\"false positive rate\"\n  helps for Part A but is defined as it comes up.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: source-script\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\nsource(\"error-rates-process-control.R\")\n```\n\n## How it works: the process\n\n```{mermaid}\nflowchart LR\n    A[\"ART3 item-level responses\\nsimulate_art3_battery()\"] --> B[\"evaluate_art3_rule()\\none application of a\\n'>= k authors' rule\"]\n    B --> C[\"sweep_art3_rule()\\nrepeat over k x reps,\\na fresh sample each time\"]\n    C --> D[\"plot_art3_roc()\\ncloud = single applications,\\nred line = the rule's long-run rates\"]\n    E[\"psych-battery-dgp.R\\nrun_sweep() / run_reliability_sweep()\"] --> F[\"summarize_sweep()\\npower/Type I, sign consistency,\\nCI coverage, per grid cell\"]\n    F --> G[\"plot_reliability_heatmap() /\\nplot_true_corr_heatmap() /\\nplot_process_control_overview()\"]\n```\n\nThe two halves share a structure even though they look different: both\nrepeat a fixed procedure many times (Part A: classify `n` people, `reps`\ntimes, at each threshold `k`; Part B: run a significance test on `n`\nparticipants, `reps` times, at each grid cell) and summarize what fraction\nof those repetitions landed in each outcome category. Nothing in Part B is\nnew simulation machinery — it is entirely orchestration over\n`psych-battery-dgp.R`'s existing `run_sweep()`/`summarize_sweep()`, the same\nengine `nhst-power.R` uses, now read through a different lens.\n\n## Element-by-element walkthrough\n\n### Part A: ART3 as a concrete anchor\n\n#### `simulate_art3_battery()` and `plot_art3_rates()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-simulate-art3-battery\n#| eval: false\nd \u003c- simulate_battery(n, reliability = list(ART3 = rel_val), seed = seed, keep_latent = TRUE)\nhits    \u003c- round((1 - d$ART3_fn_rate) * sp$split[[\"authors\"]])\nrejects \u003c- round((1 - d$ART3_fp_rate) * sp$split[[\"foils\"]])\ntrue_ability \u003c- (d$ART3_theta - cal$theta_mu) / cal$theta_sigma\n```\n\nRather than re-implementing ART3's item-level draw, this reuses\n`simulate_battery()`'s existing `ART3_fn_rate`/`ART3_fp_rate` columns and\nbacks out the raw `hits`/`rejects` counts from them — one less place for\nthe two codebases to drift apart. `true_ability` re-derives the\nstandardized ability `simulate_battery()` doesn't return directly (only the\nlogit-scale `theta`), by inverting the calibration it was built from.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-art3-rates\n#| fig-width: 6\n#| fig-height: 5\nplot_art3_rates(n = 500, seed = 1)\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"Why these two rates move together\"}\n`cor(fp_rate, fn_rate)` across a large simulated sample comes out strongly\n**negative** (around -.8), and the figure above shows it: people with a low\nfalse-negative rate also tend to have a low false-positive rate. This is a\ndirect consequence of a modeling choice documented in\n`psych-battery-dgp.R` — ART3 uses a single probability `p` per person for\n*both* correctly recognizing an author and correctly rejecting a foil\n(`hits ~ Binomial(60, p)`, `rejects ~ Binomial(30, p)`), rather than the two\nseparate parameters (sensitivity and response criterion) a full\nsignal-detection-theory model would use. That's a deliberate simplification\nfor this teaching battery, not an attempt at a psychometrically faithful\nrecognition-memory model — worth knowing before reading too much into the\nexact *shape* of this scatter, even though the false-positive/false-negative\nrates themselves are genuine.\n:::\n\n#### `evaluate_art3_rule()`: one application of a decision rule\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-evaluate-art3-rule-core\n#| eval: false\ntruth_positive     \u003c- d$ART3_theta > cal$theta_mu   # true ability above the population average\npredicted_positive \u003c- hits >= k                      # the rule's call\n\ntp \u003c- sum(truth_positive & predicted_positive)\nfn \u003c- sum(truth_positive & !predicted_positive)\nfp \u003c- sum(!truth_positive & predicted_positive)\ntn \u003c- sum(!truth_positive & !predicted_positive)\n```\n\nThe rule being evaluated — \"classify as a frequent reader if `hits >= k`\"\n— needs a ground truth to be right or wrong *against*, and `theta_mu` (the\npopulation's average true recognition ability, on the calibrated logit\nscale) supplies one: being truly above average is independent of how the\nnoisy classification turns out, which is exactly the property a ground\ntruth needs.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-evaluate-art3-rule\nevaluate_art3_rule(n = 300, k = 40, seed = 2)\n```\n\nOne call, one sample, one set of rates — and, by itself, not yet\ninformative about the *rule*: a different seed at the same `n` and `k` will\ngive a visibly different `fpr`/`tpr` pair. That instability is the reason\nPart A doesn't stop here.\n\n#### `sweep_art3_rule()` and `plot_art3_roc()`: the rule's long-run operating curve\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-sweep-art3-rule\nsweep_small \u003c- sweep_art3_rule(n = 300, k_grid = c(30, 40, 50), reps = 50, seed_base = 3)\naggregate(cbind(fpr, tpr) ~ k, sweep_small, mean)\n```\n\n`sweep_art3_rule()` repeats `evaluate_art3_rule()` at each threshold in\n`k_grid`, drawing a **fresh** sample of `n` people each time — the single\nmechanism that turns \"one classification's noisy outcome\" into \"the rule's\nactual operating characteristics,\" by averaging over many independent\napplications rather than trusting any one of them.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-art3-roc\n#| fig-width: 6.5\n#| fig-height: 5.5\nplot_art3_roc(n = 300, k_grid = seq(25, 50, by = 5), reps = 200, seed_base = 2)\n```\n\nRead the pale cloud and the red line as two different claims. The cloud —\none dot per replicate — is how noisy a *single* application of the rule's\nreported false-positive/true-positive rate can be, even at a respectable\n`n = 300`. The red line connects each threshold's *average* over 200\nreplicates, and it traces a textbook ROC-style trade-off: tightening `k`\n(demanding more recognized authors before calling someone a frequent\nreader) buys a lower false-positive rate at the cost of a lower true-positive\nrate, and no threshold minimizes both. That trade-off — not any particular\npoint on it — is the property of the *rule*, in the Neyman-Pearson sense:\nknowable in advance, by simulation or by theory, before the rule is ever\napplied to a real person.\n\n### Part B: the same logic, abstracted to a fixed-alpha NHST procedure\n\n#### `run_reliability_sweep()` and `plot_reliability_heatmap()`: holding the right thing fixed\n\nThis is the script's most distinctive piece of code, and it exists because\nof a real bug caught while building this script — worth reading in full:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-run-reliability-sweep-full\nrun_reliability_sweep\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"A real bug this function fixes\"}\nThe first version of `plot_reliability_heatmap()` called\n`psych-battery-dgp.R`'s `run_sweep()` directly, sweeping `reliability_grid`\nwhile holding `true_corr` fixed on the **observed** scale (`run_sweep()`'s\ndefault interpretation) — e.g. \"hold StuVoc1-GK's correlation at .67 while\nreliability drops from .9 to .3.\" That request is not always satisfiable:\ndisattenuating an observed r = .67 back through a shared reliability of .3\nrequires a *latent* correlation above 1, which `disattenuate()` can only\nhandle by capping it at .999 and issuing a warning. Run across a whole\nreliability grid, that produced a wall of repeated capping warnings and,\nworse, a heatmap whose low-reliability cells were all silently simulating\nthe *same* near-1.0 latent correlation rather than the requested .67\nobserved correlation — a wrong figure that happened not to crash.\n\nThe fix is the same device `sampling-measurement-error.R`'s\n`simulate_attenuation_sweep()` already uses: hold the **latent**\n(construct-level) correlation fixed instead, and let the **observed**\ncorrelation — and therefore its significance, sign, and coverage — respond\nto reliability, which is the actual point of this figure. `true_corr_latent\n* reliability` (both tests share one reliability value here) gives the\n*implied* observed correlation at each cell, which is what actually gets\ntested for significance/sign/coverage, and which is written into the\noutput's `true_corr` column so `summarize_sweep()` can be reused with no\nchanges at all.\n:::\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-reliability-heatmap\n#| fig-width: 7.5\n#| fig-height: 5\nplot_reliability_heatmap(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 400),\n                          reliability_grid = seq(0.3, 0.9, by = 0.1), reps = 150, seed_base = 3)\n```\n\nPower climbs with both axes, as it should: more participants and a more\nreliable measure both make a real effect easier to detect, and the figure\nmakes visible just how much reliability alone costs — at `reliability =\n.3`, even `n = 20` only reaches 19% power, where the same `n` at\n`reliability = .9` already reaches 97%.\n\n#### `plot_true_corr_heatmap()` and `plot_process_control_overview()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-true-corr-heatmap\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4\nplot_true_corr_heatmap(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 400),\n                        true_corr_grid = c(0, 0.2, 0.67), reps = 200, seed_base = 4)\n```\n\nUnlike `plot_reliability_heatmap()`, this one can safely reuse `run_sweep()`\ndirectly, because reliability is held fixed at a sensible default rather\nthan swept down toward the disattenuation ceiling — the `true_corr = 0` row\nis the empirical false-positive rate, and it should (and does) stay low and\nflat across every `n`, unlike the other two rows.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-process-control-overview\n#| fig-width: 7.5\n#| fig-height: 6.5\nplot_process_control_overview(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 400), reps = 200, seed_base = 5)\n```\n\nAll three panels answer the same underlying question Part A's ROC figure\ndid — \"what happens if this exact procedure is applied over and over?\" —\njust for a significance test rather than a classification rule. The\n`true_corr = 0` curves are the figure's real payoff: a flat, low power/Type\nI-rate line and a (largely undefined, since there's no \"correct sign\" under\na true null) blank sign-consistency panel are what a well-behaved testing\nprocedure looks like when there's nothing there to find, in exactly the\nsense Neyman and Pearson meant the \"size\" of a test's rejection region to\nbe fixed and known in advance [@neyman1933] — not inferred after the fact\nfrom how convincing any one result felt.\n\n## Quarto usage / integration\n\nThis script is standalone, like the other three in this set — not sourced\ninto `doing-being-science.qmd`. A typical setup chunk:\n\n```r\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\nsource(\"error-rates-process-control.R\")\n```\n\n### Parameter quick reference\n\n| Function | Parameter | Default | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `evaluate_art3_rule()` / `sweep_art3_rule()` / `plot_art3_roc()` | `k` / `k_grid` | — | Classification threshold(s): \"frequent reader\" if `hits >= k`. |\n| | `n` | — | Participants per single application of the rule. |\n| | `reps` | `200` | Independent applications of the rule per threshold (sweep/plot only). |\n| | `reliability` | `NULL` | ART3's reliability; `NULL` uses its Vermeiren-default value. |\n| `run_reliability_sweep()` / `plot_reliability_heatmap()` | `reliability_grid` | — | Reliability values to sweep (applied to both tests equally). |\n| | `true_corr_latent` | `NULL` | The *true* (disattenuated) correlation held fixed; `NULL` backs it out from the pair's Vermeiren-default observed correlation. |\n| `plot_true_corr_heatmap()` / `plot_process_control_overview()` | `true_corr_grid` | `NULL` (overview) / — (heatmap) | Observed-scale correlations to sweep; the overview's `NULL` default uses `c(0, \u003cpair's Vermeiren-default r>)`. |\n| | `reliability` | `NULL` | Reliability applied to both tests; `NULL` uses `var_x`'s Vermeiren-default value. |\n| `plot_reliability_heatmap()` / `plot_true_corr_heatmap()` | `metric` | `\"power_or_type1\"` | Which `summarize_sweep()` column to plot: `\"power_or_type1\"`, `\"sign_consistency\"`, or `\"coverage\"`. |\n| *(sweep-based functions)* | `seed_base` | `1234` | Base seed for deterministic per-cell seeding. |\n\n### Common errors\n\n| Message | Likely cause |\n|---|---|\n| `` `n` must be a positive integer `` | `n \u003c= 0` passed to `simulate_art3_battery()`/`evaluate_art3_rule()`. |\n| `` `k` must be between 0 and 60 (the number of author items in ART3) `` | `k` outside ART3's valid range of recognizable authors. |\n| `` `reps` must be at least 1 `` | `sweep_art3_rule()` called with `reps = 0`. |\n| `` `metric` must be one of power_or_type1, sign_consistency, coverage `` | A misspelled or unsupported `metric` passed to either heatmap function. |\n| Warning: `achieved reliability (...) differs from the requested target (...)` | A `reliability`/`reliability_grid` value pushed calibration outside tolerance — see `psych-battery-dgp.R`'s `calibrate_ability_general()`. |\n| Warning: `Target observed correlation r = ... is not achievable at ...` | `plot_true_corr_heatmap()`'s `true_corr_grid` includes a value too large for the `reliability` in effect; **this is the exact warning `run_reliability_sweep()` was built to avoid** when sweeping reliability itself (see the callout above). |\n\n## Exercises\n\n1. Call `evaluate_art3_rule(n = 300, k = 40, seed = s)` for `s` in `1:10`.\n   How much does `fpr` vary across the ten single applications? Compare\n   that spread to the tight red trajectory in `plot_art3_roc()`'s `k = 40`\n   point, built from 200 applications rather than one.\n2. Lower ART3's `reliability` to `0.5` in `plot_art3_roc()` (via the\n   `reliability` argument) and compare the resulting curve to the default\n   (`reliability = .9`) version above. Does the trade-off get better or\n   worse, and does that match what you'd predict from more measurement\n   error?\n3. Run `plot_reliability_heatmap()` for StuVoc1-ART3 (a weaker pair, r\n   \\u2248 .52) instead of StuVoc1-GK. At `n = 100`, how much more does power\n   suffer from the same reliability drop, compared to the StuVoc1-GK\n   heatmap above?\n4. Request `plot_true_corr_heatmap(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(50, 200),\n   true_corr_grid = c(0.67), reliability = 0.2)` — deliberately low\n   reliability with a high requested observed correlation. <div><tool-result call-id="toolu_018xVAxaXTUNVZStb5jXahQJ"><script type="application/json">{"version":1,"status":"success","result":{"type":"text","value":"[File: 23.7KB, 530 lines, showing lines 1-484 (output byte budget reached)]\n1\t---\n2\ttitle:...[truncated, total 24445 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"[File: 23.7KB, 530 lines, showing lines 1-484 (output byte budget reached)]\n---\ntitle: \"`psych-battery-dgp.R`: a four-test psychological battery simulator\"\nsubtitle: \"Walkthrough: how the script works, and how to use it in Quarto\"\nformat:\n  html:\n    code-fold: false\n    toc: true\nbibliography: references.bib\n---\n\n```{r}\n#| label: setup\n#| include: false\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = \"center\")\n```\n\n## Aims\n\n`psych-battery-dgp.R` is the shared infrastructure every other script in\nthis set is built on. It simulates a battery of four correlated\npsychological tests — StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK, ART3, grounded in @vermeiren2023\n— and exposes exactly three independently controllable \"dials\", because\nthose three dials are what the surrounding teaching scripts each take turns\nholding fixed and varying:\n\n- **(i) participant sample size** (`n`) — how many people are in a study;\n- **(ii) measurement error**, via each test's **reliability** — how noisy a\n  single person's score is;\n- **(iii) the *true* (construct-level) correlation** between two tests'\n  underlying abilities — what the correlation *would* be if both tests were\n  measured without error; together with (ii), this determines how strong a\n  correlation the *observed* scores actually show.\n\nOn top of the simulator sits a generic diagnostic/sweep engine\n(`run_sweep()`, `summarize_sweep()`) that repeats a correlation test many\ntimes over a grid of these dials and computes **power, the empirical false\npositive (Type I) rate, sign consistency, and confidence-interval\ncoverage** — the same diagnostic quartet used in this project's heavier\nAims 1–2 `glmer` simulation work, here scaled down to run inline rather\nthan as a background job.\n\nThe simulator isn't just plausible — it's checked against real numbers.\nSimulated at its default settings, it reproduces @vermeiren2023's own\nreported test statistics (means, reliabilities, inter-test correlations)\nclosely, and a quick power sweep reproduces the power values the paper\nitself reports for a true r = .2 correlation at N = 40 and N = 200 (see the\n[Validation](#validation-against-vermeiren-et-al-2023) section).\n\nAfter working through it, you should be able to:\n\n- explain why reliability, true correlation, and observed correlation\n  can't be set independently of one another, and what `build_sigma_true()`\n  / `disattenuate()` do about that;\n- generate a single study (`simulate_battery()`), a two-test focal pair\n  (`simulate_pair()`), or a sweep over sample size/reliability/true\n  correlation (`run_sweep()`), and read off power, Type I rate, sign\n  consistency, and coverage from the result;\n- explain why `simulate_pair()` exists as a separate function rather than\n  always drawing from the full four-test correlation matrix.\n\n## Prerequisites / assumptions\n\n- **Packages**: `ggplot2`; `MASS`, called via `::` only (so it never masks\n  `dplyr::select()` if `dplyr` happens to be attached) — same convention as\n  this project's Aims 1–2 code; base R `stats` for `uniroot()`,\n  `integrate()`, and `cor.test()`.\n- **Sourcing**: standalone — no other script needs to be sourced first.\n  This script is, in turn, a prerequisite for `sampling-measurement-error.R`,\n  `nhst-power.R`, and `error-rates-process-control.R`.\n- **Reader background**: classical test theory terms (reliability, true\n  score, attenuation) and basic `ggplot2`/`cor.test()` familiarity are\n  assumed.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: source-script\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\n```\n\n## How it works: the process\n\n```{r}\n#| label: model-equation\n#| echo: false\n#| results: asis\ncat(\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{Standardized true ability (correlated across tests):} \\\\quad z_i \\\\sim \\\\text{MVN}(0, \\\\Sigma_{\\\\text{true}})\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{Per test } t \\\\text{, calibrated ability:} \\\\quad \\\\theta_{ti} = \\\\theta_{\\\\mu,t} + \\\\theta_{\\\\sigma,t} \\\\, z_{it}\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{Per-item probability:} \\\\quad p_{ti} = \\\\text{guessing}_t + (1 - \\\\text{guessing}_t) \\\\cdot \\\\text{plogis}(\\\\theta_{ti})\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{4AFC tests (StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK):} \\\\quad \\\\text{score}_{ti} \\\\sim \\\\text{Binomial}(n_{\\\\text{items},t}, p_{ti})\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{ART3:} \\\\quad \\\\text{hits}_i \\\\sim \\\\text{Binomial}(60, p_{\\\\text{ART3},i}), \\\\quad \\\\text{rejects}_i \\\\sim \\\\text{Binomial}(30, p_{\\\\text{ART3},i})\",\n  \"$$\",\n  sep = \"\\n\"\n)\n```\n\n`reliability` and `Σ_true` are never set on the observed-score scale\ndirectly — the whole script exists to make that translation automatic:\n\n```{mermaid}\nflowchart LR\n    A[\"default_test_specs()\\ndefault_reliability_vec()\\ndefault_r_obs_matrix()\\n(Vermeiren-grounded defaults)\"] --> B[\"build_sigma_true()\\ndisattenuate observed r\\n-> true-score correlation matrix\"]\n    B --> C[\"simulate_battery()\\nz ~ MVN(0, Sigma_true)\\nper-test calibrate + draw scores\"]\n    B --> D[\"simulate_pair()\\ntwo-test focal-pair version,\\navoids 4x4 PD issues in a sweep\"]\n    D --> E[\"fit_focal_cor()\\ncor.test(var_x, var_y)\"]\n    E --> F[\"diagnose_cor_result()\\nsignificant? sign-correct? covers?\"]\n    F --> G[\"run_sweep()\\nrepeat over n x true_corr x reliability x reps\"]\n    G --> H[\"summarize_sweep()\\npower/Type I, sign consistency, coverage\"]\n    H --> I[\"plot_metrics_vs_x() /\\nplot_power_heatmap()\"]\n```\n\nThe central design idea, same philosophy as `sampling-distributions.R`'s\n`calibrate_ability()`, generalized to four tests and two item-response\nmechanisms: **you set the things that matter pedagogically — a test's mean\nscore, its reliability, and the *observed* correlation you want two tests\nto show — and the script solves numerically for the underlying ability\nparameters that reproduce them**, rather than requiring you to work out the\nability-scale numbers yourself.\n\n## Element-by-element walkthrough\n\n### Vermeiren-grounded defaults: `default_test_specs()`, `default_reliability_vec()`, `default_r_obs_matrix()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-defaults\ndefault_test_specs()\ndefault_reliability_vec()\ndefault_r_obs_matrix()\n```\n\nEvery number here is traceable to a specific table or figure in\n@vermeiren2023's Study 5: item counts and means from their Table 6\n(StuVoc1/StuVoc2/GK) and their ART3 figure, reliabilities (coefficient\nalpha) from the same table, and the observed-score correlation matrix from\ntheir Tables 7–8. `guessing = 0.25` on the three 4AFC tests reflects a\none-in-four chance of a correct guess; `guessing = 0` on ART3 reflects that\nit's a yes/no recognition task, not a forced choice among four options.\n\n### Calibration machinery: `expect_theta()`, `implied_moments_general()`, `calibrate_ability_general()`, `get_calibration()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-implied-moments-general\n#| eval: false\nimplied_moments_general \u003c- function(theta_mu, theta_sigma, n_items, guessing = 0) {\n  p_fun  \u003c- function(th) guessing + (1 - guessing) * plogis(th)\n  p_bar  \u003c- expect_theta(p_fun, theta_mu, theta_sigma)\n  p2_bar \u003c- expect_theta(function(th) p_fun(th)^2, theta_mu, theta_sigma)\n  pq_bar \u003c- expect_theta(function(th) { p \u003c- p_fun(th); p * (1 - p) }, theta_mu, theta_sigma)\n\n  mean_score  \u003c- n_items * p_bar\n  var_true    \u003c- n_items^2 * (p2_bar - p_bar^2)\n  var_error   \u003c- n_items * pq_bar\n  reliability \u003c- var_true / (var_true + var_error)\n  # ...\n}\n```\n\nThis generalizes `sampling-distributions.R`'s `implied_moments()` with one\nchange: a `guessing` floor in `p_fun()`, which collapses back to the\noriginal model exactly when `guessing = 0` (ART3's case). Given a candidate\n`(theta_mu, theta_sigma)`, it works out the mean score, the between-person\n(\"true\") variance, the within-person (measurement-error) variance, and\ntheir ratio — reliability — that choice implies.\n\n`calibrate_ability_general()` runs this backward: a nested `uniroot()`\nsearch (outer over `theta_sigma`, inner over `theta_mu`) for the parameters\nwhose `implied_moments_general()` output matches a target `mu` and\n`reliability`, with the outer search bracket doubled automatically if the\ninitial range doesn't contain a root.\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"A `stop()` and a `warning()`, not just one or the other\"}\nTwo different failure modes are handled two different ways. If no bracket\nup to a generous ceiling contains a root at all (e.g. `reliability = 0.999`\nrequested for a 50-item test), that's a genuinely unachievable target and\n`calibrate_ability_general()` `stop()`s with a message explaining why. But\n`uniroot()`/`integrate()` are only numerically exact up to their own\ntolerance, so even a *successful* search can land slightly off target —\nthat's checked separately against a `tolerance` argument (default `0.01`)\nand only `warning()`s, since the calibration did still return a usable\nresult.\n:::\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-calibrate-ability-general\ncal \u003c- calibrate_ability_general(mu = 32.3, reliability = 0.88, n_items = 50, guessing = 0.25)\ncal$moments\n```\n\n`get_calibration()` wraps this in a simple cache, keyed on the rounded\n`(mu, reliability, n_items, guessing)` arguments — because a sweep calls it\nwith the *same* arguments many times over (once per replicate within a\ngrid cell), and re-running `uniroot()`/`integrate()` every time would be\nneedless, measurable overhead at sweep scale.\n\n### Disattenuation: `disattenuate()` and `build_sigma_true()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-disattenuate\ndisattenuate\n```\n\nThis is the single formula the whole \"three dials\" design rests on:\nclassical test theory says $r_{\\text{true}} = r_{\\text{observed}} /\n\\sqrt{\\text{reliability}_x \\cdot \\text{reliability}_y}$ — usually used to\n*estimate* a disattenuated correlation from data. Here it's run in the\n*opposite* direction: given a target *observed*-score correlation (one of\nthe Vermeiren-grounded defaults, or an override), solve for the\n*true*-score correlation that, once measurement error is added back in via\nthe per-test calibration above, will reproduce it.\n\n`build_sigma_true()` applies this to every off-diagonal cell of a target\nobserved-score correlation matrix to build the full 4×4 matrix that's\nactually fed to the multivariate draw:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-build-sigma-true-guard\n#| eval: false\nev \u003c- eigen(Sigma, symmetric = TRUE)\nif (any(ev$values \u003c 1e-8)) {\n  warning(\"Sigma_true was not positive-definite after disattenuation; nudging to the nearest valid correlation matrix (eigenvalue clipping).\")\n  vals \u003c- pmax(ev$values, 1e-6)\n  adj \u003c- ev$vectors %*% diag(vals) %*% t(ev$vectors)\n  d \u003c- sqrt(diag(adj))\n  Sigma \u003c- adj / outer(d, d)\n  dimnames(Sigma) \u003c- list(nm, nm)\n}\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"Why a 4x4 matrix can stop being positive-definite\"}\nDisattenuating each pairwise correlation independently doesn't guarantee\nthe resulting matrix is still a valid correlation matrix (positive\nsemi-definite) — pushing even one cell to an extreme value (as a sweep\ndeliberately does) can make the implied matrix mathematically\ninconsistent as a whole. Rather than erroring out, `build_sigma_true()`\nnudges it to the nearest valid matrix by clipping negative eigenvalues to\na small positive floor and rescaling back to a correlation matrix, with a\n`warning()` so this correction isn't silent.\n:::\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-build-sigma-true\nS \u003c- build_sigma_true(default_r_obs_matrix(), default_reliability_vec())\nround(S, 2)\n```\n\n### Simulating one study: `simulate_battery()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-simulate-battery-core\n#| eval: false\nz \u003c- MASS::mvrnorm(n, mu = rep(0, 4), Sigma = Sigma_true)\ncolnames(z) \u003c- names(specs)\n\nfor (t in names(specs)) {\n  sp  \u003c- specs[[t]]\n  cal \u003c- get_calibration(sp$mu, rel[[t]], sp$n_items, sp$guessing)\n  theta \u003c- cal$theta_mu + cal$theta_sigma * z[, t]\n  p \u003c- sp$guessing + (1 - sp$guessing) * plogis(theta)\n  # 4AFC: out[[t]] \u003c- rbinom(n, sp$n_items, p)\n  # ART3: hits/rejects drawn separately, plus fp/fn rate columns\n}\n```\n\nOne `MASS::mvrnorm()` draw gives every simulated participant's correlated\ntrue abilities across all four tests at once; the loop then applies each\ntest's own calibrated item-response mechanism. This is the function to\nreach for when you want **one realistic dataset** — every test, Vermeiren-\ndefault correlations and reliabilities unless overridden:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-simulate-battery\nd \u003c- simulate_battery(n = 2000, seed = 1)\nstr(d)\nround(cor(d[c(\"StuVoc1\", \"StuVoc2\", \"GK\", \"ART3\")]), 2)\n```\n\n### Simulating a focal pair: `simulate_pair()`\n\n`run_sweep()` doesn't use `simulate_battery()` — it uses a leaner sibling,\n`simulate_pair()`, that draws only the two tests under test:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-simulate-pair\nd2 \u003c- simulate_pair(n = 300, var_x = \"StuVoc1\", var_y = \"GK\",\n                     true_corr = 0.2, corr_scale = \"observed\", seed = 2)\ncor(d2$StuVoc1, d2$GK)\n```\n\n::: {.callout-tip title=\"Why not just reuse the full 4x4 matrix for a sweep?\"}\nA sweep deliberately pushes one cell of the correlation matrix to extreme\nvalues (including 0, to measure the false-positive rate). Doing that\ninside the full 4×4 `Sigma_true` risks exactly the positive-definiteness\nproblem `build_sigma_true()`'s eigenvalue-clipping guard exists to patch —\nand patching it silently changes *other* tests' correlations too, which\nwould be a confusing side effect in a sweep meant to vary only one pair.\n`simulate_pair()` sidesteps this by only ever building a 2×2 correlation\nmatrix for the two tests actually being tested, which stays\npositive-definite for any correlation in `(-1, 1)`.\n:::\n\n`corr_scale` controls what `true_corr` means: `\"observed\"` (the default)\ntreats it as the *observed*-score correlation and disattenuates\ninternally — the right choice for NHST/power work, where the population\nparameter being tested lives on the observed scale (used throughout\n`run_sweep()`, below). `\"latent\"` treats it as the *true*-score correlation\ndirectly, with no compensation — used by `sampling-measurement-error.R`'s\nattenuation figure, where the point is to hold the construct-level\nrelationship fixed and watch the *observed* correlation respond to\nreliability.\n\n### Repeated studies: `simulate_studies_battery()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-simulate-studies-battery\nstudies \u003c- simulate_studies_battery(n = 40, n_studies = 4, seed = 3)\ntapply(studies$StuVoc1, studies$study, mean)\n```\n\nThin wrapper: call `simulate_battery()` once per study (without resetting\nthe seed between calls, so each study differs but the whole sequence is\nreproducible from one top-level `seed`), row-binding the results with a\n`study` label — same pattern as `sampling-distributions.R`'s\n`simulate_studies()`.\n\n### NHST on one dataset: `fit_focal_cor()` and `diagnose_cor_result()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-fit-diagnose\nfit \u003c- fit_focal_cor(d2, \"StuVoc1\", \"GK\")\nfit\ndiagnose_cor_result(fit, true_value = 0.2)\n```\n\n`fit_focal_cor()` is a thin wrapper around `cor.test()`, returning just the\nestimate, CI, and p-value as a one-row data frame. `diagnose_cor_result()`\nis where the *teaching* content lives: given the **true** value used to\nsimulate the data (something a real researcher never gets to know),\nclassify the fitted result as significant (CI/p excludes zero),\nsign-correct (only meaningful when the true value isn't zero — there's no\n\"correct\" nonzero sign to match under the null, hence `NA`), and whether\nthe CI covers the truth.\n\n### The sweep engine: `run_sweep()` and `summarize_sweep()`\n\nThis is the script's most distinctive piece of code — the one place the\n\"three dials, four diagnostics\" design is all visible at once — so it's\nworth reading in full rather than trimmed:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-run-sweep-full\nrun_sweep\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"Deterministic per-cell seeding\"}\n`seed_cell \u003c- seed_base + rep_i * 1e6 + n * 1e3 + round(reliability * 100) + round((true_corr + 1) * 1000)`\ngives every `(n, true_corr, reliability, rep)` combination its own fixed\nseed, derived arithmetically rather than drawn once and reused — the same\nscheme used by this project's Aims 1–2 background-job simulations. The\npractical payoff: any single cell of a sweep can be reproduced in\nisolation (useful for debugging one surprising result) without re-running\nthe whole sweep, and the whole sweep is reproducible end to end from one\n`seed_base`.\n:::\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-run-sweep\nsweep \u003c- run_sweep(n_grid = c(40, 200), true_corr_grid = c(0, 0.2, 0.67),\n                    reps = 200, var_x = \"StuVoc1\", var_y = \"GK\", seed_base = 777)\nsumm \u003c- summarize_sweep(sweep)\nsumm\n```\n\nReading this table: at `true_corr = 0` (the null), `power_or_type1` is the\nempirical **false positive rate** — it should sit near `alpha` (.05).\nEverywhere else, it's **power**. `sign_consistency` is `NA` at\n`true_corr = 0` (no correct sign to match) and otherwise the proportion of\n*significant* results that pointed the right direction. `coverage` is the\nproportion of 95% CIs that actually contained the true value — should sit\nnear .95 regardless of `true_corr`.\n\n### Figures: `plot_metrics_vs_x()` and `plot_power_heatmap()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-plot-metrics-vs-x\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4.5\nplot_metrics_vs_x(summ, x = \"n\", metrics = \"power_or_type1\", color_by = \"true_corr\")\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-plot-power-heatmap\n#| fig-width: 6\n#| fig-height: 3.5\nplot_power_heatmap(summ, x = \"n\", y = \"true_corr\")\n```\n\nBoth take `summarize_sweep()`'s output directly and are deliberately\ngeneric — any metric column (`power_or_type1`, `sign_consistency`,\n`coverage`) can be plotted against any swept dial, which is what lets the\nsame two functions serve `nhst-power.R` and\n`error-rates-process-control.R` without modification.\n\n## Quarto usage / integration\n\nThis script is standalone infrastructure — not itself wired into\n`doing-being-science.qmd`, and not meant to be used alone for a finished\nfigure; `sampling-measurement-error.R`, `nhst-power.R`, and\n`error-rates-process-control.R` each source it and build their own\nfigures/narrative on top. A typical setup chunk:\n\n```r\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\n```\n\n### Validation against Vermeiren et al. (2023) {#validation-against-vermeiren-et-al-2023}\n\n```{r}\n#| label: validation-moments\nspecs \u003c- default_test_specs()\nrel   \u003c- default_reliability_vec()\nvalidation \u003c- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(specs), function(t) {\n  sp  \u003c- specs[[t]]\n  cal \u003c- get_calibration(sp$mu, rel[[t]], sp$n_items, sp$guessing)\n  data.frame(test = t, target_mean = sp$mu, implied_mean = round(cal$moments$mean_score, 2),\n             target_reliability = rel[[t]], implied_reliability = round(cal$moments$reliability, 4))\n}))\nvalidation\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: validation-correlations\nd_val \u003c- simulate_battery(n = 5000, seed = 101)\ncat(\"Simulated observed correlations (n = 5000):\\n\")\nprint(round(cor(d_val[c(\"StuVoc1\", \"StuVoc2\", \"GK\", \"ART3\")]), 2))\ncat(\"\\nVermeiren et al. (2023) Study 5 targets:\\n\")\nprint(default_r_obs_matrix())\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: validation-power-benchmark\nbench \u003c- run_sweep(n_grid = c(40, 200), true_corr_grid = c(0, 0.2),\n                    reps = 300, var_x = \"StuVoc1\", var_y = \"GK\", seed_base = 777)\nsummarize_sweep(bench)[c(\"n\", \"true_corr\", \"power_or_type1\", \"coverage\")]\n```\n\n@vermeiren2023's own power illustration (their \"Power considerations\"\nsection) reports power ≈ .23 at N=40 and ≈ .81 at N=200 for a true\ncorrelation of r = .2 — the `true_corr = 0.2` rows above should land close\nto those values (simulation noise from only 300 replicates per cell means\nexact agreement isn't expected). The `true_corr = 0` rows give the\nempirical false-positive rate, which should sit near the nominal .05.\n\n### Parameter quick reference\n\n| Function | Parameter | Default | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `simulate_battery()` | `n` | — | Sample size (dial i). |\n| | `reliability` | `NULL` | Named override for one or more tests (dial ii); `NULL` uses Vermeiren defaults. |\n| | `Sigma_true` | `NULL` | A 4×4 true-score correlation matrix (dial iii); `NULL` builds one from `default_r_obs_matrix()` + whichever reliability is in effect. |\n| | `keep_latent` | `FALSE` | If `TRUE`, also return each test's `theta`/`p` columns. |\n| `simulate_pair()` | `var_x`, `var_y` | — | The two tests to simulate. |\n| | `true_corr` | `0` | Target correlation, on whichever scale `corr_scale` selects. |\n| | `corr_scale` | `\"observed\"` | `\"observed\"`: disattenuate internally so `true_corr` is the *observed*-score correlation. `\"latent\"`: use `true_corr` directly as the true-score correlation. |\n| `run_sweep()` | `n_grid`, `true_corr_grid`, `reliability_grid` | — / — / `NULL` | The three dials to sweep; `reliability_grid = NULL` holds reliability fixed at `var_x`'s default. |\n| | `reps` | `200` | Replicate studies per grid cell. |\n| | `alpha` | `0.05` | Significance threshold. |\n| | `seed_base` | `1234` | Base seed for deterministic per-cell seeding. |\n| *(calibration)* | `tolerance` | `0.01` | Max acceptable gap between requested and achieved reliability before `calibrate_ability_general()` warns. |\n\n### Common errors\n\n| Message | Likely cause |\n|---|---|\n| `reliability = ... is not achievable at mu = ...` | Requested reliability too close to 1 (or `mu` too close to the guessing floor/ceiling) for the given `n_items`/`guessing`. |\n| Warning: `achieved reliability (...) differs from the requested target (...)` | Calibration succeeded but landed outside `tolerance` of the target — usually near an achievability extreme; treat downstream diagnostics with caution. |\n| Warning: `Target observed correlation r = ... is not achievable at ...` | Requested observed correlation exceeds what's reachable given the two tests' reliabilities (`\\|r_true\\| > 1`);
