<div><tool-result call-id="toolu_01W83ojvbi5fhz83WYTuE3E9"><script type="application/json">{"version":1,"status":"success","result":{"type":"text","value":"[File: 17.6KB, 370 lines, showing lines 1-370]\n1\t---\n2\ttitle: \"`sampling-measurement-error...[truncated, total 19388 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"[File: 17.6KB, 370 lines, showing lines 1-370]\n---\ntitle: \"`sampling-measurement-error.R`: measurement error vs. sampling error\"\nsubtitle: \"Walkthrough: how the script works, and how to use it in Quarto\"\nformat:\n  html:\n    code-fold: false\n    toc: true\nbibliography: references.bib\n---\n\n```{r}\n#| label: setup\n#| include: false\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = \"center\")\n```\n\n## Aims\n\n`sampling-measurement-error.R` uses the four-test psychological battery\nsimulated by `psych-battery-dgp.R` (StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK, ART3, grounded in\n@vermeiren2023) to draw out a distinction that's easy to state and easy to\nblur in practice: **measurement error** and **sampling error** are different\nthings, caused by different mechanisms, fixed by different means, and this\nscript gives each one its own pair of figures so they can't be confused.\n\n- **Measurement error** is noise in *one person's* score, caused by a test\n  having only finitely many items (or author/foil names) to sample responses\n  from. It's controlled by a test's **reliability**. Lower reliability widens\n  the scatter of a person's observed score around their true ability, and —\n  the consequence that matters most for research — it **attenuates** any\n  correlation computed from that noisy score, with no change in sample size\n  at all.\n- **Sampling error** is noise in *a study's estimate* (a sample mean, a\n  sample correlation), caused by observing only `n` participants rather than\n  the whole population. It's controlled by **sample size**. A smaller `n`\n  widens the *spread* of a statistic's sampling distribution across repeated\n  studies, without shifting where that distribution is *centred*.\n\nPut the two together and you get the script's organizing claim, demonstrated\nrather than just asserted: **changing N changes the spread of a sampling\ndistribution; changing reliability changes its centre (via attenuation), not\nits spread.** `plot_sampling_distribution()` and\n`plot_attenuation_vs_reliability()` are built as a deliberate pair so this\ncontrast is visible side by side rather than left implicit.\n\nAfter working through it, you should be able to:\n\n- explain, using this script's own figures, why \"the correlation was weaker\n  than expected\" and \"the study was underpowered\" are not the same diagnosis,\n  and which error source each one points to;\n- generate a measurement-error figure (one test, one person at a time) and a\n  sampling-error figure (one statistic, repeated studies) for a battery test\n  pair of your choosing;\n- predict, roughly, how much an observed correlation will be attenuated at a\n  given reliability, using the classical test theory formula this script\n  simulates directly.\n\n## Prerequisites / assumptions\n\n- **Packages**: `ggplot2`; `ggdist`, for `plot_sampling_distribution()` only\n  (guarded the same way as `sampling-distributions.R`'s `plot_dotpile()` —\n  loading it isn't required just to source the script).\n- **Sourcing**: `psych-battery-dgp.R` must be sourced first — this script\n  uses its `default_test_specs()`, `default_reliability_vec()`,\n  `default_r_obs_matrix()`, `get_calibration()`, `simulate_pair()`, and\n  `disattenuate()` directly rather than re-implementing any calibration\n  machinery.\n- **Reader background**: classical test theory terms (reliability, true\n  score, attenuation) help but aren't required — defined as they come up.\n  Basic `ggplot2` familiarity assumed. Prior reading of\n  `sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd` is useful context (same\n  trial-level-up simulation philosophy, single test instead of a battery)\n  but not required.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: source-script\nlibrary(ggdist)\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\nsource(\"sampling-measurement-error.R\")\n```\n\n## How it works: the process\n\n```{r}\n#| label: model-equation\n#| echo: false\n#| results: asis\ncat(\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{True ability (standardized):} \\\\quad z_i \\\\sim N(0, 1)\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{Calibrated ability (logit scale):} \\\\quad \\\\theta_i = \\\\theta_\\\\mu + \\\\theta_\\\\sigma z_i\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{Per-item probability:} \\\\quad p_i = \\\\text{guessing} + (1 - \\\\text{guessing}) \\\\cdot \\\\text{plogis}(\\\\theta_i)\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"$$\",\n  \"\\\\text{4AFC tests (StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK):} \\\\quad \\\\text{score}_i \\\\sim \\\\text{Binomial}(n_{\\\\text{items}}, p_i)\",\n  \"$$\",\n  sep = \"\\n\"\n)\n```\n\nEvery figure in this script is built from the same single-test generator,\n`simulate_single_test()` (or its two-draws-per-person sibling,\n`simulate_parallel_forms_battery()`), which is itself a thin wrapper around\n`psych-battery-dgp.R`'s `get_calibration()` — the numerical solver that\nfinds the `(theta_mu, theta_sigma)` pair reproducing a target mean score and\nreliability, same device as `sampling-distributions.R`'s\n`calibrate_ability()`, generalized to handle a 4AFC guessing floor and\nART3's author/foil split.\n\n```{mermaid}\nflowchart LR\n    A[\"psych-battery-dgp.R\\nget_calibration()\\nsolves theta_mu, theta_sigma\\nfor target mu + reliability\"] --> B[\"simulate_single_test()\\nz ~ N(0,1)  (true ability)\\np = guessing + (1-guessing)*plogis(theta)\\nscore ~ Binomial(n_items, p)\"]\n    B --> C[\"plot_true_vs_observed()\\nscore vs true ability --\\nvertical scatter = measurement error\"]\n    A --> D[\"simulate_parallel_forms_battery()\\ntwo independent score draws\\nfrom the same theta_i\"]\n    D --> E[\"plot_parallel_forms()\\nform1 vs form2 --\\nr approx reliability\"]\n    A --> F[\"simulate_sampling_distribution()\\nrepeat across n_studies,\\none N at a time\"]\n    F --> G[\"plot_sampling_distribution()\\nfacet by N --\\nspread shrinks as N grows\"]\n    A --> H[\"simulate_attenuation_sweep()\\nsimulate_pair(corr_scale='latent'),\\ntrue corr fixed, reliability varied\"]\n    H --> I[\"plot_attenuation_vs_reliability()\\nobserved r vs reliability --\\ncentre shifts (attenuation)\"]\n```\n\nThe two right-hand branches are the ones to pay attention to: `F`/`G` holds\nreliability fixed and varies `n`, `H`/`I` holds `n` fixed and varies\nreliability. Same shared calibration engine, two different \"dials\" turned\none at a time.\n\n## Element-by-element walkthrough\n\n### Measurement error, one test at a time: `simulate_single_test()` and `plot_true_vs_observed()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-simulate-single-test\n#| eval: false\nsp  \u003c- specs[[test]]\ncal \u003c- get_calibration(sp$mu, rel, sp$n_items, sp$guessing)\nz     \u003c- rnorm(n)\ntheta \u003c- cal$theta_mu + cal$theta_sigma * z\np     \u003c- sp$guessing + (1 - sp$guessing) * plogis(theta)\nscore \u003c- rbinom(n, sp$n_items, p)   # ART3 branches into hits + rejects instead\n```\n\n`z` is each simulated person's **true ability**, standardized to mean 0 / SD\n1 — something a real researcher never observes directly. `score` is what a\nreal researcher *does* observe, and the gap between the two is measurement\nerror. Because `score` is drawn from a `Binomial`, not computed as a smooth\nfunction of `z`, that gap is baked into the simulation structurally, not\nadded afterwards as noise.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-true-vs-observed\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4.2\nplot_true_vs_observed(\"StuVoc1\", n = 300, seed = 1)\n```\n\nThe red curve is the *expected* score at each ability level (`n_items *\np`); every point's vertical distance from it is that person's measurement\nerror for this one administration. Lower the `reliability` argument and the\nsame plot shows a visibly fatter scatter around an unchanged curve — spread\nincreases, but the curve (and hence the relationship between true ability\nand expected score) doesn't move.\n\n### Parallel forms: `simulate_parallel_forms_battery()` and `plot_parallel_forms()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-parallel-forms\n#| eval: false\ndraw_once \u003c- function() rbinom(n, sp$n_items, p)   # same p both times\ndata.frame(id = seq_len(n), test = test, true_ability = z,\n           form1 = draw_once(), form2 = draw_once(), reliability = rel)\n```\n\nTwo independent score draws from the *same* `theta_i` (and hence the same\n`p`) is the textbook definition of reliability: it's the correlation you'd\nsee if you could test the same person twice under identical conditions.\nThat's exactly what `cor(form1, form2)` recovers:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-parallel-forms\n#| fig-width: 6\n#| fig-height: 5\nplot_parallel_forms(\"StuVoc1\", n = 500, seed = 2)\nd_pf \u003c- simulate_parallel_forms_battery(\"StuVoc1\", n = 20000, seed = 22)\ncor(d_pf$form1, d_pf$form2)\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"Why this, and not StuVoc1 vs. StuVoc2?\"}\n`simulate_parallel_forms_battery()` re-administers the *same* test, not two\ndifferent tests. StuVoc1 and StuVoc2 are highly correlated (r ≈ .82 per\n@vermeiren2023) but are not strictly parallel forms of one underlying test\n— they're two related-but-distinct vocabulary subtests. For a clean\ndemonstration that reliability *is* parallel-forms correlation, this script\nsimulates two independent administrations of one test rather than reusing\nStuVoc1/StuVoc2 for that purpose.\n:::\n\n### Sampling error across repeated studies: `simulate_sampling_distribution()` and `plot_sampling_distribution()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-sampling-distribution\n#| eval: false\nvalues \u003c- vapply(seq_len(n_studies), function(s) {\n  d \u003c- simulate_pair(n, var_x, var_y, true_corr = tc, corr_scale = \"observed\",\n                      reliability_x = rel_x, reliability_y = rel_y, seed = NULL)\n  cor(d[[var_x]], d[[var_y]])\n}, numeric(1))\n```\n\nThis is the sampling-distribution idea made concrete: simulate an entire\nstudy — not one person — `n_studies` times, each time computing the same\nstatistic (a sample mean or a sample correlation), and look at how that\ncollection of per-study estimates is spread out. Reliability stays fixed\nthroughout; only `n` (passed in from `plot_sampling_distribution()`'s\n`n_grid`) changes across panels.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-sampling-distribution\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 6\nplot_sampling_distribution(n_grid = c(30, 100, 400), n_studies = 300, statistic = \"cor\",\n                            var_x = \"StuVoc1\", var_y = \"GK\", seed = 4)\n```\n\nAll three panels are centred at roughly the same value (the population\nStuVoc1–GK correlation, ≈ .67) because reliability — and therefore\nattenuation — hasn't changed. Only the *spread* shrinks as `n` climbs from\n30 to 400, which is sampling error shrinking, not measurement error.\n\n### Attenuation: `simulate_attenuation_sweep()` and `plot_attenuation_vs_reliability()`\n\nThis is the script's most distinctive piece of code, and the one most worth\nreading in full rather than trimmed, because the single detail that makes it\nwork — `corr_scale = \"latent\"` — is easy to get backwards:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-attenuation-sweep-full\nsimulate_attenuation_sweep\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"`corr_scale = \\\"latent\\\"`, not `\\\"observed\\\"`\"}\n`simulate_pair()` (from `psych-battery-dgp.R`) supports two ways of\ninterpreting `true_corr`: `\"observed\"` treats it as the target *observed*-score\ncorrelation and disattenuates internally to find the latent correlation that\nwill produce it — the right choice for the NHST/power work, where the\npopulation parameter being tested lives on the observed scale. Here, the\nopposite is wanted: a *fixed construct-level relationship*, with reliability\nleft free to vary and the *observed* correlation left free to respond to it.\nThat's `corr_scale = \"latent\"` — `true_corr_latent` is handed to\n`simulate_pair()` untouched, and the whole point of the figure is to watch\nthe *observed* correlation move as reliability does.\n:::\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-attenuation\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4.5\nplot_attenuation_vs_reliability(reliability_grid = seq(0.2, 0.9, by = 0.1),\n                                 n = 300, reps = 300,\n                                 var_x = \"StuVoc1\", var_y = \"GK\", seed = 5)\n```\n\nThe blue line (simulated mean observed correlation, with a ribbon showing\nthe spread across the 300 replicate studies run at each reliability value)\ntracks the dashed red theoretical line almost exactly: $r_{\\text{obs}} =\nr_{\\text{true}} \\times \\text{reliability}$, the classical test theory\nattenuation formula, here simulated rather than just asserted. The dotted\nline marks the ceiling — the correlation you'd see if both tests were\nmeasured with no error at all.\n\n## Quarto usage / integration\n\nThis script is standalone — it isn't currently sourced into\n`doing-being-science.qmd` (that deck's figure sequence is built from the\nicon/number pairing in `person-grid.R` / `testing-sequence.R` /\n`sampling-distributions.R`; this script is a separate, inferential-statistics\ndemonstration). A typical setup chunk:\n\n```r\nlibrary(ggdist)\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\nsource(\"sampling-measurement-error.R\")\n```\n\nand then any of the four demo calls shown above. All four `plot_*()`\nfunctions return a plain `ggplot` object, so they combine with `patchwork`\nor further `ggplot2` layers like any other plot.\n\n### Parameter quick reference\n\n| Function | Parameter | Default | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `simulate_single_test()` / `plot_true_vs_observed()` | `test` | `\"StuVoc1\"` | Which battery test: `StuVoc1`, `StuVoc2`, `GK`, or `ART3`. |\n| | `n` | — | Number of simulated participants. |\n| | `reliability` | `NULL` | Dial (ii); `NULL` uses the test's Vermeiren-default value. |\n| `simulate_parallel_forms_battery()` / `plot_parallel_forms()` | *(same as above)* | | Two independent score draws per person from the same true ability. |\n| `simulate_sampling_distribution()` / `plot_sampling_distribution()` | `n` / `n_grid` | — | Dial (i); `plot_*()` takes a vector (`n_grid`) for a faceted comparison. |\n| | `n_studies` | — | Independent studies simulated per `n`/panel. |\n| | `statistic` | — | `\"mean\"` (one test) or `\"cor\"` (a pair, needs `var_y`). |\n| | `true_corr` | `NULL` | Population *observed*-score correlation to simulate from; `NULL` uses the Vermeiren-default for the pair. |\n| `simulate_attenuation_sweep()` / `plot_attenuation_vs_reliability()` | `reliability_grid` | — | Dial (ii), swept; applied equally to `var_x` and `var_y`. |\n| | `n` | `300` | Participants per replicate study (held fixed across the sweep). |\n| | `reps` | `200` | Replicate studies simulated per reliability value. |\n| | `true_corr_latent` | `NULL` | The fixed construct-level correlation; `NULL` backs it out from the Vermeiren-default observed correlation and reliabilities via `disattenuate()`. |\n| *(all functions)* | `seed` | `NULL` | Reproducibility. |\n\n### Common errors\n\n| Message | Likely cause |\n|---|---|\n| `` `test` must be one of StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK, ART3 `` | Misspelled or unsupported test name passed to `simulate_single_test()` / `simulate_parallel_forms_battery()`. |\n| `` `reliability` must be strictly between 0 and 1 `` | A reliability of 0, 1, or outside that range was supplied directly. |\n| `` `var_y` must be supplied when statistic = 'cor' `` | `simulate_sampling_distribution(statistic = \"cor\", ...)` called without `var_y`. |\n| `` `n_studies` must be at least 2 to show a distribution `` | `n_studies` too small to compute a spread. |\n| `` `var_x` and `var_y` must be different tests `` | Same test name passed twice to `simulate_attenuation_sweep()`. |\n| `` `reliability_grid` values must all be strictly between 0 and 1 `` | A sweep value of 0 or 1 (or outside that range) was included. |\n| `` `reps` must be at least 2 `` | `reps` too small to compute a spread at each reliability value. |\n| `Package 'ggdist' is required for plot_sampling_distribution()` | `ggdist` not installed; install with `install.packages(\"ggdist\")`. |\n\n## Exercises\n\n1. Call `plot_true_vs_observed(\"StuVoc1\", n = 300, reliability = 0.95, seed = 1)`\n   and then the same call with `reliability = 0.5`. How does the scatter\n   around the red curve change, and does the curve itself move?\n2. Run `plot_parallel_forms(\"ART3\", n = 500, seed = 2)` and confirm the\n   observed `r(form1, form2)` lands close to ART3's default reliability\n   (.90). Then try `reliability = 0.6` — does the point cloud still look\n   like a straight line, just noisier, or does its shape change?\n3. Use `simulate_sampling_distribution()` with `statistic = \"mean\"`,\n   `var_x = \"GK\"`, at `n = 20` and `n = 500` (300 studies each). Compare\n   `sd()` of the two `value` columns — is the ratio close to what you'd\n   predict from $\\sqrt{500/20}$?\n4. Using `simulate_attenuation_sweep()` for StuVoc1 and ART3 (default\n   `true_corr_latent`, backed out from their Vermeiren-default observed\n   correlation of ≈ .52), find roughly what reliability would be needed\n   for the *observed* correlation to drop below .20.\n5. Predict, then check: if reliability is fixed at .95 but `n` shrinks to\n   10, does `plot_sampling_distribution()` for the StuVoc1–GK\n   correlation look wide or narrow? Explain in your own words why that's a\n   sampling-error effect, not a measurement-error one, even though\n   reliability is high.\n\n## See also\n\n- [sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd](sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd)\n  — the single-test prior art this script generalizes: same trial-level-up\n  simulation philosophy and the same `calibrate_ability()`/parallel-forms\n  pattern, applied to one Shipley-style test rather than a four-test\n  battery.\n- [psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd](psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd) —\n  the shared calibration/simulation engine this script is built on\n  (`get_calibration()`, `simulate_pair()`, `disattenuate()`,\n  `default_test_specs()`), including its own validation check against\n  @vermeiren2023's reported test statistics.\n- [nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd](nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd) — uses the same\n  battery and the same `simulate_pair()`/disattenuation machinery to ask a\n  different question: not \"how spread out is this estimate\" but \"how often\n  would a fixed significance-testing procedure detect a real effect, or be\n  fooled by none.\"\n- [error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd](error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd)\n  — reuses this script's `simulate_attenuation_sweep()` device (hold the\n  *latent* correlation fixed, not the observed one, when sweeping\n  reliability) in its own `run_reliability_sweep()`, and explains a real\n  bug that device was built to avoid.\n\n## References\n"},"elapsedMs":0}</script></tool-result></div>

Does the gap between the simulated and Vermeiren-reported\n   power values shrink, as you'd expect from reducing simulation noise?\n\n## See also\n\n- [sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd](sampling-distributions-walkthrough.qmd)\n  — the single-test ancestor of this script's calibration approach\n  (`calibrate_ability()`/`implied_moments()`, generalized here to\n  `calibrate_ability_general()`/`implied_moments_general()` with a\n  guessing floor).\n- [sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd](sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd)\n  — uses `get_calibration()` and `simulate_pair()` from this script to\n  separate measurement error (dial ii) from sampling error (dial i).\n- [nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd](nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd) — uses\n  `run_sweep()` and `summarize_sweep()` from this script to walk through\n  NHST and power for the StuVoc1–StuVoc2 and StuVoc1–GK pairs.\n- [error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd](error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd)\n  — uses the same sweep engine, now varying all three dials together, to\n  frame power/Type I/sign-consistency/coverage as long-run Neyman–Pearson\n  process-control error rates.\n\n## References\n"},"elapsedMs":0}</script></tool-result></div>

<div><tool-result call-id="toolu_01QfsjoibCKdhTDHr5bmpxmv"><script type="application/json">{"version":1,"status":"success","result":{"type":"text","value":"[File: 14.8KB, 329 lines, showing lines 1-329]\n1\t---\n2\ttitle: \"`nhst-power.R`: null hypoth...[truncated, total 16317 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"[File: 14.8KB, 329 lines, showing lines 1-329]\n---\ntitle: \"`nhst-power.R`: null hypothesis significance testing and power\"\nsubtitle: \"Walkthrough: how the script works, and how to use it in Quarto\"\nformat:\n  html:\n    code-fold: false\n    toc: true\nbibliography: references.bib\n---\n\n```{r}\n#| label: setup\n#| include: false\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = \"center\")\n```\n\n## Aims\n\n`nhst-power.R` carries two correlation pairs from the battery simulated by\n`psych-battery-dgp.R` through the same null-hypothesis-significance-testing\nmachinery, deliberately chosen to have different effect sizes:\n\n- **StuVoc1 – StuVoc2** — observed r ≈ .82 (two related vocabulary\n  subtests)\n- **StuVoc1 – GK** — observed r ≈ .67 (vocabulary and general\n  knowledge)\n\nThe point of carrying *two* pairs through the same code, rather than one, is\nto make a fact about power concrete rather than asserted: the same test, the\nsame decision rule, applied to two real correlations from the same battery,\nneeds very different sample sizes to reach the same power, purely because\ntheir effect sizes differ. StuVoc1–StuVoc2 is reliably detectable at\nn = 10–20; StuVoc1–GK needs several times that. Nothing about the\n*test* changed between the two — only the thing being tested.\n\nThis script adds **no new simulation machinery of its own**. Every function\nhere is a thin orchestration layer over `psych-battery-dgp.R`'s\n`simulate_pair()`, `fit_focal_cor()`, `diagnose_cor_result()`, `run_sweep()`,\n`summarize_sweep()`, and `plot_metrics_vs_x()` — see\n[psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd](psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd) for\nhow those are built. What's new here is purely the *framing*: one simulated\nstudy and its decision, many studies at one sample size (a direct replica of\n@vermeiren2023's own power illustration, their \"Power considerations\"\nfigure), and many studies across a sample-size grid (power curves).\n\nAfter working through it, you should be able to:\n\n- explain, in your own words, why \"not significant\" and \"the null is true\"\n  are different claims, using this script's own true_corr = 0 curves as the\n  concrete counter-example;\n- generate a corridor plot and a power curve for a battery pair of your\n  choosing, and read off roughly what sample size reaches 80% power;\n- explain why StuVoc1–StuVoc2 and StuVoc1–GK need such different\n  sample sizes to reach the same power, despite using an identical testing\n  procedure.\n\n## Prerequisites / assumptions\n\n- **Packages**: `ggplot2` only — no new dependency beyond what\n  `psych-battery-dgp.R` already requires.\n- **Sourcing**: `psych-battery-dgp.R` must be sourced first — this\n  script uses `default_r_obs_matrix()`, `simulate_pair()`, `fit_focal_cor()`,\n  `diagnose_cor_result()`, `run_sweep()`, `summarize_sweep()`, and\n  `plot_metrics_vs_x()` directly.\n- **Reader background**: familiarity with p-values, confidence intervals,\n  and the idea of statistical power is assumed (not re-derived here); see\n  [psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd](psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd) for\n  the underlying simulation model if that's the unfamiliar part.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: source-script\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\nsource(\"nhst-power.R\")\n```\n\n## How it works: the process\n\n```{mermaid}\nflowchart LR\n    A[\"psych-battery-dgp.R\\nsimulate_pair(), fit_focal_cor(),\\ndiagnose_cor_result(), run_sweep(),\\nsummarize_sweep(), plot_metrics_vs_x()\"] --> B[\"summarize_single_study() /\\nplot_single_study()\\none simulated dataset,\\none cor.test(), one decision\"]\n    A --> C[\"plot_corridor()\\nrun_sweep() at one true_corr,\\nmany n -- a Vermeiren-Fig.-1-style\\nscatter coloured by significance\"]\n    A --> D[\"plot_power_curves()\\nrun_sweep() + summarize_sweep()\\nacross a full n grid,\\ntrue_corr = 0 and the pair's real r\"]\n```\n\nThree views of the same underlying machinery, increasing in scope: one\nstudy (`B`) shows what a single p-value is actually attached to; the\ncorridor (`C`) shows what happens if that same study were run many times at\none sample size; the power curves (`D`) show what happens across a whole\nrange of sample sizes, with the `true_corr = 0` curve kept visible\nthroughout as the benchmark for \"how often would this procedure falsely\nclaim an effect that isn't there.\"\n\n## Element-by-element walkthrough\n\n### Plain-language decisions: `format_pvalue()` and `interpret_decision()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-interpret-decision\n#| eval: false\ninterpret_decision \u003c- function(p_value, alpha = 0.05) {\n  p_label \u003c- format_pvalue(p_value)\n  if (p_value \u003c alpha) {\n    sprintf(\"reject H0 (%s, threshold %.2f) -- call this result \\\"significant\\\"\", p_label, alpha)\n  } else {\n    sprintf(\"fail to reject H0 (%s, threshold %.2f) -- call this result \\\"not significant\\\"\", p_label, alpha)\n  }\n}\n```\n\nA small thing worth calling out: both `summarize_single_study()` and\n`plot_single_study()` call this one function rather than each writing their\nown \"significant\"/\"not significant\" string, so the wording a reader sees on\na figure matches the wording in the accompanying table exactly —\navoiding a common source of confusion where a table says \"significant\" and\na figure caption says something subtly different (or vice versa).\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-interpret-decision\ninterpret_decision(0.002)\ninterpret_decision(0.31)\n```\n\n### One study: `summarize_single_study()` and `plot_single_study()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-single-study\nsummarize_single_study(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n = 200, seed = 1)\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-plot-single-study\n#| fig-width: 6\n#| fig-height: 5\nplot_single_study(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n = 200, seed = 1)\n```\n\nThis is deliberately the simplest possible figure in the whole project: one\nscatterplot, one fitted line, one estimate/CI/p-value annotated directly on\nit. Everything downstream — the corridor plot, the power curves —\nis just this exact same procedure, repeated many times and summarized.\nNothing new is introduced at the level of *what a single study's result is*;\nonly *how many times it's repeated* changes.\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"Same n, different decision, just from a different seed\"}\nRe-run the chunk above with `seed = 6` instead of `seed = 1`. At `n = 200`\nand the pair's true correlation of .67, both calls will almost certainly\nstill be significant (this pair is easy to detect) — but try the same\ncomparison at `n = 15` and the decision can flip between seeds. That\nflip is not a sign anything went wrong; it's sampling error, made visible at\nthe level of a single reported decision rather than averaged away across\nmany studies, which is exactly what the corridor plot below is built to\nshow systematically.\n:::\n\n### Many studies, one N — the corridor plot: `plot_corridor()`\n\nThis is the script's most distinctive piece of code — a direct replica\nof @vermeiren2023's own \"Power considerations\" figure, which plotted 2000\nsimulated studies' correlations against sample size, coloured by\nsignificance, and reported that at N=40 only about a quarter of studies\ntesting a true r = .2 came back significant. Worth reading in full:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-plot-corridor-full\nplot_corridor\n```\n\nIt doesn't re-simulate anything new; it just calls `run_sweep()` (from\n`psych-battery-dgp.R`) at a single `true_corr` value across a grid of sample\nsizes, and plots the *raw*, per-replicate output directly — one point\nper simulated study — rather than summarizing it first.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-plot-corridor\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 5\nplot_corridor(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(10, 15, 20, 30, 40), reps = 200, seed_base = 2)\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"Why n = 10–40 here, not Vermeiren's 40–400\"}\n@vermeiren2023's own figure swept N from 40 to 400 because they were\nillustrating power for a true correlation of r = .2 — a much weaker\neffect than any pair in this battery. StuVoc1–GK's true correlation\n(≈ .67) is strong enough that by N=40 almost every simulated study is\nalready significant (compare the earlier `psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd`\ncorridor demo, built at n = 40–400, which is solid red throughout).\nSweeping a *smaller* n range here is what's needed to see the mix of\nsignificant and non-significant outcomes that makes a corridor plot\ninformative — the right N range to sweep depends on the effect size\nbeing investigated, not on any fixed convention.\n:::\n\n### Many studies, many N — power curves: `plot_power_curves()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-plot-power-curves-core\n#| eval: false\nif (is.null(true_corr_grid)) {\n  true_corr_grid \u003c- c(0, unname(default_r_obs_matrix()[var_x, var_y]))\n}\nsweep \u003c- run_sweep(n_grid = n_grid, true_corr_grid = true_corr_grid, ...)\nsumm  \u003c- summarize_sweep(sweep)\nplot_metrics_vs_x(summ, x = \"n\", metrics = \"power_or_type1\", color_by = \"true_corr\") +\n  geom_hline(yintercept = alpha, linetype = \"dotted\", color = \"gray40\")\n```\n\nThe default `true_corr_grid` is worth noticing: it's always `c(0, \u003cthis\npair's real correlation>)`, never just the real correlation on its own. That\ndefault isn't a convenience shortcut — it's the whole point of this\nfigure. A power curve shown on its own answers \"how often would we detect\nthis real effect?\" A power curve with the null included alongside it also\nanswers the question a reader is more likely to actually need: \"how do I\ntell a detected real effect apart from a false alarm, at this same sample\nsize?\" The dotted horizontal line at `alpha` gives the second curve a\nreference point — a well-behaved false-positive rate should hover near\nit regardless of `n`, which is a different (and much flatter) shape than\npower ever takes.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-power-curves-stuvoc1-stuvoc2\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4.2\nplot_power_curves(\"StuVoc1\", \"StuVoc2\", n_grid = c(10, 20, 40, 80), reps = 300, seed_base = 3)\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-power-curves-stuvoc1-gk\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4.2\nplot_power_curves(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 400), reps = 300, seed_base = 4)\n```\n\nRead the two figures side by side: StuVoc1–StuVoc2's power curve is\nalready near 1 by `n = 20`; StuVoc1–GK needs `n` in the low hundreds to\nget there. Both true_corr = 0 curves, meanwhile, sit near the dotted .05\nline throughout — flat, low, and (within simulation noise) unaffected\nby `n`, which is exactly what a false-positive rate should look like when\nnothing about the testing procedure has changed.\n\n## Quarto usage / integration\n\nThis script is standalone — like `sampling-measurement-error.R`, it\nisn't currently sourced into `doing-being-science.qmd`. A typical setup\nchunk:\n\n```r\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\nsource(\"nhst-power.R\")\n```\n\nand then any of `summarize_single_study()`, `plot_single_study()`,\n`plot_corridor()`, or `plot_power_curves()`, each returning a plain data\nframe or `ggplot` object respectively.\n\n### Parameter quick reference\n\n| Function | Parameter | Default | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `summarize_single_study()` / `plot_single_study()` | `var_x`, `var_y` | — | The focal test pair. |\n| | `n` | — | Sample size for this one study. |\n| | `true_corr` | `NULL` | Population *observed*-score correlation to simulate from; `NULL` uses the pair's Vermeiren-default value. |\n| | `alpha` | `0.05` | Significance threshold. |\n| `plot_corridor()` | `n_grid` | — | Sample sizes to compare (one row of points each). |\n| | `reps` | `150` | Independent simulated studies per sample size. |\n| | `true_corr` | `NULL` | A single population correlation (not a grid — this figure fixes the effect size and varies `n`). |\n| `plot_power_curves()` | `n_grid` | — | Sample sizes to sweep. |\n| | `true_corr_grid` | `NULL` | Correlations to compare; `NULL` uses `c(0, \u003cpair's Vermeiren-default r>)`, always including the null. |\n| | `reliability_grid` | `NULL` | Reliability override for both tests; `NULL` uses Vermeiren defaults. |\n| | `reps` | `300` | Replicate studies per grid cell. |\n| *(all four)* | `seed` / `seed_base` | `NULL` / `1234` | Reproducibility (single-study functions take `seed`; sweep-based functions take `seed_base`, passed through to `run_sweep()`). |\n\n### Common errors\n\nThis script introduces no new validation of its own — every\n`stopifnot()`/`warning()` a user might see originates in `psych-battery-dgp.R`\n(see its own [Common errors\ntable](psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd#common-errors)), most commonly:\n\n| Message | Likely cause |\n|---|---|\n| `` `var_x`/`var_y` must each be one of StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK, ART3 `` | Misspelled or unsupported test name passed to any function here. |\n| `` `var_x` and `var_y` must be different tests `` | The same test name passed twice as both `var_x` and `var_y`. |\n| Warning: `achieved reliability (...) differs from the requested target (...)` | A `reliability`/`reliability_grid` value pushed calibration outside its tolerance — see `psych-battery-dgp.R`'s `calibrate_ability_general()`. |\n\n## Exercises\n\n1. Call `summarize_single_study(\"StuVoc1\", \"StuVoc2\", n = 15, seed = 1)` for\n   several different seeds (1 through 10). How many of the ten come back\n   significant? Does that roughly match what `plot_power_curves()` predicts\n   for `n = 15` on this pair?\n2. Build a corridor plot for StuVoc1–ART3 (r ≈ .52) using\n   `n_grid = c(10, 20, 40, 80, 150)`. <div><tool-result call-id="toolu_012wo3kWDmw8TH2Msaoup4br"><script type="application/json">{"version":1,"status":"success","result":{"type":"text","value":"[File: 18.6KB, 376 lines, showing lines 1-376]\n1\t---\n2\ttitle: \"`error-rates-process-contro...[truncated, total 20372 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"[File: 18.6KB, 376 lines, showing lines 1-376]\n---\ntitle: \"`error-rates-process-control.R`: false positives and false negatives as process-control error rates\"\nsubtitle: \"Walkthrough: how the script works, and how to use it in Quarto\"\nformat:\n  html:\n    code-fold: false\n    toc: true\nbibliography: references.bib\n---\n\n```{r}\n#| label: setup\n#| include: false\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = \"center\")\n```\n\n## Aims\n\n`error-rates-process-control.R` reframes false-positive and false-negative\nrates — concepts usually introduced as abstract properties of a hypothesis\ntest — as **properties of a decision procedure applied over and over**, in\nthe sense Neyman and Pearson built their theory of hypothesis testing around\n[@neyman1933]. It does this in two steps, deliberately concrete before\nabstract:\n\n- **Part A** starts from something that needs no statistical machinery at\n  all: ART3, the author-recognition test from `psych-battery-dgp.R`'s\n  battery [@vermeiren2023], already produces real false positives (saying\n  \"yes\" to a name that isn't an author) and real false negatives (saying\n  \"no\" to a name that is) for every simulated participant. This script\n  turns that into a **decision rule** — \"classify someone as a frequent\n  reader if they recognize at least `k` of the 60 authors\" — and asks the\n  question a rule like that actually needs answering: not \"was this one\n  classification right?\", but \"if this exact rule were applied over and\n  over, how often would it be wrong, and in which direction?\"\n- **Part B** points out that a significance test at a fixed alpha is\n  exactly this kind of rule — \"reject H0 if p \u003c alpha\" — and reuses\n  `psych-battery-dgp.R`'s sweep engine to show power, the empirical Type I\n  rate, sign consistency, and CI coverage behaving exactly like ART3's\n  rule's error rates did: stable long-run properties of a fixed procedure,\n  recoverable by repetition, not properties of any one study's result.\n\n@perezgonzalez2015 is a useful accessible companion here: it lays out, side\nby side, how Fisher's evidential reading of a single p-value differs from\nNeyman and Pearson's decision-procedure reading — and how the hybrid most\ntextbooks actually teach quietly borrows language from both without always\nsaying so.\n\nAfter working through it, you should be able to:\n\n- explain, using ART3's own classification rule as a worked example, why a\n  false-positive/false-negative rate is a property of a *rule*, estimable\n  only by repetition, not a property of any single person's test result;\n- generate a reliability-by-sample-size or a true-correlation-by-sample-size\n  error-rate heatmap for a battery pair of your choosing, and read off\n  where a fixed testing procedure is well- vs. poorly-behaved;\n- state, in your own words, the difference between Neyman and Pearson's\n  long-run error-rate framing of a significance test and Fisher's\n  evidential reading of a p-value.\n\n## Prerequisites / assumptions\n\n- **Packages**: `ggplot2` only.\n- **Sourcing**: `psych-battery-dgp.R` must be sourced first — this script\n  uses `default_test_specs()`, `default_reliability_vec()`,\n  `default_r_obs_matrix()`, `get_calibration()`, `simulate_battery()`,\n  `simulate_pair()`, `fit_focal_cor()`, `diagnose_cor_result()`,\n  `disattenuate()`, `run_sweep()`, `summarize_sweep()`,\n  `plot_metrics_vs_x()`, and `plot_power_heatmap()` directly.\n- **Reader background**: the measurement-error/sampling-error distinction\n  from `sampling-measurement-error-walkthrough.qmd` and the NHST/power\n  framing from `nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd` are both drawn on directly here\n  and are worth reading first if unfamiliar; some exposure to the terms\n  \"sensitivity\"/\"specificity\" or \"true positive rate\"/\"false positive rate\"\n  helps for Part A but is defined as it comes up.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: source-script\nsource(\"psych-battery-dgp.R\")\nsource(\"error-rates-process-control.R\")\n```\n\n## How it works: the process\n\n```{mermaid}\nflowchart LR\n    A[\"ART3 item-level responses\\nsimulate_art3_battery()\"] --> B[\"evaluate_art3_rule()\\none application of a\\n'>= k authors' rule\"]\n    B --> C[\"sweep_art3_rule()\\nrepeat over k x reps,\\na fresh sample each time\"]\n    C --> D[\"plot_art3_roc()\\ncloud = single applications,\\nred line = the rule's long-run rates\"]\n    E[\"psych-battery-dgp.R\\nrun_sweep() / run_reliability_sweep()\"] --> F[\"summarize_sweep()\\npower/Type I, sign consistency,\\nCI coverage, per grid cell\"]\n    F --> G[\"plot_reliability_heatmap() /\\nplot_true_corr_heatmap() /\\nplot_process_control_overview()\"]\n```\n\nThe two halves share a structure even though they look different: both\nrepeat a fixed procedure many times (Part A: classify `n` people, `reps`\ntimes, at each threshold `k`; Part B: run a significance test on `n`\nparticipants, `reps` times, at each grid cell) and summarize what fraction\nof those repetitions landed in each outcome category. Nothing in Part B is\nnew simulation machinery — it is entirely orchestration over\n`psych-battery-dgp.R`'s existing `run_sweep()`/`summarize_sweep()`, the same\nengine `nhst-power.R` uses, now read through a different lens.\n\n## Element-by-element walkthrough\n\n### Part A: ART3 as a concrete anchor\n\n#### `simulate_art3_battery()` and `plot_art3_rates()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-simulate-art3-battery\n#| eval: false\nd \u003c- simulate_battery(n, reliability = list(ART3 = rel_val), seed = seed, keep_latent = TRUE)\nhits    \u003c- round((1 - d$ART3_fn_rate) * sp$split[[\"authors\"]])\nrejects \u003c- round((1 - d$ART3_fp_rate) * sp$split[[\"foils\"]])\ntrue_ability \u003c- (d$ART3_theta - cal$theta_mu) / cal$theta_sigma\n```\n\nRather than re-implementing ART3's item-level draw, this reuses\n`simulate_battery()`'s existing `ART3_fn_rate`/`ART3_fp_rate` columns and\nbacks out the raw `hits`/`rejects` counts from them — one less place for\nthe two codebases to drift apart. `true_ability` re-derives the\nstandardized ability `simulate_battery()` doesn't return directly (only the\nlogit-scale `theta`), by inverting the calibration it was built from.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-art3-rates\n#| fig-width: 6\n#| fig-height: 5\nplot_art3_rates(n = 500, seed = 1)\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"Why these two rates move together\"}\n`cor(fp_rate, fn_rate)` across a large simulated sample comes out strongly\n**negative** (around -.8), and the figure above shows it: people with a low\nfalse-negative rate also tend to have a low false-positive rate. This is a\ndirect consequence of a modeling choice documented in\n`psych-battery-dgp.R` — ART3 uses a single probability `p` per person for\n*both* correctly recognizing an author and correctly rejecting a foil\n(`hits ~ Binomial(60, p)`, `rejects ~ Binomial(30, p)`), rather than the two\nseparate parameters (sensitivity and response criterion) a full\nsignal-detection-theory model would use. That's a deliberate simplification\nfor this teaching battery, not an attempt at a psychometrically faithful\nrecognition-memory model — worth knowing before reading too much into the\nexact *shape* of this scatter, even though the false-positive/false-negative\nrates themselves are genuine.\n:::\n\n#### `evaluate_art3_rule()`: one application of a decision rule\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-evaluate-art3-rule-core\n#| eval: false\ntruth_positive     \u003c- d$ART3_theta > cal$theta_mu   # true ability above the population average\npredicted_positive \u003c- hits >= k                      # the rule's call\n\ntp \u003c- sum(truth_positive & predicted_positive)\nfn \u003c- sum(truth_positive & !predicted_positive)\nfp \u003c- sum(!truth_positive & predicted_positive)\ntn \u003c- sum(!truth_positive & !predicted_positive)\n```\n\nThe rule being evaluated — \"classify as a frequent reader if `hits >= k`\"\n— needs a ground truth to be right or wrong *against*, and `theta_mu` (the\npopulation's average true recognition ability, on the calibrated logit\nscale) supplies one: being truly above average is independent of how the\nnoisy classification turns out, which is exactly the property a ground\ntruth needs.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-evaluate-art3-rule\nevaluate_art3_rule(n = 300, k = 40, seed = 2)\n```\n\nOne call, one sample, one set of rates — and, by itself, not yet\ninformative about the *rule*: a different seed at the same `n` and `k` will\ngive a visibly different `fpr`/`tpr` pair. That instability is the reason\nPart A doesn't stop here.\n\n#### `sweep_art3_rule()` and `plot_art3_roc()`: the rule's long-run operating curve\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-sweep-art3-rule\nsweep_small \u003c- sweep_art3_rule(n = 300, k_grid = c(30, 40, 50), reps = 50, seed_base = 3)\naggregate(cbind(fpr, tpr) ~ k, sweep_small, mean)\n```\n\n`sweep_art3_rule()` repeats `evaluate_art3_rule()` at each threshold in\n`k_grid`, drawing a **fresh** sample of `n` people each time — the single\nmechanism that turns \"one classification's noisy outcome\" into \"the rule's\nactual operating characteristics,\" by averaging over many independent\napplications rather than trusting any one of them.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-art3-roc\n#| fig-width: 6.5\n#| fig-height: 5.5\nplot_art3_roc(n = 300, k_grid = seq(25, 50, by = 5), reps = 200, seed_base = 2)\n```\n\nRead the pale cloud and the red line as two different claims. The cloud —\none dot per replicate — is how noisy a *single* application of the rule's\nreported false-positive/true-positive rate can be, even at a respectable\n`n = 300`. The red line connects each threshold's *average* over 200\nreplicates, and it traces a textbook ROC-style trade-off: tightening `k`\n(demanding more recognized authors before calling someone a frequent\nreader) buys a lower false-positive rate at the cost of a lower true-positive\nrate, and no threshold minimizes both. That trade-off — not any particular\npoint on it — is the property of the *rule*, in the Neyman-Pearson sense:\nknowable in advance, by simulation or by theory, before the rule is ever\napplied to a real person.\n\n### Part B: the same logic, abstracted to a fixed-alpha NHST procedure\n\n#### `run_reliability_sweep()` and `plot_reliability_heatmap()`: holding the right thing fixed\n\nThis is the script's most distinctive piece of code, and it exists because\nof a real bug caught while building this script — worth reading in full:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-run-reliability-sweep-full\nrun_reliability_sweep\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"A real bug this function fixes\"}\nThe first version of `plot_reliability_heatmap()` called\n`psych-battery-dgp.R`'s `run_sweep()` directly, sweeping `reliability_grid`\nwhile holding `true_corr` fixed on the **observed** scale (`run_sweep()`'s\ndefault interpretation) — e.g. \"hold StuVoc1-GK's correlation at .67 while\nreliability drops from .9 to .3.\" That request is not always satisfiable:\ndisattenuating an observed r = .67 back through a shared reliability of .3\nrequires a *latent* correlation above 1, which `disattenuate()` can only\nhandle by capping it at .999 and issuing a warning. Run across a whole\nreliability grid, that produced a wall of repeated capping warnings and,\nworse, a heatmap whose low-reliability cells were all silently simulating\nthe *same* near-1.0 latent correlation rather than the requested .67\nobserved correlation — a wrong figure that happened not to crash.\n\nThe fix is the same device `sampling-measurement-error.R`'s\n`simulate_attenuation_sweep()` already uses: hold the **latent**\n(construct-level) correlation fixed instead, and let the **observed**\ncorrelation — and therefore its significance, sign, and coverage — respond\nto reliability, which is the actual point of this figure. `true_corr_latent\n* reliability` (both tests share one reliability value here) gives the\n*implied* observed correlation at each cell, which is what actually gets\ntested for significance/sign/coverage, and which is written into the\noutput's `true_corr` column so `summarize_sweep()` can be reused with no\nchanges at all.\n:::\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-reliability-heatmap\n#| fig-width: 7.5\n#| fig-height: 5\nplot_reliability_heatmap(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 400),\n                          reliability_grid = seq(0.3, 0.9, by = 0.1), reps = 150, seed_base = 3)\n```\n\nPower climbs with both axes, as it should: more participants and a more\nreliable measure both make a real effect easier to detect, and the figure\nmakes visible just how much reliability alone costs — at `reliability =\n.3`, even `n = 20` only reaches 19% power, where the same `n` at\n`reliability = .9` already reaches 97%.\n\n#### `plot_true_corr_heatmap()` and `plot_process_control_overview()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-true-corr-heatmap\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4\nplot_true_corr_heatmap(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 400),\n                        true_corr_grid = c(0, 0.2, 0.67), reps = 200, seed_base = 4)\n```\n\nUnlike ## Final read-through: findings

Read all four walkthroughs in full, in the order a student would encounter them (psych-battery-dgp → sampling-measurement-error → nhst-power → error-rates-process-control). Overall the sequence holds together well: terminology (the three dials, `power_or_type1`/`sign_consistency`/`coverage`, observed-vs-latent correlation scale) is introduced once in doc 1 and reused identically throughout; the `corr_scale = "latent"` device is introduced in doc 1, demonstrated in doc 2, and correctly cited as reused in doc 4's bug-fix callout; numeric claims about effect sizes (StuVoc1–StuVoc2 ≈.82, StuVoc1–GK ≈.67, StuVoc1–ART3 ≈.52) stay consistent across all four documents; and each document's "Reader background" section correctly signals the intended reading order.

Found and fixed two real errors in the process:

1. **Sign error** (`error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd`): a callout claimed `cor(fp_rate, fn_rate)` comes out "strongly negative (around -.8)" — re-verified live and it's actually **strongly positive** (≈.80: higher true ability lowers both rates together, since a single probability `p` drives both hits and correct rejections in this simplified model). The surrounding sentence already described the relationship correctly ("low with low") — only the negative/positive label itself was backwards. Fixed.

2. **Dangling reference** (`nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd`): a callout asked the reader to "compare the earlier `psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd` corridor demo, built at n = 40–400" — confirmed by grep that no such demo exists anywhere in that document (`plot_corridor()` is never called there; it's defined in `nhst-power.R`). This was a leftover from an ad hoc console test during validation that never made it into the actual rendered walkthrough. Replaced with an honest, actionable alternative: an inline code snippet the reader can run themselves to see the same thing.

Both fixes verified live (re-ran the correlation check, confirmed the absence of the demo by grep) and both files re-rendered cleanly afterward with the bibliography and Mermaid diagrams intact. No other unverified directional claims or dangling cross-references turned up in the broader scan.

We imagine a single study, then imagine the same study repeated many times, and then ask what that repetition implies about the estimates that end up being reported.\n\n- **Part A** builds the null distribution and the Neyman–Pearson decision rule.\n- **Part B** asks what happens when the null is false, and introduces power.\n- **Part C** asks what happens to the estimates we see when only significant results are reported (the significance filter), and how precision changes with sample size.\n\nThe running example is the association between reading experience, measured by the Author Recognition Test (ART3; @vermeiren2023), and vocabulary.\n\n## Part A: Building the null distribution\n\n### One person, one score\n\nImagine I test you on vocabulary. You score 25. That number on its own tells us little.\n\n### A sample\n\nNow imagine I test you and 19 other people. We have a sample of $n = 20$ scores.\n\n### A second construct\n\nSuppose I also measure reading experience, for you and everyone else in the sample, using the ART3 [@vermeiren2023]. Each person now has two scores.\n\n### The correlation\n\nI calculate Pearson's $r$ between vocabulary and ART scores. To the extent that the tests are valid and reliable, $r$ tells us about the association between reading experience and vocabulary in *this sample*.\n\n### A test of the null hypothesis\n\nWe can ask whether the data are compatible with a population correlation of zero ($\\rho = 0$). One way is to calculate\n\n$$t = \\frac{r\\sqrt{n-2}}{\\sqrt{1-r^2}}$$\n\nwith $n - 2 = 18$ degrees of freedom.\n\n### Repeating the study, in imagination\n\nNow imagine running these steps over and over, on new samples of 20 people, in a world where $\\rho = 0$ is true. Each study gives a different $r$ and a different $t$, purely through sampling variation. This only works as a thought experiment if we say what the imagined world is: a population in which the true correlation is zero (and, for the exact $t$ distribution, in which the two variables are bivariate normal). The distribution is not built from real data. It is built from an assumption.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-null-100\n#| fig-cap: \"The t statistic in 100 imagined studies (n = 20) where the true correlation is zero. Dashed lines mark the two-tailed 5% cutoffs.\"\nset.seed(1)\nn \u003c- 20\nt_100 \u003c- sim_studies(n, rho = 0, reps = 100)$t\nhist(t_100, breaks = 20, main = \"100 studies, true null\", xlab = \"t\")\nabline(v = qt(c(.025, .975), df = n - 2), lty = 2)\n```\n\nWith 100 studies the histogram is ragged. With 10,000 it approaches the smooth $t$ distribution with 18 degrees of freedom: roughly bell-shaped, with heavier tails than the normal.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-null-10000\n#| fig-cap: \"The same exercise with 10,000 imagined studies. The curve is the t distribution with 18 degrees of freedom.\"\nset.seed(1)\nt_null \u003c- sim_studies(n, rho = 0, reps = 10000)$t\nhist(t_null, breaks = 60, freq = FALSE, main = \"10,000 studies, true null\", xlab = \"t\")\ncurve(dt(x, n - 2), add = TRUE, lwd = 2)\nabline(v = qt(c(.025, .975), df = n - 2), lty = 2)\n```\n\n### How often is $t$ \"large\"?\n\nGiven this distribution, we can say how often $|t|$ exceeds some value when the null is true. For $n = 20$ the two-tailed 5% cutoff is\n\n```{r}\nqt(.975, df = 18)\n```\n\nso $|t| \\geq 2.10$ occurs in 5% of studies, with 2.5% in each tail. The familiar 1.96 is the large-sample limit of this cutoff, and the gap between 2.10 and 1.96 is the effect of small samples on the shape of the distribution. The cutoff for $t$ corresponds to a cutoff for $r$: at $n = 20$, only $|r| \\gtrsim .44$ can be significant.\n\n```{r}\n# critical r at n = 20\ntc \u003c- qt(.975, 18); tc / sqrt(tc^2 + 18)\n```\n\n### Rejecting the null\n\nIf our observed $|t|$ exceeds the cutoff, we reject the null. Following @greenland2016, we can say the data are *incompatible* with the null, along with all the other assumptions used to compute $t$ (random sampling, normality, no selective reporting, and so on).\n\n### Error rates: the Neyman–Pearson framework\n\nThis decision-rule logic comes from @neyman1928 and @neyman1933. If we always reject when $|t| \\geq 2.10$, then in the long run we falsely reject a true null in 5% of tests. This is the Type I error rate, $\\alpha$. It is a property of the *procedure*, evaluated over the imagined repetitions. It is not the probability that any one significant result is false.\n\nThis framework differs from Fisher's use of the $p$-value as a graded measure of evidence [@fisher1925]. Modern practice mixes the two, which @gigerenzer2004 describes as the \"null ritual\", with the historical background in @gigerenzer1989 and a more recent review in @gigerenzer2018.\n\n## Part B: When the null is false\n\n### Suppose there is an association\n\nNow suppose the population correlation between ART3 and vocabulary is not zero. Say $\\rho = .3$. Nothing about our procedure changes. We test 20 people, calculate $r$, and calculate $t$ with 18 degrees of freedom.\n\n### Repeating the study, again\n\nImagine running the study over and over, each time on a new sample of 20, in a world where $\\rho = .3$.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-alt-t\n#| fig-cap: \"The t statistic in 10,000 imagined studies (n = 20) where rho = .3. The dashed curve is the null distribution from Part A; dotted lines are the cutoffs.\"\nset.seed(2)\nrho \u003c- .3\nalt \u003c- sim_studies(n, rho, reps = 10000)\ncrit \u003c- qt(.975, df = n - 2)\nhist(alt$t, breaks = 60, freq = FALSE, main = \"10,000 studies, rho = .3\", xlab = \"t\")\ncurve(dt(x, n - 2), add = TRUE, lty = 2)\nabline(v = c(-crit, crit), lty = 3)\n```\n\nThe distribution of $t$ has shifted to the right and is somewhat skewed, so it is no longer the symmetric curve from Part A. It still overlaps heavily with the null distribution. Many studies land between the cutoffs. (We call this distribution \"shifted and skewed\" rather than \"noncentral $t$\" for a reason that is explained below, after the power table.)\n\n### Power and the false negative rate\n\nUsing the same decision rule as before (reject if $|t| \\geq 2.10$):\n\n- **Power** is the proportion of studies in which we correctly reject the null.\n- The **false negative rate**, $\\beta$, is the proportion in which we *fail to reject* a null that is false. Power is $1 - \\beta$.\n\n```{r}\nmean(alt$sig)   # estimated power at rho = .3, n = 20\n```\n\nIn the Neyman–Pearson framework we fix $\\alpha$ in advance. Power then depends on three things: the true effect size, the sample size, and $\\alpha$.\n\n### Two ways to be wrong, one decision rule\n\n| | Null true | Null false |\n|---|---|---|\n| Reject | Type I error (rate $\\alpha$) | Correct (power, $1-\\beta$) |\n| Fail to reject | Correct ($1-\\alpha$) | Type II error (rate $\\beta$) |\n\nNote that rejecting a false null is a *correct* decision. The error that low power produces is failing to reject a false null.\n\n### Power across effect sizes and sample sizes\n\n```{r}\n#| label: tbl-power\n#| tbl-cap: \"Simulated power (alpha = .05, two-tailed) and the approximate n for 80% power.\"\nset.seed(5)\nrhos \u003c- c(.1, .3, .5)\ntab \u003c- data.frame(\n  rho = rhos,\n  power_n20 = sapply(rhos, function(p) mean(sim_studies(20, p, 5000)$sig)),\n  n_80 = sapply(rhos, function(p) ceiling(((qnorm(.975) + qnorm(.8)) / atanh(p))^2 + 3))\n)\nknitr::kable(tab, digits = 2,\n             col.names = c(\"True rho\", \"Power at n = 20\", \"n for ~80% power\"))\n```\n\nTwo different methods produced the numbers in this table, and it is worth being clear about what each one is. The point to take away is that realistic reading–vocabulary effects need samples far larger than 20. The next section explains where the numbers come from.\n\n### Where do power numbers come from?\n\nThere are three routes to a power figure: simulation, a formula based on Fisher's $z$, and a formula based on the noncentral $t$ distribution. They agree closely here, but they rest on different logic, and only the first is a direct implementation of \"imagine the study repeated many times\".\n\n#### Route 1: simulation (Monte Carlo)\n\nThis is the route we have been following. Generate many studies from a population with the stated $\\rho$, apply the decision rule to each, and count the proportion that reject. Its strength is that it needs no theory beyond the sampling model itself. Its limitation is that the answer carries *Monte Carlo error*. If true power is $p$ and we run $B$ simulated studies, the estimate has a standard error of about $\\sqrt{p(1-p)/B}$. With $B = 5{,}000$ and $p \\approx .25$ that is about .006, so the third decimal place is noise. Different random seeds, or different versions of R, will give slightly different values. That is why the table reports two decimals, and why the results are computed when the chapter is rendered rather than typed in.\n\n#### Route 2: the Fisher $z$ approximation\n\nA correlation is bounded between $-1$ and $1$, so its sampling distribution is skewed whenever $\\rho \\neq 0$. Fisher's transformation $z = \\operatorname{arctanh}(r)$ removes most of that skew. After transforming, $z$ is approximately normal, with mean $\\operatorname{arctanh}(\\rho)$ and a standard deviation of $1/\\sqrt{n-3}$ that does not depend on $\\rho$.\n\nThat gives a simple recipe. Define the standardised true effect\n\n$$\\delta = \\operatorname{arctanh}(\\rho)\\,\\sqrt{n-3}.$$\n\nThe test rejects when the standardised statistic exceeds $z_{1-\\alpha/2}$ in absolute value, so power is approximately\n\n$$1 - \\beta \\approx \\Phi(\\delta - z_{1-\\alpha/2}) + \\Phi(-\\delta - z_{1-\\alpha/2}).$$\n\nThe second term is almost zero for effects of this size, so we can drop it and solve for the sample size that gives a target power (80%, so $z_{1-\\beta} = 0.84$):\n\n$$n \\approx \\left(\\frac{z_{1-\\alpha/2} + z_{1-\\beta}}{\\operatorname{arctanh}(\\rho)}\\right)^2 + 3.$$\n\nThis is the formula behind the \"$n$ for ~80% power\" column. It is quick and shows how $n$ scales: halving the effect size roughly quadruples the sample size needed. It is still an approximation, because the normality of $z$ is approximate and because it uses the normal cutoff (1.96) rather than the $t$ cutoff (2.10). Its error is small for moderate $n$ and larger for very small $n$.\n\n#### Route 3: the noncentral $t$ distribution\n\nFor an ordinary $t$-test comparing two means, the statistic follows a *noncentral* $t$ distribution when the null is false. This is the distribution people usually have in mind when they say \"power is the area of the noncentral $t$ beyond the cutoff\". It is natural to expect the same to hold for the correlation test, but it holds only conditionally.\n\nThe statistic $t = r\\sqrt{n-2}/\\sqrt{1-r^2}$ is the $t$ statistic for the slope of a regression of vocabulary on ART3. If we **treated the ART3 scores as fixed numbers** (as in a designed experiment), then $t$ would follow a noncentral $t$ with $n-2$ degrees of freedom and a noncentrality parameter proportional to the spread of those fixed scores.\n\nIn our study the ART3 scores are **random**: a new sample gives new ART3 scores with a new spread. The noncentrality parameter therefore changes from study to study. It is approximately\n\n$$\\text{ncp} = \\frac{\\rho}{\\sqrt{1-\\rho^2}}\\sqrt{\\chi^2_{n-1}},$$\n\nwhere $\\chi^2_{n-1}$ is a chi-square random variable capturing how spread out the sampled ART3 scores happen to be. The distribution of $t$ across studies is then a *mixture* of noncentral $t$ distributions, with a different centre in each study. A mixture of this kind is not itself a noncentral $t$.\n\nThis explains something about the structure of Parts A and B:\n\n- **Under the null** ($\\rho = 0$) the noncentrality parameter is zero whatever the ART3 scores are, so every component of the mixture is the same central $t$ distribution. The mixture collapses, and the Part A distribution is exact.\n- **Under an alternative** ($\\rho \\neq 0$) the mixture does not collapse. The result is shifted away from zero and skewed. A single noncentral $t$ evaluated at the *average* noncentrality parameter is a good approximation, but it is not exact.\n\nThe code below checks all of this for $\\rho = .3$ and $n = 20$. It compares four power estimates: direct simulation of studies, the mixture of noncentral $t$ distributions, a single noncentral $t$ at the typical noncentrality, and the Fisher $z$ formula.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: tbl-power-methods\n#| tbl-cap: \"Four ways to estimate power for rho = .3, n = 20 (alpha = .05, two-tailed).\"\nset.seed(8)\nn \u003c- 20; rho \u003c- .3; B \u003c- 20000\ncrit \u003c- qt(.975, n - 2)\n\n# 1. Direct simulation of studies\npower_sim \u003c- mean(sim_studies(n, rho, B)$sig)\n\n# 2. Mixture: each study has its own noncentrality parameter\nncp_i \u003c- rho / sqrt(1 - rho^2) * sqrt(rchisq(B, n - 1))\nt_mix \u003c- rt(B, df = n - 2, ncp = ncp_i)\npower_mix \u003c- mean(abs(t_mix) >= crit)\n\n# 3. A single noncentral t at the typical noncentrality\nncp_1 \u003c- rho / sqrt(1 - rho^2) * sqrt(n - 1)\npower_nct \u003c- pt(-crit, n - 2, ncp_1) + pt(crit, n - 2, ncp_1, lower.tail = FALSE)\n\n# 4. Fisher z approximation\ndelta \u003c- atanh(rho) * sqrt(n - 3)\npower_fz \u003c- pnorm(delta - qnorm(.975)) + pnorm(-delta - qnorm(.975))\n\nknitr::kable(\n  data.frame(method = c(\"Simulate studies\", \"Mixture of noncentral t\",\n                        \"Single noncentral t\", \"Fisher z formula\"),\n             power = c(power_sim, power_mix, power_nct, power_fz)),\n  digits = 3, col.names = c(\"Method\", \"Power\"))\n```\n\nExpect the first two rows to agree to within Monte Carlo error, because they describe the same process: that is the evidence that the mixture explanation is right. The last two rows should be close to them but not identical, because each is a one-step approximation.\n\n#### Why the distinction matters for teaching\n\n- It reinforces the idea that every power number answers the question \"what proportion of imagined studies reject?\", under a stated set of assumptions.\n- Formulas are shortcuts to that proportion. Simulation is the definition. When the two disagree noticeably (for example at very small $n$, with non-normal data, or with a messy analysis pipeline) the simulation is the one to trust, provided it reproduces the data-generating process.\n- Assumptions are part of the answer. Both formulas assume bivariate normality. If vocabulary or ART3 scores are skewed or have ceiling effects, the simulation can be rerun with a more realistic data-generating process.\n\n### Interpreting a \"null result\"\n\nIf power is low, a non-significant result is what we would expect to see most of the time, even when the effect is real. A non-significant $t$ therefore does not show that $\\rho = 0$. Failing to reject is not accepting. A null result is hard to interpret unless we have a reason to think the test could have detected an effect of the size we care about.\n\n### Ways to deepen this\n\n- **Overlay the null and alternative distributions** and shade the $\\alpha$ and $\\beta$ regions, then vary $n$ and $\\rho$ and watch the overlap change.\n- **Look at $p$-value distributions.** Under the null, $p$ is uniform. Under an alternative, $p$ piles up near zero, more so with higher power. A $p$ of .03 therefore means different things depending on power.\n- **Positive predictive value.** The proportion of significant results that are true depends on power, $\\alpha$, and the prior proportion of true hypotheses [@ioannidis2005]. This is different from $\\alpha$.\n- **Instead of reading a non-significant result as \"no effect\"**: report a confidence interval and ask which effects it excludes; use equivalence tests against a smallest effect size of interest [@lakens2017]; run a sensitivity analysis (what is the smallest $\\rho$ we had 80% power to detect?). Avoid *post hoc* observed power, which is a transformation of the $p$-value [@hoenig2001].\n- **Plan power in advance**, with the smallest effect size of interest justified before data collection [@cohen1988; @cohen1992].\n\n## Part C: What we see when only significant results are reported\n\nPart B asked what happens when the effect is real but power is low. Part C asks what happens to the estimates we actually see.\n\n### The significance filter\n\nReuse the simulation from Part B ($\\rho = .3$, $n = 20$), keep $r$ as well as $t$, and imagine that only the significant studies reach print.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: sig-filter\nset.seed(3)\nrho \u003c- .3\nres \u003c- sim_studies(20, rho, reps = 10000)\n\nmean(res$r)               # all studies: close to .3\nmean(res$r[res$sig])      # significant only: much larger\nmean(res$r[res$sig]) / rho  # exaggeration ratio (Type M error)\nmean(res$r[res$sig] \u003c 0)  # share of significant results with the wrong sign (Type S error)\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-filter\n#| fig-cap: \"Estimated r across 10,000 imagined studies (n = 20, rho = .3). Grey: all studies. Dark: significant studies only. The vertical line marks the true value.\"\nbrk \u003c- seq(-1, 1, by = .025)\nhist(res$r, breaks = brk, col = \"grey85\", border = \"white\",\n     main = \"Which studies get reported?\", xlab = \"observed r\")\nhist(res$r[res$sig], breaks = brk, col = \"grey30\", border = \"white\", add = TRUE)\nabline(v = rho, lwd = 2)\n```\n\nTwo points to make explicit:\n\n- Nothing is wrong with any single study. The inflation comes from *selecting on significance*, whether by journals, authors, or the analyst.\n- At $n = 20$ the significance threshold is $|r| \\approx .44$, so any significant result must be at least that large. The filter forces inflation. These are the Type M (magnitude) and Type S (sign) errors of @gelman2014, and the problem of overestimated effects in low-powered research is also discussed by @button2013.\n\n### Inflation as a function of power\n\nRepeat the simulation across sample sizes and compare the exaggeration ratio with power.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-inflation\n#| fig-cap: \"Exaggeration ratio (mean significant r divided by true rho) against power, for rho = .3 at several sample sizes.\"\nset.seed(6)\nns \u003c- c(20, 30, 50, 85, 200, 500)\ninfl \u003c- do.call(rbind, lapply(ns, function(k) {\n  s \u003c- sim_studies(k, .3, 5000)\n  data.frame(n = k, power = mean(s$sig), ratio = mean(s$r[s$sig]) / .3)\n}))\ninfl\nplot(infl$power, infl$ratio, type = \"b\", xlim = c(0, 1),\n     xlab = \"power\", ylab = \"exaggeration ratio\")\nabline(h = 1, lty = 2)\n```\n\nThe ratio falls toward 1 as power rises. Low power makes significant results unreliable as well as rare.\n\n### Sampling variability across n\n\nA second way to see the problem is to treat a large dataset as a stand-in population, draw repeated subsamples of different sizes, and look at the spread of the estimates at each $n$. This is the approach used by @marek2022 for brain-wide association studies. Here we simulate the population, but real ART3 and vocabulary data from a large sample would serve equally well.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-marek\n#| fig-cap: \"Middle 95% of sample correlations at each n, drawn from a simulated population of 10,000 people with rho = .3. The dashed line is the population value.\"\nset.seed(7)\nN_pop \u003c- 10000; rho \u003c- .3\npx \u003c- rnorm(N_pop); py \u003c- rho * px + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(N_pop)\npop_r \u003c- cor(px, py)\n\nns \u003c- c(20, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000)\nband \u003c- t(sapply(ns, function(k) {\n  rr \u003c- replicate(2000, { i \u003c- sample(N_pop, k); cor(px[i], py[i]) })\n  quantile(rr, c(.025, .5, .975))\n}))\n\nplot(ns, band[, 3], type = \"b\", log = \"x\", ylim = range(band),\n     xlab = \"sample size n (log scale)\", ylab = \"sample r\")\nlines(ns, band[, 1], type = \"b\")\nlines(ns, band[, 2], lty = 3)\nabline(h = pop_r, lty = 2)\n```\n\nWhat changes with $n$ is the *spread*, not just the average. A study at $n = 20$ is drawing from a very wide distribution.\n\n### The corridor of stability\n\nThe third view follows one study as data accumulate. @schonbrodt2013 simulated studies in which participants are added one at a time, tracked the running correlation, and defined a \"corridor of stability\" around the true value. For each trajectory we can ask: after what sample size does the estimate never leave the corridor again?\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-corridor\n#| fig-cap: \"Running correlation in 100 imagined studies as participants are added one at a time (rho = .3). Dotted lines mark a corridor of plus or minus .1.\"\nset.seed(4)\nN \u003c- 1000; rho \u003c- .3; w \u003c- .1\ntraj \u003c- replicate(100, {\n  x \u003c- rnorm(N); y \u003c- rho * x + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(N)\n  sapply(20:N, function(k) cor(x[1:k], y[1:k]))\n})\nmatplot(20:N, traj, type = \"l\", lty = 1, col = \"#00000020\",\n        xlab = \"n\", ylab = \"running r\")\nabline(h = c(rho - w, rho, rho + w), lty = c(3, 1, 3))\n```\n\n```{r}\n# sample size after which each trajectory stays inside the corridor\nstable_n \u003c- apply(traj, 2, function(r) {\n  out \u003c- abs(r - rho) > w\n  if (any(out)) 20 + max(which(out)) else 20\n})\nquantile(stable_n, c(.5, .8, .95))\n```\n\n[Next offset: 381; 31 more lines, ~3.3KB]\n[Outline: showing H2-H4 of 32 headings; read a section with offset and limit]\n  25-34  ## Introduction\n 35-111  ## Part A: Building the null distribution\n  37-40  ### One person, one score\n  41-44  ### A sample\n  45-48  ### A second construct\n  49-52  ### The correlation\n  53-60  ### A test of the null hypothesis\n  61-86  ### Repeating the study, in imagination\n 87-101  ### How often is $t$ \"large\"?\n102-105  ### Rejecting the null\n106-111  ### Error rates: the Neyman–Pearson framework\n112-270  ## Part B: When the null is false\n114-117  ### Suppose there is an association\n118-135  ### Repeating the study, again\n136-148  ### Power and the false negative rate\n149-157  ### Two ways to be wrong, one decision rule\n158-175  ### Power across effect sizes and sample sizes\n176-258  ### Where do power numbers come from?\n180-183  #### Route 1: simulation (Monte Carlo)\n184-201  #### Route 2: the Fisher $z$ approximation\n202-252  #### Route 3: the noncentral $t$ distribution\n253-258  #### Why the distinction matters for teaching\n259-262  ### Interpreting a \"null result\"\n263-270  ### Ways to deepen this\n271-401  ## Part C: What we see when only significant results are reported\n275-305  ### The significance filter\n306-326  ### Inflation as a function of power\n327-353  ### Sampling variability across n\n354-386  ### The corridor of stability\n387-393  ### Things to state alongside these results\n394-401  ### What to do about it\n402-411  ## Where this leaves NHST"},"elapsedMs":7}</script></tool-result></div>

Both tell the same story about precision.\n\n### Things to state alongside these results\n\n- A corridor is about **estimation precision**, not the NHST decision rule. It reframes the problem rather than solving it within NHST.\n- The stability $n$ depends on the corridor width, the confidence level, and $\\rho$. The sampling variance of $r$ is roughly $(1-\\rho^2)^2/(n-1)$, so larger $\\rho$ stabilises faster.\n- @marek2022 concern brain-wide association studies, where true effects are tiny. It also shows where the difficulties lie.\n\n1. **The null is probably never exactly true.** After @meehl1967 and @meehl1990, we may suspect that in the social sciences everything correlates with everything to some degree (the \"crud factor\"; see also @lykken1968 and @orben2020). With enough data, every test then rejects, and the question becomes whether an effect is large enough to matter.\n2. **Small samples are noisy.** A significant $t$ at $n = 20$ is not a flaw, since 5% of true nulls will reach it by design. The problems are low power, selective reporting, and the inflated estimates that selection produces.\n3. **Small effects make all of this worse.** Power falls and the exaggeration ratio rises when the true effect is small.\n\nLow-$n$ studies and huge-$n$ studies fail in opposite ways: the former cannot detect real effects, the latter detect trivial ones. ## Same foundation, different approach

Both independently converge on the **same running example**: the Author Recognition Test (ART3) from Vermeiren, Vandendaele & Brysbaert (2023) correlated with vocabulary, used to teach the Neyman–Pearson long-run error-rate framing versus Fisher's evidential reading of a p-value. That convergence wasn't coordinated — it's a genuine sign the two projects are pointed at the same pedagogical target.

Where they differ is in form and depth:

| | `nhst-thought-process.qmd` | This conversation's four-script suite |
|---|---|---|
| Form | One self-contained narrative essay, inline base-R `replicate()` simulation | Reusable infrastructure: one shared DGP + three thin scripts, each with a separate documentation walkthrough |
| Population model | Abstract bivariate normal (no item-level mechanism) | Item-level/4AFC + signal-detection binomial model, calibrated to Vermeiren's actual reported means/reliabilities |
| Measurement error | Not modeled — only sampling error (N) varies | A first-class, independently-controllable dial, deliberately separated from sampling error |
| Power theory | Three computational routes compared (Monte Carlo, Fisher *z*, noncentral *t*), including the subtle point that a random-*X* correlation test's alternative distribution is a *mixture* of noncentral *t*'s, not a single one | Simulation only; no closed-form cross-check |
| Type S / Type M errors | Explicit "exaggeration ratio" and sign-flip rate under a significance filter (citing Gelman & Carlin 2014, Button et al. 2013) | `sign_consistency` only (≈ 1 − Type S rate among significant results); **no Type M/magnitude-inflation diagnostic at all** — a real gap relative to this document |
| "Corridor" | Schönbrodt & Perugini's (2013) literal corridor-of-stability: **one** dataset, running correlation as *n* grows, with a stability envelope | `plot_corridor()`: a Vermeiren-Fig.-1-style cross-sectional scatter of **many independent** studies at each *n*, coloured by significance |
| Further critiques | Meehl's "crud factor" (the null is probably never exactly true), Ioannidis's PPV, equivalence testing, Registered Reports | Not addressed |
| ART3 as a decision rule | Not present | `error-rates-process-control.R`'s person-level classification-rule ROC bridge (no counterpart in the other document) |

## A terminology collision worth flagging

**"Corridor" means two different things in the two documents.** Ours (`plot_corridor()` in `nhst-power.R`) replicates Vermeiren et al.'s own Fig. 1 — many independent studies at a few discrete sample sizes, coloured by significance. Theirs (`fig-corridor` in Part C) is Schönbrodt & Perugini's actual "corridor of stability" — a single accumulating dataset with a running correlation and a stability band. These are genuinely complementary views (cross-sectional vs. longitudinal, as their own doc says), but the shared name is a real risk if a reader encounters both: worth distinguishing explicitly if the two bodies of work are ever cross-referenced or merged into one teaching sequence.

## Should we add a Type M/Type S exaggeration-ratio diagnostic?

**Short answer: yes, it's a natural and cheap addition — but implementing it would mean editing already-finalized files, which runs against your earlier instruction not to touch any current `.qmd`. I'd want your go-ahead before doing it.** Here's the reasoning.

### Why it fits

Type I rate, power, sign consistency, and coverage answer "how often does this fixed procedure reach the right *decision*?" Type M answers a different, complementary question: "when it does reject, how distorted is the *number* it hands back?" `nhst-thought-process.qmd`'s significance-filter demo makes this vivid — the exaggeration ratio (mean significant *r* ÷ true ρ) is large at low power and falls toward 1 as power rises, which is exactly the kind of long-run, procedure-level property the rest of `error-rates-process-control.R` is built to illustrate. Right now our suite is silent on it entirely.

There's also a documentation-honesty angle: `psych-battery-dgp-walkthrough.qmd`'s Aims section already claims the sweep engine computes "the same diagnostic quartet used in this project's heavier Aims 1–2 `glmer` simulation work." The actual Aims-1-2 quartet was power / sign-reliability (Type S) / **Type M** / coverage — ours substitutes coverage for Type M rather than including both. Adding it would make that claim literally true instead of approximately true.

### Why it's cheap

The infrastructure is already most of the way there:

- `diagnose_cor_result(fit, true_value, alpha)` already has both `fit$estimate` and `true_value` in scope. A one-line addition — `inflation_ratio = if (true_value == 0) NA else abs(fit$estimate / true_value)` — parallels the existing `sign_correct` convention exactly (NA at the null, since "exaggeration relative to zero" isn't meaningful).
- `summarize_sweep()` already has the exact selection-on-significance pattern needed — the `sign_df <- results[results$significant & !is.na(results$sign_correct), ]` block — so a parallel `type_m_df`/`median(inflation_ratio)` aggregation is a direct copy-adapt, reporting the **median** (not mean) to match both the Aims-1-2 precedent and robustness to the occasional wild outlier that significance-filtering disproportionately selects for at small *n*.
- `plot_metrics_vs_x()` and `plot_power_heatmap()` are already metric-name-agnostic — no plotting code changes needed once the column exists. `plot_process_control_overview()` would just grow from 3 panels to 4, and `plot_reliability_heatmap()`/`plot_true_corr_heatmap()`'s `metric` validation would need one more allowed string.
