guessing_t) * plogis(theta_ti)\n#'   4AFC tests (StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK):\n#'     score_ti   ~ Binomial(n_items_t, p_ti)\n#'   ART3 (60 author + 30 foil items, no guessing floor):\n#'     hits_i             ~ Binomial(60, p_ART3,i)   -- correct \"yes\" to an author\n#'     correct_rejects_i  ~ Binomial(30, p_ART3,i)   -- correct \"no\" to a foil\n#'     score_ART3,i       =  hits_i + correct_rejects_i\n#'     false_negative_rate_i = 1 - hits_i / 60   (said \"no\" to a real author)\n#'     false_positive_rate_i = 1 - correct_rejects_i / 30 (said \"yes\" to a foil)\n#'\n#' `reliability` and `Sigma_true` aren't set directly on the observed-score\n#' scale -- `calibrate_ability_general()` solves each test's ability\n#' location/scale numerically so its *emergent* reliability matches the\n#' target, and `build_sigma_true()` converts a target *observed*-score\n#' correlation matrix into the *true*-score (disattenuated) correlation\n#' matrix that actually needs to be fed to the multivariate draw, via\n#' r_true = r_observed / sqrt(reliability_x * reliability_y). <div><thinking id="thinking-1791367393533-2qb3q">
I notice the plotting function locks the y-axis to 0-1, which works fine for power, sign consistency, and coverage since those are proportions, but type_m_ratio can exceed 1 substantially (2x, 3x inflation at low power), so forcing it into the same bounded scale would clip or misrepresent that metric.

The hardcoded y-limits of 0 to 1 are a real problem since type_m_ratio values can easily exceed 1, especially with small n or low power where inflation ratios of 1.5-3x are common — ggplot would silently clip those points off the plot. One fix is to change plot_metrics_vs_x() to use free y-scales per facet instead of a fixed range, though that would alter behavior for existing callers like the power curves and psych-battery walkthrough.

Alternatively, I could leave plot_metrics_vs_x() as-is for its current 0-1 range use cases, and instead exclude type_m_ratio from plot_process_control_overview(), creating a separate plot_type_m_curve() function with its own appropriate y-scale.

This is the safer, additive-only path that matches my earlier framing of adding a new figure rather than folding it into the existing overview, and it avoids disturbing already-validated demo chunks. I'm starting to sketch out plot_type_m_curve() as a diagnostic for the Type M exaggeration ratio.

Still writing plotting code...

I'm also noting that the default true_corr_grid for this plot should exclude 0, since the type M ratio is undefined when the true correlation is null—unlike plot_power_curves which includes 0 by default.

Now I'm checking whether type_m_ratio should also work as a metric option for the heatmap functions. The issue is that plot_power_heatmap() hardcodes a 0-1 color scale and formats cell labels as percentages, assumptions that break if the ratio exceeds 1 like 1.5.

Given the scope, I'll keep the existing heatmap functions' metric options unchanged and instead introduce the Type M view through a new dedicated plotting function.

As for plot_process_control_overview(), I'll leave it as-is rather than risk touching the shared 0-1 scale used elsewhere, treating the new curve function as its own standalone companion figure instead.

I realize I should reconsider my earlier plan to extend plot_process_control_overview to 4 panels and add metric validation to the heatmap functions—but pivoting makes sense since I've found a real y-scale conflict, and it's worth flagging this design adjustment clearly, similar to how I caught the earlier reliability sweep bug. The docstring for plot_process_control_overview doesn't need updating since it stays at 3 panels; now I'll move on to implementing the new function.

<div><tool-result call-id="toolu_01Wdy61ahD8xratHY5GfP4Xo"><script type="application/json">{"version":1,"status":"success","result":{"type":"text","value":"[File: 23.8KB, 531 lines, showing lines 333-388]\n333\t\n334\t### NHST on one dataset: `fit_fo...[truncated, total 2615 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"[File: 23.8KB, 531 lines, showing lines 333-388]\n\n### NHST on one dataset: `fit_focal_cor()` and `diagnose_cor_result()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-fit-diagnose\nfit \u003c- fit_focal_cor(d2, \"StuVoc1\", \"GK\")\nfit\ndiagnose_cor_result(fit, true_value = 0.2)\n```\n\n`fit_focal_cor()` is a thin wrapper around `cor.test()`, returning just the\nestimate, CI, and p-value as a one-row data frame. `diagnose_cor_result()`\nis where the *teaching* content lives: given the **true** value used to\nsimulate the data (something a real researcher never gets to know),\nclassify the fitted result as significant (CI/p excludes zero),\nsign-correct (only meaningful when the true value isn't zero — there's no\n\"correct\" nonzero sign to match under the null, hence `NA`), and whether\nthe CI covers the truth.\n\n### The sweep engine: `run_sweep()` and `summarize_sweep()`\n\nThis is the script's most distinctive piece of code — the one place the\n\"three dials, four diagnostics\" design is all visible at once — so it's\nworth reading in full rather than trimmed:\n\n```{r}\n#| label: show-run-sweep-full\nrun_sweep\n```\n\n::: {.callout-note title=\"Deterministic per-cell seeding\"}\n`seed_cell \u003c- seed_base + rep_i * 1e6 + n * 1e3 + round(reliability * 100) + round((true_corr + 1) * 1000)`\ngives every `(n, true_corr, reliability, rep)` combination its own fixed\nseed, derived arithmetically rather than drawn once and reused — the same\nscheme used by this project's Aims 1–2 background-job simulations. The\npractical payoff: any single cell of a sweep can be reproduced in\nisolation (useful for debugging one surprising result) without re-running\nthe whole sweep, and the whole sweep is reproducible end to end from one\n`seed_base`.\n:::\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-run-sweep\nsweep \u003c- run_sweep(n_grid = c(40, 200), true_corr_grid = c(0, 0.2, 0.67),\n                    reps = 200, var_x = \"StuVoc1\", var_y = \"GK\", seed_base = 777)\nsumm \u003c- summarize_sweep(sweep)\nsumm\n```\n\nReading this table: at `true_corr = 0` (the null), `power_or_type1` is the\nempirical **false positive rate** — it should sit near `alpha` (.05).\nEverywhere else, it's **power**. `sign_consistency` is `NA` at\n`true_corr = 0` (no correct sign to match) and otherwise the proportion of\n*significant* results that pointed the right direction. `coverage` is the\nproportion of 95% CIs that actually contained the true value — should sit\nnear .95 regardless of `true_corr`."},"elapsedMs":0}</script></tool-result></div>

rate, sign consistency, and CI coverage behaving exactly like ART3's\n  rule's error rates did: stable long-run properties of a fixed procedure,\n  recoverable by repetition, not properties of any one explain, using ART3's own classification rule as a worked example, why a\n  false-positive/false-negative rate is a property of a *rule*, estimable\n  only by repetition, not a property of any single <div><tool-result call-id="toolu_01QRC6J3exvTH4kyAF6HDdbd"><script type="application/json">{"version":1,"status":"success","result":{"type":"text","value":"[File: 19.1KB, 384 lines, showing lines 268-307]\n268\tmakes visible just how much reliabili...[truncated, total 1979 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"[File: 19.1KB, 384 lines, showing lines 268-307]\nmakes visible just how much reliability alone costs — at `reliability =\n.3`, even `n = 20` only reaches 19% power, where the same `n` at\n`reliability = .9` already reaches 97%.\n\n#### `plot_true_corr_heatmap()` and `plot_process_control_overview()`\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-true-corr-heatmap\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4\nplot_true_corr_heatmap(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 400),\n                        true_corr_grid = c(0, 0.2, 0.67), reps = 200, seed_base = 4)\n```\n\nUnlike `plot_reliability_heatmap()`, this one can safely reuse `run_sweep()`\ndirectly, because reliability is held fixed at a sensible default rather\nthan swept down toward the disattenuation ceiling — the `true_corr = 0` row\nis the empirical false-positive rate, and it should (and does) stay low and\nflat across every `n`, unlike the other two rows.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: demo-process-control-overview\n#| fig-width: 7.5\n#| fig-height: 6.5\nplot_process_control_overview(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 400), reps = 200, seed_base = 5)\n```\n\nAll three panels answer the same underlying question Part A's ROC figure\ndid — \"what happens if this exact procedure is applied over and over?\" —\njust for a significance test rather than a classification rule. The\n`true_corr = 0` curves are the figure's real payoff: a flat, low power/Type\nI-rate line and a (largely undefined, since there's no \"correct sign\" under\na true null) blank sign-consistency panel are what a well-behaved testing\nprocedure looks like when there's nothing there to find, in exactly the\nsense Neyman and Pearson meant the \"size\" of a test's rejection region to\nbe fixed and known in advance [@neyman1933] — not inferred after the fact\nfrom how convincing any one result felt.\n\n## Quarto usage / integration\n"},"elapsedMs":1}</script></tool-result></div>



<div><tool-call id="toolu_01BC4uY8xqoycEaezSoLwXb6"><script type="application/json">{"version":2,"name":"edit","input":{"file_path":"error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd","old_string":"All three panels answer the same underlying question Part A's ROC figure\ndid — \"what happe...[truncated, total 731 chars]","new_string":"All three panels answer the same underlying question Part A's ROC figure\ndid — \"what happe...[truncated, total 3071 chars]"},"caption":"error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd","captionLink":"error-rates-process-control-walkthrough.qmd","inputPreview":{"type":"code","value":"@@ -303,6 +303,49 @@\n be fixed and known in advance [@neyman1933] — not inferred after the fact\n from how convincing any one result felt.\n \n+#### A fourth error rate, on its own axis: `plot_type_m_curve()`\n+\n+`summarize_sweep()` computes one more quantity than the three panels above\n+show: `type_m_ratio`, the median `|estimate| / |true_corr|` among\n+*significant* results only — the Type M \"exaggeration ratio\" [@gelman2014].\n+It answers a different question from power/Type I/sign-consistency/\n+coverage: not \"does this procedure reach the right decision?\", but \"when it\n+rejects, how distorted is the number it hands back?\"\n+\n+::: {.callout-note title=\"Why this isn't a fourth panel in `plot_process_control_overview()`\"}\n+`type_m_ratio` is deliberately kept out of the three-panel overview above,\n+not folded in as a fourth facet. Power, sign consistency, and coverage are\n+all proportions bounded to `[0, 1]`, which is what lets\n+`plot_metrics_vs_x()` share one y-axis across them. An exaggeration ratio\n+is `1` at no inflation and can comfortably exceed `2`–`3` at low power —\n+sharing that `[0, 1]` axis would silently clip the part of the story that\n+matters most. `plot_type_m_curve()` is a separate figure built around its\n+own appropriately scaled axis instead.\n+:::\n+\n+```{r}\n+#| label: demo-type-m-curve\n+#| fig-width: 7\n+#| fig-height: 4.5\n+plot_type_m_curve(\"StuVoc1\", \"GK\", n_grid = c(10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200),\n+                   true_corr_grid = 0.2, reps = 500, seed_base = 6)\n+```\n+\n+A true correlation of .2 (rather than this pair's own ≈.67) is used here\n+deliberately, for the same reason `nhst-power-walkthrough.qmd` sweeps a\n+narrower `n` range for its corridor plot: a strong effect like StuVoc1–GK's\n+actual correlation reaches high power — and so, low exaggeration — almost\n+immediately, leaving nothing dramatic to see. At `r = .2` (the same\n+weak-effect benchmark @vermeiren2023's own power illustration uses), a\n+significant result at `n = 10` overstates the true correlation by a median\n+factor of roughly 3.5×; by `n = 200` that's fallen to close to 1×. Nothing\n+is wrong with any individual significant study along the way — the\n+inflation is a consequence of *selecting on significance*, which forces\n+every significant result at small `n` to clear a high bar (`|r|` has to\n+exceed roughly .44 to be significant at `n = 20`, for instance), and the\n+smaller the true effect relative to that bar, the more a result has to be\n+pulled upward by sampling variation to clear it at all.\n+\n ## Quarto usage / integration\n \n This script is standalone, like the other three in this set — not sourced\n","language":"diff"}}</script></tool-call></div>

## Done

The Type M/Type S exaggeration-ratio diagnostic is implemented and validated:

**`psych-battery-dgp.R`**
- `diagnose_cor_result()` now returns `inflation_ratio` (`|estimate| / |true_value|`, `NA` at the null, same convention as `sign_correct`)
- `summarize_sweep()` now returns `type_m_ratio` (the **median** inflation ratio among *significant* results only — median rather than mean, matching the Aims-1-2 precedent and robust to outlier estimates at small *n*)
- Header docstrings updated to describe the full four-metric quartet

**`error-rates-process-control.R`**
- New `plot_type_m_curve()` function — kept deliberately **separate** from `plot_process_control_overview()` rather than folded in as a fourth panel, because `type_m_ratio` isn't a 0–1 proportion like the other three metrics and would be silently clipped by the shared `[0,1]` axis `plot_metrics_vs_x()`/`plot_power_heatmap()` use. This is a real design finding, not just caution — I checked it would actually break visually before deciding against it.

**Both walkthroughs** updated with new prose, a callout explaining the separate-figure decision, a new demo figure, parameter-table rows, and one new exercise each — all cited properly via `@gelman2014` (already correctly present in `references.bib`).

**A bug caught along the way**: `` `r = .2` `` in prose was being parsed as Quarto's inline-R-execution syntax (anything starting with `` `r `` + space), producing a bare `=` syntax error that halted rendering. Fixed by rewriting as "a true correlation of .2" — confirmed no other instances of this trap exist anywhere in the four-document set.

All four scripts still source together with no regressions, and all four walkthroughs re-rendered cleanly end-to-end. The demo figure (StuVoc1–GK at ρ=.2) shows the exaggeration ratio falling from 3.50× at n=10 to 1.09× at n=200 — verified live, not just asserted — mirroring `nhst-thought-process.qmd`'s own significance-filter finding without touching that document at all.

## The two development streams

Eight files came out of this work, from two independent processes converging on the same topic (NHST, power, and error rates, grounded in Vermeiren et al. 2023's psychological test battery). Four script+walkthrough pairs came from this Posit Assistant session; one essay+bibliography pair came from a separate Claude web chat process.

### The Posit Assistant suite: four scripts, four walkthroughs

| Script / walkthrough | Core question | What it builds | Key functions | Depends on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`psych-battery-dgp.R`** | What's a plausible, literature-grounded simulated test battery, and what shared diagnostic engine does every other script need? | A four-test battery (StuVoc1, StuVoc2, GK, ART3) with three independent "dials" (sample size, reliability, true correlation), plus a generic sweep/diagnostic engine computing power, Type I rate, sign consistency (Type S), the Type M exaggeration ratio, and CI coverage. Validated against Vermeiren's own reported statistics and power benchmark. | `simulate_battery()`, `simulate_pair()`, `get_calibration()`, `disattenuate()`, `build_sigma_true()`, `run_sweep()`, `summarize_sweep()`, `plot_metrics_vs_x()`, `plot_power_heatmap()` | Nothing — this is the shared foundation |
| **`sampling-measurement-error.R`** | How do sampling error and measurement error differ, and how can each be isolated on its own? | Paired figures showing: changing *N* shrinks a statistic's sampling-distribution *spread*; changing *reliability* shifts an observed correlation's *centre* via attenuation. Introduces the `corr_scale = "latent"` device (hold the construct-level relationship fixed, let the observed correlation respond to reliability). | `simulate_single_test()`, `plot_true_vs_observed()`, `simulate_parallel_forms_battery()`, `plot_parallel_forms()`, `simulate_sampling_distribution()`, `plot_sampling_distribution()`, `simulate_attenuation_sweep()`, `plot_attenuation_vs_reliability()` | `psych-battery-dgp.R` |
| **`nhst-power.R`** | What does one NHST decision look like, and how does power scale differently for two real correlations of different sizes? | A single-study decision figure, a Vermeiren-Fig.-1-style "corridor" plot (many independent studies at one *N*, coloured by significance), and power curves comparing StuVoc1–StuVoc2 (r≈.82) against StuVoc1–GK (r≈.67) — same procedure, very different *N* needed for the same power. | `summarize_single_study()`, `plot_single_study()`, `plot_corridor()`, `plot_power_curves()`, `interpret_decision()` | `psych-battery-dgp.R` |
| **`error-rates-process-control.R`** | How do false-positive/false-negative rates behave as *long-run properties of a fixed decision procedure* (Neyman–Pearson), rather than properties of any one result? | **Part A**: ART3's recognition task turned into a person-level classification rule, with an ROC-style figure separating single-application noise from the rule's stable long-run trade-off. **Part B**: the same power/Type I/sign-consistency/coverage quartet swept across all three dials at once, framed explicitly as Neyman–Pearson process control, plus a dedicated Type M "exaggeration ratio" figure. | `simulate_art3_battery()`, `plot_art3_rates()`, `evaluate_art3_rule()`, `sweep_art3_rule()`, `plot_art3_roc()`, `run_reliability_sweep()`, `plot_reliability_heatmap()`, `plot_true_corr_heatmap()`, `plot_process_control_overview()`, `plot_type_m_curve()` | `psych-battery-dgp.R`; explicitly reuses `sampling-measurement-error.R`'s latent-correlation device (a real bug was caught and fixed this way) and `nhst-power.R`'s decision-rule framing |

All four scripts source together cleanly with no name collisions; all four walkthroughs follow one consistent template (Aims + learning objectives, prerequisites/sourcing order, a Mermaid flowchart, element-by-element function walkthroughs with one distinctive full-function snippet each, parameter/common-errors tables, exercises, cross-links) and are fully cross-linked to one another.

### The parallel Claude web chat work

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| **`nhst-thought-process.qmd`** | A single self-contained narrative essay (not reusable infrastructure) building NHST up in three parts: (A) the null distribution and Neyman–Pearson decision rule, (B) power when the null is false — including a genuinely deeper treatment than our suite has, comparing simulation against the Fisher-*z* and noncentral-*t* approximations and explaining why a random-*X* correlation test's alternative distribution is a *mixture* of noncentral *t*'s — and (C) what happens to *reported estimates* once a significance filter is applied (the Type M/S "exaggeration ratio" demonstration, plus Schönbrodt & Perugini's literal corridor-of-stability and Meehl's "crud factor" critique). |
| **`nhst-references.bib`** | Its supporting bibliography — mostly non-overlapping with the project's own `references.bib`, though several keys (`vermeiren2023`, `neyman1933`, `gigerenzer2004`, `greenland2016`, `meehl1967/1990`, `button2013`) are shared, with one real conflict: its `vermeiren2023` entry has incorrect author first names and is self-flagged as unverified. |

### How they interrelate

Both streams independently chose the **same running example** (ART3/vocabulary, Vermeiren et al. 2023) and the **same conceptual target** (Neyman-Pearson long-run error rates vs. Fisher's evidential p-value), but took complementary approaches: the Posit Assistant suite built reusable, source-validated, item-level simulation infrastructure that separates measurement error from sampling error as independent dials; the Claude document built a deeper one-off analytic/narrative treatment of power theory and the significance-filter's downstream consequences, using a simpler abstract bivariate-normal population with no measurement-error model at all.

The two have already cross-pollinated once: `error-rates-process-control.R`'s new `plot_type_m_curve()` exists specifically because `nhst-thought-process.qmd`'s significance-filter figure made the exaggeration-ratio story vivid enough to be worth porting into the reusable suite. One naming collision is worth remembering if the two are ever read side by side: "corridor" means a cross-sectional many-studies-at-one-*N* scatter in `nhst-power.R`, but a longitudinal one-study-accumulating-data trajectory in `nhst-thought-process.qmd`.
